section: Introduction > What This Manual Covers
statement: Apply this manual to business contracts: contracts between businesses experienced in handling transactions or represented by lawyers. It doesn't address consumer contracts, although much of it could apply to them.

trigger.signal: a consumer-facing contract under review

notes: The Introduction has no paragraph numbers; cited by PDF page.

section: Introduction > What This Manual Covers
statement: Except as the book indicates, treat its examples as illustrations, not models. Use as model language only text the book recommends (for example, a table entry rated ✓✓ or an 'after' version).

section: Introduction > Using This Manual Internationally
statement: Dispense with the Commonwealth usages amongst and whilst.
fix: Use among (or between; see 2.47) and while.
notes: Detailed treatment at 13.19 (another helper's range).

section: Introduction > Using This Manual Internationally
statement: Dispense with the Commonwealth use of clause to refer to a numbered provision of a contract.
fix: Refer to sections (see 4.9).
notes: Detailed treatment at 4.9 (another helper's range).

section: Introduction > Using This Manual Internationally
statement: Dispense with the Commonwealth usage endeavours.
fix: See 8.9 (efforts standards).
severity_basis: dispute risk or legally significant usage
notes: Detailed treatment at 8.9 (another helper's range).

section: Introduction > Using This Manual Internationally
statement: Dispense with the Commonwealth usage forthwith.
notes: Detailed treatment at 10.130 (another helper's range).

section: Introduction > The Significance of Caselaw
statement: Don't rely on caselaw to give a usage a specific meaning. Draft so the contract speaks directly to the reader in standard English. An errant court opinion is no reason to retreat from a recommendation.
notes: Courts tend to be overconfident about how English works (PDF p. 42).

section: Introduction > Excuses for Sticking with Traditional Contract Language
statement: Don't accept the argument that traditional contract language 'works.' Contracts are more or less clear and present more or less risk of dispute; caselaw is full of disputes caused by traditional usages.

trigger.signal: a counterparty or colleague defends a traditional usage because it 'works'

section: Introduction > Excuses for Sticking with Traditional Contract Language
statement: Don't keep a usage because courts have 'tested' it. Courts have scrutinized only some terminology; they don't all give it the same meaning; and if a court had to determine meaning, the wording failed to state intent clearly.

trigger.signal: an argument that litigated language has a settled meaning

notes: The book calls the 'tested' claim 'a lazy platitude.' GRT, Inc. v. Marathon GTF Technology, Ltd., 2011 WL 2682898 (Del. Ch. 11 July 2011), at *14 n.79.

section: Introduction > Excuses for Sticking with Traditional Contract Language
statement: Don't rely on a claimed shared understanding of what a confusing usage means. The claim rests on sweeping generalization and argumentum ad populum, and it doesn't help if the usage is clearly ambiguous.

section: Introduction > Excuses for Sticking with Traditional Contract Language
statement: Reject the claim that a confusing usage means whatever the drafter or negotiator thinks it means. In a dispute the question is what meaning the parties attributed to the usage.

section: Introduction > Excuses for Sticking with Traditional Contract Language
statement: Weigh the fear that replacing a traditional usage causes mischief: a counterparty might push back and slow the deal, but litigators are unlikely to give a clearer usage an unexpected meaning ('It's difficult to make mischief with clear').

section: Introduction > Implementing the Recommendations > When You're Drafting
statement: When drafting, expect and prepare for objections to unfamiliar prose, chiefly from the other side but also from more senior people on your side.
notes: The recommendations most likely to seem novel: not defining this Agreement (2.123-.127), states instead of represents and warrants (3.454-.463), alternatives to material (9.51-.64) (PDF pp. 40-41).

section: Introduction > Implementing the Recommendations > When You're Drafting
statement: With a traditionalist senior colleague who isn't receptive, give them what they expect on usages that don't affect meaning, but be 'gently persistent' on issues that might affect the deal or create confusion.

section: Introduction > Implementing the Recommendations > When You're Drafting
statement: Consider explaining your usages to the other side in advance, in a cover note that cites the manual and asks them not to add traditional usages unless that would make the contract clearer or better reflect the deal.

examples.after: Please don't ask that we add traditional usages to this draft unless that would make the contract clearer or would better reflect the deal as you understand it.

section: Introduction > Implementing the Recommendations > When You're Drafting
statement: Match how far you depart from traditional usage to the transaction: in a one-off, bet-the-company deal expect resistance to novel language; in a high-volume template, strip out anything wordy or extraneous and resist changes that restore dysfunction.

section: Introduction > Implementing the Recommendations > When You're Drafting
statement: Consider holding firm even on lowercase this agreement. It has no deal significance, and someone who insists on a capital A signals early that they will meddle without good reason.

section: Introduction > Implementing the Recommendations > When You're Drafting
statement: Be realistic: with traditional templates or industry forms you may have little room. Even with control, retool incrementally, starting with the provisions you use most.

section: Introduction > Implementing the Recommendations > When You're Reviewing
statement: When reviewing the other side's draft, look only for what doesn't reflect the deal as you understand it and what could create confusion. Don't try to make their draft 'a thing of beauty.'
severity_basis: sets the reviewer's threshold for raising issues

section: Introduction > Implementing the Recommendations > When You're Reviewing
statement: On the other side's draft, give a pass to traditional features that don't make sense but aren't confusing: a traditional recital of consideration, benign overuse of shall, and archaisms in the front and back of the contract.
notes: Asking for such changes risks needlessly antagonizing the other side.

section: Introduction > Implementing the Recommendations > When You're Reviewing
statement: On the other side's draft, flag anything that should be a condition but is expressed as an obligation, inherently confusing usages (for example, indemnify and hold harmless), and every instance of ambiguity.
severity_basis: ambiguity, or a category error or usage that can change meaning or invite dispute

section: Introduction > Implementing the Recommendations > When You're Reviewing
statement: Even seemingly minor glitches are worth flagging on the other side's draft if they have caused disputes, for example throat-clearing verb structures and may in restrictive relative clauses.
severity_basis: ambiguity, or a category error or usage that can change meaning or invite dispute

section: Introduction > Implementing the Recommendations > When You're Reviewing
statement: If the other drafter is a traditionalist, cite the manual to explain a requested change, to show it rests on an internationally recognized set of guidelines.

section: Introduction > Effecting Change at Organizations
statement: To make an organization's contracts clear and consistent, first adopt a style guide; the manual can serve as its foundation. Then train personnel and provide clear, modern templates.

section: Introduction > Effecting Change at Organizations
statement: Use clarity as the only criterion for choosing a usage. Where alternatives exist, use the clearest; where they are equally clear, have everyone in the organization use the same one.

section: Introduction > Effecting Change at Organizations
statement: Let competent nonlawyers (businesspeople, contract managers, paralegals) take a greater role in expressing deal terms, provided they have a good command of contract language and substance.

section: Introduction > Effecting Change at Organizations
statement: Treat AI contract review with caution: if its patterns come from traditional contracts, expect 'garbage in, garbage out.' AI review is more promising when combined with expertise about what to look for and what to tell the user.

section: Foreword to the Fourth Edition
statement: When interpreting an existing agreement that follows older, traditional approaches, treat the manual's analysis as illustrating an alternative rather than as proof of what the agreement means; citing the manual to a judge doesn't mean your client will win.

trigger.signal: interpreting or litigating a contract drafted in traditional style

notes: Vice Chancellor J. Travis Laster's foreword (reprinted from the fourth edition): the analysis 'offers less guidance for existing agreements that hew to older approaches' (PDF p. 33). Laster cited the manual in Airborne Health, Inc. v. Squid Soap, LP, 984 A.2d 126, 140 (Del. Ch. 2009).

section: Characteristics of Optimal Contract Language (opening)
statement: Draft with the limited function of business contracts in mind: they only regulate conduct, state facts, and allocate risk. Don't treat contracts as just another form of legal writing.

section: Characteristics of Optimal Contract Language (opening)
statement: Apply the 12 principles of optimal contract language when assessing any usage the manual doesn't examine.
notes: The 12 principles (1.2): not archaic; not legalistic; not confusing; express ideas without redundancy; not repeat itself; consistent; concise; accessible; not seek to persuade; restrained in attempting to preempt judicial discretion; serve a useful purpose; don't expect it to be simple.

section: Contract Language Shouldn't Be Archaic
statement: Don't use archaic usages (for example, whereas in recitals). They add no gravitas and distance the reader from the text.
notes: The Introduction says to give a pass to archaisms in the front and back of the other side's draft (PDF p. 55); in the body, treat as style-only. Trigger words other than whereas are illustrative, drawn from elsewhere in the manual.

section: Contract Language Shouldn't Be Legalistic > Omit Problematic Terms of Art
statement: Manage legal terms of art: keep those the transaction needs (for example, security interest, perfection), and avoid the flawed kinds.
exceptions: Specialized terminology is often needed to express technical transactions; purging it all can make the contract fail to express the meaning (1.10-1.11).

section: Contract Language Shouldn't Be Legalistic > Omit Problematic Terms of Art
statement: Avoid three kinds of flawed terms of art: unnecessary, improvised, and unduly complex.

section: Contract Language Shouldn't Be Legalistic > Omit Problematic Terms of Art
statement: Don't use a doctrinal term of art where simpler terminology does the job.
test: Is there a discrepancy between the term's doctrinal meaning and the semantic work the sentence needs ('a dollar word or phrase doing a nickel's worth of work')? If so, the term is unnecessary.
fix: Use the plain verb or noun that does the work (for example, grant instead of hypothecate).

examples.before: hypothecates [in a security agreement]
examples.after: grants

notes: Two mistaken assumptions behind unnecessary terms of art: that nothing else expresses the meaning, and that using the term guarantees the concept applies whatever the rest of the provision says (1.15-1.16).

section: Contract Language Shouldn't Be Legalistic > Omit Problematic Terms of Art
statement: Avoid improvised terms of art: ordinary wording onto which lawyers and judges have grafted doctrinal implications, such as hold harmless and best efforts.
severity_basis: dispute risk or legally significant usage

section: Contract Language Shouldn't Be Legalistic > Omit Problematic Terms of Art
statement: Expect courts to give effect to every word: that principle, applied zealously, gives significance to stray words and variations and to each element of a redundant string.

trigger.signal: redundant words or minor variations in wording

severity_basis: dispute risk or legally significant usage

section: Contract Language Shouldn't Be Legalistic > Omit Problematic Terms of Art
statement: Don't use unduly complex terms of art (for example, consequential damages, coupled with an interest, time is of the essence) without fully appreciating their implications; the provision might be unenforceable or have unexpected consequences.

trigger.regex_hint: \b(consequential damages|coupled with an interest|time is of the essence)\b

severity_basis: dispute risk or legally significant usage

section: Contract Language Shouldn't Be Legalistic > Omit Problematic Terms of Art
statement: Use straightforward alternatives to unnecessary, improvised, and unduly complex terms of art.

section: Contract Language Shouldn't Be Legalistic > Omit Problematic Terms of Art
statement: Before replacing an entrenched term of art, weigh the risk of confusion against the transaction cost of change; replacement might prompt fruitless debate or seem 'shockingly novel' (for example, states instead of represents and warrants).

section: Contract Language Shouldn't Be Legalistic > Omit Problematic Terms of Art
statement: To ease a change, use the term of art and also explain what it means.

section: Contract Language Shouldn't Be Legalistic > Omit Problematic Terms of Art
statement: Alternatively, use the term of art in the section heading and the clearer alternative in the section text (for example, indemnification, attornment, warranty headings).

section: Contract Language Shouldn't Be Legalistic > Omit Problematic Terms of Art
statement: Before replacing a term of art, check whether courts attribute significance to using that term instead of other wording. U.S. courts tend not to insist on specific wording.
severity_basis: dispute risk or legally significant usage

section: Contract Language Shouldn't Be Legalistic > Omit Problematic Terms of Art
statement: If an English-language contract is governed by the law of a jurisdiction whose courts work in another language, include the non-English original of each term of art after the English, in italics and in parentheses.

trigger.signal: governing law of a non-English-speaking jurisdiction plus a translated term of art

severity_basis: dispute risk or legally significant usage

examples.after: This agreement constitutes an assignment agreement (overeenkomst van opdracht) under the Dutch Civil Code.

section: Contract Language Shouldn't Be Legalistic > Use Standard English
statement: Write in a specialized version of standard English, the English used by educated native speakers, free of usages that gratuitously interfere with understanding.
notes: The manual avoids the labels plain English and plain language because they suggest simplified consumer language (1.31); standard English implies no dumbing down (1.32, 1.74).

section: Contract Language Shouldn't Be Confusing
statement: Make avoiding confusion a high priority: uncertain meaning leads to disputes, cost, and mischief, and many judges are ill-equipped to make sense of confusing language.
severity_basis: ambiguity, or a category error or usage that can change meaning or invite dispute

section: Contract Language Shouldn't Be Confusing
statement: Spare the reader miscues: structures that lead the reader to assume one reading, discover another, and have to reassess.

trigger.signal: a sentence whose structure invites a wrong first parse

section: Contract Language Should Express Ideas Without Redundancy > Limit the Use of Strings
statement: Limit strings of synonyms or near-synonyms (doublets, triplets). If one word expresses the meaning, the rest are extraneous, and a court may give an unexpected meaning to one element.

trigger.signal: two or more synonyms or near-synonyms joined by and/or

severity_basis: dispute risk or legally significant usage

examples.before: Abrams must sell, convey, assign, transfer, and deliver the shares to Chung.
examples.after: Abrams can simply sell the shares.

section: Contract Language Should Express Ideas Without Redundancy > Limit the Use of Strings
statement: If you use a string more than once, use identical wording each time or replace it with a defined term; minor variations invite argument that the meaning differs.

trigger.signal: the same string repeated with an element added or dropped

severity_basis: dispute risk or legally significant usage

examples.before: losses, liabilities, damages, and claims [in one provision]; losses, liabilities, and damages [in another]

section: Contract Language Should Express Ideas Without Redundancy > Limit the Use of Strings
statement: Prune traditional synonym strings, such as books and records and costs and expenses.

section: Contract Language Should Express Ideas Without Redundancy > Limit the Use of Strings
statement: Don't rely on strings with overly subtle distinctions if a different approach would be clearer (for example, alternatives to arising out of or relating to).

words: arising out of or relating to
arising out of or in connection with

severity_basis: dispute risk or legally significant usage

section: Contract Language Should Express Ideas Without Redundancy > Limit the Use of Strings
statement: For an improvised string of verbs, pick the word that does the work; deal with any distinct concept (such as delivery) where it belongs.

trigger.signal: a string of transfer verbs (sell, convey, assign, transfer, deliver)

fix: Use sell alone; address what deliver covers in the closing provisions (1.45).

section: Contract Language Should Express Ideas Without Redundancy > Limit the Use of Strings
statement: In granting language, use grants alone rather than a string such as grants, assigns, conveys, mortgages, pledges, hypothecates, and transfers; or, instead of stringing legal functions, refer explicitly to the relevant contexts.

examples.before: the Employee may transfer the Employee's rights under this agreement to the Employee's personal or legal representatives, executors, administrators, heirs, distributees, devisees, and legatees
examples.after: the Employee's rights under this agreement may be transferred by will or intestate succession

notes: The book notes the first version's intended scope might be broader; express any broader meaning by naming the contexts.

section: Contract Language Should Express Ideas Without Redundancy > Limit the Use of Strings
statement: In an autonomous definition, instead of a long string of synonyms, consider however referred to to show the definition refers to a concept.

examples.before: [a definition of Permit listing 17 kinds of permit]
examples.after: 'Permit' means a permit, however referred to, ... .

section: Contract Language Should Express Ideas Without Redundancy > Limit the Use of Strings
statement: Keep a string that is needed to cover the universe of possibilities, even if it includes some redundancy; don't cut it down (for example, to lien) unless you're confident the remaining word covers the rest.

examples.after: free of any lien, community property interest, equitable interest, option, pledge, security interest, or right of first refusal

section: Contract Language Should Express Ideas Without Redundancy > Limit the Use of Strings
statement: Consider every component of a string and keep it only if its meaning is usefully distinct from each other component.

section: Contract Language Should Express Ideas Without Redundancy > Omit Needless Elaboration
statement: Don't list a general term's constituent components when the general term's scope is clear (needless elaboration).

words: whether at law or in equity
trigger.regex_hint: \b(whether at law or in equity|federal, state,? or local)\b

examples.before: all claims whether at law or in equity
examples.after: all claims

examples.before: any federal, state, or local government body
examples.after: any government body

notes: The general term is also more comprehensive: a jurisdiction may have a level of government not described as federal, state, or local (1.53).

section: Contract Language Should Express Ideas Without Redundancy > Omit Needless Elaboration
statement: Don't accompany a general term with examples that obviously fall within it, whether introduced by including after the term or placed before it.

section: Contract Language Should Express Ideas Without Redundancy > Omit Needless Elaboration
statement: Omit a provision that another provision makes redundant.

trigger.signal: two provisions covering the same ground

notes: The manual treats provision-level redundancy as beyond its scope and refers to a blog post (7 Aug. 2021).

section: Contract Language Shouldn't Repeat Itself
statement: Never say the same thing twice in a contract, including a party's address and a number; repetition adds words and invites dispute if the versions differ.

trigger.signal: the same fact, address, or number stated in two places

severity_basis: dispute risk or legally significant usage

section: Contract Language Should Be Consistent
statement: Within a contract, don't use the same word or phrase to express different meanings (the most abused is shall).

trigger.signal: one word carrying two meanings

severity_basis: readers and judges may assume different wording means different meaning

section: Contract Language Should Be Consistent
statement: Within a contract, don't use different words or phrases to express the same meaning (for example, the many ways of saying may).

trigger.signal: two different words used for one concept (elegant variation)

severity_basis: readers and judges may assume different wording means different meaning

section: Contract Language Should Be Consistent
statement: Across an organization's contracts (and ideally across an industry), draw on the same usages, so no one could tell which individual drafted what.

section: Contract Language Should Be Concise
statement: Be concise: eliminate archaisms, unnecessary terms of art, redundancy, and repetition, and use other economies of English, such as the active voice and when instead of at the time at which.

examples.before: at the time at which
examples.after: when

section: Contract Language Should Be Accessible
statement: Make the contract accessible: use a sensible enumeration scheme, make blocks of text neither too long nor too short, arrange provisions sensibly, and use typography well.

section: Contract Language Shouldn't Seek to Persuade
statement: Be cautious about words associated mainly with expository or persuasive prose, such as therefore, because, and furthermore.
notes: Moreover is an illustrative addition, not in the book's list.

section: Contract Language Shouldn't Seek to Persuade
statement: Don't add rhetorical emphasis (words that say only 'and we really mean it!') to provisions that already express the meaning; delete it, or for at no time, if and only if, and under no circumstances, replace it.

trigger.regex_hint: \b(absolutely|at no time|completely|fully|if and only if|in all respects|in any manner|in any way|it is emphasized that|of any kind|strictly|under no circumstances|whatsoever|wholly)\b

exceptions: Emphatic words can be combined (wholly and fully; in any manner whatsoever) (1.66).
A word that is rhetorical emphasis in one context can serve another function, legitimate or not, in another context; check before deleting (1.66).

section: Contract Language Shouldn't Seek to Persuade > Rhetorical emphasis list (1.65)
statement: Don't use absolutely as rhetorical emphasis. Delete absolutely.
fix: Delete absolutely.
exceptions: The same words can serve a legitimate function in another context (1.66).

examples.before: The Lessee must absolutely refrain from performing actions involving cooking and/or frying in the Leased Property ... .
examples.after: The Lessee must refrain from performing actions involving cooking and/or frying in the Leased Property ... .

notes: Book example marked with strikethrough/underline (OCR of PDF pp. 74-75).

section: Contract Language Shouldn't Seek to Persuade > Rhetorical emphasis list (1.65)
statement: Don't use at no time as rhetorical emphasis. Replace at no time with not.
fix: Replace at no time with not.
exceptions: The same words can serve a legitimate function in another context (1.66).

examples.before: The Escrow Agent shall at no time acquire any ownership interest in the Offering Proceeds.
examples.after: The Escrow Agent shall not acquire any ownership interest in the Offering Proceeds.

notes: Book example marked with strikethrough/underline (OCR of PDF pp. 74-75).

section: Contract Language Shouldn't Seek to Persuade > Rhetorical emphasis list (1.65)
statement: Don't use completely as rhetorical emphasis. Delete completely.
fix: Delete completely.
exceptions: The same words can serve a legitimate function in another context (1.66).

examples.before: ... the Executive shall keep the terms of this agreement completely confidential ... .
examples.after: ... the Executive shall keep the terms of this agreement confidential ... .

notes: Book example marked with strikethrough/underline (OCR of PDF pp. 74-75).

section: Contract Language Shouldn't Seek to Persuade > Rhetorical emphasis list (1.65)
statement: Don't use fully as rhetorical emphasis. Delete and fully (or wholly and; see the wholly entry).
fix: Delete and fully (or wholly and; see the wholly entry).
exceptions: The same words can serve a legitimate function in another context (1.66).

examples.before: The Consultant is wholly and fully responsible for any taxes owed to any governmental authority ... .
examples.after: The Consultant is wholly responsible for any taxes owed to any governmental authority ... .

notes: The book's example for fully strikes 'and fully' in 'wholly and fully'; the 'after' text shown keeps wholly. OCR of PDF p. 74.

section: Contract Language Shouldn't Seek to Persuade > Rhetorical emphasis list (1.65)
statement: Don't use if and only if as rhetorical emphasis. Replace if and only if with only if.
fix: Replace if and only if with only if.
exceptions: The same words can serve a legitimate function in another context (1.66).

examples.before: This agreement will become effective if and only if Acme issues the Shares before the Termination Date.
examples.after: This agreement will become effective only if Acme issues the Shares before the Termination Date.

notes: Book example marked with strikethrough/underline (OCR of PDF pp. 74-75).

section: Contract Language Shouldn't Seek to Persuade > Rhetorical emphasis list (1.65)
statement: Don't use in all respects as rhetorical emphasis. Delete in all respects.
fix: Delete in all respects.
exceptions: The same words can serve a legitimate function in another context (1.66).

examples.before: This agreement is in all respects governed by Minnesota law.
examples.after: This agreement is governed by Minnesota law.

notes: Book example marked with strikethrough/underline (OCR of PDF pp. 74-75).

section: Contract Language Shouldn't Seek to Persuade > Rhetorical emphasis list (1.65)
statement: Don't use in any manner as rhetorical emphasis. Delete in any manner (and whatsoever).
fix: Delete in any manner (and whatsoever).
exceptions: The same words can serve a legitimate function in another context (1.66).

examples.before: No benefit payable under the Plan is subject in any manner whatsoever to alienation, sale, transfer, ... .
examples.after: No benefit payable under the Plan is subject to alienation, sale, transfer, ... .

notes: Book example marked with strikethrough/underline (OCR of PDF pp. 74-75).

section: Contract Language Shouldn't Seek to Persuade > Rhetorical emphasis list (1.65)
statement: Don't use in any way as rhetorical emphasis. Delete in any way.
fix: Delete in any way.
exceptions: The same words can serve a legitimate function in another context (1.66).

examples.before: ... none of the Buyer Indemnitees will be liable in any way for any injury, loss, or damage arising out of any such entry ... .
examples.after: ... none of the Buyer Indemnitees will be liable for any injury, loss, or damage arising out of any such entry ... .

notes: Book example marked with strikethrough/underline (OCR of PDF pp. 74-75).

section: Contract Language Shouldn't Seek to Persuade > Rhetorical emphasis list (1.65)
statement: Don't use it is emphasized that as rhetorical emphasis. Delete it is emphasized that.
fix: Delete it is emphasized that.
exceptions: The same words can serve a legitimate function in another context (1.66).

examples.before: It is emphasized that the designer of the unit is not entitled to design or change anything outside the bounds of the unit.
examples.after: The designer of the unit is not entitled to design or change anything outside the bounds of the unit.

notes: The strikethrough on 'It is emphasized that the' is not clearly visible; the underlined 'The' shows the replacement (OCR of PDF p. 75).

section: Contract Language Shouldn't Seek to Persuade > Rhetorical emphasis list (1.65)
statement: Don't use of any kind as rhetorical emphasis. Delete of any kind.
fix: Delete of any kind.
exceptions: The same words can serve a legitimate function in another context (1.66).

examples.before: ... alienation, sale, transfer, assignment, pledge, attachment, or encumbrance of any kind.
examples.after: ... alienation, sale, transfer, assignment, pledge, attachment, or encumbrance.

notes: No strikethrough is visible on 'of any kind' in the PDF image; the intended deletion is presumed (source formatting unclear).

section: Contract Language Shouldn't Seek to Persuade > Rhetorical emphasis list (1.65)
statement: Don't use strictly as rhetorical emphasis. Delete strictly.
fix: Delete strictly.
exceptions: The same words can serve a legitimate function in another context (1.66).

examples.before: The Company guarantees payment of the Guaranteed Obligations strictly in accordance with the terms of this agreement and the Notes.
examples.after: The Company guarantees payment of the Guaranteed Obligations in accordance with the terms of this agreement and the Notes.

notes: Book example marked with strikethrough/underline (OCR of PDF pp. 74-75).

section: Contract Language Shouldn't Seek to Persuade > Rhetorical emphasis list (1.65)
statement: Don't use under no circumstances as rhetorical emphasis. Replace under no circumstances with not.
fix: Replace under no circumstances with not.
exceptions: The same words can serve a legitimate function in another context (1.66).

examples.before: The Depositary will under no circumstances be liable for any incidental, indirect, special, consequential, or punitive damages.
examples.after: The Depositary will not be liable for any incidental, indirect, special, consequential, or punitive damages.

notes: Book example marked with strikethrough/underline (OCR of PDF pp. 74-75).

section: Contract Language Shouldn't Seek to Persuade > Rhetorical emphasis list (1.65)
statement: Don't use whatsoever as rhetorical emphasis. Delete whatsoever.
fix: Delete whatsoever.
exceptions: The same words can serve a legitimate function in another context (1.66).

examples.before: No Lender has any right of action whatsoever against the Administrative Agent.
examples.after: No Lender has any right of action against the Administrative Agent.

notes: Book example marked with strikethrough/underline (OCR of PDF pp. 74-75).

section: Contract Language Shouldn't Seek to Persuade > Rhetorical emphasis list (1.65)
statement: Don't use wholly as rhetorical emphasis. Delete wholly and.
fix: Delete wholly and.
exceptions: The same words can serve a legitimate function in another context (1.66).

examples.before: The Consultant is wholly and fully responsible for any taxes owed to any governmental authority ... .
examples.after: The Consultant is fully responsible for any taxes owed to any governmental authority ... .

notes: Book example marked with strikethrough/underline (OCR of PDF pp. 74-75).

section: Contract Language Shouldn't Seek to Persuade
statement: Don't use typography (bold, italics, all capitals, underlining) for rhetorical emphasis.

trigger.signal: emphasized text that adds no meaning

section: Restrained in Attempting to Preempt Judicial Discretion
statement: Be restrained in using the four techniques for preempting judicial discretion: stating that a judicial rule of interpretation doesn't apply; stating an internal rule of interpretation; stating how a court is to act; and stating that a particular standard applies.
severity_basis: dispute risk or legally significant usage
notes: Source: J. Travis Laster & Kenneth A. Adams, When Contracts Seek to Preempt Judicial Discretion, Judicature (Fall 2017).

section: Restrained in Attempting to Preempt Judicial Discretion
statement: Expect a court to be less likely to accept a statement that a judicial rule of interpretation doesn't apply if the statement could be seen as interfering with the natural reading of the contract.

words: shall not be construed against the drafter

severity_basis: dispute risk or legally significant usage

section: Restrained in Attempting to Preempt Judicial Discretion
statement: Don't rely on an internal rule of interpretation where the context suggests a different meaning; like judicial rules, internal rules are arbitrary, and a court is likely to ignore one that context contradicts.
severity_basis: dispute risk or legally significant usage

section: Restrained in Attempting to Preempt Judicial Discretion
statement: Don't tell a court how to act ('an exercise in impotence'). Instead, have the parties acknowledge that a particular outcome is appropriate or that they would want the court to interpret the contract in a specified way.
fix: The parties acknowledge that ... they would want the court to interpret this agreement as follows:
severity_basis: dispute risk or legally significant usage

section: Restrained in Attempting to Preempt Judicial Discretion
statement: Don't state that a legal standard applies unless it matches the facts; if it doesn't, a court might well hold the provision unenforceable.
severity_basis: dispute risk or legally significant usage

section: Contract Language Should Serve a Useful Purpose
statement: Omit provisions that misunderstand the transaction or the law and so serve no useful purpose (for example, survival provisions and inure provisions).

section: Don't Expect Contract Language to Be Simple
statement: Don't try to make a contract simpler than the transaction it expresses; contracts are necessarily as complex as their transactions.

section: The Front of the Contract (opening)
statement: Recognize the front of a contract as the title, introductory clause, any recitals, and the lead-in; a longer contract might also have a cover sheet, table of contents, and index of definitions.

section: The Title
statement: Place the title at the top center of the first page in all capitals, and state simply the kind of contract, without a definite or indefinite article.

trigger.signal: title with 'The' or 'An', or not in capitals

exceptions: If design matters, you could use another form of emphasis, typeface, or point size instead of or in addition to all capitals (2.2; 16.56).

examples.after: EMPLOYMENT AGREEMENT; OPTION AGREEMENT

section: The Title
statement: Don't use a title that looks at the transaction from two perspectives; choose one (and omit the unnecessary of).
exceptions: Which perspective you choose presumably depends on which side you represent (2.3).

examples.before: AGREEMENT OF PURCHASE AND SALE
examples.after: PURCHASE AGREEMENT [or SALE AGREEMENT]

section: The Title
statement: Make the title informative; don't use just AGREEMENT, or a bare PURCHASE AGREEMENT, if you can come up with something more specific.
exceptions: AGREEMENT alone is acceptable for an unusual contract or a grab bag of different elements (2.4).

examples.before: PURCHASE AGREEMENT
examples.after: ASSET PURCHASE AGREEMENT [or SECURITIES PURCHASE AGREEMENT]

section: The Title
statement: Don't cram several elements of the transaction into the title; consider a broader, conceptual title, perhaps reflecting the business goal.

examples.before: LICENSE, SUPPLY, MARKETING, AND DISTRIBUTION AGREEMENT

section: The Title
statement: Don't include party names in the title.

examples.before: ACME SOFTWARE LICENSE AGREEMENT

section: The Title
statement: Don't use jargon in the title.

examples.before: BUY-SELL AGREEMENT
examples.after: SHAREHOLDERS AGREEMENT

section: The Title
statement: If you can give a contract a standard title, do so; contract drafting doesn't prize variety for its own sake.

section: The Title
statement: Don't feel bound to track statutory terminology such as plan of merger or plan of exchange in the title.
exceptions: The book confirms this for Delaware, Nevada, and New York only; other states are 'likely' equally sensible (2.9), unverified.

examples.before: AGREEMENT AND PLAN OF MERGER
examples.after: MERGER AGREEMENT

examples.before: SHARE EXCHANGE AGREEMENT AND PLAN OF EXCHANGE
examples.after: SHARE EXCHANGE AGREEMENT

section: The Title
statement: Use agreement or contract in the title; contract is unobjectionable.
exceptions: Some contracts properly use another word: lease, insurance policy, and by tradition indenture (2.12; 13.468).

section: The Title
statement: A company with many contracts of one kind might supplement the title, for example with information below the title or by frontloading.

section: The Introductory Clause
statement: After the title, include an introductory clause that states the type of contract, perhaps gives a date, and identifies the parties.

section: The Introductory Clause
statement: Don't begin the introductory clause with know all men by these presents.

words: know all men by these presents

section: The Introductory Clause
statement: Format the introductory clause as a single paragraph; don't tabulate its elements with headings such as DATE and PARTIES.
exceptions: Tabulating can make sense if the number of parties and the information included would otherwise make the clause annoyingly long (2.18).

section: The Introductory Clause
statement: Begin the introductory clause with This plus the type of contract stated in the title, in all lowercase; thereafter refer to this agreement.
exceptions: Using just agreement in the introductory clause is unobjectionable (2.19).

examples.after: This asset purchase agreement is dated 25 September 2022 and is between ...

notes: The example is from sample 1 (PDF p. 78).

section: The Introductory Clause
statement: Use is dated (if the clause contains a date) rather than is made, is entered into, or is made and entered into; and say is between.
fix: This [type] agreement is dated [date] and is between ...

section: The Introductory Clause > Date in the Introductory Clause
statement: Use the date format 1 January 2022 in the introductory clause and for all other dates.

trigger.signal: dates in month-day-year or numeric format

section: The Introductory Clause > Date in the Introductory Clause
statement: Don't create a defined term such as Effective Date or Date of Execution for the introductory-clause date; refer to the date of this agreement.
fix: the date of this agreement
exceptions: Other circumstances might apply (2.24-2.44).

section: The Introductory Clause > Date in the Introductory Clause
statement: If the parties sign on the same day or close to it, put a date in the introductory clause and don't provide for dated signatures.

section: The Introductory Clause > Date in the Introductory Clause
statement: Don't make the introductory-clause date an as of date to reflect that a party signed on another date.
severity_basis: dispute risk or legally significant usage
notes: As-of dates are a haphazard professional courtesy and could confuse; using or not using as of is unlikely to be dispositive.

section: The Introductory Clause > Date in the Introductory Clause
statement: If the parties sign on different days and no one is inclined to ignore that, have them date their signatures (the date the last party signs is the contract date), and still state the date in the introductory clause, preferably inserted after signing manually or by e-signature software, with a placeholder rather than a blank.

trigger.signal: dated signature blocks with a blank date in the introductory clause

examples.after: [insert here the date the last party signs]

section: The Introductory Clause > Date in the Introductory Clause
statement: If you won't add the signing date to the introductory clause, choose among four inconvenient fallbacks; if you use a reference date (dated for reference), don't rely on the date of this agreement for timing; say the date the parties entered into this agreement.
fix: the date the parties entered into this agreement
severity_basis: dispute risk or legally significant usage
notes: Fallbacks: readers work out the date from signature blocks; signature blocks on page 1 (4.90); record the date in a contracts database; a reference date (awkward and potentially misleading).

section: The Introductory Clause > Date in the Introductory Clause
statement: Don't use as the date of the contract a date that reflects timing of performance (earlier to capture past performance, later for delayed performance); use the date of the contract and address timing where it makes most sense.

trigger.signal: an introductory-clause date earlier or later than signing; as of, effective date, dated for reference

severity_basis: dispute risk or legally significant usage
notes: Example (2.39-2.41): Acme and Schmidt sign on 1 March and Schmidt starts on 1 May; don't use 1 May in the introductory clause. Playing games with the date can have tax and other consequences, including civil or criminal liability (backdating) (2.45).

section: The Introductory Clause > Date in the Introductory Clause
statement: For precontract performance, describe the precontract circumstances in the recitals, address any payment in the payment provisions, state in the body that the contract governs the precontract performance, and use the date of the contract in the introductory clause.
severity_basis: dispute risk or legally significant usage

section: The Introductory Clause > Date in the Introductory Clause
statement: Don't use effective date (defined or undefined) for when performance starts; consider start date or performance date. A contract is effective when all parties have signed it.
fix: start date; performance date
severity_basis: dispute risk or legally significant usage

section: The Introductory Clause > Date in the Introductory Clause
statement: Avoid making a contract effective retroactively; retroactive effect can create problems in a series of transactions.
severity_basis: dispute risk or legally significant usage
notes: FH Partners, LLC v. Complete Home Concepts, Inc., 2012 WL 4074530 (Mo. Ct. App. 18 Sept. 2012).

section: The Introductory Clause > Between Versus Among
statement: Say the contract is between the parties, however many there are; don't use among or by and between.
fix: between
exceptions: If a traditionalist insists on among for more than two parties, conceding is painless (2.49).
notes: The OED says between is preferable even with more than two parties (2.48).

section: The Introductory Clause > Identifying the Parties
statement: Identify each individual party by full name and each entity party by its full registered name, including the entity designation (Inc., LLC, B.V., GmbH).
exceptions: If it would prevent confusion, also refer to any other name by which a party is or was known (2.50).
severity_basis: dispute risk or legally significant usage

section: The Introductory Clause > Identifying the Parties
statement: State party names in all capitals in the introductory clause.
exceptions: If showing medial capitals matters (HarperCollins, iPad), don't use all capitals (2.51).

section: The Introductory Clause > Identifying the Parties
statement: Don't enumerate the parties in the introductory clause.

section: The Introductory Clause > Identifying the Parties
statement: Don't tack including its affiliates and direct and indirect subsidiaries (or similar) onto a party's description or defined-term parenthetical; affiliates aren't parties and wouldn't be bound.
severity_basis: invites confusion over who is bound

examples.before: (including its affiliates and subsidiaries, "Acme")

section: The Introductory Clause > Identifying the Parties
statement: For a template used with little customization, you could refer to the other party named in the signature blocks below instead of naming it, but it's a nuisance for the reader.

section: The Introductory Clause > Identifying the Parties
statement: Where loose conventions govern the order of parties with defined roles, follow them (disclosing party before recipient; borrower before lender; seller before buyer).

section: The Introductory Clause > Parent Contracting on Behalf of an Affiliate
statement: Rather than relying on a parent's signing for nonparty group members, structure the transaction to give them the benefit of the contract while explicitly protecting the supplier or licensor (separate contracts, guarantor, agent, sublicensor, master agreement with statements of work, or written undertakings naming the supplier as third-party beneficiary).
severity_basis: dispute risk or legally significant usage
notes: Under Delaware law, nonparty group members might be liable if the parent signs explicitly for their benefit (Medicalgorithmics S.A. v. AMI Monitoring, Inc., Del. Ch. 18 Aug. 2016); not necessarily elsewhere.

section: The Introductory Clause > Parties with a Limited Role
statement: Highlight a party's limited role by inserting, before its name and between commas, and for purposes of only [specified provisions]; list that party last; and note the limited role in its signature block too.
exceptions: Omitting the highlight might have no repercussions; the party's role is whatever the contract says (2.61).
A limited-role party is likely also bound by boilerplate (governing law, notices) whether or not listed (2.62).
severity_basis: dispute risk or legally significant usage

section: The Introductory Clause > Parties with a Limited Role
statement: When there are too many parties to list, refer to them collectively, for example the financial institutions listed as Lenders on the signature pages of this agreement, or those listed in a schedule if you also need their addresses or other information.

section: The Introductory Clause > Describing the Parties
statement: After each entity party's name, state concisely its jurisdiction of organization and kind of entity.

words: organized and existing under the laws of
trigger.regex_hint: organized and existing under the laws of

examples.before: a corporation organized and existing under the laws of the state of Delaware
examples.after: a Delaware corporation

section: The Introductory Clause > Describing the Parties
statement: For a U.S. entity, don't include its address in the introductory clause; put addresses in the notices provision. Outside the U.S., include a registration number if it helps determine the party's history and status; a registered-office address is superfluous.

trigger.signal: street addresses in the introductory clause

exceptions: Where an individual is customarily distinguished by address, state it (full state name, plus ZIP code), unless the contract has a notices provision, in which case put all addresses there (2.71).
Some jurisdictions identify individuals by passport or national ID number (2.72) or require more (Czech Civil Code, 2.73).

examples.before: Albany, NY
examples.after: Albany, New York 12260

section: The Introductory Clause > Describing the Parties
statement: After each individual party's name, state that he or she is an individual; don't use natural person. State after every party name what kind of legal person it is.

examples.after: Suzanne Olsen, an individual

section: The Introductory Clause > Describing the Parties
statement: If a party serves an administrative function or acts for others, say so; if a party serves two roles, refer to it twice, once in each capacity; don't emphasize that it acts only or solely in a capacity.
severity_basis: dispute risk or legally significant usage

examples.after: ACME BANK, N.A., as collateral agent for the Secured Parties (in that capacity, the "Collateral Agent")

section: The Introductory Clause > Describing the Parties
statement: Make the trustee, not the trust, the party, and have the trustee sign as trustee: not in her individual capacity but as trustee, in both the introductory clause and the signature block.
exceptions: Some trusts, notably Delaware statutory trusts, are legal entities that can contract (2.79).
severity_basis: dispute risk or legally significant usage
notes: A trust generally isn't a legal person. Naming a trust doesn't necessarily invalidate the contract (Standard Bank v. Swanepoel NO [2015] ZASCA 71).

section: The Introductory Clause > Describing the Parties
statement: If an unincorporated division will perform, say so in the recitals or the party description, but make the company the party and signatory; don't make the division a party or say the company is represented by the division.
severity_basis: dispute risk or legally significant usage

examples.after: ACME CORPORATION, a Delaware corporation acting through its Widgets division (that corporation, "Acme")

section: The Introductory Clause > Describing the Parties
statement: Don't clutter the introductory clause with background information (relationships among parties, roles); put it in the recitals, or capture its essence with common-noun or collective defined terms.

examples.before: SWORDFISH ACQUISITION, INC., a California corporation and a wholly owned subsidiary of parent ("Sub")
examples.after: SWORDFISH ACQUISITION, INC., a California corporation ("Sub")

section: The Introductory Clause > Describing the Parties
statement: Don't assert in the introductory clause that a party is represented by a duly authorized representative, that it is duly organized and validly existing, or that the agreement states the parties' binding agreement; address the first two in statements of fact if relevant, and omit the third.

section: The Introductory Clause > Describing the Parties
statement: Generally, don't state anywhere in the contract that the parties intend to be legally bound.
exceptions: Use it if a quirk of governing law makes it necessary or advantageous, notably Pennsylvania's Uniform Written Obligations Act (2.88, 2.186).
notes: Restatement (Second) of Contracts § 21; English law presumes intent in commercial contracts (Edwards v. Skyways [1964] 1 All ER 494).

section: Defined Terms for Party Names
statement: Create in the introductory clause a defined term for each party name.

section: Defined Terms for Party Names
statement: Use an integrated definition with the defined term in parentheses, in quotation marks and bold (don't bold the quotation marks or the), without introductory text such as hereinafter referred to as.

trigger.regex_hint: \bhereinafter( referred to as)?\b|\breferred to herein as\b

notes: The book's cross-reference '2.106' for the definite article appears to mean 2.105 (as printed).

section: Defined Terms for Party Names
statement: For an entity, place the defined-term parenthetical after the jurisdiction reference.

examples.after: Excelsior Corporation, a Delaware corporation ("Excelsior")

section: Defined Terms for Party Names
statement: Don't state in a defined-term parenthetical that the defined term includes the party's successors; cover succession by default rules or targeted provisions.
severity_basis: dispute risk or legally significant usage

section: Defined Terms for Party Names
statement: Don't use all capitals or other emphasis for party-name defined terms throughout the contract.

section: Defined Terms for Party Names > Kinds of Defined Term
statement: Base a party defined term on the party's name (slightly more accessible) or on a common noun (the Company, the Shareholder); common nouns work well for standard roles, single-entity contracts, or unknown signers.
exceptions: Mixing approaches can make sense, for example a name-based term for your company and the Licensee for the changing counterparty in a template (2.98).

section: Defined Terms for Party Names > Kinds of Defined Term
statement: For an individual, use the last name (or the first name if two individuals share a last name); add an honorific if the last name alone is too stark or to show respect.

section: Defined Terms for Party Names > Kinds of Defined Term
statement: For a company, use a word or two from its name rather than an abbreviation where possible, and avoid abbreviations with unrelated meanings or connotations (DOG, SAD).
exceptions: An abbreviation might be best if affiliates have similar names, the name includes the abbreviation, the party is commonly known by it, or the name precludes anything better (BNJ) (2.101).

examples.before: Sargasso Realty Holdings, Inc. ("SRH")
examples.after: Sargasso Realty Holdings, Inc. ("Sargasso")

section: Defined Terms for Party Names > Kinds of Defined Term
statement: Don't use paired defined terms that differ only in their final syllable.
notes: Full list (2.104): Acquiror-Acquiree, Appellant-Appellee, Assignor-Assignee, Bailor-Bailee, Covenantor-Covenantee, Donor-Donee, Employer-Employee, Endorser-Endorsee, Farmor-Farmee, Grantor-Grantee, Guarantor-Guarantee, Indemnitor-Indemnitee, Lessor-Lessee, Licensor-Licensee, Mortgagor-Mortgagee, Obligor-Obligee, Offeror-Offeree, Optionor-Optionee, Payor-Payee, Transferor-Transferee, Vendor-Vendee, Warrantor-Warrantee. 2.98 itself uses 'the Licensee' as an example common-noun term; the rule bars pairing it with 'the Licensor'.

section: Defined Terms for Party Names > Kinds of Defined Term
statement: Use the definite article with a common-noun party defined term (the Purchaser, not Purchaser), and be consistent.

trigger.signal: common-noun defined term without 'the'

examples.before: Purchaser
examples.after: the Purchaser

section: Defined Terms for Party Names > Kinds of Defined Term
statement: Don't offer alternative defined terms for a party.
severity_basis: dispute risk or legally significant usage

examples.before: "Widgetco" or the "Company"
"Widgetco," sometimes referred to herein as the "Company"

section: Defined Terms for Party Names > Kinds of Defined Term
statement: Choose among Vendor, Seller, and Supplier deliberately: vendor suggests a party in the business of selling the goods; seller suggests it isn't; supplier suggests it is and is supplying over time.
notes: In Commonwealth countries vendor is standard for someone selling a house.

section: Defined Terms for Party Names > Kinds of Defined Term
statement: Consider the Employee as the default defined term for an employee; the Executive seems unnecessary and perhaps old-fashioned.
exceptions: Alternatively, use the last name with an honorific (2.108).

section: Defined Terms for Party Names > Collective Terms and Generic Labels
statement: Define a collective party term in the singular or the plural but not both, and don't use a singular defined term (the Lender) for two or more parties via collectively or together with.
severity_basis: dispute risk or legally significant usage

section: Defined Terms for Party Names > Collective Terms and Generic Labels
statement: Don't define the Parties for all the parties; say the parties, and drop the pair individually a "Party" and collectively the "Parties."

section: Defined Terms for Party Names > Collective Terms and Generic Labels
statement: In a provision saying only the parties may enforce the contract, refer to the parties by name or to the signatories, because a court might read the parties to include intended third-party beneficiaries.
severity_basis: dispute risk or legally significant usage

section: Defined Terms for Party Names > Collective Terms and Generic Labels
statement: Don't use party of the first part and party of the second part, even only in the introductory clause.
severity_basis: easily transposed labels invite confusion and litigation

section: Defined Terms for Party Names > Collective Terms and Generic Labels
statement: Avoid Party A and Party B as party defined terms; they say nothing about each party's role.
exceptions: The convention is used in ISDA forms and in translations for Chinese, South Korean, and Japanese legal writing (2.116).

section: Defined Terms for Party Names > Collective Terms and Generic Labels
statement: Where either party might play a given role, use generic labels that describe the role (the withdrawing member, the Indemnifying Party), defined if used often; avoid that party / the other party in complex provisions and contextless labels like X and Y. Choose labels carefully: a label can carry unintended consequences.
severity_basis: dispute risk or legally significant usage

examples.before: the non-breaching party
examples.after: the party claiming breach

notes: Powertech Technology, Inc. v. Tessera, Inc., 2014 WL 171830 (N.D. Cal. 15 Jan. 2014): the label non-breaching party required the terminating party to have substantially complied itself.

section: The Defined Term This Agreement
statement: Don't create the defined term this Agreement; refer to this agreement, lowercase, without defining it (likewise this amendment, this assignment).

examples.before: this Agreement [defined term]
examples.after: this agreement [undefined, lowercase]

notes: Introduction suggests holding firm on lowercase this agreement in your own drafts (PDF p. 54).

section: The Defined Term This Agreement
statement: Don't define this agreement to include its attachments; mentioning an attachment in a provision brings it within the contract.

section: The Defined Term This Agreement
statement: Don't use an abbreviation of the title (APA, NDA, MSA) as the contract's reference to itself.
fix: this agreement

section: Recitals > Function
statement: Use recitals only for background the parties regard as relevant: context recitals (circumstances leading up to the contract), purpose recitals (the parties' goals, succinctly and broadly), and simultaneous-transaction recitals.

section: Recitals > Function
statement: Don't address deal terms or facts in any detail in the recitals; put them in the body. Courts typically look to recitals only for indications of intent.

trigger.signal: obligations, prices, or detailed facts in the recitals

severity_basis: substantive terms in recitals might not be enforced

section: Recitals > Function
statement: If the transaction is straightforward and lacks any back story, dispense with recitals.

section: Recitals > Function
statement: Don't use the recital that the parties desire to enter into the agreement.

section: Recitals > Heading, Enumeration, Prose
statement: Don't use WITNESSETH (or any variant) before the recitals.

section: Recitals > Heading, Enumeration, Prose
statement: Don't give the recitals a heading; don't use WHEREAS as one. RECITALS or BACKGROUND is better than those but still unneeded.
exceptions: If a heading would make the contract's users more comfortable, use one; little is at stake (2.141).

section: Recitals > Heading, Enumeration, Prose
statement: Don't number or letter the recitals.

trigger.signal: recitals labeled A, B, C or 1, 2, 3

section: Recitals > Heading, Enumeration, Prose
statement: Write recitals as straightforward narrative prose in complete sentences and conventional paragraphs; don't begin each recital with WHEREAS or end it with a semicolon.

examples.after: Hastings Sub 1 is a wholly owned subsidiary of Hastings.

notes: The example is from sample 2 (PDF p. 106).

section: Recitals > Verb in Purpose Recitals
statement: In purpose recitals, use wants; avoid desires to, wishes to, intends to, seeks to, would like to, is desirous of, and is agreeable to.

trigger.regex_hint: \b(desires to|wishes to|is desirous of|is agreeable to|would like to)\b

examples.before: is desirous of [transferring]
examples.after: wants to [transfer]

notes: Book's verdicts (2.147): desires to 'oddly steamy'; wishes to 'a little genteel'; intends to inappropriate (suggests a plan outside the contract); seeks to means try; would like to too genteel; is desirous of archaic; is agreeable to clumsy. Sample 2 itself uses wishes (as printed).

section: Recitals > Premature References, Incorporation, True and Correct, Defined Terms
statement: In a purpose recital, don't say the parties propose to act in accordance with or subject to the terms of this agreement, or that this agreement contemplates something; express a general intent not tied to the terms (and no broader than the body). In a context recital, don't say a party has agreed to do something subject to the terms of this agreement.

words: subject to the terms of this agreement

section: Recitals > Premature References, Incorporation, True and Correct, Defined Terms
statement: Don't incorporate the recitals by reference; keep substantive provisions out of the recitals and move any into the body.
severity_basis: dispute risk or legally significant usage
notes: Jones Apparel Group, Inc. v. Polo Ralph Lauren Corp., 791 N.Y.S.2d 409 (App. Div. 2005).

section: Recitals > Premature References, Incorporation, True and Correct, Defined Terms
statement: Don't rely on a statement that the recitals are true and correct; if recital matters might be inaccurate, state them as statements of fact in the body.
severity_basis: weak basis for a claim if a recital is inaccurate

section: Recitals > Premature References, Incorporation, True and Correct, Defined Terms
statement: You may define terms in the recitals, but don't use autonomous definitions there, don't overload them, and don't use terms defined only later in the contract.

section: The Lead-In > Wording
statement: Use the lead-in The parties agree as follows: or, after recitals, The parties therefore agree as follows:

examples.after: The parties agree as follows: / The parties therefore agree as follows:

section: The Lead-In > Wording
statement: In the lead-in, don't add extraneous verbs such as covenant and agree, don't use hereby, don't say the parties hereby enter into this agreement, and don't name the parties.

words: intending to be legally bound, hereby agree

section: The Lead-In > Wording
statement: If the body would be a single one-sentence provision (for example, a straightforward amendment), you can wrap it into the lead-in, followed by the concluding clause.

section: The Lead-In > Consideration
statement: Don't use recitals of consideration (including 'backstop' recitals of unspecified consideration) just before the body; they don't establish consideration and serve no purpose.

trigger.regex_hint: (?i)\b(now,? therefore|in consideration of the premises|good and valuable consideration|receipt and sufficiency)\b

examples.before: NOW, THEREFORE, in consideration of the premises and the mutual covenants set forth herein and for other good and valuable consideration, the receipt and sufficiency of which are hereby acknowledged, the parties hereto covenant and agree as follows:
examples.after: The parties therefore agree as follows:

notes: Introduction: give a pass to a traditional recital of consideration on the other side's draft (PDF p. 55). A few courts have given backstop recitals weight (Network Protection Sciences v. Fortinet, 2013 WL 4479336 (N.D. Cal.); Urban Sites of Chicago v. Crown Castle USA, 979 N.E.2d 480 (Ill. App. Ct. 2012)), but relying on them is 'too depressingly speculative' (2.177).

section: The Lead-In > Consideration
statement: Don't include a backstop recital to invoke a rebuttable presumption of consideration; avoid disputes by stating the deal clearly.
notes: Disagrees with Tina L. Stark, Drafting Contracts 86 (2d ed. 2014).

section: The Lead-In > Consideration
statement: State any actual consideration clearly in the body, not as a recital of consideration; if a transaction (such as a disadvantageous amendment) lacks consideration, arrange consideration and state it.
severity_basis: a contract lacking consideration may be unenforceable

section: The Lead-In > Consideration
statement: As alternatives for a transaction lacking consideration, the performing party could waive consideration and acknowledge the other party's reliance (research governing law first), or use a contract under seal where governing law dispenses with consideration for sealed contracts.
severity_basis: dispute risk or legally significant usage
notes: Pennsylvania's Uniform Written Obligations Act: a statement of intent to be legally bound can substitute for consideration, but courts limit it (Socko v. Mid-Atlantic Systems of CPA, Inc., 126 A.3d 1266 (Pa. 2015)).

section: The Lead-In > Consideration
statement: Delete (other) good and valuable consideration and the receipt and sufficiency of which are hereby acknowledged.

section: The Lead-In > Consideration
statement: If two contracts are a package deal, describe the connection in the recitals and state in the body of each the implications for one contract of performance under the other.
severity_basis: dispute risk or legally significant usage
notes: TA Operating LLC v. Comdata Inc., C.A. No. 12954-CB (Del. Ch. 11 Sept. 2017).

section: The Lead-In > Consideration
statement: For an option contract, set a plausible option price, recite it, and make sure it's paid; if you rely on the Restatement § 87(1) approach, recite nominal consideration rather than a backstop recital.
exceptions: You can dispense with consideration for options governed by a statute that says none is needed (New York General Obligations Law; UCC § 2-205 firm offers) (2.201).
severity_basis: dispute risk or legally significant usage
notes: 1464-Eight v. Joppich, 154 S.W.3d 101 (Tex. 2004) endorses the Restatement approach, a minority position.

section: The Lead-In > Consideration
statement: In a guarantee of an existing debt, state the guarantor's actual consideration rather than relying on pretense consideration; if you rely on the Restatements, use nominal consideration rather than a backstop recital.
severity_basis: dispute risk or legally significant usage

section: The Lead-In > Consideration
statement: Dispense with the word consideration and express the exchange accurately, including when payment occurs; for a release, say it is in exchange for a specified action or promise.

examples.before: In consideration of $10,000, Able hereby sells the Equipment to Baker.
examples.after: Able hereby purchases the Equipment from Baker for $10,000, which Able shall pay Baker no later than 30 days after the date of this agreement.

notes: As printed, 2.209 has Able selling to Baker while 2.210-2.211 have Able purchasing from Baker; the roles flip in the book.

section: The Lead-In > Consideration
statement: Apply the same analysis to U.S.-style recitals of consideration in Canadian and U.S.-connected international contracts; in a contract governed by civil law, delete any recital of consideration.

trigger.signal: a recital or acknowledgment of consideration in a civil-law-governed contract

section: Body Heading; Cover Sheet, Table of Contents, Index
statement: Don't insert a heading such as OPERATIVE PROVISIONS between the lead-in and the body.

section: Body Heading; Cover Sheet, Table of Contents, Index
statement: For a contract over 20 pages, consider a table of contents (articles, sections, page numbers, attachments) from the first draft, preceded by an uncluttered cover sheet and followed by any index of defined terms.

section: Categories of Contract Language (introduction)
statement: For every sentence and clause in the body, first choose the category of contract language (agreement, performance, obligation, discretion, prohibition, policy, declaration, intention, recommendation, or a way of expressing a condition), then use that category's verb structure; don't go straight to shall, will, must, or another verb.

trigger.signal: any verb structure in the body of the contract

severity_basis: verb choice tracks meaning; the wrong category can change legal effect

section: Categories of Contract Language (introduction)
statement: Treat the categories of contract language as a construct based on standard English, adjusted so different categories map to different verb structures; they aren't rules of grammar.

section: Categories of Contract Language (introduction)
statement: Use figure 1 as the quick reference mapping each category to its verb structure.
notes: Figure 1 (OCR, PDF pp. 127-130): agreement - agree, lead-in only; performance - hereby + simple present (absence of performance: negative present continuous as policy); obligation on subject - shall; obligation on someone else - must (alternative: shall cause); discretion - may; absence of obligation - is not required to; absence of prohibition - is not prohibited from (superseded; see R-rider-2025-11-19-nothing-prohibits); prohibition - shall not; policy - simple present on effectiveness or for a stated time, will for contingent future events; conditional clause - simple present, matrix clause will; condition via policy - It is a condition to ... that + present perfect or present; condition via obligation - To [infinitive] ... must; declaration - states (fact the declarant knows), acknowledges (fact the other party knows); intention - intends that + will; recommendation - recommends (figure also lists advises and encourages, though 3.504 prefers recommends over advises).

section: Categories of Contract Language (introduction)
statement: Read table references this way: [3-3] is the third example in table 3; [3-3b] is the second variation of [3-3].

section: Categories of Contract Language (introduction)
statement: Read table ratings as: ✓✓ recommended; ✓ acceptable but can be improved, use with caution, or acceptability depends on context; × not recommended; ×× don't use.
notes: The PDF p. 130 legend prints a single × on both of its last two lines; reading × as 'not recommended' and ×× as 'don't use' is an inference from the tables, which use both as distinct ratings, and from the legend's order.

section: General Considerations > Use the Third Person
statement: In business contracts, use the third person (Acme shall purchase ...), not first or second person (we, us, our, you, your).
exceptions: First and second person are primarily used in consumer contracts (3.12).
severity_basis: readers lose track of who we and you are; no good collective reference

examples.after: Acme shall purchase the Shares from Ahmad.

section: General Considerations > Use the Active Voice Unless the Passive Voice Is Appropriate
statement: Recognize the passive voice: the subject is acted on (The peach was eaten by Marie); the would-be active subject becomes the 'by-agent,' which can be omitted (The peach was eaten).

trigger.signal: form of be + past participle

section: General Considerations > Use the Active Voice Unless the Passive Voice Is Appropriate
statement: Use the active voice unless there's a clear benefit to the passive; in particular, use the active voice to express action by a party. The passive adds words (with a by-agent) and disrupts subject-verb-object order.

trigger.signal: passive verb with a party as by-agent

fix: Make the actor the subject.

examples.before: The rent shall be paid by the Tenant on the first of every month.
examples.after: The Tenant shall pay the rent on the first day of every month.

section: General Considerations > Use the Active Voice Unless the Passive Voice Is Appropriate
statement: Don't use a passive verb without a by-agent to express what a party does or must do; it hides the actor, and the consequences can be drastic.

trigger.signal: passive verb with no by-agent describing party action (is terminated, shall be delivered, must be given)

fix: State the actor: If Acme terminates Player's employment ...
severity_basis: omitting the actor can change who is covered (East Texas Copy Systems)

examples.before: If Jason Player's employment with Buyer is terminated prior to two years from the date of this Agreement for any reason other than a for cause termination, this Non-Compete Agreement will no longer be binding.

notes: East Texas Copy Systems, Inc. v. Player, 2016 WL 6638865 (Tex. App. 10 Nov. 2016): 'is terminated' covered the employee's resignation, so the noncompete fell away. Also 2620-2630 Fountainview, LP v. ASR 2620-2630 Fountainview GP, LLC, 2019 WL 470240 (Tex. App. 7 Feb. 2019).

section: General Considerations > Use the Active Voice Unless the Passive Voice Is Appropriate
statement: The passive may be appropriate if the by-agent is a nonparty or isn't a person, or if leading with the thing acted on keeps the focus where it belongs.

examples.after: if a Necessary Project Approval is revoked
No party will be bound by this amendment until the Parent, the Borrowers, and the Required Lenders have signed a counterpart.

examples.before: French law governs this agreement.
examples.after: This agreement is governed by French law. [either is fine]

section: General Considerations > Throat-Clearing
statement: Eliminate throat-clearing: extraneous verb structures tacked onto the front of a sentence (Acme acknowledges that, agrees that, covenants that, represents that, It is agreed that ...). Reviewers should consider doing so too.

words: represents, warrants, covenants, and agrees that

test: Delete the introductory verb structure; if the sentence still says the same thing in its proper category, it was throat-clearing.
severity_basis: can be mistaken for the principal verb structure and has caused disputes

examples.before: The Lead Manager hereby agrees that it undertakes that it shall: (i) submit ...
examples.after: The Lead Manager shall: (i) submit ...

examples.before: It is further agreed that the insurer undertakes that it shall not contend ...
examples.after: The insurer shall not contend ...

notes: UBS Securities LLC v. Highland Capital Management, L.P., 906 N.Y.S.2d 784 (Sup. Ct. 2009), rev'd, 893 N.Y.S.2d 869 (App. Div. 2010): the court gave substantive weight to 'agree that' (3.33). The Introduction lists throat-clearing among minor glitches worth flagging on the other side's draft.

section: General Considerations > Throat-Clearing
statement: Before deleting apparent throat-clearing, check whether it is a poorly chosen principal verb; if the sentence states a fact, use language of declaration (acknowledge) and might for possibility.

examples.before: ABC and XYZ agree that each of them may obtain Confidential Information of the other.
examples.after: ABC and XYZ each acknowledge that each of them might obtain Confidential Information of the other.

section: General Considerations > Using the Subjunctive Mood
statement: Don't use the subjunctive in ordinary conditions; it's archaic. Use the indicative.

examples.before: If the Borrower be in default ...
examples.after: If the Borrower is in default ...

examples.before: It is a condition to closing that the Buyer have received an opinion ...
examples.after: It is a condition to closing that the Buyer has received an opinion ...

notes: 3.35: using the subjunctive has no implications for the deal; deploy it if you grasp modern usage.

section: General Considerations > Using the Subjunctive Mood
statement: Keep the subjunctive where the clause expresses a demand or suggestion, even inside a conditional clause (requires that Widgetco pay; recommends that the Employee retain).

examples.before: If Acme requires that Widgetco pays the purchase price in Canadian dollars ...
examples.after: If Acme requires that Widgetco pay the purchase price in Canadian dollars ...

examples.before: The Company recommends that the Employee retains a lawyer ...
examples.after: The Company recommends that the Employee retain a lawyer ...

section: General Considerations > Structure and Consolidation
statement: Think carefully before stating a shared subject and verb (Acme shall:) followed by enumerated clauses; the reader must supply them in each clause, and limiting a section to one category can be constraining.

trigger.signal: '[Party] shall:' followed by tabulated or integrated enumerated clauses

exceptions: Appropriate if the clauses are short, simple, and address a theme, like a checklist of steps (3.42).

section: General Considerations > Structure and Consolidation
statement: Consider consolidating related deal points into one verb structure rather than a separate sentence for each.

examples.before: The Licensee shall make all regulatory filings. The Licensee shall decide in which countries to file for regulatory approval.
examples.after: The Licensee shall make all regulatory filings in those countries in which it decides to seek Regulatory Approval for a Product.

examples.before: Acme shall pay each invoice no later than 30 days after it receives that invoice. For Acme's payment of an invoice to be valid, Acme must pay that invoice by bank transfer.
examples.after: Acme shall pay each invoice by bank transfer no later than 30 days after it receives that invoice.

section: General Considerations > Structure and Consolidation
statement: Don't treat one category as stronger or weaker than another; avoid mere condition, mere covenant, mere obligation, and merely in such comparisons. The categories have different consequences.
notes: Failure to satisfy a condition precludes the dependent result; failure to comply with an obligation gives a damages claim and might relieve the other party.

section: Language of Agreement
statement: Use language of agreement (agree) only once, in the lead-in (agree as follows); elsewhere agrees that is throat-clearing.

section: Language of Agreement
statement: Don't use hereby in language of agreement; hereby belongs to language of performance.

section: Language of Performance
statement: Use language of performance for speech acts that accomplish an action involving a change in status by signing the contract (Acme hereby grants the License to Smith); use the present tense.

examples.after: [1-1] ✓✓: Acme hereby purchases the Assets from Jackson.

notes: The term echoes the linguistics term 'performative'; it is unrelated to performance under a contract (3.49). Table ratings per 3.9 legend: ✓✓ recommended; ✓ acceptable but improvable or context-dependent; × not recommended; ×× don't use (× vs ×× reading inferred from the tables; the PDF p. 130 legend prints a single × on both last lines). See R-3.9-rating-legend.

section: Language of Performance > Using Hereby
statement: Use hereby in language of performance; it signals that the act is accomplished by the speech act and excludes a habitual reading.
fix: Acme hereby purchases ...
exceptions: You could omit hereby ([1-1a] is rated ✓); the habitual reading is unlikely to confuse, but it could distract (3.50-3.51).

examples.before: [1-1a] ✓: Acme purchases the Assets from Jackson.
examples.after: [1-1] ✓✓: Acme hereby purchases the Assets from Jackson.
