notes: Table ratings per 3.9 legend: ✓✓ recommended; ✓ acceptable but improvable or context-dependent; × not recommended; ×× don't use (× vs ×× reading inferred from the tables; the PDF p. 130 legend prints a single × on both last lines). See R-3.9-rating-legend.

section: Language of Performance > Using Hereby
statement: Don't replace hereby with by this agreement; hereby relates to the particular language of performance and is shorter.

section: Language of Performance > Using Hereby
statement: Omit hereby wherever it is used other than in language of performance.
test: Is the clause a speech act that changes status on signing? If not, delete hereby.

section: Language of Performance > Using Now
statement: Don't use now in language of performance: it's primarily oral, a little old-fashioned, and could be read as habitual.

examples.before: [1-1b] ××: Acme now purchases the Assets from Jackson.
examples.after: [1-1] ✓✓: Acme hereby purchases the Assets from Jackson.

examples.before: the Collaborator now assigns the Acme Foreground Intellectual Property to Acme

notes: Table ratings per 3.9 legend: ✓✓ recommended; ✓ acceptable but improvable or context-dependent; × not recommended; ×× don't use (× vs ×× reading inferred from the tables; the PDF p. 130 legend prints a single × on both last lines). See R-3.9-rating-legend.

section: Language of Performance > Problematic Usages
statement: Always use the active voice in language of performance, to make the actor clear.

trigger.signal: hereby + passive verb

severity_basis: passive performance can omit who is acting

examples.before: [1-1c] ××: The Assets are hereby purchased from Jackson.
examples.after: [1-1] ✓✓: Acme hereby purchases the Assets from Jackson.

notes: Table ratings per 3.9 legend: ✓✓ recommended; ✓ acceptable but improvable or context-dependent; × not recommended; ×× don't use (× vs ×× reading inferred from the tables; the PDF p. 130 legend prints a single × on both last lines). See R-3.9-rating-legend.

section: Language of Performance > Problematic Usages
statement: Don't use the present continuous in language of performance; performance is instantaneous, not an unfolding event.

examples.before: [1-1d] ××: Acme is hereby purchasing the Assets from Jackson.
examples.after: [1-1] ✓✓: Acme hereby purchases the Assets from Jackson.

notes: Table ratings per 3.9 legend: ✓✓ recommended; ✓ acceptable but improvable or context-dependent; × not recommended; ×× don't use (× vs ×× reading inferred from the tables; the PDF p. 130 legend prints a single × on both last lines). See R-3.9-rating-legend.

section: Language of Performance > Problematic Usages
statement: Don't use do as an auxiliary in language of performance (does hereby), and don't use doth or hath; they're archaisms.

examples.before: [1-1e] ××: Acme does hereby purchase the Assets from Jackson.
examples.after: [1-1] ✓✓: Acme hereby purchases the Assets from Jackson.

notes: Table ratings per 3.9 legend: ✓✓ recommended; ✓ acceptable but improvable or context-dependent; × not recommended; ×× don't use (× vs ×× reading inferred from the tables; the PDF p. 130 legend prints a single × on both last lines). See R-3.9-rating-legend.

section: Language of Performance > Problematic Usages
statement: Don't use agrees to, or agrees to and does hereby, as language of performance; it invites a fight over whether the clause is performance or obligation.

examples.before: [1-1f] ××: Acme agrees to purchase the Assets from Jackson.
examples.after: [1-1] ✓✓: Acme hereby purchases the Assets from Jackson.

examples.before: [1-1g] ××: Acme agrees to and does hereby purchase the Assets from Jackson.
examples.after: [1-1] ✓✓: Acme hereby purchases the Assets from Jackson.

notes: Table ratings per 3.9 legend: ✓✓ recommended; ✓ acceptable but improvable or context-dependent; × not recommended; ×× don't use (× vs ×× reading inferred from the tables; the PDF p. 130 legend prints a single × on both last lines). See R-3.9-rating-legend.

section: Language of Performance > Problematic Usages
statement: Don't use by these presents, alone or preceded by does, in language of performance.

examples.before: [1-1h] ××: Acme by these presents purchases the Assets from Jackson.
examples.after: [1-1] ✓✓: Acme hereby purchases the Assets from Jackson.

notes: Table ratings per 3.9 legend: ✓✓ recommended; ✓ acceptable but improvable or context-dependent; × not recommended; ×× don't use (× vs ×× reading inferred from the tables; the PDF p. 130 legend prints a single × on both last lines). See R-3.9-rating-legend.

section: Language of Performance > Problematic Usages
statement: Don't try to turn language of obligation into performance by adding (as) of the date of this agreement; it imposes an obligation to act sometime on that date rather than effecting a transfer on signing.

words: as of the date of this agreement
on the date of this agreement

severity_basis: ambiguity, or a category error or usage that can change meaning or invite dispute

examples.before: [1-1i] ××: Acme shall purchase the Assets from Jackson as of the date of this agreement.
examples.after: [1-1] ✓✓: Acme hereby purchases the Assets from Jackson.

notes: The prose (3.61) says 'on the date of this agreement'; table entry [1-1i] reads 'as of the date of this agreement'. Table ratings per 3.9 legend: ✓✓ recommended; ✓ acceptable but improvable or context-dependent; × not recommended; ×× don't use (× vs ×× reading inferred from the tables; the PDF p. 130 legend prints a single × on both last lines). See R-3.9-rating-legend.

section: Language of Performance > Problematic Usages
statement: Don't use is pleased to in language of performance; it doesn't make clear that the speech act accomplishes the action.
severity_basis: dispute risk or legally significant usage

examples.before: [1-1j] ××: Acme is pleased to purchase the Assets from Jackson.
examples.after: [1-1] ✓✓: Acme hereby purchases the Assets from Jackson.

examples.before: Acme Trust is pleased to retain Summit Consulting, LLC ...

notes: Table ratings per 3.9 legend: ✓✓ recommended; ✓ acceptable but improvable or context-dependent; × not recommended; ×× don't use (× vs ×× reading inferred from the tables; the PDF p. 130 legend prints a single × on both last lines). See R-3.9-rating-legend.

section: Language of Performance > Problematic Usages
statement: Don't use irrevocably, unconditionally, absolutely, or forever in language of performance; absent contrary language, an action taken can't be undone, so they're redundant.

examples.before: [1-1k] ××: Acme hereby irrevocably purchases the Assets from Jackson.
examples.after: [1-1] ✓✓: Acme hereby purchases the Assets from Jackson.

notes: Restatement (Second) of Torts § 892A cmt. i; Reyes v. Lincoln Automotive Financial Services, 2017 WL 2675363 (2d Cir. 22 June 2017) (a consent granted in a contract is irrevocable at common law). Table ratings per 3.9 legend: ✓✓ recommended; ✓ acceptable but improvable or context-dependent; × not recommended; ×× don't use (× vs ×× reading inferred from the tables; the PDF p. 130 legend prints a single × on both last lines). See R-3.9-rating-legend.

section: Language of Performance > Problematic Usages
statement: Use irrevocably with appoint if you don't want the appointing party to be able to remove the appointee, because the power to appoint might include the power to remove; or say so explicitly.
severity_basis: dispute risk or legally significant usage

section: Language of Performance > Problematic Usages
statement: If a party consents to ongoing conduct (not a one-time action), use irrevocably so the consenting party can't later change its mind.
severity_basis: without it, a consent to ongoing conduct might be withdrawn

section: Language of Performance > Actions That Don't Work; Absence of Performance; Future Performance
statement: Don't use language of performance for an action other than a change in status of a person or thing; you can't pay someone just by saying so.
severity_basis: dispute risk or legally significant usage

examples.before: The Buyer hereby pays the Seller ...

section: Language of Performance > Actions That Don't Work; Absence of Performance; Future Performance
statement: To state that a party is not taking an action on signing, don't use language of performance in the negative; use language of policy with the negative present continuous.
severity_basis: dispute risk or legally significant usage

examples.before: [1-2] ××: The Buyer does not hereby assume the Excluded Liabilities.
examples.after: [1-2b] ✓✓: In this agreement the Buyer is not assuming any Excluded Liabilities.

examples.before: [1-2a] ××: The Buyer hereby does not assume the Excluded Liabilities.
examples.after: [1-2b] ✓✓: In this agreement the Buyer is not assuming any Excluded Liabilities.

notes: Table ratings per 3.9 legend: ✓✓ recommended; ✓ acceptable but improvable or context-dependent; × not recommended; ×× don't use (× vs ×× reading inferred from the tables; the PDF p. 130 legend prints a single × on both last lines). See R-3.9-rating-legend.

section: Language of Performance > Actions That Don't Work; Absence of Performance; Future Performance
statement: To state the consequences of entering into a contract or issuing a document in the future, don't use will ... thereby; use will be deemed.
severity_basis: dispute risk or legally significant usage

examples.before: [1-3] ×: When the Company issues a Purchase Order, it will thereby hire the Contractor to perform the services stated in that Purchase Order.
examples.after: [1-3a] ✓✓: When the Company issues a Purchase Order, it will be deemed to have hired the Contractor to perform the services stated in that Purchase Order.

notes: Table ratings per 3.9 legend: ✓✓ recommended; ✓ acceptable but improvable or context-dependent; × not recommended; ×× don't use (× vs ×× reading inferred from the tables; the PDF p. 130 legend prints a single × on both last lines). See R-3.9-rating-legend.

section: Language of Performance > Buying and Selling; Services
statement: For a purchase on signing, use one perspective (Acme hereby purchases ... or Jackson hereby sells ...); using both verbs is unnecessary.
exceptions: Drafters may want reciprocity shown even at the cost of redundancy; be prepared to be asked to use both (3.71).

examples.after: Acme hereby purchases the Assets from Jackson. [or] Jackson hereby sells the Assets to Acme.

section: Language of Performance > Buying and Selling; Services
statement: Use language of obligation as the default for performance of services; use language of performance (appoints, employs, retains) only where the services define the performer by a label such as agent or employee.

examples.before: Acme hereby appoints ABC to perform for Acme ... the administrative, bookkeeping, and pricing services stated in appendix A.
examples.after: ABC shall perform for Acme ... the administrative, bookkeeping, and pricing services stated in appendix A.
The Fund hereby appoints the Agent as its Investor Servicing Agent ... [label: language of performance sounds natural]

section: Language of Performance > Advantages of Granting Language
statement: Use granting language (hereby grants ... a license) in contracts dealing with rights to software and intellectual property, where it's entrenched and lets you use sublicense; resist it elsewhere, using language of discretion instead.

examples.before: [1-4a] ✓: Acme hereby grants Widgetco the right to use the Marks in ... .
examples.after: [1-4] ✓✓: Acme hereby grants Widgetco a license to use the Marks in ... .

examples.before: [1-4b] ×× (in a license): Widgetco may use the Marks in ... .
examples.after: [1-4] ✓✓: Acme hereby grants Widgetco a license to use the Marks in ... .

examples.before: The Customer hereby grants Acme a perpetual, nonexclusive, and irrevocable license to use data on performance and output of the Covered Equipment.
examples.after: During the term of this agreement and thereafter, Acme may use data on performance and output of the Covered Equipment.

notes: 3.76 says [1-4], [1-4a], and [1-4b] mean the same; the ×× rating for [1-4b] applies in the IP-license context. [1-4a] is ✓ here, but the general form 'hereby grants ... the right to' is ×× in table 4 ([4-1o], 3.281). Table ratings per 3.9 legend: ✓✓ recommended; ✓ acceptable but improvable or context-dependent; × not recommended; ×× don't use (× vs ×× reading inferred from the tables; the PDF p. 130 legend prints a single × on both last lines). See R-3.9-rating-legend.

section: Language of Performance > Advantages of Granting Language
statement: Prefer grants ... a license to the verb license: the noun takes adjectives (nonexclusive, irrevocable, perpetual) more simply, and Acme hereby licenses alone could make Acme either licensee or licensor.

examples.before: [1-4c] ×: Acme hereby licenses to Widgetco the right to use the Marks in ... .
examples.after: [1-4] ✓✓: Acme hereby grants Widgetco a license to use the Marks in ... .

notes: Table ratings per 3.9 legend: ✓✓ recommended; ✓ acceptable but improvable or context-dependent; × not recommended; ×× don't use (× vs ×× reading inferred from the tables; the PDF p. 130 legend prints a single × on both last lines). See R-3.9-rating-legend.

section: Language of Performance > Advantages of Granting Language
statement: For leases, the verb lease remains conventional (Jones hereby leases to Smith); Jones hereby grants Smith a lease would be unorthodox.

section: Language of Performance > Advantages of Granting Language
statement: Omit to after grant: hereby grants Widgetco a license, not hereby grants to Widgetco a license. The same applies to other verbs, such as pay.

examples.before: [1-4d] ×: Acme hereby grants to Widgetco a license to use the Marks in ... .
examples.after: [1-4] ✓✓: Acme hereby grants Widgetco a license to use the Marks in ... .

notes: Little rides on this distinction (3.86). Table ratings per 3.9 legend: ✓✓ recommended; ✓ acceptable but improvable or context-dependent; × not recommended; ×× don't use (× vs ×× reading inferred from the tables; the PDF p. 130 legend prints a single × on both last lines). See R-3.9-rating-legend.

section: Language of Obligation
statement: Use language of obligation to state any duty the contract imposes on a party; it comes in two structures: obligation imposed on the subject of the sentence and obligation imposed on someone other than the subject. It is also one way to express a condition.

section: Language of Obligation > Obligation Imposed on the Subject > Use Shall to Mean Only Has a Duty To
statement: Use shall only to impose a duty on the subject of the sentence, when the subject is a party; don't use shall to express any other meaning.

trigger.signal: shall + verb in any sentence

test: Substitute 'has a duty to' for 'shall'. If the result doesn't make sense, shall is misused (3.92).
fix: Use the verb the category calls for: must for a duty on someone other than the subject, may for discretion, the present tense or will for policy, the present tense in conditional and relative clauses, must with a to-clause for a condition.
severity_basis: ambiguity, or a category error or usage that can change meaning or invite dispute

examples.after: [2-1] ✓✓: Acme shall purchase the Shares from Hughes.

notes: Courts generally accept shall as expressing obligation: Vandertoll v. Kentucky, 110 S.W.3d 789, 791 (Ky. 2003) ('Shall means shall'). PacifiCorp v. Sempra Energy Trading Corp. (E.D. Cal. 2 July 2004) held shall can mean should, an outlier relying on statutory interpretation (3.90-3.91). Overuse of shall for future time is benign and can be let pass on the other side's draft (3.103); see R-3.98-shall-future-time. Table ratings per 3.9 legend: ✓✓ recommended; ✓ acceptable but improvable or context-dependent; × not recommended; ×× don't use (× vs ×× reading inferred from the tables; the PDF p. 130 legend prints a single × on both last lines). See R-3.9-rating-legend.

section: Language of Obligation > Obligation Imposed on the Subject > Use Shall to Mean Only Has a Duty To
statement: Apply the has a duty test to every shall: replace shall with has (or have) a duty to and check that the provision still makes sense and imposes a duty on a party that is the subject. Shall with an inanimate subject fails at once.
severity_basis: ambiguity, or a category error or usage that can change meaning or invite dispute

examples.before: The rent shall be paid by the Tenant on the first of every month. [fails: abstract-noun subject]
examples.after: The Tenant shall pay the rent on the first day of every month.

examples.before: Jones shall be entitled to have her expenses reimbursed promptly. [fails]
examples.after: Acme shall promptly reimburse Jones's expenses.

examples.before: The auditors shall submit the report no later than 90 days after the Claim Date. [fails: nonparty; use must (3.150)]
Acme shall be authorized to disclose ... [fails]
examples.after: Acme may disclose ...

examples.before: "Releasor" shall mean ... [fails]
examples.after: "Releasor" means ...

examples.before: This agreement shall be governed by New York law. [fails]
examples.after: This agreement is governed by New York law.

examples.before: This agreement shall terminate on 23 August 2024. [fails]
examples.after: This agreement terminates on 23 August 2024.

examples.before: When ABC repurchases Jones's Shares, Jones shall cease to be a Shareholder. [fails]
examples.after: When ABC repurchases Jones's Shares, Jones will cease to be a Shareholder.

examples.before: This agreement shall be amended by written agreement of the parties. [fails: express as a condition]
examples.after: To be effective, an amendment to this agreement must be in writing and signed by both parties.

examples.before: Patterson shall submit any Dispute Notice no later than five Business Days after she receives the related invoice. [fails: should be a condition]
examples.after: To dispute an invoice, Patterson must submit a Dispute Notice no later than five Business Days after she receives the related invoice.

examples.before: If Acme shall sell the Assets ... [fails]
examples.after: If Acme sells the Assets ...

examples.before: If a Bankruptcy Event shall occur ... [fails]
examples.after: If a Bankruptcy Event occurs ...

examples.before: ... to an account Widgetco shall designate in writing [fails]
examples.after: ... to an account that Widgetco designates in writing

notes: Passing cases in 3.121: no. 1 'ABC shall perform the Services for XYZ' (obligation) and no. 2 'The Employee shall not disclose Confidential Information' (prohibition). The 'after' texts for nos. 11-12 come from the condition boxes at 3.546 and 3.548. The test depends on context (3.121); 'duty' is used only because it's shorter than 'obligation' (3.92, 3.192).

section: Language of Obligation > Obligation Imposed on the Subject > Overuse of Shall
statement: Don't use shall to mark future time where standard English would use the simple present (This agreement shall terminate ...; shall be governed by ...). On the other side's draft, such benign overuse rarely confuses and can be let pass.
test: Has a duty test (3.92).
notes: Overuse violates one word, one meaning (1.57) and distances contract prose from standard English, making drafters oblivious to the obligation-versus-condition distinction (3.99).

section: Language of Obligation > Obligation Imposed on the Subject > Overuse of Shall
statement: Address overuse of shall through disciplined use (shall only for a duty on the subject), not by eliminating shall; replacing shall with must or will doesn't fix the only routine dispute (obligation versus condition) and spreads the multiple-meaning problem.
severity_basis: dispute risk or legally significant usage
notes: Authorities discussed: Garner's Dictionary of Legal Usage 953-54; Michèle M. Asprey, Plain Language for Lawyers 205-16 (4th ed. 2010); Garner's Modern English Usage 993 ('shall seems likely to persist'). The bigger problem is chaotic verb structures generally (3.115).

section: Language of Obligation > Obligation Imposed on the Subject > Overuse of Shall
statement: Don't use must for an obligation imposed on a party that is the subject; must is needed for obligations on others and for conditions, and muddying obligations and conditions is particularly unhelpful.
exceptions: Use must with a to-infinitive or for clause to express a condition (3.386, 3.391); use must for obligations on someone other than the subject (3.154).

examples.before: [2-1a] ×: Acme must purchase the Shares from Hughes.
examples.after: [2-1] ✓✓: Acme shall purchase the Shares from Hughes.

notes: Table ratings per 3.9 legend: ✓✓ recommended; ✓ acceptable but improvable or context-dependent; × not recommended; ×× don't use (× vs ×× reading inferred from the tables; the PDF p. 130 legend prints a single × on both last lines). See R-3.9-rating-legend.

section: Language of Obligation > Obligation Imposed on the Subject > Overuse of Shall
statement: Don't use will to impose an obligation on the subject; will primarily expresses future time and would then do triple duty (obligation on the subject, obligation on others, future time).
severity_basis: will is also used for policy and future time, so a will-obligation can be read as a prediction or policy

examples.before: [2-1b] ×: Acme will purchase the Shares from Hughes.

section: Language of Obligation > Obligation Imposed on the Subject > Mood, Tense, Is Responsible For
statement: Express obligations in the indicative mood, not the imperative (as the Construction Specifications Institute recommends for specifications); to avoid wordy passives, use The Contractor shall do the following: plus tabulated clauses.

examples.after: The Contractor shall do the following: [tabulated enumerated clauses]

section: Language of Obligation > Obligation Imposed on the Subject > Mood, Tense, Is Responsible For
statement: Don't use the simple present to express obligations (as The New Engineering Contract does); in standard English, the third-person present doesn't impose obligations.

trigger.signal: a party subject + simple present verb stating what it must do

severity_basis: a present-tense statement may be read as a description, not a duty

... and the other party provides it.

section: Language of Obligation > Obligation Imposed on the Subject > Mood, Tense, Is Responsible For
statement: Don't use is responsible for + present participle to express a duty owed to another party; it is long-winded and unclear whether it creates a duty or acknowledges one from another source.
severity_basis: dispute risk or legally significant usage

section: Language of Obligation > Obligation Imposed on the Subject > Mood, Tense, Is Responsible For

words: is responsible for paying any taxes

examples.after: Acme is responsible for paying any taxes ... .

section: Language of Obligation > Obligation Imposed on Someone Other Than the Subject
statement: Recognize six contexts in which a sentence imposes an obligation on someone other than its subject: a passive verb (with or without a by-agent); a subject that isn't a legal person; a nonparty subject or by-agent; receive with a party subject; is entitled to with a noun or passive complement clause; and an obligation expressed as imposed by the other party or the contract.

severity_basis: imposes a duty the party may be unable to perform; invites a fight

section: Language of Obligation > Feasibility, Preventing Events, Only, Compliance
statement: Before imposing an obligation, decide whether it makes sense: does the party have enough control, and is compliance feasible? If not, use a reasonable efforts obligation, a condition, and a risk-allocation provision (for example, for landlord consent).

trigger.signal: an obligation to obtain a nonparty's act or to achieve something outside the party's control

severity_basis: an infeasible obligation could confuse or be held unenforceable
notes: Landlord-consent example (3.173): instead of obliging Widgetco to obtain consent, Acme should impose a reasonable efforts obligation (8.5), make consent a closing condition, and consider a termination fee or indemnity (13.425).

section: Language of Obligation > Feasibility, Preventing Events, Only, Compliance
statement: To stop an undesirable event not fully within a party's control, use two provisions: a reasonable efforts obligation to take steps to prevent it, and a risk-allocation provision making the party liable for resulting losses if it happens anyway. Avoid shall prohibit (unclear how much is required) and shall prevent (liable regardless?).
severity_basis: dispute risk or legally significant usage

section: Language of Obligation > Feasibility, Preventing Events, Only, Compliance
statement: Don't use shall not permit or shall not allow for events a party doesn't fully control; permit can mean merely allowing something to happen, so the extent of the duty is ambiguous.
fix: Use a reasonable efforts obligation plus risk allocation (3.176, 3.180).
severity_basis: ambiguity, or a category error or usage that can change meaning or invite dispute

section: Language of Obligation > Feasibility, Preventing Events, Only, Compliance
statement: Don't use only in an obligation that provides for the only possible means of performing; it's redundant. Keep it if other means are possible and you want to exclude them.
fix: Delete a redundant only.

examples.before: BioLab shall pay HealthLab only in United States dollars. [only one means]
BuildCo shall use untreated cedar timber in building the deck. [other materials possible]
examples.after: BuildCo shall use only untreated cedar timber in building the deck.

notes: In 3.182 the book shows only inserted.

section: Language of Obligation > Feasibility, Preventing Events, Only, Compliance
statement: Don't impose an obligation to comply with an obligation stated elsewhere in the contract; say that the other provision applies, unless it would apply anyway.
fix: Say that the other provision applies, or omit the sentence if it would apply anyway.

examples.before: Upon termination ..., ABC shall comply with its obligations ... stated in article 12.

section: Language of Obligation > Related Terminology
statement: Use obligation, not covenant, including when grouping obligations (signing-to-closing, while debt is outstanding).
notes: Covenant has a 'quaint Old Testament (or Raiders of the Lost Ark) quality'; Mellinkoff calls it 'an old synonym for contract and agreement' (3.187).

section: Language of Obligation > Related Terminology
statement: Covenant not to compete is a term of art; noncompetition provision would be less fusty.

section: Language of Obligation > Related Terminology
statement: Don't distinguish affirmative and negative covenants, and don't refer to obligations and prohibitions; obligation covers both doing and not doing.

section: Language of Obligation > Related Terminology
statement: Choose obligation or duty and use it consistently; the choice has no implications for the transaction (the manual prefers obligation for contract duties).

section: Language of Obligation > Related Terminology
statement: Don't modify obligations with irrevocable, absolute, or unconditional.
notes: You revoke something that benefits the other party, not something imposed on you; absolute has unclear purpose; unconditional is redundant if no conditions apply.

section: Language of Obligation > Related Terminology
statement: Use comply with and compliance with for obligations, not perform, performance, discharge, or fulfill; an obligation can be a duty not to act.

section: Language of Obligation > Related Terminology
statement: Prefer breach to violation, nonperformance, or noncompliance; use breach as a mass noun (no article) unless referring to multiple breaches.

examples.before: Any such disclosure will constitute a breach of the Recipient's obligations under this section 5.2.
examples.after: Any such disclosure will constitute breach of the Recipient's obligations under this section 5.2.

section: Language of Obligation > Related Terminology
statement: Where you can, use the verb breach instead of the noun; it's more concise and keeps the actor (the mass noun can drop it).

trigger.regex_hint: \b(result in a breach of|constitute (a )?breach of|in the event of (a )?breach)\b

examples.before: ... do not ... conflict with, result in a breach of, or constitute a default under ... .
examples.after: ... do not ... conflict with, breach, or constitute a default under ... .

examples.before: will constitute breach of
examples.after: will breach

examples.before: Any purported assignment or delegation in breach of this section 20.4 will be void.
examples.after: Any purported assignment or delegation that breaches this section 20.4 will be void.

examples.before: In the event of breach of this section 6.7 ...
examples.after: If Acme breaches this section 6.7 ...

section: Language of Discretion > Using May to Grant Discretion
statement: Use language of discretion to state that a party has discretion to take or not take a specified action.

section: Language of Discretion > Using May to Grant Discretion
statement: Grant discretion with may in the active voice; don't use wordier or less precise alternatives (is authorized to, is entitled to, shall have the right to, reserves the right to, is permitted to, is allowed to, is free to, is hereby empowered to, is at liberty to).

trigger.regex_hint: \b(is authorized to|shall have the right to|reserves the right to|is permitted to|is allowed to|is free to|is (hereby )?empowered|is at liberty to|has the right to)\b

examples.before: [4-1a] ×: Acme is authorized to ... .
examples.after: [4-1] ✓✓: Acme may appoint one or more subcontractors.

examples.before: [4-1b] ×: Acme is entitled to ... .
[4-1c] ××: Acme shall have the right to ... .
[4-1d] ××: Acme reserves the right to ... .
[4-1e] ××: Acme is permitted to ... .
[4-1f] ××: Acme is allowed to ... .
[4-1g] ××: Acme is free to ... .
[4-1h] ××: Acme is hereby empowered by the Customer to ... .
[4-1i] ××: Acme is at liberty to ... .

notes: Has the right to is an illustrative trigger (the table lists shall have the right to). Is entitled to has a legitimate discretion use when one party's discretion depends on another's performance (3.290). Table ratings per 3.9 legend: ✓✓ recommended; ✓ acceptable but improvable or context-dependent; × not recommended; ×× don't use (× vs ×× reading inferred from the tables; the PDF p. 130 legend prints a single × on both last lines). See R-3.9-rating-legend.

section: Language of Discretion > Using May to Grant Discretion
statement: Don't use may with a passive verb; make the party with discretion the subject.

examples.before: [4-2] ✓: The Option may be exercised by Smith before 1 January 2024.
examples.after: [4-2b] ✓✓: Smith may exercise the Option before 1 January 2024.

examples.before: [4-2a] ✓: The Option may be exercised before 1 January 2024.
examples.after: [4-2b] ✓✓: Smith may exercise the Option before 1 January 2024.

notes: The prose says 'don't use the passive voice' with may, but table 4 rates [4-2] and [4-2a] ✓, not ×. Table ratings per 3.9 legend: ✓✓ recommended; ✓ acceptable but improvable or context-dependent; × not recommended; ×× don't use (× vs ×× reading inferred from the tables; the PDF p. 130 legend prints a single × on both last lines). See R-3.9-rating-legend.

section: Language of Discretion > May; Dual Verb Structures > May But Is Not Required To
statement: Don't add but is not required to (or but is not obligated to, or shall have the right but not the obligation to) after may; discretion inherently carries no obligation.

words: but shall not be obligated to

examples.before: [4-1j] ××: Acme may but is not required to ... .
... the Company may (but is not required to) increase the Conversion Rate ... .
examples.after: ... the Company may increase the Conversion Rate ... .

notes: Table ratings per 3.9 legend: ✓✓ recommended; ✓ acceptable but improvable or context-dependent; × not recommended; ×× don't use (× vs ×× reading inferred from the tables; the PDF p. 130 legend prints a single × on both last lines). See R-3.9-rating-legend.

section: Language of Discretion > Using May to Grant Discretion
statement: Don't use freely with may; it's redundant.

examples.before: [4-1k] ××: Acme may freely ... .

notes: Table ratings per 3.9 legend: ✓✓ recommended; ✓ acceptable but improvable or context-dependent; × not recommended; ×× don't use (× vs ×× reading inferred from the tables; the PDF p. 130 legend prints a single × on both last lines). See R-3.9-rating-legend.

section: Language of Discretion > Using May to Grant Discretion
statement: Don't use can to grant discretion; can expresses ability, not discretion.
severity_basis: dispute risk or legally significant usage

examples.before: [4-1l] ××: Acme can ... .

notes: Table ratings per 3.9 legend: ✓✓ recommended; ✓ acceptable but improvable or context-dependent; × not recommended; ×× don't use (× vs ×× reading inferred from the tables; the PDF p. 130 legend prints a single × on both last lines). See R-3.9-rating-legend.

section: Language of Discretion > Using May to Grant Discretion
statement: Don't frame discretion as granted by the contract (This agreement allows Acme to ...).

examples.before: [4-1m] ××: This agreement allows Acme to ... .

notes: Table ratings per 3.9 legend: ✓✓ recommended; ✓ acceptable but improvable or context-dependent; × not recommended; ×× don't use (× vs ×× reading inferred from the tables; the PDF p. 130 legend prints a single × on both last lines). See R-3.9-rating-legend.

section: Language of Discretion > Using May to Grant Discretion
statement: Don't express discretion with a buried-actor policy such as The Option is exercisable; make the party the subject of may.

examples.before: [4-2c] ××: The Option is exercisable before 1 January 2024.
examples.after: [4-2b] ✓✓: Smith may exercise the Option before 1 January 2024.

notes: Table ratings per 3.9 legend: ✓✓ recommended; ✓ acceptable but improvable or context-dependent; × not recommended; ×× don't use (× vs ×× reading inferred from the tables; the PDF p. 130 legend prints a single × on both last lines). See R-3.9-rating-legend.

section: Language of Discretion > When Language of Discretion Is Inappropriate
statement: Don't use language of discretion to say what someone is free to do anyway; at best it's redundant, and at worst the other party might argue the discretion exists only because of the contract. To remind the parties, use language of declaration with acknowledges.

trigger.signal: may + an action the party could take without the contract (inspect, rely, consult)

fix: Delete it, or introduce the reminder with language of declaration using acknowledges (3.209).
severity_basis: dispute risk or legally significant usage

examples.before: The Buyer may inspect the Goods after they are received ... .

notes: See also R-rider-2025-whether-world-at-large (Acme states that it may ...).

section: Language of Discretion > When Language of Discretion Is Inappropriate
statement: Don't constrain, in language of discretion, what a party is free to do anyway (inspect within a reasonable time); if timing matters only as a condition, put it in a conditional clause.
severity_basis: suggests late action is a breach when it can only be a failed condition

examples.before: The Buyer may within a reasonable time inspect the Goods ... .
examples.after: If on inspecting the Goods within a reasonable time after delivery the Buyer determines that any fail to meet the Specifications, the Buyer may return the Goods ... .

section: Language of Discretion > Limited Discretion; May ... Only; Exclusive Option
statement: Be explicit about whether discretion is limited. A specific grant of discretion (Acme may sell the Shares to Ferguson) suggests, through the expectation of relevance, that other options are excluded, and courts may invoke expressio unius.

trigger.signal: may + a specific option where the party might have others

severity_basis: ambiguity, or a category error or usage that can change meaning or invite dispute

examples.before: Acme may sell the Shares to Ferguson.
examples.after: Unlimited: Acme may sell the Shares to any Person.  Limited: The only Person to whom Acme may sell the Shares is Ferguson. [or] Acme shall not sell the Shares to anyone other than Ferguson.

notes: Arkel International, L.L.C. v. Parsons Global Services, 2008 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 1624 (M.D. La. 8 Jan. 2008): 'either party may institute suit in the Superior Court ... or, if mutually agreed ..., the dispute shall be settled by arbitration' held permissive though probably meant to be mandatory. Ener-G Holdings plc v. Hormell [2012] EWCA Civ. 1059: were two specified notice methods exclusive?

section: Language of Discretion > Limited Discretion; May ... Only; Exclusive Option
statement: Don't use may ... only to express limited discretion; it's ambiguous between 'may elect to do only X' and 'the only thing it may do is X,' and repositioning only won't cure it.
severity_basis: ambiguity, or a category error or usage that can change meaning or invite dispute

examples.before: Acme may close one or more Contract Stores for any reason, and in doing so it may consider only its own interests.
examples.after: ... and in doing so it may elect to consider only its own interests.

examples.before: Widgetco may sell only the 1965 Ford Mustang.
examples.after: Widgetco shall sell no vehicle other than the 1965 Ford Mustang.

section: Language of Discretion > Limited Discretion; May ... Only; Exclusive Option
statement: If a party's only choices are to take a specified action or do nothing, use language of discretion and say that the choice offered is the only choice.
severity_basis: without a statement of exclusivity, a party may argue it can pursue other routes

examples.before: Any controversy or claim ... shall be settled by arbitration administered by the American Arbitration Association.
examples.after: As the exclusive means of initiating adversarial proceedings to resolve any dispute ..., a party may demand that the dispute be resolved by arbitration administered by the American Arbitration Association ... .

notes: Williams-Sonoma Stores, Inc. v. DDK/WE Hospitality Partners, LLC (Del. Ch. 27 June 2019) (transcript): may without an exclusivity statement prompted an argument that a party could go to court instead.

section: Language of Discretion > Using Might, Not May, to Express Possibility
statement: Use may only to grant discretion; use might to express possibility. Using may for possibility creates ambiguity between authorization and possibility.
test: Can you replace may with 'has discretion to'? If not, and you mean possibility, use might.
fix: If you mean possibility, use might (and introduce it with language of declaration, 3.234); or recast as a condition: If the Investigator provides ... then ... (3.233).
severity_basis: ambiguity, or a category error or usage that can change meaning or invite dispute

examples.before: The Investigator may provide the Sponsor with confidential information.

notes: Cambridge Grammar 200: might suggests slightly lower possibility than may, but relative degrees are irrelevant in contracts (3.235).

section: Language of Discretion > Using Might, Not May, to Express Possibility
statement: Because might states a fact, introduce it with language of declaration, such as The parties acknowledge that.

section: Language of Discretion > Using Might, Not May, to Express Possibility
statement: Don't rely on a distinction between might and expects to; use might, or state explicitly the basis for any expectation.
severity_basis: dispute risk or legally significant usage

section: Language of Discretion > Using Might, Not May, to Express Possibility
statement: Don't abandon may for is permitted to out of fear that may will be read as might; the risk is not meaningful, and may remains the best way to express discretion.
notes: As printed, 3.237 cites [4-1d] for is permitted to, but table 4 shows it at [4-1e].

section: Language of Discretion > May Require; May Request
statement: Where may require frames one party's discretion over what is really the other party's obligation, use language of obligation and state the trigger: At X's request, Y shall ... .
severity_basis: dispute risk or legally significant usage

examples.before: The Company may require a Participant to retain the shares ...
examples.after: At the Company's written request, a Participant shall retain the shares ...

examples.before: The Bank may require each Borrower to establish a lockbox ...
examples.after: At the Bank's written request, each Borrower shall establish a lockbox ...

section: Language of Discretion > May Require; May Request
statement: Where may require indicates possibility, use might.
severity_basis: ambiguity, or a category error or usage that can change meaning or invite dispute

examples.before: The issuer of these securities may require an opinion of counsel ...
examples.after: The issuer of these securities might require an opinion of counsel ...

section: Language of Discretion > May Require; May Request
statement: In a restrictive relative clause, may is superfluous; use the simple present (as the Bank requires).
severity_basis: dispute risk or legally significant usage

examples.before: such other documentation as the Bank may require
examples.after: such other documentation as the Bank requires

section: Language of Discretion > May Require; May Request
statement: Where may request actually imposes an obligation on another party, say At the request of X, Y shall ... ; if a separate document (such as an Issuer Order) reflects the request, omit the may request language.
fix: At the request of X, Y shall ... .
exceptions: May request as a main verb might simply mean a party may ask, for example for assistance (3.245).
severity_basis: dispute risk or legally significant usage

examples.before: the Issuer may request and the Trustee, upon receiving an Issuer Order, shall authenticate ...
examples.after: the Trustee, upon receiving an Issuer Order, shall authenticate ...

examples.before: the Trustee may request that the Company deliver an officers' certificate ...

section: Language of Discretion > Don't Use At Its Sole Discretion with May
statement: Don't use at its sole discretion with may. If it's rhetorical emphasis, delete it; if it tries to address a real issue (such as the implied duty of good faith), address that issue directly.
severity_basis: may be read as an attempt to waive the implied duty of good faith, with unpredictable enforceability

examples.before: [4-1n] ××: Acme may at its sole discretion ... .
examples.after: [4-1] ✓✓: Acme may ... . [address any real concern directly]

notes: A party generally must exercise contractual discretion in good faith in the U.S. (Restatement (Second) of Contracts § 205; UCC § 1-304) and many other countries, but not England (3.250-3.252). Table ratings per 3.9 legend: ✓✓ recommended; ✓ acceptable but improvable or context-dependent; × not recommended; ×× don't use (× vs ×× reading inferred from the tables; the PDF p. 130 legend prints a single × on both last lines). See R-3.9-rating-legend.

section: Language of Discretion > Don't Use At Its Sole Discretion with May
statement: Don't use absolute instead of or with sole (sole and absolute), or uncontrolled; it's legalistic redundancy.
severity_basis: dispute risk or legally significant usage

section: Language of Discretion > Don't Use At Its Sole Discretion with May
statement: Don't refer to good-faith discretion; it's redundant.

section: Language of Discretion > Don't Use At Its Sole Discretion with May
statement: Be aware that reasonable discretion might curtail discretion: a reasonableness standard could be read as stricter than good faith.
severity_basis: dispute risk or legally significant usage

section: Language of Discretion > Don't Use At Its Sole Discretion with May
statement: Eliminate any language that could be construed as waiving the implied duty of good faith (sole discretion defined as without regard to reasonableness, for any reason or no reason), even if it favors your client.

words: for any reason or no reason
without regard to any standard of reasonableness
not subject to a reasonableness standard
trigger.regex_hint: \bfor any reason or no reason\b|\bwithout regard to any standard of reasonableness\b|\bnot subject to (a|any) reasonableness standard\b

severity_basis: enforceability varies by jurisdiction; caselaw is confused
notes: Cases: Cussler v. Crusader Entertainment, 2010 WL 718007 (Cal. Ct. App. 2010) (sole and absolute discretion enforced); Automatic Sprinkler Corp. v. Anderson, 257 S.E.2d 283 (Ga. 1979); contra A.W. Fiur Co. v. Ataka & Co., 422 N.Y.S.2d 419 (App. Div. 1979). UCC § 1-302: good faith 'may not be disclaimed by agreement'.

section: Language of Discretion > Don't Use At Its Sole Discretion with May
statement: Instead of sole discretion, address the concern directly: make the discretion subject to stated conditions, or have the other party acknowledge that specified adverse consequences are irrelevant to the exercise of discretion.
severity_basis: dispute risk or legally significant usage

examples.before: Acme may at any time close any one or more Contract Stores. [adding at its sole discretion is reckless to rely on]
examples.after: Acme may close one or more Contract Stores for any reason, and in doing so it may elect to consider only its own interests and will not be required to consider the effect ... on Widgetco ... .

notes: VTR, Inc. v. Goodyear Tire & Rubber Co., 303 F. Supp. 773 (S.D.N.Y. 1969); UCC § 1-302 lets parties set standards 'not manifestly unreasonable'.

section: Language of Discretion > Don't Use At Its Sole Discretion with May
statement: If you can't or won't craft explicit language, either use at its discretion and warn the client it might not ensure unfettered discretion, or (more prudent) omit it.

section: Language of Discretion > Don't Use At Its Sole Discretion with May
statement: Where neither conditions nor acknowledgments can work (subjective judgments that cost the discretion holder nothing, as in Cussler), eliminate the problematic discretion, for example by making an approved item final or giving one party unilateral control.
severity_basis: dispute risk or legally significant usage

section: Language of Discretion > Don't Use At Its Sole Discretion with May
statement: Treat at its sole discretion in conditional clauses and restrictive relative clauses the same way: address a real deal issue directly, or delete a legalistic habit.
severity_basis: dispute risk or legally significant usage

examples.before: If Acme at its sole discretion buys more widgets ...
at a price acceptable to Widgetco in its sole discretion

section: Language of Discretion > Hereby Grants the Right To; Cooperation; Waivers; Is Entitled To
statement: Instead of Party X hereby grants Party Y the right to [verb] (discretion disguised as performance), say Party Y may [verb].
exceptions: Granting a license (noun) remains appropriate for software and IP (3.76-3.77).

examples.before: [4-1o] ××: The Customer hereby grants Acme the right to ... .
The Borrower hereby grants to the Holder the right to set off against this note upon occurrence of an Event of Default.
examples.after: The Holder may set off against this note upon occurrence of an Event of Default.

notes: Table ratings per 3.9 legend: ✓✓ recommended; ✓ acceptable but improvable or context-dependent; × not recommended; ×× don't use (× vs ×× reading inferred from the tables; the PDF p. 130 legend prints a single × on both last lines). See R-3.9-rating-legend.

section: Language of Discretion > Hereby Grants the Right To; Cooperation; Waivers; Is Entitled To
statement: Instead of Party X hereby consents to Party Y [verb]ing, say Party Y may [verb].

examples.before: [4-1p] ××: The Customer hereby consents to Acme appointing ... .
examples.after: [4-1] ✓✓: Acme may appoint ... .

notes: Table ratings per 3.9 legend: ✓✓ recommended; ✓ acceptable but improvable or context-dependent; × not recommended; ×× don't use (× vs ×× reading inferred from the tables; the PDF p. 130 legend prints a single × on both last lines). See R-3.9-rating-legend.

section: Language of Discretion > Hereby Grants the Right To; Cooperation; Waivers; Is Entitled To
statement: Where exercising discretion requires another party's cooperation, make the implicit obligation explicit with language of obligation; will be given the opportunity to only hints at it.

words: will be given the opportunity to

severity_basis: the cooperating party's duty is otherwise unstated

examples.before: One or more Acme representatives may inspect Widgetco's financial records ... .
examples.after: Widgetco shall permit one or more Acme representatives to inspect Widgetco's financial records during business hours at Widgetco's principal office.

section: Language of Discretion > Hereby Grants the Right To; Cooperation; Waivers; Is Entitled To
statement: When hereby waives the right to really means the other party doesn't have to do something, say that (is not required to).

examples.before: Acme hereby waives any right to inspect or approve of any finished photographs.
examples.after: Photoco is not required to permit Acme to inspect or approve of any finished photographs.

examples.before: The Employee hereby waives his right to receive any severance other than under this agreement.
examples.after: The Company will not be required to pay the Employee any severance other than under this agreement.

examples.before: The Borrower hereby waives its right to elect to make payments under this agreement in a currency other than U.S. dollars.
examples.after: The Lender is not required to accept payments under this agreement in a currency other than U.S. dollars.

notes: Before and after texts are read from the book's strikethrough revisions (OCR of PDF p. 197); the first example's strikethrough is missing in the book (probably a typesetting slip).

section: Language of Discretion > Hereby Grants the Right To; Cooperation; Waivers; Is Entitled To
statement: Is entitled to with an active complement clause expresses discretion that depends on another party's performance, which may doesn't capture; but it's much clearer to ignore that distinction and state the other party's obligation.
exceptions: In statutory drafting, expressing 'a person is entitled to vote' as an obligation would be awkward; the fix works in contracts because they have few actors (3.291).
severity_basis: dispute risk or legally significant usage

examples.before: [5-1] ✓: No later than five days after Rubin exercises the Option, Rubin will be entitled to purchase a number of Shares equal to ... .
examples.after: [5-1c] ✓✓: No later than five days after Rubin exercises the Option, Acme shall sell to Rubin, at Rubin's election, a number of shares equal to ... .

examples.before: [5-1a] ××: Exercise of the Option will entitle Rubin to purchase within five days a number of Shares equal to ... .
examples.after: [5-1c] ✓✓ [as above]

examples.before: [5-1b] ×: No later than five days after Rubin exercises the Option, Rubin may purchase a number of Shares equal to ... .
examples.after: [5-1c] ✓✓ [as above]

examples.before: [5-2] ✓: Wagner is entitled to serve on Investco's board of directors.
examples.after: [5-2b] ✓✓: Investco shall at Wagner's option appoint Wagner a member of its board of directors.

examples.before: [5-2a] ×: Wagner may serve on Investco's board of directors.
examples.after: [5-2b] ✓✓ [as above]

notes: Table ratings per 3.9 legend: ✓✓ recommended; ✓ acceptable but improvable or context-dependent; × not recommended; ×× don't use (× vs ×× reading inferred from the tables; the PDF p. 130 legend prints a single × on both last lines). See R-3.9-rating-legend.

section: Language of Discretion > Is Not Required To
statement: Express absence of obligation with is not required to + verb; don't use nothing in this agreement requires, this agreement does not require, in no event is ... required to, is not obligated to, is not obliged to, or is not bound to.

trigger.regex_hint: \b(nothing in this agreement requires|this agreement does not require|in no event (is|will|shall)|is not (obligated|obliged|bound) to)\b

examples.before: [6-1a] ××: Nothing in this agreement requires Acme to replace the Widget Equipment.
examples.after: [6-1] ✓✓: Acme is not required to replace the Widget Equipment.

examples.before: [6-1b] ✓: Acme is not [obligated] [obliged] to replace the Widget Equipment.
examples.after: [6-1] ✓✓: Acme is not required to replace the Widget Equipment.

examples.before: [6-1c] ××: Acme is not bound to replace the Widget Equipment.
examples.after: [6-1] ✓✓: Acme is not required to replace the Widget Equipment.

notes: Absence of obligation isn't strictly discretion but is grouped with it (3.292). The book prints [6-1b] above [6-1a]. Table ratings per 3.9 legend: ✓✓ recommended; ✓ acceptable but improvable or context-dependent; × not recommended; ×× don't use (× vs ×× reading inferred from the tables; the PDF p. 130 legend prints a single × on both last lines). See R-3.9-rating-legend.

section: Language of Discretion > Is Not Required To
statement: Don't use may not to mean 'is authorized not to'; may not has three possible meanings.
severity_basis: ambiguity, or a category error or usage that can change meaning or invite dispute

section: Language of Discretion > Is Not Required To
statement: Use the active voice after is not required to.

examples.before: [6-3] ×: Amounts collected from Participants are not required to be held in a segregated account.
examples.after: [6-3a] ✓✓: Widgetco is not required to hold in a segregated account any amounts collected from Participants.

notes: Table ratings per 3.9 legend: ✓✓ recommended; ✓ acceptable but improvable or context-dependent; × not recommended; ×× don't use (× vs ×× reading inferred from the tables; the PDF p. 130 legend prints a single × on both last lines). See R-3.9-rating-legend.

section: Language of Discretion > Is Not Required To
statement: Don't use shall not be required to; don't use will not be required to unless you are addressing the consequences of a contingent future event.
exceptions: Will not be required to is acceptable for consequences of a contingent future event (3.296; 3.334).

examples.before: [6-1d] ××: Acme shall not be required to replace the Widget Equipment.
examples.after: [6-1] ✓✓: Acme is not required to replace the Widget Equipment.

examples.before: [6-1e] ×: Acme will not be required to replace the Widget Equipment.
examples.after: [6-1] ✓✓: Acme is not required to replace the Widget Equipment.

examples.before: [6-3b] ××: Amounts collected from Participants shall not be required to be held in a segregated account.
examples.after: [6-3a] ✓✓: Widgetco is not required to hold in a segregated account any amounts collected from Participants.

notes: Table ratings per 3.9 legend: ✓✓ recommended; ✓ acceptable but improvable or context-dependent; × not recommended; ×× don't use (× vs ×× reading inferred from the tables; the PDF p. 130 legend prints a single × on both last lines). See R-3.9-rating-legend.

section: Language of Discretion > Is Not Required To
statement: Don't confuse not imposing an obligation on Party A with imposing that obligation on Party B.
severity_basis: category confusion changes who bears the duty

examples.before: [6-1f] ××: Widgetco shall replace the Widget Equipment. [where the intent is only that Acme need not]
examples.after: [6-1] ✓✓: Acme is not required to replace the Widget Equipment.

notes: Table ratings per 3.9 legend: ✓✓ recommended; ✓ acceptable but improvable or context-dependent; × not recommended; ×× don't use (× vs ×× reading inferred from the tables; the PDF p. 130 legend prints a single × on both last lines). See R-3.9-rating-legend.

section: Language of Discretion > Is Not Required To
statement: Don't impose limits on Party A when Party B's concern is only that it not be responsible beyond a limit; state what must be done, with a cap.
severity_basis: restricts conduct the other party doesn't care about

examples.before: [6-2a] ××: The Consultant's annual expenses must not exceed $10,000.
examples.after: [6-2b] ✓✓: Acme shall reimburse the Consultant's expenses up to $10,000 per year.

examples.before: [6-2] ✓: Acme is not required to reimburse the Consultant for annual expenses in excess of $10,000.
examples.after: [6-2b] ✓✓: Acme shall reimburse the Consultant's expenses up to $10,000 per year.

notes: Table ratings per 3.9 legend: ✓✓ recommended; ✓ acceptable but improvable or context-dependent; × not recommended; ×× don't use (× vs ×× reading inferred from the tables; the PDF p. 130 legend prints a single × on both last lines). See R-3.9-rating-legend.

section: Language of Discretion > Is Not Required To
statement: Instead of is not entitled to + a passive complement clause or + a noun, focus on the party not subject to the obligation.

examples.before: [6-1g] ✓: Widgetco is not entitled to have the Widget Equipment replaced.
examples.after: [6-1] ✓✓: Acme is not required to replace the Widget Equipment.

examples.before: Acme is not entitled to advance notice.
examples.after: Levine is not required to give Acme advance notice.

notes: Table ratings per 3.9 legend: ✓✓ recommended; ✓ acceptable but improvable or context-dependent; × not recommended; ×× don't use (× vs ×× reading inferred from the tables; the PDF p. 130 legend prints a single × on both last lines). See R-3.9-rating-legend.

section: Language of Discretion > Is Not Required To
statement: Don't use need not; need is used colloquially for both lack and obligation, and need not can also mean 'should not' or 'has no reason to.'
severity_basis: dispute risk or legally significant usage

examples.before: [6-1h] ××: Acme need not replace the Widget Equipment.
examples.after: [6-1] ✓✓: Acme is not required to replace the Widget Equipment.

notes: Table ratings per 3.9 legend: ✓✓ recommended; ✓ acceptable but improvable or context-dependent; × not recommended; ×× don't use (× vs ×× reading inferred from the tables; the PDF p. 130 legend prints a single × on both last lines). See R-3.9-rating-legend.

section: Language of Discretion > Is Not Required To
statement: Don't use may refuse to, may decline to, or may abstain from to express absence of obligation, and don't say one party does not expect the other to act.
severity_basis: refusal discretion suggests the obligation persists unless refused

examples.before: [6-1i] ××: Acme may refuse to replace the Widget Equipment.

section: Language of Discretion > Is Not Required To
statement: If it wouldn't make sense to impose an obligation on a party, don't negate it with is not required to or a variant; address the real issue, for example with language of policy stating the party will not be liable.
fix: Say instead, in language of policy, that the owner and architect will not be liable if the contractor doesn't pay subcontractors (3.303).
severity_basis: dispute risk or legally significant usage

examples.before: Neither the Owner nor Architect shall have an obligation to pay or see to the payment of money to a Subcontractor or supplier except as may otherwise be required by law.

section: Language of Discretion > Is Not Prohibited From
statement: MSCD5: express absence of prohibition with is not prohibited from; except to avoid confusion, don't use this agreement does not prohibit or nothing in this agreement prohibits. You could use may instead, but if Acme could act anyway absent the contract, don't suggest its ability comes from the contract.

trigger.regex_hint: \bis not prohibited from\b|\bnothing in this agreement prohibits\b|\bthis agreement does not prohibit\b

examples.after: Acme is not prohibited from removing the Widget Equipment. [figure 1]

notes: SUPERSEDED by blog rider R-rider-2025-11-19-nothing-prohibits (19 Nov 2025): use language of declaration, 'The parties acknowledge that nothing in this agreement prohibits Acme from ...'. Apply the rider, not this paragraph.

section: Language of Discretion > Is Not Prohibited From (blog rider)
statement: To express absence of prohibition, use language of declaration rather than language of discretion: The parties acknowledge that nothing in this agreement prohibits Acme from [verb]ing. Don't use is not prohibited from.

trigger.regex_hint: \bis not prohibited from\b|\bnothing in this agreement prohibits\b|\bthis agreement does not prohibit\b

fix: The parties acknowledge that nothing in this agreement prohibits [Party] from [verb]ing ... .
severity_basis: discretion wording can suggest that the ability arises only under the contract

examples.before: Acme is not prohibited from selling the Widgets.
examples.after: The parties acknowledge that nothing in this agreement prohibits Acme from selling the Widgets.

notes: Source: Kenneth A. Adams, '“Is Not Prohibited From”: I’ve Changed My Mind!', Adams on Contract Drafting, 19 November 2025, https://www.adamsdrafting.com/acme-is-not-prohibited-from-selling-the-widgets-ive-changed-my-mind/. Quotations (WebFetch, verbatim): 'I’ve now changed my mind about how it should be treated.' 'The parties acknowledge that nothing in this agreement prohibits Acme from selling the Widgets.' The post says the issue 'should [be] addressed using not language of discretion, but language of declaration.' Supersedes MSCD5 3.304 and the figure 1 row for is not prohibited from. 'Before' is the MSCD5-style form.

section: Language of Prohibition
statement: Express prohibition with shall not (has a duty not to) imposed on a party that is the subject of the sentence.
test: Has a duty not to: if the subject isn't a party, shall not doesn't work (3.155).
severity_basis: ambiguity, or a category error or usage that can change meaning or invite dispute

examples.after: [7-1] ✓✓: The Customer shall not modify the Equipment without Acme's prior written consent.

section: Language of Prohibition
statement: Don't use must not instead of shall not for a prohibition on a party that is the subject.
severity_basis: dispute risk or legally significant usage

examples.before: [7-1a] ×: The Customer must not modify the Equipment ... .
examples.after: [7-1] ✓✓: The Customer shall not modify the Equipment ... .

notes: Table ratings per 3.9 legend: ✓✓ recommended; ✓ acceptable but improvable or context-dependent; × not recommended; ×× don't use (× vs ×× reading inferred from the tables; the PDF p. 130 legend prints a single × on both last lines). See R-3.9-rating-legend.

section: Language of Prohibition
statement: Don't use may not for prohibition; Acme may not transfer the Shares could mean Acme might not transfer, is authorized not to transfer, or isn't authorized to transfer.
exceptions: With a negative subject (no party, neither party), may is the better choice (3.324).
severity_basis: ambiguity, or a category error or usage that can change meaning or invite dispute

examples.before: [7-1b] ×: The Customer may not modify the Equipment ... .
examples.after: [7-1] ✓✓: The Customer shall not modify the Equipment ... .

section: Language of Prohibition
statement: Use is not entitled to + active complement clause only when the prohibition rests on another party's not being obligated (Mancini is not entitled to serve on Widgetco's board); otherwise don't use it for prohibition, and don't use has no right to.

trigger.regex_hint: \b(is not entitled to|has no right to|shall have no right to)\b

examples.before: [7-1c] ×: The Customer is not entitled to modify the Equipment ... .
examples.after: [7-1] ✓✓: The Customer shall not modify the Equipment ... .

examples.before: Acme shall not convert its Shares ... .
examples.after: Acme is not entitled to convert the Shares except as provided in section 3.2.

section: Language of Prohibition > Suboptimal Usages
statement: Don't use shall refrain from; refrain is polite deference suited to social contexts. Use shall not.

examples.before: [7-1d] ××: The Customer shall refrain from modifying the Equipment ... .
examples.after: [7-1] ✓✓: The Customer shall not modify the Equipment ... .

section: Language of Prohibition > Suboptimal Usages
statement: Don't use hereby waives the right to (or any right to) to express prohibition; use shall not.

examples.before: [7-1e] ××: The Customer hereby waives the right to modify the Equipment ... .
examples.after: [7-1] ✓✓: The Customer shall not modify the Equipment ... .

examples.before: Acme hereby waives the right to sell the Shares.
examples.after: Acme shall not sell the Shares.

section: Language of Prohibition > Suboptimal Usages
statement: For jury-trial waivers, you could use prohibition (Each party shall not demand a trial by jury), but because waiver language is universal, you might find it expedient to keep it.

words: waives any right to a trial by jury

notes: Fed. R. Civ. P. 38: a party secures a jury trial by demand.

section: Language of Prohibition > Suboptimal Usages
statement: Don't use shall never; if an obligation should continue perpetually, even after termination, say so explicitly.
severity_basis: never could be read to last only until termination

examples.before: [7-1f] ××: The Customer shall never modify the Equipment ... .
examples.after: [7-1] ✓✓: The Customer shall not modify the Equipment ... .

statement: Don't use shall in no way; it's rhetorical emphasis.

examples.before: [7-1g] ××: The Customer shall in no way modify the Equipment ... .
examples.after: [7-1] ✓✓: The Customer shall not modify the Equipment ... .

statement: Don't use cannot or agrees not to in language of prohibition.

examples.before: [7-1h] ××: The Customer cannot modify the Equipment ... .
examples.after: [7-1] ✓✓: The Customer shall not modify the Equipment ... .

examples.before: [7-1i] ××: The Customer agrees not to modify the Equipment ... .
examples.after: [7-1] ✓✓: The Customer shall not modify the Equipment ... .

section: Language of Prohibition > Suboptimal Usages
statement: Don't say the contract doesn't authorize a party to do something; express it as a prohibition.

examples.before: [7-1j] ××: Nothing in this agreement gives the Customer the right to modify the Equipment ... .
examples.after: [7-1] ✓✓: The Customer shall not modify the Equipment ... .

notes: Table ratings per 3.9 legend: ✓✓ recommended; ✓ acceptable but improvable or context-dependent; × not recommended; ×× don't use (× vs ×× reading inferred from the tables; the PDF p. 130 legend prints a single × on both last lines). See R-3.9-rating-legend.

section: Language of Prohibition > Collective Nouns; Nor Shall; Exceptions
statement: With a collective-noun subject, express prohibition with a negative subject (neither for two, no for more) plus may, or with a singular subject and a negative verb (each party shall not); avoid neither party shall and the parties shall not ... their.

examples.before: [7-2] ×: Neither party shall assign any of its rights ... .
examples.after: [7-2a] ✓: Neither party may assign any of its rights ... .

examples.before: [7-2b] ×: The parties shall not assign any of their rights ... .
examples.after: [7-2c] ✓: Each party shall not assign any of its rights ... .

notes: No option earns ✓✓. Neither party shall fails the has a duty test (it reads as absence of duty). The parties ... their raises collective-versus-individual questions (11.16). See R-3.9-rating-legend.

section: Language of Prohibition > Collective Nouns; Nor Shall; Exceptions
statement: Don't use nor shall to continue a prohibition; start a new sentence with language of prohibition.

examples.before: The Receiving Party shall not use Confidential Information other than as authorized ... under the SOW, nor shall the Receiving Party disclose any Confidential Information ... .
examples.after: The Receiving Party shall not use Confidential Information other than as authorized ... under the SOW. The Receiving Party shall not disclose any Confidential Information ... .

section: Language of Prohibition > Collective Nouns; Nor Shall; Exceptions
statement: To express a prohibition as an exception to language of discretion, state it explicitly rather than relying on the expectation of relevance.
severity_basis: dispute risk or legally significant usage

examples.before: Widgetco may sell one or more of the Vehicles except the 1965 Ford Mustang.
examples.after: Widgetco may sell one or more of the Vehicles but not the 1965 Ford Mustang. [or: ..., except that it shall not sell the 1965 Ford Mustang]

section: Language of Prohibition > Collective Nouns; Nor Shall; Exceptions
statement: To express a prohibition as an exception to language of obligation, be explicit; merely carving the item out of the obligation says nothing about whether the party may do it.
severity_basis: ambiguity, or a category error or usage that can change meaning or invite dispute

examples.before: Widgetco shall sell all Vehicles except the 1965 Ford Mustang.
examples.after: Widgetco shall sell one or more of the Vehicles, except that it shall not sell the 1965 Ford Mustang.

section: Language of Policy > Verbs in Language of Policy
statement: Use language of policy for rules the parties must observe that don't, at least expressly, require or permit action or inaction: rules governing a thing, event, or circumstance, and rules on the scope, meaning, or duration of the contract.

section: Language of Policy > Verbs in Language of Policy
statement: Use the present tense for policies that apply on effectiveness of the contract (governing law, entire agreement, definitions) and for policies that state a fixed time of effectiveness or lapse.

trigger.signal: governing law, entire-agreement, definition, or fixed-date termination in will or shall

examples.before: [8-2a] ×: The laws of the state of New York will govern ... .
examples.after: [8-2] ✓✓: The laws of the state of New York govern all matters arising out of this agreement.

examples.before: [8-5a] ×: This agreement will terminate on 31 December 2019.
examples.after: [8-5] ✓✓: This agreement terminates on 31 December 2019.

notes: Table ratings per 3.9 legend: ✓✓ recommended; ✓ acceptable but improvable or context-dependent; × not recommended; ×× don't use (× vs ×× reading inferred from the tables; the PDF p. 130 legend prints a single × on both last lines). See R-3.9-rating-legend.

section: Language of Policy > Verbs in Language of Policy
statement: Use will for policies about contingent future events, meaning events that might not happen or whose timing is uncertain (will terminate upon the closing of a Qualified IPO; will be void).

trigger.signal: a policy tied to an uncertain future event stated in the present tense or with shall

severity_basis: tense signals whether the event is contingent; the wrong tense can mislead on timing

examples.before: [8-6a] ×: This agreement terminates upon the closing of a Qualified IPO.
examples.after: [8-6] ✓✓: This agreement will terminate upon the closing of a Qualified IPO.

examples.before: [8-1] ×: Any attempted transfer of Shares in violation of this agreement is void.
examples.after: [8-1a] ✓✓: Any attempted transfer of Shares in violation of this agreement will be void.

notes: Table ratings per 3.9 legend: ✓✓ recommended; ✓ acceptable but improvable or context-dependent; × not recommended; ×× don't use (× vs ×× reading inferred from the tables; the PDF p. 130 legend prints a single × on both last lines). See R-3.9-rating-legend.

section: Language of Policy > Verbs in Language of Policy
statement: Don't use shall in language of policy; policy imposes no obligation.

examples.before: [8-1b] ××: Any attempted transfer of Shares in violation of this agreement shall be void.
examples.after: [8-1a] ✓✓: ... will be void.

examples.before: [8-2b] ××: The laws of the state of New York shall govern ... .
examples.after: [8-2] ✓✓: The laws of the state of New York govern ... .

examples.before: [8-3a] ××: This agreement shall constitute ... .
examples.after: [8-3] ✓✓: This agreement constitutes the entire agreement of the parties regarding the subject matter of this agreement.

examples.before: [8-4a] ××: "GAAP" shall mean ... .
examples.after: [8-4] ✓✓: "GAAP" means generally accepted accounting principles, consistently applied.

examples.before: [8-5b] ××: This agreement shall terminate [on 31 December 2019] ... .
examples.after: [8-5] ✓✓: This agreement terminates on 31 December 2019.

examples.before: [8-6b] ××: This agreement shall terminate [upon the closing of a Qualified IPO] ... .
examples.after: [8-6] ✓✓: This agreement will terminate upon the closing of a Qualified IPO.

section: Language of Policy > Buried-Actor Policies; Passive Voice; Obfuscation
statement: Rephrase buried-actor policies (exercisable, payable, recoverable) as language of obligation, language of discretion, or a conditional clause; they often omit the responsible party, and The fee is payable by 20 April could mean an obligation, discretion, or a condition.
severity_basis: ambiguity, or a category error or usage that can change meaning or invite dispute

examples.before: [8-7] ✓: Interest is payable at a rate of 8% per year.
examples.after: [8-7b] ✓✓: The Borrower shall pay interest ... .

examples.before: [8-7a] ××: Interest shall be payable ... .
examples.after: [8-7b] ✓✓: The Borrower shall pay interest ... .

examples.before: [8-8] ✓: The Option is exercisable until midnight at the end of 31 December 2019.
examples.after: [8-8b] ✓✓: Smith may exercise the Option ... .

examples.before: [8-8a] ××: The Option shall be exercisable ... .
examples.after: [8-8b] ✓✓: Smith may exercise the Option ... .
