section: Language of Policy > Buried-Actor Policies; Passive Voice; Obfuscation
statement: Rephrase is due as language of obligation.
severity_basis: dispute risk or legally significant usage

examples.before: The First Installment is due by 1 March 2024.
examples.after: The Purchaser shall pay the First Installment by 1 March 2024.

section: Language of Policy > Buried-Actor Policies; Passive Voice; Obfuscation
statement: Instead of is subject to + abstract noun with an abstract-noun subject, use may + verb with a party as subject; instead of is eligible for, state the obligation.
severity_basis: dispute risk or legally significant usage

examples.before: The Employee's position and assignments are subject to change.
examples.after: The Company may change the Employee's position and assignments.

examples.before: The Employee will be eligible for a bonus if ...
examples.after: The Company shall pay the Employee a bonus if ...

section: Language of Policy > Buried-Actor Policies; Passive Voice; Obfuscation
statement: The passive voice in language of policy is unremarkable; where the missing by-agent is the world at large, prevent any implication that someone must act by adding automatically or by switching to an active verb with the same subject.
exceptions: Don't switch will be deemed to the active voice (3.340; 13.209-.210).

examples.before: the Option Price will be increased
examples.after: the Option Price will increase

section: Language of Policy > Buried-Actor Policies; Passive Voice; Obfuscation
statement: Don't turn provisions about party actions into opaque language of policy through jargon (lead-time, net 30); state the action and the actor, even at the cost of extra words.
severity_basis: dispute risk or legally significant usage

examples.before: Acme will have a lead-time of up to 45 days from accepting a Purchase Order for scheduling Services.
examples.after: No later than 45 days after it receives a Purchase Order, Acme shall notify the Customer of the schedule for performing the Services requested in that Purchase Order.

examples.before: Payment terms are net 30 from the date of the invoice.
examples.after: The Customer shall pay each invoice no later than 30 days from the date of the invoice.

section: Expressing Conditions (general)
statement: Treat a condition as a future and uncertain event or circumstance on which a legal relation depends; express it by a conditional clause, language of obligation (must + to-clause), or language of policy (It is a condition to ... that), choosing by context.

section: Expressing Conditions (general)
statement: Say condition, not condition precedent; never use condition subsequent (state that if X happens, Y will cease); and say a condition is satisfied or not satisfied, not breached or complied with.
severity_basis: condition subsequent is unclear to clients and many lawyers; breach language conflates conditions and obligations

section: Expressing Conditions > Conditional Clause
statement: A conditional clause (introduced by if, unless, where, when, as long as, so long as, or on condition that) modifies a matrix clause in language of obligation, discretion, prohibition, or policy; it isn't itself a category.

examples.after: If Acme has not exercised the Option by 31 December 2022, Smith may transfer the Shares to another Person.

section: Expressing Conditions > Conditional Clause
statement: Put a short conditional clause first and a long one after the matrix clause; put it first if it contains enumerated clauses; if both clauses have several elements, use two sentences.

trigger.signal: long conditional clause before the matrix clause, or text continuing after enumerated clauses

section: Expressing Conditions > Conditional Clause
statement: Use then at the start of the matrix clause only when a complex conditional clause comes first and then would prevent a reader miscue; omit it after a short conditional clause.

examples.after: If a Government Body grants to Acme a compulsory license ... on more favorable terms ..., then for as long as that compulsory license is in effect the terms of that compulsory license will control.

section: Expressing Conditions > Conditional Clause
statement: Use the present tense in conditional clauses and other subordinate clauses (notwithstanding, even if); don't use shall, should, or the subjunctive there.

examples.before: [9-1b] ××: If Investco shall receive a Violation Notice, ... .
examples.after: [9-1] ✓✓: If Investco receives a Violation Notice, it shall promptly notify Widgetco.

examples.before: [9-1c] ××: If Investco shall have received a Violation Notice, ... .
examples.after: [9-1] ✓✓: If Investco receives a Violation Notice, ... .

examples.before: [9-1d] ×: If Investco should receive a Violation Notice, ... .
examples.after: [9-1] ✓✓: If Investco receives a Violation Notice, ... .

examples.before: [9-2b] ××: If Acme shall receive a Notice of Consent, ... .
examples.after: [9-2] ✓✓: If Acme receives a Notice of Consent, it may transfer the Shares.

examples.before: [9-2c] ××: If Acme shall have received a Notice of Consent, ... .
examples.after: [9-2] ✓✓: If Acme receives a Notice of Consent, ... .

examples.before: [9-3a] ××: If the Borrower shall be in default, ... .
examples.after: [9-3] ✓: If the Borrower is in default, the Lender may accelerate the Loan.

examples.before: [9-3b] ××: If the Borrower be in default, ... .
examples.after: [9-3] ✓: If the Borrower is in default, ... .

examples.before: even if any such nondisclosure and nonuse may prevent the Employee from competing with RMA ...
examples.after: even if any such nondisclosure and nonuse prevents the Employee from competing with RMA ...

notes: Benign shall; the Introduction lets it pass on the other side's draft. 'Should' tentativeness is unhelpful; the subjunctive serves no purpose (3.360). See R-3.9-rating-legend.

section: Expressing Conditions > Conditional Clause
statement: The present perfect in a conditional clause is acceptable if satisfying the condition is part of the transaction rather than a response to a contingency, but use the present tense for consistency.

examples.before: [9-1a] ×: If Investco has received a Violation Notice, ... .
examples.after: [9-1] ✓✓: If Investco receives a Violation Notice, ... .

examples.before: [9-2a] ✓: If Acme has received a Notice of Consent, ... .
examples.after: [9-2] ✓✓: If Acme receives a Notice of Consent, it may transfer the Shares.

notes: Table ratings per 3.9 legend: ✓✓ recommended; ✓ acceptable but improvable or context-dependent; × not recommended; ×× don't use (× vs ×× reading inferred from the tables; the PDF p. 130 legend prints a single × on both last lines). See R-3.9-rating-legend.

section: Expressing Conditions > Conditional Clause
statement: With a stative verb in a conditional clause, address any fear that the condition must be met at signing by adding at any time, or better, switch to a dynamic verb.

trigger.signal: if + is/has (stative) describing a state that could arise later

severity_basis: a stative condition might be read as tested only at signing

examples.before: [9-3] ✓: If the Borrower is in default, the Lender may accelerate the Loan.
examples.after: [9-3d] ✓✓: If the Borrower defaults, ... .

examples.before: [9-3] ✓: If the Borrower is in default, ... .
examples.after: [9-3c] ✓: If the Borrower is at any time in default, ... .

notes: Table ratings per 3.9 legend: ✓✓ recommended; ✓ acceptable but improvable or context-dependent; × not recommended; ×× don't use (× vs ×× reading inferred from the tables; the PDF p. 130 legend prints a single × on both last lines). See R-3.9-rating-legend.

section: Expressing Conditions > Conditional Clause
statement: In a matrix clause following a conditional clause, use will where the verb would otherwise be in the present tense; don't use the present tense or shall. Shall, may, and must are unaffected by a conditional clause.

trigger.signal: matrix clause after if/unless with a present-tense or shall policy verb

examples.before: [10-1a] ××: If Jones ceases to be employed by the Company, the Option shall terminate.
examples.after: [10-1] ✓✓: If Jones ceases to be employed by the Company, the Option will terminate.

examples.before: [10-1b] ×: If ... , the Option terminates.
examples.after: [10-1] ✓✓: If ... , the Option will terminate.

examples.before: [10-2a] ××: If ..., that transfer shall be valid only ... .
examples.after: [10-2] ✓✓: If a Stockholder transfers all its Shares to a Person that is not a Stockholder, that transfer will be valid only if the Person acquiring those Shares agrees to be bound by this agreement.

examples.before: [10-2b] ×: If ..., that transfer is valid only ... .
examples.after: [10-2] ✓✓ [as above]

notes: Table ratings per 3.9 legend: ✓✓ recommended; ✓ acceptable but improvable or context-dependent; × not recommended; ×× don't use (× vs ×× reading inferred from the tables; the PDF p. 130 legend prints a single × on both last lines). See R-3.9-rating-legend.

section: Expressing Conditions > Positive or Negative Matrix Clause; Unless
statement: Choose between may ... only if and shall not ... unless based on what the client expects or prefers; to avoid relying on the expectation of relevance, say: Acme shall not sell the Shares, except that it may sell the Shares if Widgetco consents.

words: may sell the shares only if

severity_basis: dispute risk or legally significant usage

examples.before: Acme may sell the Shares only if Widgetco consents. / Acme shall not sell the Shares unless Widgetco consents.
examples.after: Acme shall not sell the Shares, except that it may sell the Shares if Widgetco consents.

section: Expressing Conditions > Positive or Negative Matrix Clause; Unless
statement: In language of policy, use the negative unless form for a condition that is necessary but not sufficient (amendments): will not be effective unless ..., not will be effective if ... .
severity_basis: dispute risk or legally significant usage

examples.before: An amendment to this agreement will be effective if it is in writing and signed by both parties.
examples.after: An amendment to this agreement will not be effective unless it is in writing and signed by both parties.

section: Expressing Conditions > Positive or Negative Matrix Clause; Unless
statement: When an obligation using a verb of activity (keep confidential, maintain) is coupled with an unless clause, replace the unless clause with except that + is not required to (or will no longer be required to) + an if clause.

trigger.signal: shall + activity verb (keep, maintain, continue) + unless

severity_basis: the unless form invites a dispute over when the obligation starts (Total Recall v. Luckey)

examples.before: A shall keep the information confidential unless by 1 July 2012 B has not paid A $10,000.
examples.after: A shall keep the information confidential, except that if by 1 July 2012 B has not paid A $10,000, A will no longer be required to keep the information confidential.

notes: Total Recall Technologies v. Luckey, 2016 WL 199796 (N.D. Cal. 16 Jan. 2016): the court said 'unless' tended to support reading the payment as a precondition; the author says that reading is unreasonable. With momentary-action verbs, if and unless versions mean the same (3.376-3.377).

section: Expressing Conditions > Using Language of Obligation
statement: To express a condition through language of obligation, use must plus a to-infinitive clause or a for clause that makes the condition explicit; must alone or shall alone will likely be read as an obligation, and need only is too colloquial.
severity_basis: an unmarked condition will likely be treated as an obligation, changing the remedy

examples.before: [11-1a] ××: Acme must submit to Widgetco ... [each invoice within 90 days].
examples.after: [11-1] ✓✓: To be reimbursed, Acme must submit to Widgetco no later than 90 days after Acme receives it each invoice for expenses that Acme incurs.

examples.before: [11-1b] ××: Acme shall submit to Widgetco ... .
examples.after: [11-1] ✓✓ [as above]

examples.after: [11-1] ✓✓ [as above]

Courts treat doubtful provisions as obligations: Murray on Contracts § 103; 13 Williston § 38:13; Mind & Motion Utah Investments v. Celtic Bank, 367 P.3d 994 (Utah 2016); Howard v. Federal Crop Insurance Corp., 540 F.2d 695 (4th Cir. 1976). An obligation with a time limit is a less clear alternative (3.392). section: Expressing Conditions > Using Language of Policy
statement: To express a single condition in language of policy most concisely, begin with It is a condition to ... that; subject to satisfaction of the condition later in the sentence is wordy.

words: is subject to satisfaction of the condition

examples.before: [12-1e] ××: Tanaka's employment as the Company's chief financial officer is subject to satisfaction of the condition that Tanaka has settled the Litigation.
examples.after: [12-1] ✓✓: It is a condition to Tanaka's employment as the Company's chief financial officer that Tanaka has settled the Litigation.

section: Expressing Conditions > Using Language of Policy
statement: Introduce a group of closing conditions with ... are subject to satisfaction of the following conditions: and state each as a tabulated that-clause; for one condition, say ... are subject to the condition that ... . Without that, a condition can read as a statement of fact or, with shall, an obligation.

words: subject to satisfaction of the following conditions

severity_basis: unmarked closing conditions can be read as statements of fact or obligations

examples.before: [12-2] ××: Acme's statements of fact are accurate at the Closing as though made at the Closing; ... .
examples.after: [12-2a] ✓✓: that Acme's statements of fact are accurate ... .

examples.before: [12-3] ××: the Buyer has received an opinion of Acme's counsel in the form of exhibit A ... .

section: Expressing Conditions > Using Language of Policy
statement: In conditions stated in language of policy, use the present tense or the present perfect; don't use shall (have), must (have), will (have), or the subjunctive.

examples.after: [12-1] ✓✓ [as above]

examples.before: [12-1d] ××: ... that Tanaka have settled the Litigation.
examples.after: [12-1] ✓✓ [as above]

section: Expressing Conditions > Comparing Methods; Conditions That Can Be Ignored; Other Conditions
statement: Pick the way of expressing a condition that context allows: for termination on cessation of employment, only a conditional clause is plausible; elsewhere (amendments, dispute notices) all three work and the difference is concision.

examples.before: *For the Option to terminate, Becker must cease to be employed by the Company. / *It is a condition to the Option terminating that Becker ceases to be employed by the Company.
examples.after: If Becker ceases to be employed by the Company, the Option will terminate.

notes: Asterisks mark versions the book calls not plausible (3.400).

section: Expressing Conditions > Comparing Methods; Conditions That Can Be Ignored; Other Conditions
statement: If a party could ignore a condition before taking the action it governs, use an obligation instead; use a condition only if satisfying it depends on something outside the control of the party that would act.
severity_basis: an ignorable condition leaves the other party without a clear remedy

examples.before: It is a condition to Acme's conducting a public sale of widgets that Acme notify Widgetco in advance ... .
examples.after: Before conducting a public sale of widgets, Acme shall notify Widgetco in advance of the date and location of that sale.

section: Expressing Conditions > Comparing Methods; Conditions That Can Be Ignored; Other Conditions
statement: Recognize that a stated condition might not be the only condition; a court might read others into the contract (an invoice 'valid only if' timely still wouldn't be valid at triple the agreed price).
severity_basis: dispute risk or legally significant usage

section: Language of Obligation > The Has a Duty Test > AAA Clause
statement: Don't use the standard AAA arbitration clause (... shall be settled by arbitration ...); it fails the has a duty test, and an obligation on the parties to arbitrate every dispute makes no sense. Use exclusive discretion: a party may demand arbitration as the exclusive means of initiating adversarial proceedings.
severity_basis: dispute risk or legally significant usage

examples.before: Any controversy or claim ... shall be settled by arbitration administered by the American Arbitration Association.
examples.after: As the exclusive means of initiating adversarial proceedings to resolve any dispute ..., a party may demand that the dispute be resolved by arbitration administered by the American Arbitration Association ... .

section: Language of Declaration
statement: Use language of declaration (a verb of speaking) to declare facts so the declaring party is seen to assert them: states for a fact the declaring party knows and the other party wants asserted as accurate; acknowledges for a fact the other party knows and wants the declaring party to accept.

examples.after: [13-1] ✓✓: Acme states that the Equipment is listed in schedule A.
[13-2] ✓✓: The Investor acknowledges that it has received a copy of each SEC Document.

notes: Table ratings per 3.9 legend: ✓✓ recommended; ✓ acceptable but improvable or context-dependent; × not recommended; ×× don't use (× vs ×× reading inferred from the tables; the PDF p. 130 legend prints a single × on both last lines). See R-3.9-rating-legend.

section: Language of Declaration
statement: Don't use hereby with language of declaration.

examples.before: [13-1a] ×: Acme hereby states ... .
examples.after: [13-1] ✓✓: Acme states that the Equipment is listed in schedule A.

examples.before: [13-2a] ×: The Investor hereby acknowledges ... .
examples.after: [13-2] ✓✓: The Investor acknowledges that it has received a copy of each SEC Document.

notes: Table ratings per 3.9 legend: ✓✓ recommended; ✓ acceptable but improvable or context-dependent; × not recommended; ×× don't use (× vs ×× reading inferred from the tables; the PDF p. 130 legend prints a single × on both last lines). See R-3.9-rating-legend.

section: Language of Declaration > Statements of Fact: Represents and Warrants
statement: Don't pile other verbs onto represents or warrants (represents and acknowledges; represents, warrants, covenants, and agrees); it makes no sense.
severity_basis: dispute risk or legally significant usage

section: Language of Declaration > Statements of Fact: Represents and Warrants
statement: Treat warrant and warranty for goods in a sale-of-goods contract as a separate function; using represents and warrants there probably won't cause a fight but conflates two confusing concepts.

section: Language of Declaration > Statements of Fact: Represents and Warrants
statement: Don't assume that using represents, warrants, or both determines whether an inaccurate statement supports a misrepresentation claim, a breach-of-warranty claim, or both (the 'remedies rationale'); in the U.S. it is of no practical relevance.
severity_basis: dispute risk or legally significant usage
notes: Remedies rationale: Tina L. Stark, Drafting Contracts 15, 137-38 (2d ed. 2014) (permissive); Garner's Dictionary of Legal Usage 775 (restrictive). Contrary caselaw: Aspect Systems v. Lam Research, 2008 WL 2705154 (D. Ariz.); Quality Wash Group V v. Hallak, 58 Cal. Rptr. 2d 592 (Ct. App. 1996); UCC § 2-313(2).

section: Language of Declaration > Statements of Fact: Represents and Warrants
statement: Don't match the verb to the timeframe (represents for past or present facts, warrants for future facts); it is inconsistent with warranty law and makes no semantic sense.
severity_basis: dispute risk or legally significant usage
notes: Timeframe rationale: ABA Model Stock Purchase Agreement with Commentary 77 (2d ed. 2011); Krys v. Henderson, 69 S.E.2d 635 (1952).

section: Language of Declaration > Statements of Fact: Represents and Warrants
statement: In contracts governed by English law, don't rely on warrants alone (the standard English practice) to exclude misrepresentation claims and rescission; courts give the restrictive remedies rationale 'significant but not overwhelming support.' Address remedies expressly instead.
severity_basis: English caselaw is split on whether warrants-only statements can support misrepresentation
notes: Sycamore Bidco Ltd v. Breslin [2012] EWHC 3443 (Ch) and Idemitsu Kosan v. Sumitomo [2016] EWHC 1909 (Comm) (warranties only); contra Invertec Ltd v. De Mol Holding BV [2009] EWHC 2471 (Ch); MAN Nutzfahrzeuge v. Freightliner [2005] EWHC 2347; Chandelor v. Lopus (1603).

section: Language of Declaration > Statements of Fact: Represents and Warrants
statement: Whether it's your draft or the other side's, rearrange provisions so that only statements of fact follow represents and warrants (or states); move obligations and future facts to where they belong.

trigger.signal: obligations (will, shall) or predictions inside a list of representations

severity_basis: obligations and predictions hidden among statements of fact get the wrong remedy

examples.before: [Consultant represents and warrants that:] it will use industry best practices to prevent the introduction of any viruses ... .
examples.after: [book's classification] Obligation; see 3.89.

examples.before: [Consultant represents and warrants that:] the Services will be performed in a professional manner ... .
examples.after: [book's classification] Passive-voice obligation; see 3.148.

examples.before: [Consultant represents and warrants that:] all Services and Deliverables will materially conform to the Specifications for a period of one year from Acceptance;
examples.after: [book's classification] Future fact; see 3.474.

notes: The book classifies each item (OCR, PDF p. 242) but doesn't redraft them. The book classifies the pending-litigation item as a future fact.

section: Language of Declaration > Statements of Fact: Using States
statement: Don't use represents, warrants, or represents and warrants to introduce statements of fact; use states. Use the noun statement of fact, not representation and warranty, and don't use asserts or confirms.

examples.before: [13-1b] ×: Acme represents ... .
examples.after: [13-1] ✓✓: Acme states that the Equipment is listed in schedule A.

examples.before: [13-1c] ××: Acme represents and warrants ... .
examples.after: [13-1] ✓✓: Acme states that the Equipment is listed in schedule A.

notes: On the other side's draft, changing represents and warrants to states can be more trouble than it's worth (3.461); hence let-pass. Table ratings per 3.9 legend: ✓✓ recommended; ✓ acceptable but improvable or context-dependent; × not recommended; ×× don't use (× vs ×× reading inferred from the tables; the PDF p. 130 legend prints a single × on both last lines). See R-3.9-rating-legend.

section: Language of Declaration > Statements of Fact: Using States
statement: To introduce a series of statements of fact, say [Party name] states that the following facts are accurate: so a full independent clause precedes the colon. No signal is needed that an inaccurate statement supports a remedy.

words: states that the following facts are accurate

section: Language of Declaration > Statements of Fact: Using States
statement: To allay fears about states, add: The verb used to introduce a statement of fact in this agreement does not affect the remedies available for inaccuracy of that statement of fact.

examples.after: The verb used to introduce a statement of fact in this agreement does not affect the remedies available for inaccuracy of that statement of fact.

section: Language of Declaration > Statements of Fact: Using States
statement: In slow-changing practice areas (one-off M&A deals) or when marking up the other side's draft in higher-volume deals, states may cause more consternation than it's worth; if stuck with represents and warrants in a U.S. contract, rely on a no-reliance provision and add the 3.459 sentence.
severity_basis: dispute risk or legally significant usage
notes: No-reliance provision: Glenn D. West, Global Private Equity Watch (2 Aug. 2016) (3.462).

section: Language of Declaration > Statements of Fact: Using States
statement: If remedies for inaccurate statements of fact are an issue, address them explicitly (for example, state that a party may claim misrepresentation, breach of warranty, or both, or that misrepresentation claims are precluded); relying on any combination of represents and warrants is irresponsible.
exceptions: Utility is uncertain: enforceability is mixed; a bare preclusion leaves room for extracontractual claims (use a no-reliance provision); rote limits may not suit the deal; the analysis is speculative; indemnification, liquidated damages, or liability limits may be simpler (3.467-3.471).
severity_basis: dispute risk or legally significant usage
notes: Kenneth A. Adams, Eliminating the Phrase Represents and Warrants from Contracts, 16 Tennessee Journal of Business Law 203 (2015).

section: Language of Declaration > Future Facts; Terminology
statement: Don't present predictions ('future facts') as statements of fact. If the stating party controls the matter, impose an obligation; you can also or instead state a remedy; if it lacks control, allocate the risk (indemnification, liquidated damages, breakup fee).

trigger.signal: statement of fact using will about the future

severity_basis: a prediction can't be accurate or inaccurate when made, so remedies are unclear

examples.before: The Units will comply with the Specifications.
examples.after: The Seller shall sell to the Buyer Units that comply with the Specifications.

examples.before: The Units will comply with the Specifications.
examples.after: If a Unit fails to comply with the Specifications, then ... .

examples.before: On the Closing Date the market price of unobtanium will be above US$5 million per gram. [stating party lacks control: allocate the risk]

section: Language of Declaration > Future Facts; Terminology
statement: Say a statement of fact is accurate or inaccurate, not breached (you breach an obligation), and don't say a statement can become inaccurate.
severity_basis: dispute risk or legally significant usage

section: Language of Declaration > Future Facts; Terminology
statement: Don't lump statements of fact with obligations, for example by providing for cure of 'breached' representations; an inaccurate statement can't later be made accurate.
severity_basis: conflates the remedies for inaccuracy and breach

section: Language of Declaration > Acknowledgments
statement: Use acknowledge when the declaring party accepts as accurate a fact offered by another party; it precludes later challenge. Don't use understand, accept, or concede instead.

examples.after: Acme acknowledges that the Consultant is in the business of providing services and consulting advice to others.
Each Shareholder acknowledges that the Merger Shares have not been registered under the Securities Act and are instead being issued under an exemption from registration.

section: Language of Declaration > Acknowledgments
statement: Put background facts in the recitals, which need no language of declaration; if a fact is important, have the declaring party acknowledge it in the body.

section: Language of Declaration > Acknowledgments
statement: Use acknowledge only to introduce a fact asserted by another party, not language that falls in another category; and never combine acknowledge with another verb (acknowledges and agrees).
severity_basis: dispute risk or legally significant usage

examples.before: Each Lender acknowledges that it shall conduct its own independent investigation of the financial condition and affairs of each Borrower.
examples.after: Each Lender shall conduct its own independent investigation of the financial condition and affairs of each Borrower.

examples.before: The parties acknowledge that this agreement does not supersede, modify, or otherwise affect the terms of any stock options ... .
examples.after: This agreement does not supersede, modify, or otherwise affect the terms of any stock options ... .

section: Language of Declaration > Acknowledgments
statement: Don't use unconditionally acknowledge or expressly acknowledge; it's rhetorical emphasis.

section: Language of Intention
statement: When a status can't be addressed definitively because it depends on circumstances after signing (independent-contractor status), state what the parties intend: The parties intend that ... will ... . Don't use obligation, policy, acknowledgment, or shall be construed.

trigger.regex_hint: \b(shall|will) be (deemed )?an independent contractor\b|\b(shall|is to) be construed\b

severity_basis: dispute risk or legally significant usage

examples.before: [14-1a] ××: The Consultant shall be an independent contractor.
examples.after: [14-1] ✓✓: The parties intend that the Consultant will be an independent contractor.

examples.before: [14-1b] ×: The Consultant will be an independent contractor.
examples.after: [14-1] ✓✓ [as above]

examples.before: [14-1c] ×: The Consultant acknowledges that she will be an independent contractor.
examples.after: [14-1] ✓✓ [as above]

examples.before: [14-1d] ××: The Consultant shall be construed to be an independent contractor.
examples.after: [14-1] ✓✓ [as above]

examples.before: [14-1e] ×: The Consultant is to be construed to be an independent contractor.
examples.after: [14-1] ✓✓ [as above]

notes: 19 Williston on Contracts § 54:2: a factor is 'whether the parties believe they are creating the relation of master and servant' (3.499). Table ratings per 3.9 legend: ✓✓ recommended; ✓ acceptable but improvable or context-dependent; × not recommended; ×× don't use (× vs ×× reading inferred from the tables; the PDF p. 130 legend prints a single × on both last lines). See R-3.9-rating-legend.

section: Language of Intention
statement: Use language of policy, not intention, where the contract's choice applies unless a court later finds it fails minimum legal requirements, as with governing law.

examples.before: The parties intend that New York governs ... . [awkward]
examples.after: New York law governs this agreement. [figure 1 policy example]

section: Language of Recommendation
statement: A party with greater bargaining power may include a recommendation to the other party using recommends (not advises, which suggests a relationship of trust), without hereby.
exceptions: Encourages and reminds are other possibilities; alternatively, have the other party acknowledge the recommendation or release liability for failing to follow it (3.504-3.505).

examples.before: [15-1a] ×: The Company advises the Participant to consult with his or her personal legal advisor ... .
examples.after: [15-1] ✓✓: The Company recommends that the Participant consult with his or her personal legal advisor if the Participant is uncertain whether the insider rules apply.

notes: Table ratings per 3.9 legend: ✓✓ recommended; ✓ acceptable but improvable or context-dependent; × not recommended; ×× don't use (× vs ×× reading inferred from the tables; the PDF p. 130 legend prints a single × on both last lines). See R-3.9-rating-legend.

section: Shall and May in Restrictive Relative Clauses
statement: Don't use shall in a restrictive relative clause; use the present tense.

examples.before: [16-1a] ××: ... to any account that Acme shall specify in writing.
examples.after: [16-1] ✓✓: Jones shall pay the Purchase Price by wire transfer to any account that Acme specifies in writing.

notes: Table ratings per 3.9 legend: ✓✓ recommended; ✓ acceptable but improvable or context-dependent; × not recommended; ×× don't use (× vs ×× reading inferred from the tables; the PDF p. 130 legend prints a single × on both last lines). See R-3.9-rating-legend.

section: Shall and May in Restrictive Relative Clauses
statement: With a stative verb in a relative clause (Shares it owns), say explicitly whether after-acquired items are covered, rather than using shall.

trigger.signal: relative clause with own/hold/possess where after-acquired property matters

severity_basis: unclear whether after-acquired shares are covered

examples.before: [16-2a] ××: ... any Shares it shall own.
examples.after: [16-2b] ✓✓: ... any Shares it currently owns or any additional Shares it acquires.

examples.before: [16-2] ✓: Other than under the terms of this agreement, no Stockholder may transfer any Shares it owns.
examples.after: [16-2b] ✓✓ [as above]

notes: Table ratings per 3.9 legend: ✓✓ recommended; ✓ acceptable but improvable or context-dependent; × not recommended; ×× don't use (× vs ×× reading inferred from the tables; the PDF p. 130 legend prints a single × on both last lines). See R-3.9-rating-legend.

section: Shall and May in Restrictive Relative Clauses
statement: Don't use may in a restrictive relative clause; if it means might it is redundant, and it can be read to cover any plausible candidate whether or not the event occurs. Usually just omit may.

words: with which tenant may be merged

severity_basis: caselaw: 'may be merged' covered contemplated mergers (383 Madison)

examples.before: [16-3a] ××: If Acme sells Assets to one or more buyers that Singh may introduce to Acme ... .
examples.after: [16-3] ✓✓: If Acme sells Assets to one or more buyers that Singh introduces to Acme ... .

notes: 383 Madison LLC v. Bear Stearns Companies, Inc., 2008 WL 5380443 (N.Y. Sup. Ct. 18 Dec. 2008): an exemption for an entity 'with which Tenant may be merged' applied to a contemplated merger. The Introduction lists may in restrictive relative clauses among glitches worth flagging. Table ratings per 3.9 legend: ✓✓ recommended; ✓ acceptable but improvable or context-dependent; × not recommended; ×× don't use (× vs ×× reading inferred from the tables; the PDF p. 130 legend prints a single × on both last lines). See R-3.9-rating-legend.

section: Dual Verb Structures
statement: Don't use two verb structures with the same verb in one clause (be and hereby is; shall grant and hereby grants; has granted and hereby grants; may but is not required to; has no authority to and shall not; shall and continue to); none the author has seen makes sense.

trigger.signal: two verb structures sharing one main verb
trigger.regex_hint: \bbe and (it )?(is )?hereby\b|\bshall \w+,? and (does )?hereby \w+|\bha(s|ve) \w+ed and hereby\b|\band continue to\b

severity_basis: dispute risk or legally significant usage

section: Dual Verb Structures
statement: In resolutions, use only performative resolutions (resolved, that ... hereby is authorized), not be and hereby is; in contracts, use only language of performance with hereby (and you can't both amend a contract and express an intention to amend it).
fix: Use only language of performance with hereby (3.519).

examples.before: Section 1(c) of the Employment Agreement be and hereby is deleted in its entirety and replaced in full by the following:

notes: Kenneth A. Adams, Legal Usage in Drafting Corporate Resolutions, Practical Lawyer (Sept. 2002).

section: Dual Verb Structures
statement: Don't combine an obligation to grant with a present grant (shall grant, and hereby grants). Put the language of performance in one sentence, and in a separate sentence require the assigning party, at the other party's request, to sign whatever documents are needed if the present assignment proves ineffective.

words: agrees to assign and hereby assigns
hereby assigns and agrees to assign

exceptions: Where no fallback rationale applies (for example, an access grant to real property), the structure is 'just silly' (3.523).
severity_basis: dispute risk or legally significant usage

examples.before: Upon termination, Acme shall grant, and hereby grants, to PharmaCo a nonexclusive, worldwide license ... .

section: Dual Verb Structures
statement: Don't say a party has granted and hereby grants; if a belt-and-suspenders fallback is intended, say so in separate sentences.

examples.before: Trustor by executing and delivering this Deed of Trust has granted and hereby grants to Beneficiary, as security for the Debt, a security interest in the Trust Property ... .

section: Dual Verb Structures
statement: Don't say a person has no authority to, and shall not, act as agent; use shall not alone (it makes clearer that you have a remedy), and consider stating that the person isn't an agent of the company.

words: has no authority to, and shall not
has no authority to and shall not
trigger.regex_hint: \bhas no authority to,? and shall not\b

fix: Use shall not alone; a sensible starting point is to state that the person isn't an agent of the company (3.530).

examples.before: The Contractor has no authority to, and shall not, act as agent for or on behalf of Client ... .

section: Dual Verb Structures
statement: Don't add and continue to (or keep, as in insure and keep insured, indemnify and keep indemnified) to an obligation; shall already imposes an ongoing obligation. If timing or duration is in question, address it explicitly.

examples.before: Acme agrees to pay and continue to pay all fees ... .
the Employee shall and continue to participate ...
shall insure and keep insured; shall indemnify and keep indemnified

section: Not a Category: Standard Terms; Assumptions
statement: In unsigned standard terms, don't use will for the company's obligations and must for the customer's ('bizarre'); the habitual present (Acme initiates reimbursement ...) is expedient but ducks the category question and could cause confusion if a provision is disputed.

trigger.signal: standard terms describing company duties in the simple present or with will

severity_basis: dispute risk or legally significant usage

examples.before: Acme initiates reimbursement five Business Days after the day it receives the Data File.
Acme calculates payment terms based on the date invoices are delivered.

notes: The book presents the habitual present as expedient but risky and gives no model rewrite.

section: Not a Category: Standard Terms; Assumptions
statement: Recast each statement-of-work assumption using the appropriate category of contract language (obligation, condition, policy); assumptions leave unclear what happens if they fail.
severity_basis: consequences of a failed assumption are unclear
notes: Likely to challenge an organization's process, since SOWs and contracts are usually handled by different groups (3.543).

section: Selecting Which Category of Contract Language to Use
statement: To transfer rights or assets on signing, use language of performance (Acme hereby assigns ...). Don't rely on language of obligation (shall assign, agrees to assign) or language of policy (will be the property of, will vest in).

trigger.regex_hint: \b(shall|agrees? to) assign\b|\b(will|shall) (be the (sole and exclusive )?property of|vest in)\b

severity_basis: courts have refused to treat obligation or policy wording as a present transfer

examples.before: Acme shall assign the Intellectual Property ... . / Acme agrees to assign the Intellectual Property ... .
examples.after: Acme hereby assigns the Intellectual Property ... .

examples.before: The Intellectual Property will be the property of Acme ... .
examples.after: Acme hereby assigns the Intellectual Property ... .

notes: Stanford University v. Roche Molecular Systems, 563 U.S. 776 (2011); IpVenture v. Prostar Computer, 503 F.3d 1324 (Fed. Cir. 2007); Pelopidas, LLC v. Keller, 2021 WL 3501988 (Mo. Ct. App. 10 Aug. 2021); Omni MedSci v. Apple, 7 F.4th 1148 (Fed. Cir. 2021) ('shall be the property of the University' was 'a statement of intended disposition and a promise of a potential future assignment').

section: Selecting Which Category of Contract Language to Use
statement: Express what is required to amend the contract as a condition; language of obligation, prohibition, or limited discretion presupposes breach and a remedy, which make no sense here. The obligation-based condition is most concise.

trigger.regex_hint: \b(shall be amended|may be amended only|shall not (be )?amend(ed)?|may amend this agreement only)\b

severity_basis: dispute risk or legally significant usage

examples.before: The parties may amend this agreement only by a writing signed by both parties.
examples.after: To be effective, an amendment to this agreement must be in writing and signed by both parties. [17 words]

examples.before: The parties shall not amend this agreement, except by written agreement of the parties.
examples.after: An amendment to this agreement will not be effective unless it is in writing and signed by both parties. [19 words]

notes: Policy version (22 words, least concise): It is a condition to an amendment to this agreement being effective that it is in writing and signed by both parties.

section: Selecting Which Category of Contract Language to Use
statement: Don't say a party may rely on information the other furnishes; it's free to rely anyway, and discretion doesn't address what happens if the information is inaccurate. Use language of policy allocating liability.
severity_basis: dispute risk or legally significant usage

examples.before: The Contractor may rely on the accuracy of information furnished by the Owner.
examples.after: The Owner will be liable for any damages the Contractor incurs arising from inaccurate information the Owner provides to the Contractor.

section: Selecting Which Category of Contract Language to Use
statement: Express a deadline for disputing an invoice (or similar notice) as a condition, not an obligation; the only sensible consequence of lateness is losing the right to dispute.

trigger.signal: shall submit/give notice within X days, where lateness should forfeit a right

severity_basis: ambiguity, or a category error or usage that can change meaning or invite dispute

examples.before: Patterson shall submit any Dispute Notice no later than five Business Days after she receives the related invoice.
examples.after: Patterson may dispute an invoice if she submits a Dispute Notice no later than five business days after she receives that invoice.

examples.before: Patterson shall submit any Dispute Notice ... .
examples.after: To dispute an invoice, Patterson must submit a Dispute Notice no later than five Business Days after she receives the related invoice.

notes: Both condition forms run 22 words; the policy form (It is a condition to disputing an invoice that ...) works but is least concise (26 words).

section: Selecting Which Category of Contract Language to Use
statement: Decide whether a tenant (or other party) should get a remedy for unreasonably withheld consent or permission to proceed; if permission, the clearest form is prohibition plus an exception in language of discretion.

words: consent unreasonably withheld will be deemed
trigger.regex_hint: \b(shall|will) not (be )?unreasonably with(hold|held)\b|\bnot to be unreasonably withheld\b

severity_basis: the choice is a deal point that the usual wording may not reflect

examples.before: The Tenant shall not assign this lease without the Landlord's consent, which the Landlord shall not unreasonably withhold. [remedy for breach]
examples.after: The Tenant shall not assign this lease without the Landlord's consent, except that the Tenant may assign this lease if the Landlord unreasonably withholds consent. [permission]

notes: Less clear alternatives: '... unless the Landlord unreasonably withholds consent' (conditional clause), and 'Consent unreasonably withheld will be deemed to have been given' (deem; less clear). The book doesn't choose between remedy and permission.

section: Selecting Which Category > Stating How a Court Is to Conduct Itself
statement: Don't use verb structures that tell a court what it may do, may not do, or must do (the court shall/will be entitled to, shall have the power to, no court shall construe, X shall not be construed as, X is to be construed, shall be admissible); a judge is likely to think 'Says who!' Of the discretion forms, only the court may interpret is not suboptimal.

words: nothing in this agreement is to be construed
shall be entitled to specific performance
trigger.regex_hint: \b(court|courts|tribunal|arbitrator)s? (shall|will|may)( not)? (be entitled|have|construe|interpret|modify|deem)\b|\b(shall|may|is|are)( not)? (to )?be construed\b|\bshall( not)? be admissible\b|\bshall be entitled to (specific performance|equitable relief|injunctive relief)\b

severity_basis: a court might ignore or reject the provision

examples.before: The courts shall be entitled to modify the duration and scope of any restriction contained herein ... .
examples.after: The parties acknowledge that if a dispute ... arises ..., they would want the court to interpret this agreement as follows: ... .

examples.before: The principle of ejusdem generis shall not be used to limit ... .
No prior drafts of this agreement ... shall be admissible in any court to vary or interpret the terms of this agreement.

notes: AM General Holdings LLC v. Renco Group, Inc., 2015 WL 9487922, at *3 (Del. Ch. 29 Dec. 2015): a stipulation that a party 'shall be entitled to specific performance' couldn't assure expedited relief. The book's lists are incomplete (3.553, 3.555, 3.557).

section: Selecting Which Category > Stating How a Court Is to Conduct Itself
statement: To aim for a result in court without appearing to boss the court around, put the focus on the parties: The parties acknowledge that if a dispute between the parties arises out of this agreement or its subject matter, they would want the court to interpret this agreement as follows: ... .
severity_basis: dispute risk or legally significant usage

examples.after: The parties acknowledge that if a dispute between the parties arises out of this agreement or the subject matter of this agreement, they would want the court to interpret this agreement as follows:

section: Language of Discretion > When Language of Discretion Is Inappropriate (blog rider)
statement: When a party's ability (or requirement) to act arises outside the contract, from the world at large, and isn't granted or imposed by the contract, say so with a statement of fact: Acme states that it may sell the Widgets (or Acme states that it must sell the Widgets), adding the basis if helpful (Acme states that because of X, it may sell the Widgets in accordance with Y).

trigger.signal: may or must describing a freedom or requirement that exists independently of the contract

fix: [Party] states that [because of X,] it may [or must] [verb] ... .
severity_basis: a bare may or must invites the argument that the discretion or duty arises only under the contract

examples.before: Acme may sell the Widgets. [meaning nothing in the world at large prevents it]
examples.after: Acme states that it may sell the Widgets.

examples.before: Acme may sell the Widgets. [freedom based on an outside source]
examples.after: Acme states that because of X, it may sell the Widgets in accordance with Y.

notes: Source: Kenneth A. Adams, 'Whether Discretion and Obligation Arise Under the Contract or Reflect the World at Large', Adams on Contract Drafting, https://www.adamsdrafting.com/whether-discretion-and-obligation-arise-under-the-contract-or-reflect-the-world-at-large/. Publication date not shown on the page (WebFetch, 5 Nov. 2026); the page carries the note 'Updated 19 November 2025'; caller dates it Nov. 2025. Verbatim: 'Does it mean that under the contract, Acme has the discretion to sell the widgets?' 'Or is Acme asserting the fact that nothing in the world at large prevents Acme from selling the widgets?' The post says that to express the second meaning 'the burden is on you to make that meaning clear.' The post's earlier suggestion 'Acme states that it is not prohibited from selling the Widgets' is noted on the page as superseded by the 19 Nov. 2025 post (see R-rider-2025-11-19-nothing-prohibits). Relation to MSCD5: 3.209 says to remind parties of what someone is free to do anyway using acknowledges; this rider uses states, where the declaring party itself asserts the fact (3.457). No sentence in the post refers to changing MSCD or a sixth edition. Reclassified as an elaboration: it adds a usage MSCD5 does not address (3.208-3.211 is related) and does not state a change to MSCD5.

section: Layout > The MSCD Enumeration Scheme
statement: Use the MSCD enumeration scheme, in its "articles" version (sections grouped into articles) or its "sections" version.

trigger.signal: contract body enumerated with another scheme, such as a first-line-indent scheme

fix: Reformat the body to the MSCD scheme (hanging indents; sections, subsections (a), clauses (1)).
notes: Sample 3 shows the articles version.

section: Layout > The MSCD Enumeration Scheme
statement: Don't use a first-line-indent enumeration scheme; indenting the first line of enumerated text makes no more sense than indenting the first line of unenumerated text.

trigger.signal: first line of each enumerated section or subsection indented, with following lines flush left

section: Layout > Components of the Body
statement: The body of the contract consists of sections (which can be grouped into articles), subsections, and enumerated clauses.
notes: Subdividing text makes it easier to read, permits cross-referencing, and helps readers find their way.

section: Layout > Components of the Body
statement: Don't use footnotes in contracts.

trigger.signal: footnote markers or footnote text in a contract

fix: Move the footnote text into the body or delete it.
severity_basis: readability; footnotes can also suggest the footnote text is of lesser significance

section: Layout > Components of the Body > Articles
statement: Consider grouping sections that share a theme into articles once a contract has more than 25 or so sections.

trigger.signal: more than about 25 sections with no articles

test: Count the sections; if more than about 25 and none are grouped, consider articles.

section: Layout > Components of the Body > Articles
statement: Use article, not section, for a group of sections.

trigger.signal: a group of sections labeled "section" (for example, section 1 containing sections 1.1 and 1.2)

fix: Call the group an article.
severity_basis: section 1 becomes ambiguous between a single provision and a group

section: Layout > Components of the Body > Articles
statement: Don't use the UK term clause for articles or sections; use article and section. Reserve clause for enumerated clauses.

trigger.signal: "clause 12" or "this clause" used to refer to a section or article

severity_basis: clause would otherwise have three meanings

section: Layout > Components of the Body > Articles
statement: Give each article a simple, all-encompassing heading in all capitals.
exceptions: Miscellaneous is acceptable as an article heading; it is understood to refer to the boilerplate at the back of the contract (but not as a section heading; 4.25).

section: Layout > Components of the Body > Articles
statement: Number articles with Arabic digits, not words or Roman numerals, and without multiple numeration: article 1, not article one, article I, or article 1.0.

examples.before: article one
examples.after: article 1

examples.before: article 1.0
examples.after: article 1

section: Layout > Components of the Body > Articles
statement: Don't number the first article 0 (zero).

section: Layout > Components of the Body > Sections > Function
statement: In the boilerplate, combine unrelated provisions in one section only when they are brief enough that giving each its own section would waste space.

trigger.signal: one section addressing two or more unrelated topics

fix: Give each provision its own section unless each is very brief.
severity_basis: the context of one provision could influence interpretation of another in the same section (Williams v. CDP, Inc., 4th Cir. 2012)

section: Layout > Components of the Body > Sections > Function
statement: Don't use subsections in a section that combines unrelated provisions; if the provisions merit subsections, make them sections.

trigger.signal: omnibus section divided into (a), (b), (c) for unrelated topics

section: Layout > Components of the Body > Sections > Function
statement: Don't combine more than two unrelated provisions in a single section, and give the section a heading that names each (for example, Amendment; Waiver).

trigger.signal: section combining three or more unrelated provisions

severity_basis: economy is more than offset by the potential for confusion

section: Layout > Components of the Body > Sections > Function
statement: Put all text in the body of the contract within a section.

trigger.signal: unenumerated text between sections or after an article heading

exceptions: When statements of fact form an article to themselves, place the introductory language (for example, Acme states that the following facts are accurate) after the article heading and before the sections, so the statements of fact can be sections with headings.

section: Layout > Components of the Body > Sections > Enumeration
statement: Number each section. Don't put Section before each section number, and don't bold section numbers.

trigger.signal: "Section 4.2" printed before a section heading, or bold section numbers

fix: Use the bare number (4.2) in roman type.

section: Layout > Components of the Body > Sections > Enumeration
statement: Without articles, number sections 1, 2, 3 (not 1.0, 2.0). With articles, use multiple numeration 1.1, 1.2 (not 1.01 or 1.1.).

trigger.signal: section numbers with an extra zero (1.01), a trailing period (1.1.), or .0

section: Layout > Components of the Body > Sections > Enumeration
statement: Use the automatic-numbering function in Word, or paragraph-numbering software, for sections, subsections, and tabulated enumerated clauses.
severity_basis: spares renumbering when text is added, deleted, or moved

section: Layout > Components of the Body > Sections > Enumeration
statement: Don't enumerate sections FIRST:, SECOND:, THIRD:, as some litigator-drafted settlement agreements do.

section: Layout > Components of the Body > Sections > Enumeration
statement: Enumerate a section even if it is the only section in its article.

trigger.signal: article containing one unnumbered section

severity_basis: consistent enumeration; a cross-reference to section 5.1 tells the reader more than article 5

section: Layout > Components of the Body > Sections > Headings
statement: Give each section a heading: a bolded word or short phrase in headline-style capitalization. Don't use underlining, all capitals, or bold plus italics.

trigger.signal: section with no heading, or a heading underlined, in all capitals, or bold italic

section: Layout > Components of the Body > Sections > Headings
statement: Make any heading you create clear and brief; don't use a heading that promises more than the section delivers or is otherwise misleading.
test: Compare the heading with what the section actually provides.
exceptions: A provision saying headings are for convenience only is of questionable value (15.18).
severity_basis: courts have refused to enforce provisions with uninformative or misleading headings

section: Layout > Components of the Body > Sections > Headings
statement: For a section addressing two distinct issues, you may give a word or phrase for each, separated by a semicolon (Amendment; Waiver).

section: Layout > Components of the Body > Sections > Headings
statement: Don't use Miscellaneous as a section heading for unrelated topics; consider creating several shorter sections.

trigger.signal: section (not article) headed Miscellaneous

section: Layout > Components of the Body > Sections > Headings
statement: Don't use etc. to broaden a heading (Notices, etc.); divide the section instead. Don't use etc. anywhere in a contract.

section: Layout > Components of the Body > Sections > Headings
statement: Don't use a subject and verb as a heading (Acme Agrees To) with the section made of enumerated clauses that each complete the sentence.

trigger.signal: heading ending in a verb (Acme Agrees To, The Seller Shall) followed by clauses that complete it

severity_basis: separates subject and verb from the rest of the sentence and limits the section to one category of contract language

section: Layout > Components of the Body > Subsections
statement: Divide a section into two or more enumerated subsections if each addresses a different aspect of one topic or the section would otherwise be too long to read comfortably.

section: Layout > Components of the Body > Subsections
statement: Don't divide a section into unenumerated paragraphs, and don't mix an unenumerated paragraph into a section divided into subsections.

trigger.signal: section broken into paragraphs without (a), (b), or a hanging unenumerated paragraph after subsections

fix: Enumerate every paragraph as a subsection, or make the unenumerated text its own section.
severity_basis: caused confusion over what a provision applies to (Karmely v. Wertheimer, 2d Cir. 2013)

section: Layout > Components of the Body > Subsections
statement: Use the (a) hierarchy for subsections. If a section has ten or more subsections, consider grouping them into two or more sections rather than shifting to (aa).

section: Layout > Components of the Body > Subsections
statement: Don't use the multiple-numeration system for subsections (4.3.1, 4.3.2).
severity_basis: takes more space, makes section 1.1 ambiguous between article 1's first section and section 1's first subsection, and clashes with the (1) clause hierarchy

section: Layout > Components of the Body > Subsections
statement: Don't give subsections headings.

trigger.signal: bold or italic heading at the start of a subsection

severity_basis: subsection headings detract from section headings

section: Layout > Components of the Body > Enumerated Clauses > Function
statement: "Enumerated clauses" are parts of a sentence in a section or subsection, preceded by introductory text, each designated by a number or letter in parentheses, with the next-to-last followed by and or or.

examples.after: Schedule 3.3 lists (1) the name of each financial institution in which Acme has an account ..., (2) the one or more names in which each account or box is held, (3) the type of account, and (4) ...

section: Layout > Components of the Body > Enumerated Clauses > Function
statement: Use enumerated clauses whenever a list or series is anything other than a short string of brief clauses.

trigger.signal: long series of items separated only by commas or semicolons, without (1), (2)

fix: Enumerate the items (1), (2), (3).

section: Layout > Components of the Body > Enumerated Clauses > Function
statement: A clause may contain subclauses and sub-subclauses, but treat three levels as generally a sign of undue complexity.

trigger.signal: enumeration nested to (i) within (A) within (1)

section: Layout > Components of the Body > Enumerated Clauses > Structure
statement: Don't begin an enumerated clause with a capital letter unless the word otherwise requires one.

trigger.signal: enumerated clause beginning with a capitalized ordinary word

severity_basis: enumerated clauses are parts of a sentence

section: Layout > Components of the Body > Enumerated Clauses > Structure
statement: Put the only sentence-ending period in a set of enumerated clauses at the end of the last clause; don't end one sentence and begin another inside the set.

trigger.signal: a period followed by a new sentence inside an enumerated clause that is not the last

section: Layout > Components of the Body > Enumerated Clauses > Structure
statement: Always precede enumerated clauses with introductory text.

trigger.signal: enumeration from one hierarchy followed immediately by enumeration from the next hierarchy down, for example (a) followed directly by (1)

fix: Add introductory text or restructure as separate sentences.
severity_basis: without introductory text the items are not a list but loosely related matter better stated as separate sentences
notes: The book prints "Enumerated clauses lacking enumerated text"; context indicates introductory text is meant.

section: Layout > Components of the Body > Enumerated Clauses > Structure
statement: Don't continue a sentence after a set of enumerated clauses, whether the continuation modifies each clause or is unrelated.

trigger.signal: text after the last enumerated clause, before the period (for example, "..., or (3) X, in each case ..." or "..., and (3) Y, unless ...")

fix: Move the continuation into the introductory text, or state it in a separate sentence.
severity_basis: makes the reader work harder and risks miscues

section: Layout > Components of the Body > Enumerated Clauses > Punctuation
statement: Use a colon to introduce any set of enumerated clauses more than about three lines long.

section: Layout > Components of the Body > Enumerated Clauses > Punctuation
statement: Make whatever precedes a colon a full independent clause, with a subject and verb, that can stand alone; convert a fragment by adding the following or as follows.

trigger.signal: a colon after a fragment (for example, "has not:" or "the Seller shall:")

examples.before: Since 30 March 2022, the Company has not: (1) incurred any obligation ...
examples.after: Since 30 March 2022, the Company has not done any of the following: (1) incurred any obligation ...

section: Layout > Components of the Body > Enumerated Clauses > Punctuation
statement: The following or as follows need not come last before the colon if it is in the only or last independent clause, but don't let one or more other independent clauses separate it from the colon.

trigger.signal: "the following" separated from its colon by another independent clause

examples.after: Acme shall transfer to Widgetco each of the following, with its certificate of title attached:

section: Layout > Components of the Body > Enumerated Clauses > Punctuation
statement: Separate long, complex, or internally punctuated enumerated clauses with semicolons, and use semicolons whenever the clauses justify a preceding colon; otherwise, and always when no colon precedes the clauses, use commas.

trigger.signal: semicolons between short clauses with no colon, or commas between clauses introduced by a colon

section: Layout > Components of the Body > Enumerated Clauses > Tabulation
statement: You may tabulate enumerated clauses so each stands alone; the more clauses and the longer they are, the more likely tabulation helps.

section: Layout > Components of the Body > Enumerated Clauses > Tabulation
statement: Don't tabulate subclauses if their clauses are integrated (and likewise for sub-subclauses within integrated subclauses).

section: Layout > Components of the Body > Enumerated Clauses > Tabulation
statement: Keep integrated any clauses that are not preceded by a full independent clause and a colon and are separated by commas.
severity_basis: tabulating them leaves an unpunctuated introduction and clauses ending in commas

section: Layout > Components of the Body > Enumerated Clauses > Tabulation
statement: Put tabulated enumerated clauses at the end of a sentence, so no "dangling" text starts flush left below the last clause; end the section or subsection after the clauses rather than adding unenumerated sentences.

trigger.signal: flush-left text after a set of tabulated clauses

notes: Sample 5.

section: Layout > Components of the Body > Enumerated Clauses > Enumeration
statement: Use (1) for enumerated clauses, (A) for subclauses, and (i) for sub-subclauses; reserve (a) for subsections.

trigger.signal: enumerated clauses lettered (a) or numbered (i) at the first level

section: Layout > Components of the Body > Enumerated Clauses > Enumeration
statement: Don't use "commingled enumeration": in a section without subsections, don't use (a) for first-level tabulated clauses.

section: Layout > Components of the Body > Enumerated Clauses > Enumeration
statement: Don't use multiple numeration (1.1.1, 6.15.4.5.3) for tabulated enumerated clauses, and don't adopt the AIA .1 hierarchy.
severity_basis: clauses are parts of a sentence, multiple numeration can't serve integrated clauses, forces commingling, and gets cumbersome

section: Layout > Components of the Body > Enumerated Clauses > Enumeration
statement: Don't use bullets for tabulated enumerated clauses.

section: Layout > Components of the Body > Enumerated Clauses > Enumeration
statement: Don't follow enumeration from one hierarchy immediately, with no intervening text, by enumeration from the next hierarchy down (for example, (2) followed directly by (A)); restructure to fix both this and the missing introductory text.

section: Layout > Components of the Body > Enumerated Clauses > Enumeration
statement: Don't use two sets of tabulated clauses with different hierarchies in one section or subsection; remove enumeration from one set or move one set to its own section or subsection.

section: Layout > Components of the Body > Enumerated Clauses > Enumeration
statement: Don't give tabulated enumerated clauses headings.

section: Layout > The MSCD Enumeration Scheme (indents)
statement: Indent all section text, and indent section and subsection text equally; don't move subsections one tab further in.
severity_basis: subsections are not a lower taxonomic level; indenting them differently misleads and wastes space

section: Layout > The MSCD Enumeration Scheme (indents)
statement: Distinguish subsections by indenting the subsection enumeration slightly more than the section number.

section: Layout > The MSCD Enumeration Scheme (indents)
statement: Don't put a period after a section number or after a section heading.

trigger.signal: "4.2." or "Notices." as a section number or heading

section: Layout > The MSCD Enumeration Scheme (indents)
statement: Indent tabulated enumerated clauses one tab setting further in than sections and subsections, with the enumeration at the left edge of the text.

section: Layout > The MSCD Enumeration Scheme (indents)
statement: Adopt the MSCD scheme by setting up Microsoft Word styles; templates for both versions are at adamsdrafting.com/resources.

section: Layout > Block Length
statement: If a section or subsection runs more than about 15 lines, consider dividing it into two or more sections or subsections, or tabulating its enumerated clauses.

trigger.signal: section or subsection longer than about 15 lines

test: Count lines in each section or subsection.
severity_basis: long blocks wear the reader out and make it easier to lose one's place

section: Layout > Block Length
statement: At the other extreme, consider keeping the shortest components consolidated; gauge balance by the white space on the page.

trigger.signal: very short subsections and tabulation of even short clauses (shopping-list text)

section: Layout > Two-Column Format
statement: Use a two-column format rarely, if at all; minimizing page count ranks below concision, readability, and ease of work.
exceptions: The MSCD scheme can be used in two columns (4.68).
severity_basis: requires small fonts that are harder to read, discourages comments, and forces scrolling on screen

section: Layout > Arranging Provisions
statement: Arranging the body involves three concurrent processes: deciding what topics sections address (custom mostly dictates this), allocating provisions to sections, and determining the sequence.

section: Layout > Arranging Provisions
statement: Usually have each section address a specific deal issue; devoting a section to one party's obligations is usually too constraining, and such sections end up more mixed than advertised.

trigger.signal: section headed "Obligations of [Party]" or "Covenants of [Party]"

section: Layout > Arranging Provisions
statement: Put more-important and more-frequently consulted provisions first, balanced against the conventional sequence (for an acquisition: deal terms, statements of fact, preclosing obligations, closing conditions, termination, indemnification, miscellaneous).
severity_basis: consistency saves time and helps navigation and checking for completeness

section: Layout > Arranging Provisions
statement: Don't "bury" a contentious provision.

trigger.signal: contentious provision placed among boilerplate or in an unexpected place

severity_basis: in consumer contracts burying can make a provision unenforceable; between sophisticated parties it can sour the relationship and is unlikely to fool anyone

section: Layout > Frontloading and Backending
statement: Frontload selected deal information (for example, in a table at the top) only if transactional and administrative benefits justify it.
exceptions: If the information is retrievable elsewhere (for example, customer contacts in the invoicing system), nothing is gained by frontloading it (4.88).
notes: 4.85 cross-refers to 4.71 for the standard approach to arranging; the arranging discussion starts at 4.72.

section: Layout > Frontloading and Backending
statement: Move frontloaded information out of the body; don't state it in two places.

trigger.signal: the same deal term stated in a cover table and in the body

fix: Delete one statement and refer to the other.
severity_basis: repetition invites unconforming revisions and inconsistency (conflict)

section: Layout > Frontloading and Backending
statement: Be cautious about frontloading signature blocks: it shows at once whether the contract is signed, but it may encourage signing without reading, and dissuading readers from reading the boilerplate invites later claims of ignorance.

section: Layout > Frontloading and Backending
statement: "Backending" puts deal-specific information in a schedule; it makes more sense when that information is voluminous.
notes: 4.91 ends mid-sentence in the book ("You could frontload the schedules and").

section: Layout > Frontloading and Backending
statement: A master agreement with statements of work is analogous to backending, driven by serial transactions between the same parties; purchase orders with separate terms are analogous to both frontloading and backending.
notes: Some companies retitle "master" agreements (for example, "framework agreement").

section: Layout > Cross-References > Function
statement: Don't cross-refer to a sentence or part of a sentence (the penultimate sentence of section 2.10; the proviso in the final sentence of this section 3).
fix: Drop the sentence reference if unnecessary, or isolate the text in its own section or subsection.
severity_basis: makes the reader work and can't be automated, so it goes stale

section: Layout > Cross-References > Function
statement: Use as few cross-references as possible; each provision should be understandable on its own. Treat many prioritizing cross-references (notwithstanding, subject to, except as provided in) as a sign of inefficient structure.

section: Layout > Cross-References > Wording
statement: In a cross-reference, say whether a section or an article is meant, plus its enumeration; don't use the section mark (§).

examples.after: section 4.2

section: Layout > Cross-References > Wording
statement: Don't add of this agreement or hereof to internal cross-references, and don't add above or below.

section: Layout > Cross-References > Wording
statement: When a provision refers to itself, include its enumeration (this section 4), even for a section.

section: Layout > Cross-References > Wording
statement: When referring to two or more sections, don't repeat section: sections 5 and 7, not section 5 and section 7.

examples.before: section 5 and section 7
examples.after: sections 5 and 7

section: Layout > Cross-References > Wording
statement: Refer to a subsection as a section (this section 4(c)), not as subsection or this subsection (c); for two or more subsections of one section, repeat the section number (section 6(b) or 6(c)).

examples.before: section 6(b) or (c)
examples.after: section 6(b) or 6(c)

section: Layout > Cross-References > Wording
statement: Refer to an enumerated clause as clause (2) of section 4(b) or as section 4(b)(2); for multiple clauses repeat the section and subsection numbers (sections 6(b)(2) and 6(b)(3)).

examples.before: sections 6(b)(2) and (3)
examples.after: sections 6(b)(2) and 6(b)(3)

section: Layout > Cross-References > Wording
statement: Don't use initial capitals for section and article in cross-references, and don't emphasize cross-references with bold, italics, or underlining.

trigger.signal: "Section 4.2" mid-sentence, or emphasized cross-references

section: Layout > Cross-References > Wording
statement: Don't include the heading in each cross-reference (article 12 (Indemnification)); if desired, insert the automated cross-reference as a hyperlink instead.
severity_basis: refers to the same thing twice and invites inconsistency

section: Layout > Cross-References > Updating
statement: Use Word's automatic cross-referencing only in the master version; in copies sent for comment, convert field codes to text, and make next-draft changes in the master.
severity_basis: others unaware of field codes create chaos, and some metadata-removal software treats field codes as metadata

section: Layout > Cross-References > Updating
statement: When deleting text would make cross-references inaccurate, you may replace the deleted text with [Intentionally omitted] and keep the enumeration.
notes: Useful for high-volume template users even with automatic cross-references.

section: Layout > Headers and Footers
statement: Number pages in Arabic numerals, leaving the first page unnumbered; with a cover sheet, use lowercase Roman numerals for the associated materials (table of contents, index of definitions).

section: Layout > Headers and Footers
statement: Generally center page numbers in the footer; if the footer holds other information, consider placing them flush right, perhaps with the word Page.

section: Layout > Headers and Footers
statement: For the contract proper, Page x of y (or x/y) is probably not worth its clutter.

section: Layout > Headers and Footers
statement: For multiple attachments, number pages either consecutively (as one document, where Page x of y is more useful) or nonconsecutively (each attachment separately, for example C-5); choose for the transaction, and don't use both in one set.
exceptions: C-5 style numbering is awkward if attachments are enumerated by section number (5.81).

section: Layout > Headers and Footers
statement: Use headers or, more usually, footers for file names and draft lines.

section: Layout > Headers and Footers
statement: You may mark working drafts Confidential. Don't mark drafts exchanged with the other side Privileged and Confidential (it may suit drafts with explanatory notes shared only with the client), and don't mark draft contracts Attorney Work Product.
severity_basis: the work-product doctrine covers materials prepared in anticipation of litigation

section: Layout > Headers and Footers
statement: Don't fear that a logo in headers, footers, or a cover sheet makes the organization the "drafter" for contra proferentem purposes; other evidence of who drafted what is available.

section: Back of the Contract > Concluding Clause
statement: The "back of the contract" is the concluding clause, the signature blocks, and any attachments; the concluding clause is the sentence that usually precedes the signature blocks.

section: Back of the Contract > Concluding Clause
statement: If the introductory clause states the contract date and signers don't date their signatures, use: The parties are signing this agreement on the date stated in the introductory clause. Don't name the parties.
notes: Sample 6.

section: Back of the Contract > Concluding Clause
statement: If signers date their signatures, use: Each party is signing this agreement on the date specified for that party's signature.
notes: Sample 7.

section: Back of the Contract > Concluding Clause
statement: Omit the concluding clause unless you consider its modest narrative function and long tradition reason enough to use it; if you do, go ahead.
severity_basis: it adds no information but closes the body as the lead-in opens it
notes: Counterparty review: the Introduction says to give a pass to archaisms in the front and back of the contract on the other side's draft.

section: Back of the Contract > Concluding Clause
statement: In the concluding clause, refer to signing, not to executing or executing and delivering.
severity_basis: execute adds nothing beyond sign and can't cure a missing element of validity or give comfort on authority; delivery isn't required except for a contract under seal or an English deed
notes: Counterparty review: the Introduction says to give a pass to archaisms in the front and back of the contract on the other side's draft.

section: Back of the Contract > Concluding Clause
statement: Use the present progressive (the parties are signing), not the past (signed) or present perfect (have signed, have caused to be signed).
severity_basis: the contract speaks at the moment of signing; the present perfect suggests completion in the past
notes: Counterparty review: the Introduction says to give a pass to archaisms in the front and back of the contract on the other side's draft.

section: Back of the Contract > Concluding Clause
statement: For consistency, revise a statement such as This agreement has been validly executed by Acme to This agreement is being validly signed by Acme (whether the statement serves any purpose is a separate question).

examples.before: This agreement has been validly executed by Acme.
examples.after: This agreement is being validly signed by Acme.

section: Back of the Contract > Concluding Clause
statement: Don't use as of for a date in the introductory or concluding clause; but if you use it in one, use it in the other.
severity_basis: a haphazardly observed courtesy that could be confusing (2.27)

section: Back of the Contract > Concluding Clause
statement: Don't use the traditional concluding clause or its archaisms: IN WITNESS WHEREOF, these presents, the day and year first above written.

words: the day and year first above written
trigger.regex_hint: (?i)in witness whereof|these presents|first above written|day and year first

examples.before: IN WITNESS WHEREOF, the parties hereto, intending to be legally bound, have by their proper and duly authorized officers duly executed and delivered these presents as of the day and year first above written.

notes: 5.24 says a "standard alternative, set forth above" is imprecise too, without identifying it. Counterparty review: the Introduction says to give a pass to archaisms in the front and back of the contract on the other side's draft.

section: Back of the Contract > Concluding Clause
statement: Don't rely on a statement that the signer is authorized (in the concluding clause or elsewhere); ask for confirmation such as a board resolution or a list of authorized employees with specimen signatures. A reminder to your own people not to sign without authority belongs in the signature blocks.
severity_basis: vagueness, dispute risk, or legally significant usage

section: Back of the Contract > Concluding Clause
statement: Don't use the traditional "Each individual signing for an entity hereby personally warrants his or her legal authority to bind that entity"; it is peculiarly worded, and a remedy against the signer is a low priority.

section: Back of the Contract > Concluding Clause
