statement: Don't say the parties are intending to be legally bound; it is generally pointless.
notes: Counterparty review: the Introduction says to give a pass to archaisms in the front and back of the contract on the other side's draft.

section: Back of the Contract > Concluding Clause
statement: Don't say the parties accept the terms of the agreement; signing suffices to show assent.
notes: Counterparty review: the Introduction says to give a pass to archaisms in the front and back of the contract on the other side's draft.

section: Back of the Contract > Concluding Clause
statement: If signers date their signatures, consider adding: This agreement will become effective when all parties have signed it. The date of this agreement will be the date this agreement is signed by the last party to sign it (as indicated by the date specified for that party's signature).
exceptions: Unnecessary if the introductory clause states the date the contract was signed (2.24-.46).

section: Back of the Contract > Concluding Clause
statement: If the parties are also parties to other contracts, refer in the concluding clause to the type of agreement rather than this agreement, or use a signature-page notation.

section: Back of the Contract > Signature Blocks > Format
statement: Use a signature block for each party, and don't use the name of an unincorporated division; it lacks capacity to contract.

trigger.signal: signature block in the name of a division

severity_basis: a party without capacity to contract

section: Back of the Contract > Signature Blocks > Format
statement: For a legal entity, put its name in all capitals above the signature line; don't state its defined term above the name or its jurisdiction of organization after it.

trigger.signal: "SELLER:" or "ACME CORPORATION, a Delaware corporation" above a signature line

section: Back of the Contract > Signature Blocks > Format
statement: Don't put two or more entity names above one signature line; use a separate signature block for each entity.
severity_basis: English law requires separate signature in each capacity (Companies Act 2006 s 44(6)); separate blocks are clearer everywhere

section: Back of the Contract > Signature Blocks > Format
statement: Put By: next to the signature line; beneath it note the signer's name and title in lowercase with initial capitals, and any special capacity (for example, trustee). Use Name: and Title: only if you don't know who will sign; otherwise state the name and title instead of those labels.

section: Back of the Contract > Signature Blocks > Format
statement: To remind an entity party's signer to obtain management approval, add and authorized signatory (or and authorized signer) after the signer's name and title.

section: Back of the Contract > Signature Blocks > Format
statement: Have two persons sign for a company when needed to manage risk, when organizational documents require it, when the other party wants a statutory presumption of authority (for example, California Corporations Code § 313), or when the contract isn't otherwise valid (English law in some circumstances).
severity_basis: vagueness, dispute risk, or legally significant usage

section: Back of the Contract > Signature Blocks > Format
statement: The Canadian practice of placing I have authority to bind [the Corporation] under a block isn't clearly better than other approaches, except where it facilitates recording that requires a statement of signer authority.

section: Back of the Contract > Signature Blocks > Format
statement: If the signer for an entity is itself an entity, use a signature block within a signature block.
notes: Sample 6 (Jarrow Holdings LLC).

section: Back of the Contract > Signature Blocks > Format
statement: For an individual party, put the individual's name in capitals under the signature line, add in his [or her] own capacity if confusion is a risk, and don't state the defined term above.
severity_basis: capitals distinguish an individual party from an individual signing for an entity

section: Back of the Contract > Signature Blocks > Format
statement: If signers date their signatures, put Date: to one side of each signature line or directly beneath it.
notes: Sample 7.

section: Back of the Contract > Signature Blocks > Format
statement: Align signature blocks one above the other or side by side; don't use the English arrangement with block information on the left and a vertical line of closing parentheses with the signature to the right.
severity_basis: signers may sign in the printed-name blank and think they're done

section: Back of the Contract > Signature Blocks > Format
statement: Use a Read before signing notation only where a party is an individual not represented by counsel; otherwise it is pointless.

section: Back of the Contract > Signature Blocks > Format
statement: To avoid requesting a new dated signature page, add to the effectiveness provision: If a party signs this agreement but fails to date their signature, the date the other party receives the signing party's signature will be deemed to be the date the signing party signed this agreement. With more than two parties, name one party (for example, the Company) as the recipient.
exceptions: Change their to its if all parties are entities (5.44).
On receiving an undated signature, handwrite the date with the notation Determined in accordance with the relevant section and send the pages to the other parties (5.45).

section: Back of the Contract > Signature Blocks > Format
statement: If the introductory clause highlights a party's limited role, do so in its signature block too: add , for purposes of only [specified provisions] immediately after the party name.

section: Back of the Contract > Signature Blocks > Seals and Deeds
statement: Know where sealing still matters in the United States: (1) consideration (a sealed contract binds without consideration or raises a presumption of it); (2) limitation periods (for example, Delaware allows 20 years for actions on contracts under seal versus three years); (3) authorization (N.Y. Business Corporation Law § 107 makes the corporate seal prima facie evidence of authorized execution).
severity_basis: requirements vary arbitrarily by jurisdiction; Delaware requires the word seal next to the signature lines (Sunrise Ventures, Del. Ch. 2010)

section: Back of the Contract > Signature Blocks > Seals and Deeds
statement: Rather than rely on sealing to deal with consideration or limitation periods, address those issues explicitly in the contract.
severity_basis: a formality's significance isn't evident from the formality; most states have abolished or weakened the sealed/unsealed distinction, and UCC § 2-203 abolished it for sales of goods

section: Back of the Contract > Signature Blocks > Seals and Deeds
statement: Outside the United States, observe local signing formalities: in England, a deed must be described as a deed or state it is executed as a deed, be signed by the appropriate persons, be witnessed, and be delivered; Australia also recognizes deeds; in China and Russia, practice is to sign and apply the corporate seal.
severity_basis: formalities can defeat deed status (400 George Street v. BG International, QSC 2010, where a heading Background instead of Recitals was a factor)

section: Back of the Contract > Signature Blocks > Seals and Deeds
statement: If the law requires signing formalities for enforceability, or observing them gives a legal advantage, provide for them; for a required corporate seal, consider the notation Corporate seal here next to each block.
severity_basis: vagueness, dispute risk, or legally significant usage

section: Back of the Contract > Signature Blocks > Seals and Deeds
statement: Otherwise, eliminate all references to sealing and other irrelevant signing formalities.
notes: Counterparty review: the Introduction says to give a pass to archaisms in the front and back of the contract on the other side's draft.

section: Back of the Contract > Signature Blocks > Witnessing, Notarizing, E-Signature, Counsel
statement: To provide for witnessing (required by law for some contracts, such as mortgages in some states), put a witness signature block preceded by Witness: next to the block being witnessed; Attest: is an alternative but obscure to many readers.

section: Back of the Contract > Signature Blocks > Witnessing, Notarizing, E-Signature, Counsel
statement: Some U.S. state laws require signatures on certain contracts to be acknowledged before a notary or other official (for example, Colorado for independent-contractor agreements); contracts often require notarization even when the law doesn't, presumably to avoid identity disputes.

section: Back of the Contract > Signature Blocks > Witnessing, Notarizing, E-Signature, Counsel
statement: E-signature software applies signatures and dates to signature blocks whatever their format; it differs from scanning a signature stamp.

section: Back of the Contract > Signature Blocks > Witnessing, Notarizing, E-Signature, Counsel
statement: Don't have counsel sign a settlement agreement under APPROVED AS TO FORM AND CONTENT; if the aim is to show the parties had legal advice, have the parties say so in the agreement.

words: approved as to form and content

severity_basis: the notation didn't preclude a finding that the lawyers were personally bound (Monster Energy Co. v. Schechter, Cal. 2019)

section: Back of the Contract > Consents and Signature Page
statement: Signature blocks may be followed by a consent (or acknowledgment) in which nonparties consent to something in the contract, such as guarantors consenting to restructured debt; check whether it is necessary, because guarantees usually allow modification without guarantor consent.

section: Back of the Contract > Consents and Signature Page
statement: Keep the concluding clause and signature blocks together on one page; if that leaves blank space after the body, add [Signature page follows] rather than [The remainder of this page has been intentionally left blank].

trigger.regex_hint: (?i)remainder of this page (has been |is )?intentionally left blank

section: Back of the Contract > Consents and Signature Page
statement: As an alternative to naming the agreement type in the concluding clause, state at the bottom of the signature page the contract type and, as necessary, the date and party names; this is particularly useful when signature blocks span more than one page.

examples.after: [Signature page to Acme Corporation credit agreement dated 17 July 2022]

section: Back of the Contract > Attachments > Kinds
statement: Follow the prevailing U.S. convention: call a stand-alone document an exhibit, and call information that could have been in the body a schedule.
test: Ask whether the attachment is a stand-alone document (exhibit) or information that could have been in the body (schedule).
exceptions: Other jurisdictions differ (Australia uses annexure for stand-alone documents).
severity_basis: consistent labeling helps readers once a contract has enough attachments

section: Back of the Contract > Attachments > Kinds
statement: With only a few attachments, don't feel bound by the exhibit/schedule distinction; a generic term (appendix, annex, attachment) works, and four attachments beats three exhibits and one schedule.

section: Back of the Contract > Attachments > Kinds
statement: Put schedules before exhibits, and place attachments after the signatures (U.S. convention).
severity_basis: readers flip more between the body and schedules; putting signatures between schedules and exhibits (Australian practice) makes them harder to find

section: Back of the Contract > Attachments > References
statement: Don't use hereto or to this agreement in references to attachments, alone or after attached.
severity_basis: a reference to an attachment is reasonably assumed to be to that contract

examples.before: exhibit A attached hereto
examples.after: exhibit A

section: Back of the Contract > Attachments > References
statement: Don't emphasize references to attachments (italics, bold, underlining), don't put the enumeration in quotation marks (exhibit "A"), and don't use initial capitals (use exhibit A, schedule 3.2).

section: Back of the Contract > Attachments > Enumeration
statement: Enumerate attachments sequentially (1, 2, 3 or A, B, C) or by the number of the section they relate to; use section-number enumeration mainly in contracts with articles and multiple numeration.
severity_basis: without articles, section-number enumeration risks miscues (is attachment 10 sequential or section 10?)

section: Back of the Contract > Attachments > Enumeration
statement: Consider a hybrid: enumerate schedules by section number and exhibits by consecutive letters, so schedule 3.2 can't be confused with exhibit 3.2.

section: Back of the Contract > Attachments > Exhibits and Schedules
statement: An exhibit is a stand-alone document, either currently in effect (for example, organizational documents) or a form to be signed later (for example, an employment agreement to be signed at closing).

section: Back of the Contract > Attachments > Exhibits and Schedules
statement: A schedule holds material that could be in the body but is placed after it, such as a list of parties or banking information.

section: Back of the Contract > Attachments > Exhibits and Schedules
statement: Link each disclosure schedule to its provision by saying that schedule X states (or lists) all instances of the thing at issue; alternatively, say that other than as stated in schedule X there are no such instances, when the thing is undesirable or present in limited quantities.
severity_basis: an unclear link between schedule and statement of fact invites dispute over what was disclosed

section: Back of the Contract > Attachments > Exhibits and Schedules
statement: Use disclosure schedules for volume, because the party collecting the information often isn't the drafter, because collection runs on a different process and timetable, and for sensitivity (schedules can be omitted from circulated drafts and, under Regulation S-K Item 601(b)(2), often from merger-agreement filings).

section: Back of the Contract > Attachments > Exhibits and Schedules
statement: If no scheduled information turns out to be needed, delete the reference rather than send readers to a schedule saying None or Not applicable.

section: Back of the Contract > Attachments > Exhibits and Schedules
statement: Put provisions governing the effect of disclosure schedules in the body, not on a cover sheet to the schedules.

trigger.signal: cover sheet to disclosure schedules stating how disclosures qualify statements of fact

severity_basis: they are provisions like any other, so they belong in the body

section: Back of the Contract > Attachments > Exhibits and Schedules
statement: Don't place contract sections in a schedule, especially contentious provisions (burying) or ostensibly routine ones.
exceptions: Relegating standardized, non-negotiable provisions to a schedule is sometimes simplest (5.94).
Some drafters put especially sensitive terms, such as pricing, in a schedule to limit disclosure (5.94).
Don't put the definition section in a pull-out schedule; handle definitions so it is unnecessary (5.94, 6.89-.98).
severity_basis: makes them less convenient to refer to; burying a contentious provision risks enforceability and the relationship (4.83)

section: Back of the Contract > Attachments > Exhibits and Schedules
statement: Say in schedule X, not on schedule X.
severity_basis: on fits a single page; use in for any other component

examples.before: on schedule 3.2
examples.after: in schedule 3.2

section: Back of the Contract > Attachments > Saying Attachments Are Part of the Contract
statement: Don't state that attachments are part of the contract.

words: as though fully set forth herein
trigger.regex_hint: (?i)(made|constitutes?|form(s|ing)?) a part (of|hereof)|as (though|if) fully set forth herein|incorporated herein by reference

severity_basis: a reference to an attachment presumptively refers to that contract's attachments and by itself brings it within the contract

examples.before: All exhibits and schedules annexed hereto are expressly made a part of this agreement as though fully set forth herein.

section: Back of the Contract > Attachments > Saying Attachments Are Part of the Contract
statement: If schedules hold self-contained sets of provisions (some master-agreement structures) and the body doesn't otherwise mention them, state in the body that they are part of the contract.

trigger.signal: schedule of terms that the body never refers to

severity_basis: because the body doesn't otherwise mention those schedules, stating that they are part of the contract is necessary to make them part of it

section: Back of the Contract > Attachments > Virtual Attachments
statement: A "virtual attachment" is an ancillary document made part of a contract without being physically attached, such as an employee handbook or a web page of general terms.

section: Back of the Contract > Attachments > Virtual Attachments
statement: Say expressly that a virtual attachment is part of the contract.

trigger.signal: contract that refers to a handbook, policy, or web page of terms without saying it is part of the contract

fix: State that the [document] is part of this agreement.
severity_basis: otherwise a court may hold the document is not part of the contract

section: Back of the Contract > Attachments > Virtual Attachments
statement: Don't say the contract is subject to a virtual attachment, and don't merely say where it can be found (for example, on a specified web page).
severity_basis: a court might hold subject to doesn't adequately express intent to be bound (Affinity Internet v. Consolidated Credit Counseling, Fla. Dist. Ct. App. 2006; Manasher v. NECC Telecom, E.D. Mich. 2007)

section: Back of the Contract > Attachments > Virtual Attachments
statement: Be cautious about using a definition to bring in a virtual attachment (for example, "Support Services" means services described at a website at any given time).

trigger.signal: definition pointing to terms on a website "at any given time" or "as updated from time to time"
trigger.regex_hint: (?i)(at any given time|from time to time).{0,60}(website|http)|(website|http).{0,80}(at any given time|from time to time)

severity_basis: it may seem a low-key way to allow unilateral amendment, but a court could hold the description isn't part of the contract

examples.before: "Support Services" means Product support services described in the description of support services provided at the Acme Licenses website (http://www.acme.com/licenses) at any given time.

section: Back of the Contract > Attachments > Virtual Attachments
statement: Whether a party may unilaterally amend a virtual attachment, and whether and how it must notify the other party, are contentious issues outside MSCD's scope; address them deliberately.
severity_basis: vagueness, dispute risk, or legally significant usage

section: Back of the Contract > Indicating the End of the Contract
statement: End of Agreement (or a variant) might be useful at the end of a contract whose signatures are at the front, and after attachments, but less awkward alternatives may be preferable.

section: Back of the Contract > Indicating the End of the Contract
statement: Don't use End of Agreement right after the body and before the signature blocks; if the concern is blank space, use Signature page follows.
severity_basis: the signature blocks themselves signal the end

section: Back of the Contract > Indicating the End of the Contract
statement: Don't use End of Agreement after signature blocks at the back.
severity_basis: without attachments it adds nothing; with attachments it misleads, because attachments are part of the contract

section: Back of the Contract > Indicating the End of the Contract
statement: With frontloaded signature blocks, consider Page x of y or blank space at the bottom of the last page to signal the end, rather than the awkward End of Agreement; don't use a dinkus (* * *), which usually denotes omission or a break.

section: Back of the Contract > Indicating the End of the Contract
statement: For clickwrap, shrinkwrap, or other unsigned contracts squeezed unformatted into a webpage, readme file, or dialog box, End of Agreement or an equivalent may be the clearest and most prudent option.

section: Back of the Contract > Indicating the End of the Contract
statement: Rather than End of Agreement after attachments, number the pages of the whole set of attachments Page x of y and identify the kind of attachment in a header or footer on every page.
severity_basis: end notations don't reveal missing pages or attachments in between

section: Back of the Contract > Indicating the End of the Contract
statement: Don't put End of Article x after every article.
exceptions: Some government contracts use End of Clause because the regulations they restate use it (5.119).

section: Defined Terms > Purpose and Nature
statement: Treat words and phrases for which the contract provides definitions as "defined terms"; each definition is either autonomous (linked to the defined term by a definitional verb) or integrated (part of a regular sentence, with the defined term in a parenthetical).

section: Defined Terms > Purpose and Nature
statement: Use a defined term to make the contract easier to read (a short term replaces a longer definition) and to ensure that whatever is defined is expressed consistently.

section: Defined Terms > Purpose and Nature
statement: You may repeat the defined term inside its own definition; a contract defined term is only a convenient substitute for its definition in that contract, so this isn't circular.

examples.after: "Trademark" means a registered trademark or service mark or any trademark or service mark that is the subject of any application, registration, or renewal.

section: Defined Terms > Purpose and Nature
statement: Defined terms are usually nouns (common or proper) or noun phrases; occasionally a verb (transfer) or a prepositional phrase (to Acme's knowledge).

section: Defined Terms > Purpose and Nature
statement: Define a common-noun defined term in the singular, unless the plural is simpler.

section: Defined Terms > Purpose and Nature
statement: Don't define a term in both singular and plural forms ("Note" and "Notes" mean ...; each a "Member" and collectively the "Members").
severity_basis: a reasonable reader isn't confused by switching between singular and plural; defining both is silly and distracting

examples.before: "Note" and "Notes" mean ...

section: Defined Terms > Purpose and Nature
statement: Don't address in an internal rule of interpretation the practice of defining in the singular and using in the plural, or vice versa.

section: Defined Terms > Purpose and Nature
statement: Don't use as alternative defined terms both a word or phrase and its abbreviation ("Customer Service Request" or "CSR" means ...); use one or the other.

examples.before: "Customer Service Request" or "CSR" means ...

section: Defined Terms > Purpose and Nature
statement: Use initial capitals for every defined term, even routine ones such as Person or Subsidiary, with no exceptions; if many instances make the text harder to read, find a way to omit the defined term rather than drop the capitals.

trigger.signal: a defined term appearing in lowercase

severity_basis: a lowercase instance invites the question whether it was a mistake or meant something else

section: Defined Terms > Purpose and Nature
statement: Don't use bold, italics, all capitals, or quotation marks each time you use a defined term.

trigger.signal: defined term bolded, italicized, or quoted at each use

section: Defined Terms > Consistency
statement: Provide definitions for all abbreviations, even widely known ones such as SEC.

trigger.signal: abbreviation used without a definition

severity_basis: readers will eventually be confused because readership is broader than expected

section: Defined Terms > Consistency
statement: Make sure every instance of a defined term uses initial capitals; use case-sensitive search to check.
test: Search case-sensitively for the lowercase form of each defined term.
fix: Capitalize the instance, or use a different word if a different meaning is intended.
severity_basis: a contract defining Obligations as bonds used lowercase obligations in a crucial provision; the panel read it to cover any obligations (Economist, 2019)

section: Defined Terms > Consistency
statement: Don't use a lowercase version of a defined word or phrase to express a different meaning; use a different word or phrase.
exceptions: Unavoidable if the defined term is a common word, for example Bank.
severity_basis: readers can't tell whether the lowercase form was a mistake or intended a different meaning

section: Defined Terms > Consistency
statement: Don't use a word or phrase that differs from a defined term but is close enough to make the reader wonder whether it refers to the defined term.

trigger.signal: phrase resembling a defined term (for example, "services are substantially completed" alongside defined "Substantial Completion")

severity_basis: held ambiguous in Clinton Ass'n for a Renewed Environment v. Monadnock Construction (N.Y. Sup. Ct. 2013)

section: Defined Terms > Consistency
statement: Don't use a defined term that refers to a single item in a way that suggests there are more than one (for example, any Note when Note is a specific note).
severity_basis: National Housing Partnership v. Municipal Capital Appreciation Partners I (D.C. 2007)

section: Defined Terms > Abbreviations
statement: You may use abbreviations (acronyms, read as words, like ERISA; initialisms, read as letters, like SEC) as defined terms.

section: Defined Terms > Abbreviations
statement: Before an abbreviation used as a common noun, choose a or an by the sound of its first syllable, go with the pronunciation you and your colleagues use, and apply it consistently throughout the contract.

section: Defined Terms > Abbreviations
statement: Don't use acronyms and initialisms to excess; they turn contracts into alphabet soup.

section: Defined Terms > Selecting Defined Terms
statement: If a conventional defined term exists for the meaning (Business Day, the Code, GAAP, Indemnifiable Losses), use it.
severity_basis: contract drafting favors predictability over novelty

section: Defined Terms > Selecting Defined Terms
statement: If you give a conventional defined term an unorthodox definition, modify the term to alert the reader (Adjusted Net Operating Income instead of Net Operating Income).
severity_basis: a reader will assume the conventional meaning

section: Defined Terms > Selecting Defined Terms
statement: For a definition unique to the transaction, use a term that is concise yet informative and specific enough to distinguish it from other defined terms in that contract (the Property; the Acmetown Property; the 144 Ninth Street Acmetown Property).

section: Defined Terms > Autonomous Definitions > Structure
statement: An autonomous definition links the defined term to the definition by a definitional verb; the term also covers the whole sentence.

section: Defined Terms > Autonomous Definitions > Structure
statement: Place the defined term before the definition ("Exchange Act" means the Securities Exchange Act of 1934), not after (Any such transfer is referred to in this agreement as a "Permitted Transfer").

trigger.regex_hint: (?i)(is|are|shall be) referred to (in this agreement|herein) as

examples.before: Any such transfer is referred to in this agreement as a "Permitted Transfer".

section: Defined Terms > Autonomous Definitions > Structure
statement: In an autonomous definition, don't put the, a, an, or The term before the defined term.

section: Defined Terms > Autonomous Definitions > Structure
statement: Introduce a single autonomous definition with In this agreement, followed by a comma; introduce a set with In this agreement, the following definitions apply, followed by a colon. Don't use wordier alternatives such as For purposes of this agreement, the following terms have the following meanings.

words: the following terms have the following meanings

section: Defined Terms > Autonomous Definitions > Structure
statement: In a set, state each autonomous definition as a separate paragraph without first-line indent, end each with a period (not a semicolon), and put the set in alphabetical order.

section: Defined Terms > Autonomous Definitions > Structure
statement: Don't add text at the end of the paragraph that constitutes an autonomous definition, including another sentence that builds on the definition; address that topic elsewhere.

trigger.signal: a second sentence in a definition paragraph

section: Defined Terms > Autonomous Definitions > Structure
statement: Don't enumerate a set of autonomous definitions.
severity_basis: alphabetical order is organization enough; (a) schemes reach (cccccccccc)

section: Defined Terms > Autonomous Definitions > Placement and Emphasis
statement: Place an autonomous definition either in a definition section or on-site; put on-site autonomous definitions (a sentence among others, or their own subsection if more than a couple of lines) right after the provisions that use the defined terms.
severity_basis: definitions given before the provisions puzzle readers; definitions given later, after unrelated text, make them work harder

section: Defined Terms > Autonomous Definitions > Placement and Emphasis
statement: Put the defined term in quotation marks and bold, in both autonomous definitions and defined-term parentheticals; don't bold the quotation marks.

trigger.signal: defined term at its definition not in bold quotation marks

section: Defined Terms > Autonomous Definitions > Definitional Verbs
statement: If the definition is full (it gives the entire meaning), use means.

section: Defined Terms > Autonomous Definitions > Definitional Verbs
statement: Don't use mean as the definitional verb, even when the defined term is plural; treat the defined term as a label.

examples.before: "Products" mean the MegaSonic motors listed in exhibit A.
examples.after: "Products" means the MegaSonic motors listed in exhibit A.

section: Defined Terms > Autonomous Definitions > Definitional Verbs
statement: Don't use is or are as the definitional verb.
severity_basis: is and are suit expository prose; means is simpler

examples.before: "Salvage" is cargo that has been damaged ...

section: Defined Terms > Autonomous Definitions > Definitional Verbs
statement: An enlarging definition (part of the meaning) uses includes; a limiting definition (excluding something) uses does not include. Used alone, both leave the full scope unstated and can create mischief.
severity_basis: Mattel v. MGA Entertainment (9th Cir. 2010): "includes, but is not limited to" let the parties fight over whether inventions covered ideas

section: Defined Terms > Autonomous Definitions > Definitional Verbs
statement: To avoid the uncertainty of enlarging or limiting definitions used alone, combine a full definition with either or both: W means X [and includes Y] [but does not include Z].
fix: Rewrite as "W" means X and includes Y but does not include Z.
severity_basis: vagueness, dispute risk, or legally significant usage

section: Defined Terms > Autonomous Definitions > Definitional Verbs
statement: Don't use means and includes, and don't use includes only.
severity_basis: a meaning can't be complete and incomplete at once; includes only equals means but is wordier and less clear

section: Defined Terms > Autonomous Definitions > Definitional Verbs
statement: Don't use a dash or a colon instead of a definitional verb.

examples.before: "ERISA"—the Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974

section: Defined Terms > Autonomous Definitions > Definitional Verbs
statement: State the definitional verb in the present tense; don't use shall mean or shall have the meaning.
severity_basis: definitions are language of policy; no duty is expressed

section: Defined Terms > Autonomous Definitions > Part of Speech
statement: With means, includes, or does not include, make the part of speech of the defined term match that of the definition; otherwise use refers to (for example, "Register", "Registered", and "Registration" refer to ...).

trigger.signal: a verb or adjective form defined with means by a noun phrase

test: Substitute the definition for the defined term in a sentence that uses it; if the grammar breaks, the parts of speech don't match.
severity_basis: vagueness, dispute risk, or legally significant usage

section: Defined Terms > Autonomous Definitions > Part of Speech
statement: If a term has identical noun and verb forms (Control, Transfer), you may define each separately: "[Defined Term]" means, when used as a noun, [first definition], and when used as a verb, [second definition].

section: Defined Terms > Autonomous Definitions > Part of Speech
statement: Be wary of an internal rule of interpretation giving defined terms corresponding meanings in other parts of speech; it could have unexpected consequences. If confusion is possible, define each form, and if you have an alternative to defining several forms, use it.
severity_basis: vagueness, dispute risk, or legally significant usage

section: Defined Terms > Autonomous Definitions > Stuffed Definitions
statement: Don't include in an autonomous definition anything beyond what the defined term means.
fix: Move conditions, obligations, makeup, and function into operative provisions.
severity_basis: stuffing sweeps complexity into defined terms and makes the reader unpack it; it also causes repetition elsewhere

section: Defined Terms > Autonomous Definitions > Stuffed Definitions
statement: Treat shall, must, may, or will in a definition as a symptom of stuffing; state the obligation elsewhere using language of obligation.
severity_basis: vagueness, dispute risk, or legally significant usage

examples.before: "Acme Financial Statements" means ... which Acme shall deliver no later than three months after the end of each Acme fiscal year.

section: Defined Terms > Autonomous Definitions > Stuffed Definitions
statement: Address conditions, requirements, and prohibitions (such as trustee approval not to be unreasonably withheld), and the makeup and function of a thing, separately from the definition of its identity.
severity_basis: vagueness, dispute risk, or legally significant usage

examples.after: Committee limited to "the Acme stock option committee," with its makeup and function addressed separately

section: Defined Terms > Autonomous Definitions > Stuffed Definitions
statement: Don't put an integrated definition inside an autonomous definition (... declared effective by the Securities and Exchange Commission (the "SEC")); define the term elsewhere and use just the defined term.
severity_basis: lengthens the definition, and a reader wouldn't look in an autonomous definition for another term's definition

section: Defined Terms > Integrated Definitions > Structure
statement: An integrated definition is part of a regular sentence, with the defined term stated in parentheses after the definition, in a "defined-term parenthetical."

examples.after: ... file with the SEC (those documents, the "Dynaco SEC Documents")

section: Defined Terms > Integrated Definitions > Structure
statement: If a defined-term parenthetical at the end of a list creates syntactic ambiguity about how far back the definition goes, consider prefacing the list with the following plus a colon, with the parenthetical between the following and the colon; or clarify the scope (6.75), or use an autonomous definition.

trigger.signal: defined-term parenthetical after the last item in a series

severity_basis: can change meaning or invite dispute

examples.after: the Promoter shall supply the Band with the following (the "Requirements"): (1) ...

section: Defined Terms > Integrated Definitions > Structure
statement: Don't use hereafter, hereinafter referred to as, or similar legalistic fluff in a defined-term parenthetical.

section: Defined Terms > Integrated Definitions > Structure
statement: In a defined-term parenthetical, include the, a, or an as appropriate (needed only for common nouns), and put it before (outside) the opening quotation mark.

examples.before: ("the Equipment")
examples.after: (the "Equipment")

section: Defined Terms > Integrated Definitions > Structure
statement: Don't put a defined-term parenthetical after a possessive.
severity_basis: the definition and the defined term aren't grammatically equivalent

examples.before: If a customer's (a "Terminating Customer") contract with Acme terminates ...

section: Defined Terms > Integrated Definitions > Structure
statement: Don't put a defined-term parenthetical in a section heading, and don't nest parentheses inside one.

section: Defined Terms > Integrated Definitions > Placement
statement: Put the defined-term parenthetical at the end of the definition, not in the middle; mid-definition placement is usually awkward but can change meaning.
test: Ask whether the words after the parenthetical are meant to be part of the definition.
severity_basis: can change meaning or invite dispute

examples.before: all contracts, oral or written ("Contracts"), to which Dynaco is a party
examples.after: all contracts, oral or written, to which Dynaco is a party (each such contract, a "Contract")

section: Defined Terms > Integrated Definitions > Placement
statement: Don't place a defined-term parenthetical beyond the end of the definition.

examples.before: The lease for Blackacre must be substantially in the form of exhibit B (the "Lease").
examples.after: The lease for Blackacre (the "Lease") must be substantially in the form of exhibit B.

section: Defined Terms > Integrated Definitions > Placement
statement: For an amount of money, put the defined-term parenthetical after the description of what the amount represents, not after the amount.
severity_basis: not every amount of $3 million is the Purchase Price

examples.before: The purchase price for the Shares is $3 million (the "Purchase Price").
examples.after: The purchase price for the Shares (the "Purchase Price") is $3 million.

section: Defined Terms > Integrated Definitions > Placement
statement: When creating the party-name defined term for an entity, place the defined-term parenthetical after the jurisdiction reference (see 2.93).

section: Defined Terms > Integrated Definitions > Scope, Collectively, Boosting, Stacking
statement: If it might be unclear how far back an integrated definition goes, put in the parenthetical, just before the defined term, a reference to the pertinent noun (that litigation, the "Acme Litigation"; each such consent, a "Required Consent").

trigger.signal: defined-term parenthetical after a long noun phrase or series with no scope-clarifying noun

severity_basis: unclear scope of a definition is syntactic ambiguity (12.1)

examples.after: (those documents, the "Dynaco SEC Documents")

section: Defined Terms > Integrated Definitions > Scope, Collectively, Boosting, Stacking
statement: If the definition consists of enumerated clauses, say so in the parenthetical: (the litigation listed in clauses (1) through (4) of this section 4(b), the "Acme Litigation").
severity_basis: can change meaning or invite dispute

section: Defined Terms > Integrated Definitions > Scope, Collectively, Boosting, Stacking
statement: If an integrated definition covers a whole string of nouns, you may add collectively to the parenthetical, just before the defined term and after any scope-clarifying language; if the last element is a plural noun, consider whether readers might apply collectively only to it.
severity_basis: can change meaning or invite dispute

examples.after: the Company, the Parent, and their respective subsidiaries and affiliates (collectively, the "Acme Entities")

section: Defined Terms > Integrated Definitions > Scope, Collectively, Boosting, Stacking
statement: You may supplement an integrated definition by adding language (generally together with) in the parenthetical, just before the defined term and after any scope language and collectively ("boosting"); don't use boosting inappropriately to add affiliates or subsidiaries to a party-name defined term.
severity_basis: vagueness, dispute risk, or legally significant usage

examples.after: ... and other Affiliates (collectively, together with the Company, the "Company Group")

section: Defined Terms > Integrated Definitions > Scope, Collectively, Boosting, Stacking
statement: You may define more than one term in one parenthetical, separated by a semicolon and each with its scope clarified ("stacking"); don't stack more than two, and you may boost the second term.

examples.after: (that agreement, the "Merger Agreement"; that merger, the "Merger")

section: Defined Terms > Integrated Definitions > Scope, Collectively, Boosting, Stacking
statement: In integrated definitions, match the part of speech of the defined term to the definition, adding transition language before the defined term if needed, or restructure the provision or define the term elsewhere.
severity_basis: vagueness, dispute risk, or legally significant usage

examples.after: At the Effective Time, Merger Sub will merge into Acme (the merger thus effected, the "Merger").

section: Defined Terms > Choosing and Placing Definitions
statement: Choose between integrated and autonomous definitions partly by length: a short definition is probably more efficient as an integrated definition, a long one as an autonomous definition; also consider where you create the term.

section: Defined Terms > Choosing and Placing Definitions
statement: Put a definition in a definition section or on-site. A definition section lists autonomous definitions alphabetically; head it Definitions, not Glossary.

section: Defined Terms > Choosing and Placing Definitions
statement: Don't use the Commonwealth two-column format for a definition section, or a variant that omits the definitional verb.
severity_basis: chops each sentence in two; omitting the verb implies means and precludes enlarging and limiting definitions and refers to

section: Defined Terms > Choosing and Placing Definitions
statement: To define a term on-site, place the definition where the contract makes most use of the term, not merely where it is first used; put an on-site autonomous definition right after the provision that uses it.
severity_basis: defining at first use makes the reader flip between the definition and the part that uses the term most

section: Defined Terms > Choosing and Placing Definitions
statement: Decide where to define a term by how far it can be understood without its definition: define entirely clear terms (SEC, ERISA, GAAP) and largely clear terms (Affiliate, Business Day) in the definition section; define custom-built terms (Equity Infusion, Excess Insurance Proceeds) on-site.
notes: The book's 6.92 cites "(6.92)" for "entirely clear"; the category is in 6.93.

section: Defined Terms > Choosing and Placing Definitions
statement: Don't put the definition section at the beginning of the body; pare it down to inherently familiar terms and move it toward the back, among the miscellaneous provisions (or dispense with it and define the few terms on-site).
severity_basis: readers care most about deal provisions; a reader who starts with definitions will need to reread them later

section: Defined Terms > Choosing and Placing Definitions
statement: Don't put the definition section in an attachment.

section: Defined Terms > Cross-Referencing to Definitions
statement: Avoid cross-references in the definition section to terms defined elsewhere ("Material Permits" has the meaning given that term in section 3.4).
severity_basis: wordy, and scattered alphabetically so readers still flip pages

section: Defined Terms > Cross-Referencing to Definitions
statement: Use an index of definitions listing all defined terms alphabetically in two columns with the page number (not section number) of each definition; call it an index of definitions, not an index of defined terms, and place it after the table of contents.
exceptions: A contract too short for a table of contents is presumably too short for an index (6.103).

section: Defined Terms > Cross-Referencing to Definitions
statement: Create the index with Word's indexing feature early, not just before signing; an index at the end of the definition section listing only on-site terms is less useful.

section: Defined Terms > Cross-Referencing to Definitions
statement: Don't say in the first section that some or all defined terms are defined in the definition section.

section: Defined Terms > Cross-Referencing to Definitions
statement: Don't put a cross-reference parenthetical such as (as defined in section x) after a defined term; use an index of definitions instead.
exceptions: Occasional use is unobjectionable if the contract has no index and a term is defined in a far corner where a reader might wonder (6.109).

section: Defined Terms > Mistakes in Using Defined Terms
statement: If the definition is the same as the defined term, supplement the definition or eliminate the defined term.

examples.before: The standstill period (the "Standstill Period") begins on the date of this agreement ...

section: Defined Terms > Mistakes in Using Defined Terms
statement: Eliminate a defined term whose meaning is already expressed in the sentence that uses it.

examples.before: The Buyer shall designate in writing a Buyer's Representative to act on its behalf.
examples.after: The Buyer shall designate in writing an individual to act on its behalf.

section: Defined Terms > Mistakes in Using Defined Terms
statement: Don't follow a defined term with something that is already a component of its definition.

examples.before: "Seller" means the entity providing Products or performing Services under the Master Services Agreement.
examples.after: "Seller" means the entity providing Products or performing Services.

examples.before: perform any of the Services specified in an SOW without ...
examples.after: perform any of the Services without ...

section: Defined Terms > Mistakes in Using Defined Terms
statement: Don't define term A by reference to term B and term B by reference to term A; anchor one definition to an external reality.
test: For each definition that uses another defined term, check whether that term's definition refers back.
severity_basis: a circular definition has no fixed meaning

examples.before: "Bonus Date" means a date on which Acme determines that a Bonus Period concludes. / "Bonus Period" means a period that ... concludes on a Bonus Date.

section: Defined Terms > Mistakes in Using Defined Terms
statement: Avoid defined terms that a reader might think combine other defined terms (Licensor, Software, and Licensor Software; Control and Change of Control); usually you can choose terms that eliminate the overlap.
severity_basis: vagueness, dispute risk, or legally significant usage

section: Defined Terms > Mistakes in Using Defined Terms
statement: Use autonomous and integrated definitions, not improvised alternatives.

examples.before: The following events shall be deemed "Events of Default" ...
... the Annual Delivery Period, which shall be defined for purposes hereof as ...

notes: The book prints "Although they might otherwise be objectionable"; the sense appears to be "might not otherwise be."

section: Defined Terms > Mistakes in Using Defined Terms
statement: As you revise, check that no defined term is defined but not used, or used but not defined; technology can help.
test: List every defined term; search for each one's uses; list every capitalized term in use and confirm it is defined.
severity_basis: vagueness, dispute risk, or legally significant usage

section: Defined Terms > Value Versus Cost
statement: Weigh each defined term's benefit (the economy it offers and how often it is used) against its cost (breaks in the text, parenthetical clutter, capitals, and the mental link to the definition); a short definition needs frequent use to justify a defined term.
exceptions: A sufficiently complex concept may warrant an autonomous definition even if used once (6.129).
If revising a template leaves only one or two instances, it might not be worth eliminating the term (6.130).

examples.before: "Agreement Term" used twice in a 12-page employment letter
examples.after: term of this agreement (and, for the other use, after termination)

section: Defined Terms > Value Versus Cost
statement: Don't rely on provisions that tie meaning to a dictionary, whether general (Oxford English Dictionary) or for a specific term (disparage).
severity_basis: meaning divorced from context is unpromising; a court is unlikely to limit itself to a dictionary for a term of art

section: Defined Terms > Value Versus Cost
statement: Don't use herein so called; it serves no evident purpose.

section: Sources of Uncertain Meaning > Introduction
statement: Distinguish six sources of uncertain meaning: ambiguity, not being sufficiently specific, mistake, conflict, not addressing an issue, and vagueness. Don't lump them all under "ambiguity," as courts and Black's Law Dictionary do.
severity_basis: each operates differently; misdiagnosis leads to the wrong fix
notes: Ambiguity, insufficient specificity, mistake, and conflict are presumably unintentional; not addressing an issue may be intentional; vagueness is an essential tool used with restraint (7.3).

section: Sources of Uncertain Meaning > Ambiguity
statement: Text is ambiguous if it can express two or more inconsistent meanings. Aim to eliminate ambiguity from contracts.
test: Can a reasonable reader give the text two or more meanings that are inconsistent with each other? If so, it is ambiguous.
exceptions: For ambiguity of the part versus the whole, it is unrealistic to eliminate all possible alternative meanings (7.5; 11.152-.156).
severity_basis: can change meaning or invite dispute
notes: Other kinds of ambiguity: time references (chapter 10), part versus whole (chapter 11), syntactic (chapter 12), language of discretion (3.222-.240).

section: Sources of Uncertain Meaning > Ambiguity
statement: Describe language as ambiguous even if the broader context resolves the ambiguity, rather than calling it unambiguous.
fix: Revise the text so it bears only the intended meaning without relying on context (7.5).
severity_basis: saying the language is ambiguous but resolved by context better reflects how ambiguity operates (7.6)

section: Sources of Uncertain Meaning > Ambiguity
statement: Don't engage in "creative ambiguity" (deliberately ambiguous wording meant to invoke a hidden meaning later).
severity_basis: antithetical to a successful relationship; might violate ethics rules; may be barred by the forthright negotiator principle (United Rentals v. RAM Holdings, Del. Ch. 2007); contra proferentem works against the party responsible

section: Sources of Uncertain Meaning > Ambiguity
statement: Train yourself to spot ambiguity; it doesn't come naturally, and most ambiguity is subtle enough to go unnoticed.
severity_basis: can change meaning or invite dispute

section: Sources of Uncertain Meaning > Ambiguity
statement: Lexical ambiguity: a word or phrase with more than one meaning, whether homonymy (unrelated meanings: bank of a river versus a financial institution) or polysemy (related senses: bank as an institution or its building).

trigger.signal: a word with two or more established meanings used where either could apply

test: List the established meanings of the word; ask whether more than one fits the provision. Homonymy rarely confuses in contracts; polysemy is the usual risk.
fix: State the intended meaning instead of the ambiguous word, or make the word a defined term.
exceptions: Routine instances (represents, material, year) have routine fixes; nonroutine words take imagination to spot (7.15).
severity_basis: whether foreclosure meant foreclosure proceedings or a foreclosure sale (Provident Bank v. Tennessee Farmers Mutual Insurance Co., 6th Cir. 2007)

section: Sources of Uncertain Meaning > Ambiguity
statement: Antecedent ambiguity: a pronoun or other referring word or phrase (said, such, thereof, it, those, the fee) for which two or more antecedents present themselves.

trigger.signal: a referring word whose antecedent could be either of two or more earlier nouns or noun phrases

test: For each referring word, list every earlier noun phrase it could point to; if more than one fits grammatically and sensibly, it is ambiguous.
fix: Make clear which antecedent you mean: repeat the noun, use a defined term, or restructure. Replace archaic referring words (said, thereof, such meaning those).
severity_basis: Loso v. Loso (Conn. App. Ct. 2011) (said cost); Trustees of First Union v. Mandell (7th Cir. 1993) (thereof); SCA Promotions v. Yahoo! (5th Cir. 2017) (the fee); Rainy Sky v. Kookmin Bank [2011] UKSC 50 (such sums)

examples.before: The defendant agrees to pay for one-half the cost of Sarah's college educational expenses ... subject to the limitation that said cost shall not exceed the tuition for a full-time residential student at UCONN-Storrs.
examples.after: The defendant shall pay half the cost of Sarah's college educational expenses for a four-year degree net of any scholarships and grants, up to an amount equal to half the tuition for a full-time residential student at UCONN-Storrs.

notes: Three of the four cited examples involve archaisms, so antecedent ambiguity is harder to spot in traditional contract language (7.22).

section: Sources of Uncertain Meaning > Ambiguity
statement: Contract-reference ambiguity: here-words (herein, hereunder, hereof, hereto, hereinbelow) and pointing words (above, below, the foregoing, as aforesaid) leave unclear whether they refer to part of the contract or the whole, or which part; hereunder can also be read as "below" rather than "by operation of."

trigger.signal: a here-word or pointing word instead of a reference to a specific section

test: Ask whether the word could mean the whole contract, the current section, or the text immediately before or after; if more than one reading is possible, it is ambiguous.
fix: Refer to the whole contract as this agreement or to a specific section by number (section 4.2); use hereby only in language of performance.
severity_basis: herein (Pronschinske Trust v. Kaw Valley, 7th Cir.; Karmely v. Wertheimer, 2d Cir. 2013; Bayerische Landesbank v. Aladdin, 2d Cir. 2012); hereunder (Medicis v. Anacor, Del. Ch. 2013; Weichert v. Faust, Md. 2011; Yosemite v. Nationwide, S.D.N.Y. 2016); the foregoing (Karmely); except as provided below (In re Lehman Bros., 2d Cir. 2013)
notes: The book prints the Pronschinske Trust citation as 899 F.2d 470 (7th Cir. 2018); the reporter series appears to be a misprint (unverified).

section: Sources of Uncertain Meaning > Ambiguity
statement: Don't use here-words, except hereby in language of performance.
fix: Use this agreement, or a specific section reference.
severity_basis: can change meaning or invite dispute

section: Sources of Uncertain Meaning > Ambiguity
statement: When pointing to other parts of a contract, refer to specific sections, not above, below, the foregoing, or as aforesaid.
severity_basis: can change meaning or invite dispute

section: Sources of Uncertain Meaning > Ambiguity
statement: Don't call a provision ambiguous merely because the parties attribute alternative meanings to it; an ill-informed dispute isn't enough (and courts too may see ambiguity where none exists).

section: Sources of Uncertain Meaning > Ambiguity
statement: Don't be satisfied with unambiguous drafting; aim to avoid fights. For example, don't rely on a comma to establish meaning.

trigger.signal: meaning that depends on the presence or absence of a comma

fix: Restructure so the meaning doesn't depend on punctuation.
severity_basis: can change meaning or invite dispute

section: Sources of Uncertain Meaning > Other Sources
statement: Not being sufficiently specific: a word or phrase too general for the issue it must decide (full-time basis, subcontractor, cohabitation, offshore, computer gaming business) can lead to fights over which more specific meaning was intended. Courts call it ambiguity; "insufficiently specific" is more accurate.

trigger.signal: a general word or phrase that must decide a borderline question (who counts, what counts, how much)

test: Ask what borderline cases the parties could argue about, and whether the text answers them.
fix: Specify the criteria (for example, hours, duration, employee versus consultant).
exceptions: Insufficient specificity can result from changing circumstances rather than a drafting glitch (7.34; Richey v. Metaxpert, 9th Cir. 2010).
severity_basis: In re C.P.Y. (Tex. App. 2012) (full-time basis); Graev v. Graev (N.Y. 2008) (cohabitation); Jones v. Francis Drilling Fluids (S.D. Tex. 2008) (offshore)

section: Sources of Uncertain Meaning > Other Sources
statement: Mistake: the parties are mistaken about the facts and the contract reflects that mistake (two ships named Peerless, Raffles v. Wichelhaus). Don't label this "latent ambiguity"; the text doesn't present alternative meanings.
test: Check that each name, identifier, and factual reference picks out the thing both parties intend.
fix: Identify things by unique particulars (date, number, location).
severity_basis: vagueness, dispute risk, or legally significant usage

section: Sources of Uncertain Meaning > Other Sources
statement: Conflict: two or more components of a contract aren't compatible, often through careless repetition (words and digits that don't match) or entire provisions that conflict (remedies provisions; an establishing-jurisdiction provision versus a consent-to-jurisdiction provision).

trigger.signal: the same matter addressed in two places, or amounts stated in both words and digits

test: Find every provision addressing the same subject and confirm they can all apply together.
fix: State each point once; reconcile or delete conflicting provisions.
severity_basis: United Rentals v. RAM Holdings (Del. Ch. 2007); NB Alternatives Advisers v. VAT Master (Del. Ch. 2021)

section: Sources of Uncertain Meaning > Other Sources
statement: Not addressing an issue: by oversight, the drafter doesn't address an issue that should have been addressed (Sabatini v. Roybal: a "private garage" restriction said nothing about size). It is harder to avoid than other sources, because you must figure out what's missing.
test: For each provision, ask what a party could do that complies with the words but defeats the purpose (size, number, timing, who decides).
exceptions: The parties may intentionally leave an issue unaddressed when negotiating it isn't worth the time given the limited likelihood it arises; that might involve risk (7.45).
severity_basis: can change meaning or invite dispute

section: Sources of Uncertain Meaning > Vagueness
statement: Vague words include prompt, reasonable, material, negligent, satisfactory, substantial, and related adverbs. Vagueness involves no clear demarcation (borderline cases) and dependence on context, judged by what a reasonable person would do in the circumstances.
severity_basis: vagueness, dispute risk, or legally significant usage

section: Sources of Uncertain Meaning > Vagueness
statement: Prefer a specific standard (no later than five days after) to a vague one (promptly) where you can.
severity_basis: vagueness brings the possibility of dispute

examples.before: promptly
examples.after: no later than five days after

section: Sources of Uncertain Meaning > Vagueness
statement: Use vagueness when lack of control over the future or someone else's conduct makes a precise standard senseless (for example, reimbursing reasonable legal expenses), or when addressing an issue precisely would make negotiations longer or more contentious than the parties want.
severity_basis: vagueness, dispute risk, or legally significant usage
notes: Different vague words pose different challenges: promptly may have clear-cut time constraints; substantial leaves the parties wondering where on a spectrum it falls (7.50).

section: Sources of Uncertain Meaning > Vagueness
statement: Use vagueness only if not too much is at stake and the context is commonplace enough that the parties and any court have a basis for determining what is reasonable in the circumstances.
severity_basis: vagueness, dispute risk, or legally significant usage

section: Sources of Uncertain Meaning > Vagueness
statement: Reduce the scope of vagueness, for example by adding specific obligations alongside a reasonable efforts obligation.
severity_basis: vagueness, dispute risk, or legally significant usage

section: Sources of Uncertain Meaning > Vagueness
statement: Treat gradations of vagueness as unhelpful, as with negligent, grossly negligent, reckless, and wanton, and especially a supposed spectrum of efforts standards.
exceptions: In the right context a spectrum can be subdivided coherently, as with MSCD's distinction between material (dealbreaker) and nontrivial (7.55).
severity_basis: vagueness, dispute risk, or legally significant usage

section: Sources of Uncertain Meaning > Blurred Boundaries
statement: The categories blend: lexical ambiguity and insufficient specificity differ by degree, as do insufficient specificity and failing to address an issue; a usage can be both vague and ambiguous (best efforts, material).
severity_basis: vagueness, dispute risk, or legally significant usage

section: Reasonable Efforts > Thesis and Function
statement: An "efforts standard" is a phrase featuring the word efforts; an "efforts provision" is a contract sentence that includes an efforts standard.

section: Reasonable Efforts > Thesis and Function
statement: Don't treat efforts standards as a hierarchy: best efforts, reasonable efforts, commercially reasonable efforts, and the rest all come down to reasonableness.
severity_basis: requiring more than reasonable effort is unreasonable and unworkably uncertain, and the hierarchy gives best, commercially, and all meanings inconsistent with colloquial English (8.79); U.S. courts mostly reject a hierarchy, English and Canadian courts endorse it (8.2)

section: Reasonable Efforts > Thesis and Function
statement: Use an efforts standard when one party wants another to further a goal that nonparties (or weather or other unpredictable natural events) have a say in achieving, such as obtaining a permit or consents, or promoting sales.

trigger.signal: unqualified obligation to achieve a result outside the obligor's control (Acme shall obtain the Permits) or to promote a goal (Jones shall promote the sale of Widgets)

test: Ask whether achieving the goal is entirely within the party's control. If not, an unqualified obligation makes the party liable however hard it worked.
severity_basis: an unqualified obligation to promote invites argument over whether negligible or all-consuming performance is required
notes: Efforts standards save time and reduce contention but are inherently vague; the expedience comes at the risk of disagreement after signing (8.5-.6). The chapter addresses explicit efforts standards, not implied ones (8.7; Wood v. Lucy, Lady Duff Gordon).

section: Reasonable Efforts > Components
statement: An efforts standard has components: a noun (efforts or endeavours); "qualitative" adjectives (reasonable, best, good-faith, diligent, and others, alone or combined, as in reasonable best efforts); postpositive modifiers (efforts that are reasonable; efforts in good faith); activity adjectives; determiners; and a verb. The variety adds confusion and nothing of value.

trigger.regex_hint: (?i)\befforts? (that are|in good faith|consistent with)\b|\b(reasonable best|best good[- ]faith|reasonable and prudent)\s+efforts\b

severity_basis: vagueness, dispute risk, or legally significant usage
notes: Figure 4 surveys EDGAR usage (8.8, 8.11).

section: Reasonable Efforts > Components
statement: Use efforts rather than endeavours (or endeavors); the difference is only one of style, endeavours is in long decline, and the modern choice is efforts.
exceptions: English and Australian drafters favor endeavours; nothing suggests English judges would treat the switch as changing meaning (8.171).

section: Reasonable Efforts > Components
statement: Don't use other nouns in place of efforts (for example, actions); they offer only needless variety.
notes: On degree of care, see Adams blog post of 11 Oct. 2022 (8.10).

section: Reasonable Efforts > Components
statement: Don't use an "activity" adjective in an efforts standard (reasonable sales efforts); it inflicts abstract nouns on the reader and invites redundancy.

examples.before: Acme shall use reasonable sales effort to sell ...

section: Reasonable Efforts > Components
statement: Don't use commercially (or commercial) in an efforts standard; it is redundant and invites legalistic arguments for a different meaning. If you mean something other than reasonable efforts, say so explicitly.
fix: Use reasonable efforts.
severity_basis: AB Stable VIII v. Maps Hotels (Del. Ch. 2020) held commercially redundant; Menn v. ConMed (Del. Ch. 2022) read commercially best efforts as best efforts

section: Reasonable Efforts > Components
statement: Don't use very (very best efforts), all (all reasonable efforts), or every (every reasonable effort) in an efforts standard; they are delexicalized flourishes that invite attribution of meaning. Use efforts in the plural.
severity_basis: UBH v. Standard Life (Q.B. 1986) treated all reasonable endeavours as a middle position; the meaning attributed to all can't be explained

section: Reasonable Efforts > Components
statement: Use the verb use with an efforts standard (use reasonable efforts); don't vary the verb and don't add a pronoun (use its reasonable efforts).

examples.before: use its reasonable efforts
examples.after: use reasonable efforts

section: Reasonable Efforts > Components
statement: Don't combine an efforts standard with a substitute verb (use reasonable efforts to endeavor; endeavor to use reasonable efforts), and don't say a party shall not negligently permit an act instead of requiring it to use reasonable efforts to stop the act.

words: to the best of its ability

severity_basis: silly redundancy; substitutes (utmost, aggressively, to the best of its ability) add needless variety

section: Reasonable Efforts > Components
statement: Don't use on a best-efforts basis as a wordy alternative to a conventional efforts provision.
exceptions: On a best-efforts basis remains a securities term of art (8.19).

examples.before: The parties shall work together on a best-efforts basis to obtain ... all necessary Work Authorizations.
examples.after: The parties shall together use reasonable efforts to obtain ... all necessary Work Authorizations.

section: Reasonable Efforts > Enforceability
statement: If a provision makes an arrangement contingent on future agreement, use a good-faith standard (negotiate in good faith) rather than an efforts standard, and don't use future agreement to put off negotiations.
exceptions: Illinois holds a best-efforts promise too vague to bind if the parties fail to articulate what performance it requires (Kraftco v. Kolbus, Ill. App. Ct. 1971) (8.20).
Sometimes contingency on future agreement is unavoidable (8.22).
severity_basis: some courts hold an obligation to use efforts to agree unenforceable (Pinnacle Books v. Harlequin, S.D.N.Y. 1981; Phillips Petroleum v. Enron [1997] CLC 329); the Seventh Circuit equated it with negotiating in good faith (Denil v. DeBoer, 2011)

section: Reasonable Efforts > Enforceability
statement: Because efforts standards are vague, compliance depends on the circumstances of the case, with the uncertainty that entails.
severity_basis: Martin v. Monumental Life (3d Cir. 2001); Triple-A Baseball Club v. Northeastern Baseball (1st Cir. 1987)

section: Reasonable Efforts > Commentary and Caselaw
statement: Don't rely on commentary describing a hierarchy (ABA M&A Committee "general sense of a hierarchy"; Garner; Stark); much of it is insubstantial or misdescribes U.S. caselaw. English and Canadian commentators treat the hierarchy as established fact.
severity_basis: vagueness, dispute risk, or legally significant usage

section: Reasonable Efforts > Commentary and Caselaw
statement: U.S. courts, with a few isolated exceptions, reject the idea that best efforts requires every conceivable effort and decline to recognize a hierarchy; they variously equate best efforts with good faith, more than good faith, diligence, or reasonableness, and often with reasonable efforts.
exceptions: Only three opinions suggest best efforts is more onerous, without explanation, and none has been followed: In re Hyman Cos. (Bankr. E.D. Pa. 2010); In re Chateaugay (S.D.N.Y. 1996); Krinsky v. Long Beach Wings (Cal. Ct. App. 2002) (8.37).
severity_basis: Coady v. Toyota (1st Cir. 2004): "cannot mean everything possible under the sun"; Bloor v. Falstaff (2d Cir. 1979); Stewart v. O'Neill (2002); Soroof Trading (S.D.N.Y. 2012)

section: Reasonable Efforts > Commentary and Caselaw
statement: Don't use good-faith efforts; it brings back uncertainty, because courts will likely apply whatever standard they use for the implied duty of good faith (which might require dishonesty for breach, or rest on reasonableness), and whether good faith is objective or subjective is unsettled.
severity_basis: vagueness, dispute risk, or legally significant usage

section: Reasonable Efforts > Commentary and Caselaw
statement: Delaware courts don't distinguish efforts standards in practice: Williams v. Energy Transfer (Del. 2017) read commercially reasonable efforts and reasonable best efforts alike as requiring all reasonable steps; Akorn (Del. Ch. 2018) drew no distinction; AB Stable (Del. Ch. 2020) held commercially redundant. Strine's Williams dissent is a nonbinding exception.
severity_basis: vagueness, dispute risk, or legally significant usage

section: Reasonable Efforts > Commentary and Caselaw
statement: Under UCC § 2-306(2), a lawful exclusive-dealing agreement imposes, unless otherwise agreed, best efforts to supply and to promote; Official Comment 5 equates that with reasonable diligence and good faith, which appears to preclude treating best efforts as more onerous for Article 2.
severity_basis: vagueness, dispute risk, or legally significant usage

section: Reasonable Efforts > Commentary and Caselaw
statement: Know that English and Canadian courts endorse a hierarchy (Rhodia v. Huntsman: reasonable endeavours "probably" requires one reasonable course, best endeavours all of them, in obiter dicta; Atmospheric Diving Systems (B.C.S.C. 1994): best efforts is higher, yet means all reasonable steps), although Jet2.com v. Blackpool Airport (EWCA 2012) treated best and all reasonable endeavours as meaning the same.
severity_basis: a drafter in those jurisdictions faces a court that may read best efforts as requiring more than reasonable performance

section: Reasonable Efforts > Commentary and Caselaw
statement: The High Court of Australia reads best endeavours as requiring what a party reasonably can do "but no more" (Hospital Products, 1984; Electricity Generation v. Woodside, 2014); Singapore's Court of Appeal (KS Energy, 2014) found all reasonable endeavours not usefully distinguishable from best endeavours yet more onerous than reasonable endeavours.
severity_basis: vagueness, dispute risk, or legally significant usage

section: Reasonable Efforts > Why a Hierarchy Fails
statement: Don't use best efforts: in colloquial English best is a delexicalized flourish that doesn't signal acting more than reasonably, but legalistic readers attribute extra meaning to it, so best efforts is ambiguous as well as vague.
fix: Use reasonable efforts, ideally as a defined term (8.155).
severity_basis: can change meaning or invite dispute

section: Reasonable Efforts > Why a Hierarchy Fails
statement: Reasonable efforts is a legal construct absent from colloquial English, best understood as the profession's response to fears that judges would ignore the idiomatic meaning of best efforts.
notes: 8.106 prints 28 of 44 COCA examples as "67%"; the arithmetic gives about 64% (confirmed as printed, p. 403).

section: Reasonable Efforts > Why a Hierarchy Fails
statement: Don't try to impose an obligation to act more than reasonably through an efforts standard; there is no basis for deciding how much more than reasonable is required, as with the chaotic degrees of negligence.
severity_basis: vagueness, dispute risk, or legally significant usage

section: Reasonable Efforts > Interpreting Efforts Provisions
statement: Recognize that neither side of the efforts debate offers a plausible explanation: U.S. courts reject a hierarchy without stating a rationale, and cases and commentary supporting one merely assert it (Rhodia's one-course/all-courses distinction; Brooke Homes; Atmospheric Diving Systems; law-firm newsletters), expressed in equivocal terms (probably, might, normally) that make relying on them rash.
severity_basis: no court has applied the Rhodia construct, and guidance divorced from the facts is unhelpful because circumstances give endeavours provisions meaning (8.70, 8.76)

section: Reasonable Efforts > Interpreting Efforts Provisions
statement: When interpreting efforts provisions, watch for two elements used to justify a hierarchy against the evidence: the conceptual explanation (it's valid because many think so; words mean what people think; different words express different meanings) and the semantics explanation (intuition about reasonable meaning "moderate" and best meaning "excelling all others").
severity_basis: the presumption that different words carry different meanings is only a presumption to weigh against other considerations

section: Reasonable Efforts > Interpreting Efforts Provisions
statement: Don't look to English endeavours caselaw for drafting guidance: because the courts can't articulate the distinction, and endeavours provisions depend on their circumstances, caselaw can tell you nothing reliable about the hierarchy.
severity_basis: vagueness, dispute risk, or legally significant usage

section: Reasonable Efforts > How to Draft Efforts Provisions
statement: Choose reason and clarity over legalistic hair-splitting; don't defer to court-interpreted "tested" language, which was tested because it was confusing.
severity_basis: vagueness, dispute risk, or legally significant usage

section: Reasonable Efforts > How to Draft Efforts Provisions
statement: Use efforts provisions only if the party lacks complete control over achieving the goal; be cautious about using them as an expedient substitute for being specific.
test: Is achieving the goal entirely within the obligor's control? If so, state an unqualified obligation.
severity_basis: vagueness leads to disputes and unpredictable outcomes

section: Reasonable Efforts > How to Draft Efforts Provisions
statement: Use only reasonable efforts, and stick with efforts rather than something more colloquial such as shall try.
fix: Change to reasonable efforts.
severity_basis: any other standard carries significant risk of confusion and won't reliably deliver what many think it promises

section: Reasonable Efforts > How to Draft Efforts Provisions
statement: To reduce vagueness, supplement a reasonable efforts obligation with unqualified obligations for related tasks within the party's control (for example, require Acme to apply for the permit by a specified date).

trigger.signal: reasonable efforts to obtain something with no specific steps or deadlines

severity_basis: vagueness, dispute risk, or legally significant usage

section: Reasonable Efforts > How to Draft Efforts Provisions
statement: If the other side balks at reasonable efforts, explain that the notion that best efforts is more onerous doesn't make sense, and that caselaw doesn't support it (U.S.) or is confused (England, Canada).

section: Reasonable Efforts > How to Draft Efforts Provisions
statement: Don't use best efforts against an other side unaware of U.S. caselaw in the hope it will exert itself more; seek a meeting of the minds instead.
severity_basis: vagueness, dispute risk, or legally significant usage

section: Reasonable Efforts > How to Draft Efforts Provisions
statement: Always incorporate in a reasonable efforts obligation a standard for measuring performance (how many, how quickly, how soon); a vague one such as promptly suffices.

trigger.signal: efforts obligation with no goal, quantity, or timing

test: Ask: against what goal or deadline would a court measure whether the efforts were enough?
exceptions: Some courts (New York, per TPTCC NY v. Radiation Therapy Services, S.D.N.Y. 2011) expect unrealistic detail; drafters can't be expected to offer much in the way of guidelines (8.143).
severity_basis: Kevin M. Ehringer Enterprises v. McData (5th Cir. 2011): a best efforts promise without a goal or guideline was unenforceable; Herrmann Holdings v. Lucent (5th Cir. 2002): "as promptly as practicable" made it enforceable

section: Reasonable Efforts > How to Draft Efforts Provisions
statement: Instead of creating a new standard, consider referring to a benchmark courts have used: past performance, promises in negotiations, industry practice, the promisor's efforts under similar contracts, or how the promisor would act if promisor and promisee were one entity.
severity_basis: vagueness, dispute risk, or legally significant usage
notes: The less specific the standards, the more likely a court balances the obligation against the promisor's broader business constraints (8.145; Martin v. Monumental Life).

section: Reasonable Efforts > How to Draft Efforts Provisions
statement: Consider how other provisions affect the performance an efforts provision requires: a right to terminate for missed sales targets may lead a court to treat the targets as minimum acceptable performance, but keep the reasonable efforts obligation, which preserves a breach claim and a basis to terminate without waiting for a missed target.
severity_basis: vagueness, dispute risk, or legally significant usage

section: Reasonable Efforts > How to Draft Efforts Provisions
statement: Delete to the extent possible and similar phrases from an efforts provision; an efforts provision already implies the party might be unable to comply.

examples.before: Acme shall use reasonable efforts to cancel or mitigate, to the extent possible, each obligation that would cause Acme to incur expenses ...
examples.after: Acme shall use reasonable efforts to cancel or mitigate each obligation that would cause Acme to incur expenses ...

section: Reasonable Efforts > How to Draft Efforts Provisions
statement: Don't refer to good faith or diligence in a reasonable efforts provision, and don't place any other modifier after efforts.

examples.before: Each party shall use reasonable efforts, undertaken diligently and in good faith, to obtain all Consents before Closing.
examples.after: Each party shall use reasonable efforts to obtain all Consents before Closing.

section: Reasonable Efforts > How to Draft Efforts Provisions
statement: Don't use more than one efforts standard in a contract; harmonize a template's standards if necessary.
