test: Search for every efforts standard; all should be the same phrase.
severity_basis: multiple standards invite the argument that each means something different

section: Reasonable Efforts > Defining Reasonable Efforts
statement: Consider making Reasonable Efforts a defined term, stating its core meaning and anything excluded: "Reasonable Efforts" means, regarding conduct by a party, the efforts that a reasonable person in the position of that party would use to engage in that conduct competently and promptly.
severity_basis: vagueness, dispute risk, or legally significant usage

section: Reasonable Efforts > Defining Reasonable Efforts
statement: Make the Reasonable Efforts definition work in every context it appears (obligations, conditions, statements of fact); state expectations about maintaining a status or stopping something in the provision itself; otherwise customize the core definition.
severity_basis: vagueness, dispute risk, or legally significant usage

section: Reasonable Efforts > Defining Reasonable Efforts
statement: Don't use a Reasonable Efforts definition that lists actions a party must take; state any absolute requirement as a freestanding obligation.
severity_basis: vagueness, dispute risk, or legally significant usage

examples.before: "Reasonable Efforts" means, among other things, that the Company shall submit to the SEC, within two business days after ... a request for acceleration of effectiveness ...

section: Reasonable Efforts > Defining Reasonable Efforts
statement: Limit extreme interpretations with specific carve-outs from reasonable efforts (for example, incurring expenses over stated amounts, incurring liabilities, changing business strategy, disposing of significant assets, violating law, imperiling existence or solvency, initiating litigation), using a clearer device than the traditional proviso.
severity_basis: Rex Medical v. Angiotech (S.D.N.Y. 2010) held financial hardship irrelevant to a commercially reasonable efforts obligation

section: Reasonable Efforts > Defining Reasonable Efforts
statement: Some common carve-outs (for example, actions that would result in a material adverse change in that party) likely fall outside reasonable efforts anyway, but a party may include them to make doubly sure.

section: Reasonable Efforts > Defining Reasonable Efforts
statement: If you intend compliance to require more than reasonable conduct, say so in the definition or provision (for example, acknowledging that the money and personnel a reasonable person would devote are unlimited); expect few to accept it.
severity_basis: vagueness, dispute risk, or legally significant usage

examples.after: Acme acknowledges that the money that a reasonable person in Acme's position would be willing to expend on, and the personnel ... devote to, complying with its obligations under this section 11 are unlimited.

section: Reasonable Efforts > Negotiating Efforts Provisions
statement: Don't tolerate anything in the contract or negotiation record suggesting you accept a hierarchy of efforts standards; an unsophisticated court might find it meaningful.
severity_basis: In re Hyman Cos. (Bankr. E.D. Pa. 2010) relied on an amendment from reasonable efforts to best efforts as showing reasonable efforts would not satisfy the duty

section: Reasonable Efforts > Negotiating Efforts Provisions
statement: If you agree to best efforts to get the deal done, put on the record that you don't accept that it requires more than reasonable performance; if you agree to change best efforts to reasonable efforts, put on the record that you do so as a matter of clear drafting, not because it changes meaning.
severity_basis: can change meaning or invite dispute

section: Material > Usage and Caselaw Meanings
statement: Drafters use material and materially (modifying adjectives and verbs) to narrow a broad provision to what matters; material also appears in material adverse change (MAC) and material adverse effect (MAE).
severity_basis: vagueness, dispute risk, or legally significant usage

section: Material > Usage and Caselaw Meanings
statement: Treat material as ambiguous as well as vague: it can mean "nontrivial" (worth a reasonable person's attention) or "dealbreaker" (enough to affect whether a reasonable person would do the deal), and caselaw hasn't addressed that.
test: For each use, ask whether a reasonable reader could read it as nontrivial or as dealbreaker, and which the client needs.
fix: Replace with nontrivial (or trivial) or dealbreaker, or use Material as a defined term (9.51-.64).
severity_basis: the Salesforce sentence could mean "except trivial changes" or "not to a dealbreaker extent," and has no plain meaning (9.42-.44); ambiguity on top of vagueness hides the implications (9.45)

examples.before: SFDC will not materially decrease the overall security of the Services ...
examples.after: SFDC will not decrease more than trivially the overall security of the Services.

notes: Second printing deleted the 9.3 summary sentence that "you'll look in vain for some shared understanding of what material means"; no rule changed. The cited article is 21 Scribes J. Legal Writing (2023-2024); first page given as 85 in the second-printing post but 83 in Adams's resume (unresolved).

section: Material > Usage and Caselaw Meanings
statement: Don't assume every contract use of material breach means common-law material breach (nonperformance that goes to the root of the contract); because material is ambiguous, say which meaning you intend.
severity_basis: 14 Williston on Contracts §§ 43:5-43:6 (material = goes to the root, heart, or essence)
notes: It would seem unhelpful to exclude common-law material breach from an otherwise comprehensive termination provision (9.6).

section: Material > Usage and Caselaw Meanings
statement: Under TSC Industries v. Northway (U.S. 1976), an omitted fact is material if there is a substantial likelihood a reasonable shareholder would consider it important in deciding how to vote; courts apply this to disclosure generally and to contracts (Frontier Oil v. Holly, Del. Ch. 2005).
severity_basis: vagueness, dispute risk, or legally significant usage

section: Material > Usage and Caselaw Meanings
statement: Under IBP v. Tyson Foods (Del. Ch. 2001), a MAE closing condition protects the acquirer from unknown events that substantially threaten the target's overall earnings potential in a durationally significant manner; a buyer must make a "strong showing" (a "heavy burden," Snow Phipps, Del. Ch. 2021) to invoke it.
severity_basis: vagueness, dispute risk, or legally significant usage

section: Material > Usage and Caselaw Meanings
statement: Under Akorn v. Fresenius Kabi (Del. Ch. 2018), in all material respects excludes "small, de minimis, and nitpicky issues" and sets a standard less onerous than common-law material breach, limited to issues significant in the context of the contract.
severity_basis: vagueness, dispute risk, or legally significant usage

section: Material > Usage and Caselaw Meanings
statement: Don't look to caselaw for clear drafting of materiality: courts resolve disputes over dysfunctional language, and caselaw on materiality is patchwork from unrelated contexts.

section: Material > Expressing the Two Meanings
statement: Don't use significant to express a materiality threshold; it is ambiguous between "worthy of attention" and the weakened sense "noticeable" (in effect, not insignificant). Use nontrivial instead.
fix: Use nontrivial (or trivial), or dealbreaker.
severity_basis: can change meaning or invite dispute

section: Material > Expressing the Two Meanings
statement: Don't use words of importance that show "free-floating vagueness" (minor, significant, important, substantial, essential, major) to set thresholds, and don't build a hierarchy of levels from them.
severity_basis: uncertainty about the quantum, with no guarantee the other party agrees; hierarchies are unworkable, as with efforts standards and degrees of negligence

section: Material > Expressing the Two Meanings
statement: Use "inflection-point vagueness," tying importance to a change in incentives. The first inflection point is nontrivial: something a reasonable person in the party's position would pay attention to, equating with TSC Industries and Akorn's exclusion of small, de minimis, and nitpicky issues.
severity_basis: vagueness, dispute risk, or legally significant usage

section: Material > Expressing the Two Meanings
statement: The second inflection point is dealbreaker: the deal depends on it, equating with common-law material breach and IBP's strong showing. Delaware applies the dealbreaker meaning to MAC, but semantics gives no basis to confine it there.
severity_basis: vagueness, dispute risk, or legally significant usage

section: Material > Expressing the Two Meanings
statement: To gauge what material probably means in a provision, consider what is at stake: in provisions about the economic bargain (statements of fact, obligations) it sensibly means nontrivial; in provisions that let a party call off the deal (closing conditions, termination for material breach) a committed party would want it to mean dealbreaker.
severity_basis: can change meaning or invite dispute

examples.before: Alpha is not in material breach of any Gamma Contract.

notes: Because material is ambiguous, you can't be certain what drafters intended in a given contract (9.41).

section: Material > Expressing the Two Meanings
statement: Use materially, not in all material respects, as the adverbial form of material: is materially accurate, not is accurate in all material respects.
severity_basis: in all material respects is wordier and more legalistic and doesn't work in some contexts (at a price materially below Fair Market Value); materially always works

examples.before: is accurate in all material respects
examples.after: is materially accurate

examples.before: is in all material respects in compliance with
examples.after: is materially in compliance with

section: Material > Alternatives to Material
statement: Omit material from contracts; express its two meanings with nontrivial (and trivial) and dealbreaker, or use Material as a defined term for the dealbreaker meaning.
severity_basis: can change meaning or invite dispute

section: Material > Alternatives to Material
statement: Use nontrivial for the lower threshold; no nontrivial is a legitimate double negative, equal to the two positive forms (only trivial litigation, or no litigation).
severity_basis: vagueness, dispute risk, or legally significant usage

examples.before: There is no material litigation pending against the Company.
examples.after: There is no nontrivial litigation pending against the Company.

section: Material > Alternatives to Material
statement: Consider dealbreaker for the higher threshold; it needn't be a defined term. It has no negative form, so use it in a negative structure (not dealbreaker inaccurate).
severity_basis: vagueness, dispute risk, or legally significant usage

examples.before: were materially accurate on the date of this agreement and are materially accurate at Closing
examples.after: were not dealbreaker inaccurate on the date of this agreement and are not dealbreaker inaccurate at Closing

section: Material > Alternatives to Material
statement: If the contract uses MAC, use Material as a defined term rather than dealbreaker, for consistency.
severity_basis: readers would be confused by material (in MAC) and dealbreaker elsewhere expressing the same meaning

section: Material > Alternatives to Material
statement: If you keep material, define it for the dealbreaker standard, referring to both entry and consummation: "Material" and "Materially" refer to a [dealbreaker] level of significance that would have affected the decision of a reasonable person in the Buyer's position regarding whether to enter into this agreement or would affect [that] decision regarding whether to consummate the transaction. If more than one party is subject to materiality standards, define it "regarding a given Person."
severity_basis: vagueness, dispute risk, or legally significant usage

section: Material > Alternatives to Material
statement: When a statement of fact has two nouns materiality could modify, modify the noun that is the focus of the statement of fact.
severity_basis: modifying the wrong noun can be overinclusive (any default under a nontrivial contract) or underinclusive (both nouns qualified)

examples.before: The Seller is not in default under any nontrivial contract to which it is party.
examples.after: The Seller is not in nontrivial default under any contract to which it is party.

section: Material Adverse Change > Using MAC
statement: MAC issues fall into using MAC provisions and defining MAC. MAC is entrenched, so MSCD assumes it rather than Dealbreaker Adverse Effect; where the nontrivial meaning suits, you can use nontrivial adverse effect.

section: Material Adverse Change > Using MAC
statement: An "absolute MAC provision" states that no MAC has occurred since a date (Since 31 December 2021, no MAC has occurred). A court should aggregate events even without individually or in the aggregate (as in IBP).

words: no material adverse change has occurred

severity_basis: vagueness, dispute risk, or legally significant usage

section: Material Adverse Change > Using MAC
statement: A "modifying MAC provision" qualifies a statement of fact about some aspect of operations (contain no inaccuracies except for inaccuracies that would not reasonably be expected to result in a MAC); a mass noun or plural count noun makes individually or in the aggregate unnecessary.
severity_basis: vagueness, dispute risk, or legally significant usage

section: Material Adverse Change > Using MAC
statement: Don't repeat MAC statements of fact as closing conditions; the standard bringdown condition already covers them.

section: Material Adverse Change > Using MAC
statement: Draft a MAC provision as a statement of fact rather than a condition: a condition only lets a party walk, while an inaccurate statement of fact can also support a damages or indemnification claim.
severity_basis: vagueness, dispute risk, or legally significant usage
notes: Other uses: an obligation to notify of any MAC; a right to terminate a license on a MAC affecting the other party; a credit-agreement event of default (9.75).

section: Material Adverse Change > Using MAC
statement: As an alternative to a modifying MAC provision, use dealbreaker or defined Material (contains no Material inaccuracies); nontrivial is unlikely to fit. Use MAC where the concern is an adverse effect on the other party's fortunes, and Material where the concern is a direct effect on your client.
exceptions: Not every Material provision can become a MAC provision; a static noun such as contract can't express change (9.77).
severity_basis: vagueness, dispute risk, or legally significant usage

section: Material Adverse Change > Bringdown Condition
statement: In a materiality-qualified bringdown condition, use Materially accurate (as a defined term) rather than accurate in all material respects: that individually and in the aggregate, the statements of fact made by the Seller in article 2 were Materially accurate on the date of this agreement and are Materially accurate at Closing. If both sides' bringdowns use materiality, state whose perspective applies.

words: true and correct in all material respects
trigger.regex_hint: (?i)(true and correct|accurate) in all material respects

severity_basis: vagueness, dispute risk, or legally significant usage

section: Material Adverse Change > Bringdown Condition
statement: Use individually and in the aggregate in the bringdown to capture the cumulative effect of inaccuracies (it benefits the buyer); if you omit it, refer to each statement of fact, making clear the cumulative effect doesn't count.
severity_basis: in the aggregate alone might arguably work, but the longer phrase is clearer

section: Material Adverse Change > Bringdown Condition
statement: In a MAC-qualified bringdown, don't say a failure to be true and correct would not reasonably be expected to have a MAC; an inaccuracy doesn't cause a MAC, the circumstances behind it might. Say: except for any statements of fact that are inaccurate such that the events or circumstances giving rise to those inaccuracies have not had and would not reasonably be expected to have a Material Adverse Effect.

words: failure to be true and correct

severity_basis: vagueness, dispute risk, or legally significant usage

section: Material Adverse Change > Bringdown Condition
statement: Carve statements of fact (such as capitalization) out of the bringdown materiality qualification only if they have no materiality qualification of their own, and recognize the carve-out may accomplish little.

section: Material Adverse Change > Bringdown Condition
statement: Don't contort drafting to neutralize "double materiality" (stripping statement-of-fact qualifiers for bringdown purposes, or applying the bringdown qualifier only to unqualified statements); it is an illusion if the bringdown uses the dealbreaker standard, because both provisions then look to the same external standard.

words: without giving effect to any materiality
trigger.regex_hint: (?i)double materiality|disregarding (all|any) (qualifications|materiality)|without (giving effect to|regard to) any (materiality|material adverse)

severity_basis: vagueness, dispute risk, or legally significant usage

section: Material Adverse Change > Bringdown Condition
statement: Optionally, state that double materiality doesn't apply: the level of inaccuracy permitted by the bringdown's materiality qualification will not be affected by a materiality qualification to which a statement of fact is subject.

section: Material Adverse Change > Verbs in MAC Provisions
statement: In MAC provisions, use would [or would not] reasonably be expected to result in a MAC; don't use will (inaccurate only if a MAC materializes or becomes certain), could (any remote path makes it inaccurate), could reasonably be expected, or would result.

trigger.regex_hint: (?i)\b(could|will|would)( reasonably be expected to)? (result in|have) a material adverse

severity_basis: the verb shifts the risk dramatically between the parties
notes: Don't expect mathematical certainty about the level of likelihood in expect (9.100; 13.522).

section: Material Adverse Change > Verbs in MAC Provisions
statement: In an absolute MAC provision use the present perfect (no MAC has occurred), and for the party with the benefit, graft on a modifying provision: Since [date], there has not occurred any MAC or any events or circumstances that would reasonably be expected to result in a MAC.
severity_basis: vagueness, dispute risk, or legally significant usage

section: Material Adverse Change > Defining MAC
statement: Use one defined term, and make it Material Adverse Change; don't use both MAC and MAE.
severity_basis: no MAE has occurred sounds odd; fixes add causation language that can cut buyer protection (Great Lakes Chemical v. Pharmacia, Del. Ch. 2001); using both is confusing and unnecessary because the broader definition works everywhere

section: Material Adverse Change > Defining MAC
statement: Specify a baseline date in an absolute MAC statement of fact (signing date; date of the latest audited or unaudited financial statements, the buyer generally preferring audited; date of formation; a lender's commitment date).

trigger.signal: absolute MAC statement with no "since [date]"

severity_basis: a required element: an absolute MAC provision measures change from that date

section: Material Adverse Change > Defining MAC
statement: Use Material Adverse Change as a defined term, spelled out rather than abbreviated.

section: Material Adverse Change > Defining MAC
statement: Use a basic MAC definition such as: "Material Adverse Change" means any Material adverse change in the business, results of operations, assets, liabilities, or financial condition of the Seller, as determined from the perspective of a reasonable person in the Buyer's position.
severity_basis: vagueness, dispute risk, or legally significant usage

section: Material Adverse Change > Defining MAC
statement: Define MAC as a material adverse change in something, not as an event or circumstance that would reasonably be expected to result in one, nor both; put the would reasonably be expected formula in the MAC provisions instead.
severity_basis: vagueness, dispute risk, or legally significant usage

section: Material Adverse Change > Defining MAC
statement: Say any material adverse change in ..., not any change, effect, development, or circumstance materially adverse to ...; the extra nouns are superfluous.

section: Material Adverse Change > Defining MAC
statement: State whose perspective determines materiality in the MAC definition (from the perspective of the Buyer, or of a reasonable person in the Buyer's position).
severity_basis: can change meaning or invite dispute

section: Material Adverse Change > Defining MAC
statement: Generally don't add quantitative thresholds to a MAC definition: indicia are many and partial coverage is arbitrary, they complicate negotiation, illustrative indicia risk a court rejecting dissimilar changes, and quantifiable concerns belong elsewhere.
exceptions: An aggressive buyer or one with ample bargaining power might want favorable thresholds (9.130).
severity_basis: vagueness, dispute risk, or legally significant usage

section: Material Adverse Change > Field of Change
statement: For a buyer acquiring a company, define the "field of change" as the business, results of operations, assets, liabilities, or financial condition of the target, adjusted to the transaction (for example, the assets acquired in an asset purchase; in credit agreements, effects on lender rights or the borrower's ability to perform).
severity_basis: vagueness, dispute risk, or legally significant usage

section: Material Adverse Change > Field of Change
statement: Read liabilities in the field of change in its broad sense (any legal responsibility); if the contract defines Liabilities broadly elsewhere, use that defined term.
severity_basis: vagueness, dispute risk, or legally significant usage

section: Material Adverse Change > Field of Change
statement: To cover a target's planned new line of business, refer in the field of change to the business as it is currently being conducted or as the target currently proposes to conduct it, or, if plans are sufficiently developed, add specific statements of fact or conditions about the expansion.
severity_basis: vagueness, dispute risk, or legally significant usage

section: Material Adverse Change > Field of Change
statement: Omit properties (overlaps assets), operations (within business), and capitalization (ambiguous between share structure and market value) from the field of change, and use financial condition rather than condition (financial or otherwise). Don't assume stock-price changes fall within a field that excludes capitalization; address them explicitly.
severity_basis: vagueness, dispute risk, or legally significant usage

section: Material Adverse Change > Field of Change
statement: Keep elements beyond business in the field of change despite arguable surplusage; some courts read a business-only field narrowly.
severity_basis: Pine State Creamery v. Land-O-Sun Dairies (E.D.N.C. 1997) held operating profits outside "any material adverse change in the Business" (reversed by the 4th Cir. 1999)

section: Material Adverse Change > Field of Change
statement: If a party wants to walk when specific industry-wide or general developments cause a MAC, say so in the contract, preferably in a statement of fact, condition, or other provision rather than as including examples in the MAC definition.
severity_basis: caselaw is mixed: Borders v. KRLB (Tex. App. 1987) and Pittsburgh Coke v. Bollo (E.D.N.Y. 1976) held industry-wide changes weren't a MAC; IBP declined to exclude them

section: Material Adverse Change > Prospects
statement: Omit prospects from the field of change and use the "back door" instead: consistently use would [or would not] reasonably be expected to result in a MAC in modifying provisions, and add or any event or circumstance that would reasonably be expected to result in a MAC to absolute provisions.
severity_basis: the analysis is largely the same and may spare the usual skirmish; Pacheco (D. Mass. 2000) and Goodman v. Raytheon (S.D.N.Y. 1999) rejected treating a change in prospects as a MAC where prospects was absent

section: Material Adverse Change > Prospects
statement: A buyer wanting certainty about publicly announced projections should make it a closing condition that no event or circumstance exists that is reasonably expected to result in the target failing to meet any publicly announced financial projections, rather than rely on Pacheco.
severity_basis: vagueness, dispute risk, or legally significant usage

section: Material Adverse Change > Prospects
statement: Address specific concerns (matters that might fall within prospects, partly controlled or uncontrolled changes, and any issue that might support a claim or a right to walk) in statements of fact, conditions, or termination provisions, stated as broadly as possible, so the absolute MAC provision is needed only for matters unforeseeable at signing.
severity_basis: examples given as including in the MAC definition raise the risk a court won't treat a dissimilar change as a MAC (13.378)

section: Material Adverse Change > Whose MAC and Aggregation
statement: Say whose MAC (of the Seller; or the Seller and its Subsidiaries, taken as a whole). When both sides benefit from MAC provisions, give each its own defined term (Buyer MAC, Seller MAC), use the multi-party Material definition, and don't use a MAC definition that applies to one party in a provision applying to another.
severity_basis: can change meaning or invite dispute

section: Material Adverse Change > Whose MAC and Aggregation
statement: A target normally forgoes MAC protection when paid in cash; when paid in buyer stock, whether to seek it depends on the exchange ratio and other mechanisms addressing major changes in the buyer's business.

section: Material Adverse Change > Whose MAC and Aggregation
statement: Don't build aggregation into the MAC definition (when considered individually or together with each other such adverse change); it makes little sense for modifying provisions. Use the expanded absolute MAC provision for broad aggregation.
severity_basis: vagueness, dispute risk, or legally significant usage

section: Material Adverse Change > Inclusions and Carve-Outs
statement: Don't specify changes the buyer wants to walk over as including examples in the MAC definition; state their nonoccurrence in statements of fact, closing conditions, or termination provisions.
severity_basis: examples raise the risk a court won't treat a dissimilar change as a MAC

section: Material Adverse Change > Inclusions and Carve-Outs
statement: Word MAC carve-outs generally, not as historical facts, and introduce them with other than [or except for, or but does not include] any of the following, either alone or in combination. Common carve-outs: general economic conditions; industry-wide changes (perhaps unless disproportionate); announcement of the transaction; stock price or trading volume; labor disruptions; failure to meet estimates; actions contemplated by the agreement or requested by the buyer; actions required by law.
severity_basis: vagueness, dispute risk, or legally significant usage

section: Material Adverse Change > Inclusions and Carve-Outs
statement: Target counsel should weigh bargaining power, the nature of the business (carve-outs are associated with technology deals), and deal practice; a restrained seller position carves out economy-wide and industry changes and changes attributable to the deal. Omitting a carve-out doesn't mean a court would find a MAC.

section: Material Adverse Change > Relation to Other Provisions
statement: Recognize that other provisions can limit a MAC: a narrower specific provision may control (Gordon v. Dolin, Ill. App. Ct. 1982), and silence on a topic can suggest it wasn't material (Northern Heel v. Compo, 1st Cir. 1988).
severity_basis: can change meaning or invite dispute

section: References to Time > Functions and Dates
statement: A reference to time does one of four things: gives a date to something; specifies a point in time; specifies a period of time that begins or ends at a stated point and has a stated duration; or apportions a quantity per unit of time. Paired points in time are equivalent to a period.

examples.after: Acme may exercise the Option from 1 July 2023 to 28 September 2023.

section: References to Time > Functions and Dates
statement: State dates in day-month-year format (1 January 2022); U.S. drafters should consider switching to it.
exceptions: Under month-day-year, omit the comma after the year when the date is used as an adjective; any date ending introductory matter takes a comma (10.8).
severity_basis: it creates no confusion, streamlines prose (no commas), and is used in most of the world

examples.before: January 1, 2022
examples.after: 1 January 2022

section: References to Time > Functions and Dates
statement: Don't use the format this 24th day of October, 2022; it is archaic and long-winded.

examples.before: this 24th day of October, 2022
examples.after: 24 October 2022

section: References to Time > Functions and Dates
statement: Don't use two digits for the day (07 November 2022).

section: References to Time > Functions and Dates
statement: Don't use purely numerical dates (10/9/2022).
fix: Write the date as 9 October 2022 (or 10 September 2022).
severity_basis: too informal and confusing: the U.S. puts the month first and much of the world puts the day first, so 10/9/2022 has two readings

section: References to Time > Functions and Dates
statement: Don't add A.D. before the year; it is eccentric.

section: References to Time > Functions and Dates
statement: If you refer to a day without anchoring it in time, use day rather than date.
exceptions: Date instead of day can't cause confusion, so insisting on it gains little; changing closing date to closing day would be pedantic (10.16).

examples.before: interest from the beginning of the date the disputed payment was originally due through the date before the date of payment
examples.after: interest from the beginning of the day the disputed payment was originally due through the day before the day of payment

section: References to Time > Functions and Dates
statement: Omit the date that is (before the date that is, no later than the date that is); it is almost always clutter.
exceptions: Appropriate in the definition of a defined term that uses the word date (10.18).

examples.before: If the Exchange Offer is not completed on or before the date that is 270 days after the Closing Date ...
examples.after: If the Exchange Offer is not completed by 270 days after the Closing Date ...

section: References to Time > Functions and Dates
statement: Don't use the date notified; say the date that ABC specifies by notice to XYZ.

examples.before: "First Hand Date" means the date notified by ABC to XYZ upon which the first hand of poker is played ...

section: References to Time > Points in Time
statement: Fix a point in time by reference to a date or other day (on 9 April 2024; the Closing Day) or an anniversary; on expresses something happening by reference to a day.

section: References to Time > Points in Time
statement: Inclusive-versus-exclusive ambiguity: a preposition marking the beginning or end of a period (from, after, until, to, by, between) can leave unclear whether the stated day is included.

trigger.signal: a period bounded by a day using from, after, until, to, by, or between

test: Ask whether the boundary day itself falls inside the period. Caselaw: from and after mostly exclusive; until, to, and by split; between mostly exclusive at both ends; starting and commences on likely inclusive; before likely exclusive; through likely inclusive.
fix: State the time of day for each boundary (10.33), or use starting [day] and ending on or through [day], or say expressly inclusive or exclusive.
exceptions: Even where caselaw is consistent, a court could hold otherwise on the circumstances, and the parties may not have had that effect in mind (10.27-.28).
severity_basis: can change meaning or invite dispute

section: References to Time > Points in Time
statement: Prefer prepositions courts read consistently: starting [day] and commences on (likely inclusive), through (likely inclusive), before (likely exclusive). Avoid until, to, and by for ending points and from, after, and between for beginning points, because courts split or default to exclusive.
severity_basis: can change meaning or invite dispute
notes: MSCD table in 10.24-.25 summarizes caselaw; see ocr-tables.md.

section: References to Time > Points in Time
statement: Recognize that fixing a point in time by reference to a day is insufficiently specific: a beginning or ending point could fall at the midnight starting or ending the day, and a party might claim it had some other time in mind.

trigger.signal: deadline or period stated by day with no time of day

test: Ask at what moment on the day the period begins or ends.
fix: State a time of day (10.33); or say from the beginning of 15 April 2023 to the end of 30 April 2023 (which could be read as business hours); or state inclusive or exclusive expressly (legalistic); or add a comprehensive interpretation section.
severity_basis: can change meaning or invite dispute

section: References to Time > Points in Time
statement: State a time of day for each beginning and ending point (the Option expires at 2:00 p.m. on 25 September 2022); avoid close of business and opening of business, which can cause disputes.
severity_basis: Lehman Brothers International v. ExxonMobil [2016] EWHC 2699 (Comm); Re Electron Holdings [2013] IEHC 495

section: References to Time > Points in Time
statement: Prefer midnight as the time of day: it lets you deal in entire days and reduces disputes over when a notice or payment was received.

section: References to Time > Points in Time
statement: Don't refer to midnight or noon as 12:00 a.m. or 12:00 p.m.; they are boundaries between a.m. and p.m. hours.
fix: Say noon, or midnight at the beginning [or end] of [date].
severity_basis: can change meaning or invite dispute

section: References to Time > Points in Time
statement: Midnight ambiguity: midnight on [date] could mean the midnight beginning or the midnight ending that day; the convention that it means the end isn't clearly universal or known to the parties.

trigger.signal: midnight on a date, or 12:01 a.m. / 11:59 p.m. used to dodge the issue

test: Ask whether midnight on the date could be read as the start of that day.
fix: Say midnight at the beginning [or end] of [date]. Don't use 12:01 a.m. or 11:59 p.m., which is clumsy.
severity_basis: can change meaning or invite dispute

section: References to Time > Points in Time
statement: Treat a time of day as a boundary between periods, not a minute-long period; don't state hours, minutes, and seconds, and watch for a draft that states a time a minute more or less than expected (5:01 p.m.).
severity_basis: the misconception can cause fights over an extra minute (Kanye West campaign v. Wisconsin Elections Commission, 2020)

section: References to Time > Points in Time
statement: Don't use at to state a deadline; use a beginning or ending point in time.
fix: Say before [time] on [date], or no later than [time] on [date].
severity_basis: a time of day occupies no time, so it is unclear how much time before or after the party has; a court might accept action in the following minute (Bradscot v. Hamilton-Wentworth, O.C.A. 1999)

section: References to Time > Points in Time
statement: State a time of day in digits (5:30 p.m., not five thirty p.m. or both), without o'clock, with lowercase a.m. and p.m. with periods; use the 24-hour system (17:30) where customary, but without seconds.

section: References to Time > Points in Time
statement: If the parties are in different time zones or business crosses them, specify the governing time zone, preferably by city (6:00 p.m., New York time) to avoid daylight-saving errors (PST versus PDT; Arizona) and states spanning more than one zone.
severity_basis: can change meaning or invite dispute

examples.before: 1:00 p.m. PST on 5 July 2022
examples.after: 1:00 p.m. PDT on 5 July 2022

section: References to Time > Points in Time
statement: Use upon (or on) for an event only to express something that happens automatically when it occurs (The Option will expire upon sale of the Acme Assets); when language of discretion or obligation is tied to an event, state a period for acting.
severity_basis: IPE Asset Management v. Fairview Block (N.Y. App. Div. 2014): an option exercisable "upon expiration of a 15-month period after closing" was held ambiguous as to how long the buyer had

examples.after: If during the 30 days after that 15-month period the Buyer notifies the Seller it wishes to sell the Property back to the Seller ...

section: References to Time > Periods of Time
statement: In a forward-looking period (from, following, after), the convention excludes the day you count from and includes the last day; be explicit about how the ending date is determined, and if you know both ends, use paired points in time instead.
exceptions: The convention doesn't apply if the period clearly must consist of entire days (both terminal days excluded) or the parties clearly intend the first day to be included (10.63).
severity_basis: can change meaning or invite dispute

examples.after: Smith may exercise the Option during the ten days from his receipt of the Option Notice. (Notice on 1 January: day one is 2 January; exercise before midnight at the end of 11 January.)

section: References to Time > Periods of Time
statement: Backward-looking period ambiguity: in a period counted back from an event (before, prior to), especially minimum notice (at least ten days' prior notice), courts split between counting one terminal day and requiring "clear" or "entire" days that exclude both.

trigger.signal: minimum notice or a period counted back from a date or event

test: Count back both ways (exclude one terminal day; exclude both) and see whether the last valid day differs (for a 31 December transfer with ten days' notice: 21 December versus 20 December).
fix: Be explicit about how the beginning date is determined; you could denote the period in entire days.
severity_basis: can change meaning or invite dispute

section: References to Time > Periods of Time
statement: Don't measure a period from a point in time that could cause argument over when or whether it occurred (final resolution of any disputes).

trigger.signal: period keyed to an event of uncertain timing

severity_basis: can change meaning or invite dispute

section: References to Time > Periods of Time
statement: Within ambiguity: within X days of an event can denote a period running forward, backward, or both (within seven days of the first anniversary), and within X days prior to can mean "during the X days before" or "at least X days before."

trigger.signal: within X days (or months) of, or within X days prior to, an event or date

test: Ask whether the period could run before the reference point, after it, or both.
fix: Say no later than seven days after it receives a Sale Notice (or during the X days before, or at least X days before).
severity_basis: Wilson v. Gentile (Cal. Ct. App. 1992): within 30 days prior to meant different things for option and renewal provisions

examples.before: within seven days of receiving a Sale Notice
examples.after: no later than seven days after it receives a Sale Notice

section: References to Time > Units of Time
statement: Choose the unit of time deliberately; for days, often prefer business days, defined as a day other than a weekend or public holiday in a specified jurisdiction, or a day banks are open.
severity_basis: business days track working days and ensure the last day is a business day

section: References to Time > Units of Time
statement: Don't use calendar days instead of days; it is unnecessary and potentially confusing.

section: References to Time > Units of Time
statement: Don't use nonbusiness day; say a day other than a business day.

section: References to Time > Units of Time
statement: Consider months for periods longer than about 90 days; a month counted forward ends at midnight at the beginning of the corresponding day of the next month (or the last day of that month if none corresponds).

section: References to Time > Units of Time
statement: Don't use weeks for periods; they give no advantage over days or months.

section: References to Time > Units of Time
statement: A period of years runs through the day before the relevant anniversary of the first day included; when a period is measured from a stated point, don't fear a court will read month or year as a calendar month or year.

section: References to Time > Units of Time
statement: Bi- and semi- ambiguity: biannual and semiannual both mean twice a year, but some dictionaries give biannual the meaning of biennial; bimonthly and biweekly invite similar confusion.

trigger.signal: a frequency word with the prefix bi- or semi-

test: Ask whether the word could mean twice per unit or once every two units.
fix: Say twice a year (month, week) or every two years (months, weeks).
severity_basis: can change meaning or invite dispute

section: References to Time > Units of Time
statement: Instead of agreeing not to start bankruptcy proceedings until one year and a day after repayment, say no sooner than one year after.
severity_basis: under the standard counting convention, no sooner than one year after already clears the Bankruptcy Code § 547 one-year preference period

section: References to Time > Units of Time
statement: When an act must occur on a specified date, the period is that day's 24 hours; no beginning or ending point need be stated, though you may add a time of day.

section: References to Time > Units of Time
statement: To state how many units of time satisfy a condition, use at least X (not not less than X or X or more); don't use any of these in language of obligation or prohibition, where they suggest the duration is open-ended.

trigger.regex_hint: (?i)\b(shall|shall not|must not)\b[^;\n]{0,100}?\b(not less than|no less than|at least)\s+\w+\s+(\(\d+\)\s+)?(days|months|years)

exceptions: If you use that form, say not less than, not no less than (10.85).
severity_basis: Pam's Academy of Dance v. Marik (Ill. App. Ct. 2018): dispute over a restriction "for a period of not less than three (3) years"

examples.before: The Company shall retain copies ... for a period of not less than six years from the date thereof.

examples.after: Each arbitrator must be a licensed commercial real estate broker with at least 15 years' experience ...

section: References to Time > Ambiguous Period Constructions
statement: Time-of-day-at-end ambiguity: before 2:00 p.m. on the date that is 20 Business Days after the Closing can mean any time up to 2:00 p.m. on day 20, or only on day 20 before 2:00 p.m.

trigger.signal: before [time] on the [date] that is X days after [event]

test: Ask whether delivery on day 19 (or earlier) counts, or only delivery on day 20 before the stated time.
fix: For the first meaning: between the Closing and 2:00 p.m. 20 Business Days after the Closing. For the second: on the 20th Business Day after the Closing, before 2:00 p.m.
severity_basis: can change meaning or invite dispute

section: References to Time > Ambiguous Period Constructions
statement: Point-for-period ambiguity: tying a figure that pertains to a period to the point marking its end (the Revenues as of the 24-Month Revenue Measurement Point) invites a fight over which part of the period the figure covers.

trigger.signal: a cumulative figure (revenues, sales, income) measured "as of" a point that ends a multi-part period

test: Ask whether the figure covers the whole period or only the last segment before the point.
fix: Refer to the period itself (the Revenues for the 24 months ending ...).
severity_basis: can change meaning or invite dispute

section: References to Time > Ambiguous Period Constructions
statement: Don't use during the period or during a period to establish a period; use while or from ... to.
exceptions: During that period, during the period specified in, and similar phrases referring to a period stated elsewhere are fine (10.93).

examples.before: During the period that the Warrant is outstanding, the Company shall ...
examples.after: While the Warrant is outstanding, the Company shall ...

section: References to Time > Ambiguous Period Constructions
statement: Will-have ambiguity: saying a party will have a period to do something leaves unclear whether you mean an obligation or a condition.

trigger.signal: a party will have (or shall have) a period to do something

test: Ask whether failing to act is a breach (obligation) or just loss of a right (condition).
fix: For an obligation: No later than 60 days after termination, Acme shall return ... For a condition: To validly exercise the Option, Acme must no later than 60 days after termination notify Widgetco that it is doing so.
severity_basis: can change meaning or invite dispute

section: References to Time > Ambiguous Period Constructions
statement: Before-scope ambiguity: a condition such as If any of the Assets are destroyed or damaged prior to Completion can cover only damage between signing and completion, or any time before completion, including before signing.

trigger.signal: a condition about something happening before (prior to) Closing or Completion, with no start date

test: Ask whether the period could start before signing.
fix: Address the condition of the assets at signing expressly.
severity_basis: Gwynt Y Môr OFTO v. Gwynt Y Môr Offshore Wind Farm [2020] EWHC 850 (Comm)

section: References to Time > Apportioning Quantities per Unit of Time
statement: When apportioning a quantity per unit of time, address two issues: the alternative meanings of the unit, and short periods at the beginning or end of the contract.
severity_basis: vagueness, dispute risk, or legally significant usage

section: References to Time > Apportioning Quantities per Unit of Time
statement: Unit-of-time ambiguity in apportioning: year (per year, annual) can mean a year from the agreement date and each anniversary, or the 12 months from any 1 January (most courts); month can mean to the corresponding day of the next month, or a calendar month; week can mean any seven consecutive days or a traditional week.

trigger.signal: a quantity, payment, or limit apportioned per year, month, or week

test: Ask whether the unit runs from the contract date or from the calendar boundary.
fix: State what year or month means, by a more specific alternative (each 12-month period starting on the date of this agreement or an anniversary; each calendar quarter) or a defined term if used several times.
severity_basis: can change meaning or invite dispute

section: References to Time > Apportioning Quantities per Unit of Time
statement: Don't rely on calendar year, civil year, calendar month, or a reference to the Gregorian calendar to fix the meaning: U.S. courts likely read calendar year as 1 January-31 December and calendar month as a month of the year, but English courts tend to read calendar month as running to the corresponding day of the next month.
fix: State the period expressly (1 January through 31 December).
severity_basis: can change meaning or invite dispute

section: References to Time > Apportioning Quantities per Unit of Time
statement: If year or month means a calendar year or month, state how to treat a short period between signing and the next unit and between the last complete unit and termination (prorate the number or amount, with rounding; apply the percentage to the short-period portion of the index; or prorate the percentage of the full index), or arrange beginning and ending short periods.

trigger.signal: annual or monthly entitlement, bonus, or cap with no provision for partial periods

severity_basis: can change meaning or invite dispute
notes: Each approach has caveats: seasonal concentration of revenue, indexes that can't be split, and bonuses that depend on performance before hiring or require waiting until year-end (10.108-.109).

section: References to Time > Apportioning Quantities per Unit of Time
statement: Block-of-time ambiguity: when the thing apportioned is itself a unit of time (two months of each year), it is unclear whether it must be taken as a single block.

trigger.signal: a number of days, weeks, or months to be taken within a year or month

test: Ask whether the time may be split into several shorter blocks.
fix: To require a block, use consecutive (two consecutive months each year; convert one month to 30 consecutive days). If not, say so (over the course of one or more visits, each no shorter than five business days).
severity_basis: can change meaning or invite dispute

examples.after: Over the course of one or more visits, each no shorter than five business days, excluding travel days, the Employee shall work in Acme's Budapest office for two months of each year.

section: References to Time > Speed, Frequency, and Duration
statement: Treat promptly and immediately (and prompt and immediate) as meaning the same thing in contracts: courts apply a reasonableness standard to both.
exceptions: Immediately also means "without intermediary" (the immediately preceding Business Day); that use is not a speed standard (10.119).
severity_basis: State v. Chesson (Ala. Civ. App. 2006); Doe Fund v. Royal Indemnity (N.Y. App. Div. 2006); Buck v. Scalf (Tenn. Ct. App. 2003) (promptly means within a reasonable time); Dwoskin v. Rollins (5th Cir. 1981) and Briggs Ave v. Insurance Corp. of Hannover (S.D.N.Y. 2006) (immediately is subject to reasonableness)

section: References to Time > Speed, Frequency, and Duration
statement: Don't say as promptly as possible [or practicable]; promptly already depends on the circumstances.

section: References to Time > Speed, Frequency, and Duration
statement: Omit immediately and use promptly; don't use both promptly and immediately in one contract.
severity_basis: using both invites argument for gradations of meaning

section: References to Time > Speed, Frequency, and Duration
statement: Don't use synonyms of promptly (quickly, as soon as practicable, expeditiously, forthwith, right away) or without undue delay.
fix: Use promptly, or a precise deadline.
exceptions: Under German law, without undue delay may be appropriate as the English equivalent of unverzüglich (10.130).
severity_basis: vagueness, dispute risk, or legally significant usage

section: References to Time > Speed, Frequency, and Duration
statement: If you can state a precise deadline, do so; if promptly may not convey enough urgency, use a precise deadline (no later than 60 minutes after learning of that event) or combine vague and absolute limits (promptly, but not later than x days after).
severity_basis: vagueness, dispute risk, or legally significant usage

examples.after: promptly, but not later than x days after ...

section: References to Time > Speed, Frequency, and Duration
statement: Don't use at any time in language of discretion (may already lets the party act whenever it wishes) or in language of obligation or conditional clauses.
exceptions: If an instance of language of discretion is particularly important, at any time may preclude argument (10.133); see 3.359 for conditional clauses.

examples.before: Each party shall at any time before the Effective Time ...
examples.after: Each party shall before the Effective Time ...

section: References to Time > Speed, Frequency, and Duration
statement: To make explicit that a right (or obligation or condition) isn't one-time-only, use on one or more occasions instead of from time to time.
exceptions: Unnecessary for a right that can be exercised only once or an ongoing process (10.137).
severity_basis: from time to time means "once in a while," but a party might act twice in quick succession; making it explicit denies a desperate litigant even a weak argument

examples.before: The Bank may from time to time adjust the Advance Rate ...
examples.after: The Bank may on one or more occasions adjust the Advance Rate ...

section: References to Time > Speed, Frequency, and Duration
statement: Don't use at all times: an ongoing obligation applies at all times without saying so; if a provision could be read as applying only at one moment, use always; for a statement of fact, state a time period (since 1 January 2022).
severity_basis: vagueness, dispute risk, or legally significant usage

section: References to Time > Speed, Frequency, and Duration
statement: Use if instead of so long as, whether it means "on condition that" or "for as long as."

examples.before: So long as the Indemnifying Party is conducting the defense of the Nonparty Claim ...
examples.after: If the Indemnifying Party is conducting the defense of the Nonparty Claim ...

section: References to Time > Speed, Frequency, and Duration
statement: Don't use periodically; be specific (state intervals, or whenever the client asks); to express that something changes over time, use then (the Agent's loan procedures then in effect).
severity_basis: vagueness, dispute risk, or legally significant usage

examples.before: the Agent's loan procedures periodically in effect
examples.after: the Agent's loan procedures then in effect

section: References to Time > Adding a Time Component
statement: Time-component ambiguity: a reference to things that pertain to a party (affiliates, subsidiaries, clients, shares, applicable law) can mean those existing at signing or those existing at some later time.

trigger.signal: a class of persons or things belonging to a party (affiliates, subsidiaries, clients, shares) or applicable law, with no time reference

test: Ask whether the class could grow or change after signing, and which members the provision should cover.
fix: Say so in the provision or definition: "Subsidiary" means, for a Person [on the date of this agreement] [at a given time], ... ; say whether shares includes shares acquired later.
severity_basis: GTE Wireless v. Cellexis (1st Cir. 2003); Ellington v. EMI Music (N.Y. 2014) (affiliates); Alliantgroup v. Solanji (Tex. App. 2014) (client); Kia Motors America v. Glassman (6th Cir. 2013) (applicable law)

section: Part Versus the Whole > Introduction
statement: Ambiguity of "the part versus the whole": plural nouns and the words and, or, every, each, all, and any can leave unclear whether a provision refers to one member of a group or to the whole group. MSCD examples: numbered sentences are the text at issue; numbered-and-lettered italic sentences state its possible meanings.
severity_basis: can change meaning or invite dispute

section: Part Versus the Whole > Whether Singular Means Plural
statement: Singular-for-plural ambiguity: a provision that refers to a thing or unnamed person in the singular (a non-affiliated third party; notice) may or may not apply to more than one.

trigger.signal: singular noun naming a counterparty, event, or document that could occur more than once

test: Ask whether the provision should apply regardless of number, only to one, or only to more than one; usually you want regardless of number.
fix: Make the intended scope explicit (one or more non-affiliated persons); sometimes a further sentence is needed.
severity_basis: Coral Production v. Central Resources (Neb. 2007): sale to "a non-affiliated third party" held to cover sale to more than one; ION Geophysical v. Fletcher (Del. Ch. 2010): "notice" held to allow more than one notice

section: Part Versus the Whole > Whether Singular Means Plural
statement: Use one or more rather than X or Xs (one or more widgets, not the widget or widgets).

examples.before: the widget or widgets
examples.after: one or more widgets

section: Part Versus the Whole > Whether Singular Means Plural
statement: Don't rely on an internal rule of interpretation (the singular includes the plural) to make provisions apply regardless of number.
severity_basis: such rules are clumsy and can't be assumed to prevent a fight; the Coral Production contract had one

section: Part Versus the Whole > Whether Singular Means Plural
statement: Don't count on any to extend a provision to more than one; any can mean any one member of the class, like a. Use one or more (if Acme files a complaint with one or more government bodies).
fix: Replace any with one or more where more than one should be covered.
severity_basis: can change meaning or invite dispute

section: Part Versus the Whole > Whether Singular Means Plural
statement: Use one or more only where the context poses a greater risk of dispute; making every singular provision expressly cover the plural produces ponderous prose.

section: Part Versus the Whole > Plural Nouns
statement: Plural-subject ambiguity: with a plural subject (The Stockholders shall notify Acme), it can be unclear whether members act individually or collectively; in language of discretion (may) there is a third meaning (one or more may act, or only if all do). Adding all of doesn't change the analysis.

trigger.signal: plural noun (or all of the [noun]s) as the subject of shall, may, must, or will

test: Ask: must each member act, or the members together? With may: can one member act alone, or only if all act?
fix: Say Each Stockholder shall ..., One or more Stockholders may ..., or The Stockholders, acting collectively, ...; or appoint an agent to act for the group.
exceptions: Some plural sentences are unambiguous (The Acme Subsidiaries are Delaware corporations) (11.15).
severity_basis: can change meaning or invite dispute

examples.before: The Stockholders shall notify Acme.
examples.after: Each Stockholder shall notify Acme.

section: Part Versus the Whole > Plural Nouns
statement: Plural-direct-object ambiguity: with a plural direct object (Acme shall notify the Stockholders; Acme may sell the Shares), it can be unclear whether the subject acts as to each member or the group collectively, and in language of discretion whether it must act as to all or may act as to some.

trigger.signal: plural noun as the object of a verb of obligation, discretion, or prohibition

test: Ask whether the action must cover all members, may cover some, or treats them as a group.
fix: Say each of the Stockholders, the Stockholders considered collectively, one or more Shares, or but only if it sells all of them.
exceptions: When collective treatment makes no sense (Acme shall sell the Shares), the meanings narrow (11.18).
severity_basis: can change meaning or invite dispute

section: Part Versus the Whole > Plural Nouns
statement: Plural-subject-and-object ambiguity: with a plural subject and a plural object (The Stockholders shall promptly submit the completed questionnaires), it can be unclear whether the object relates to each subject member separately or to all together.

trigger.signal: plural subject plus plural object

test: Ask whether each member must submit one, each must submit all, or the group submits them together.
fix: Say Each Stockholder shall promptly submit a completed questionnaire (or the questionnaires), or The Stockholders, acting collectively, ...
exceptions: Context often makes the meaning clear (11.20).
severity_basis: can change meaning or invite dispute

examples.before: The Stockholders shall promptly submit the completed questionnaires.
examples.after: Each Stockholder shall promptly submit a completed questionnaire.

section: Part Versus the Whole > And
statement: And concerns a set in its totality, and is often unambiguous (Acme and Widgetco are Delaware corporations), but it can mean "together" or "together and separately," and can leave unclear whether nouns act or are acted on individually or collectively, depending on grammatical context.
severity_basis: can change meaning or invite dispute
notes: 11.23 cross-refers to 11.6 for individual versus collective action; that discussion is at 11.16 (possible cross-reference error).

section: Part Versus the Whole > And
statement: And-subject ambiguity: parties linked by and as the subject (Able and Baker shall notify Acme) can act individually or collectively; with may, it can also mean both must act, or either or both may act.

trigger.signal: two or more parties joined by and as the subject of shall or may

test: Ask whether each may (or must) act alone, or whether all must act together.
fix: Say Able and Baker shall each notify Acme; Able or Baker, or both of them, may notify Acme; or ..., acting collectively, ...
severity_basis: Spanski Enterprises v. Telewizja Polska (2d Cir. 2020): "TVP and SEI may extend its term" led to a fight over whether each could extend or both had to agree

examples.before: TVP and SEI may extend its term by subsequent 10 year periods.
examples.after: The term of this agreement, as extended in accordance with this section 10.1, will be extended by ten years if the parties so agree in writing.

section: Part Versus the Whole > And
statement: And-direct-object ambiguity: nouns linked by and as direct objects (Acme shall notify Able and Baker) raise individual-versus-collective meanings; with may, whether both, one, or either is meant (Acme may dissolve Subsidiary A and Subsidiary B); with shall not, whether both are prohibited separately or only the combination.

trigger.signal: two or more nouns joined by and as the object of shall, may, or shall not

test: For shall not: is each act prohibited, or only doing both? For may: must the party act as to both, or may it act as to one?
fix: Say shall not notify Able and shall not notify Baker; may dissolve one or both of Subsidiary A and Subsidiary B; or both ..., as opposed to one or the other.
exceptions: When the objects can't be considered collectively (Acme shall dissolve Subsidiary A and Subsidiary B), the ambiguity is reduced (11.28).
severity_basis: can change meaning or invite dispute

section: Part Versus the Whole > And
statement: Distributive-versus-joint ambiguity: with and in both subject and object (Able and Baker shall notify Acme and Widgetco), it is unclear whether each subject acts as to each object, each acts as to one object respectively, or they act collectively.

trigger.signal: and joining two subjects and and joining two objects in one sentence

test: Ask whether the pairing is each-to-each, one-to-one (respectively), or joint.
fix: Say Able and Baker shall each notify Acme and Widgetco; or ... notify Acme and Widgetco, respectively; or ..., acting collectively, ...
severity_basis: can change meaning or invite dispute

section: Part Versus the Whole > And
statement: Multiple-verb-phrase ambiguity: one may governing two verb phrases joined by and (Acme may sell assets and make capital expenditures) can mean the party may do both only together, or each separately.

trigger.signal: may followed by two or more verb phrases joined by and

test: Ask whether the party may do one without the other.
fix: Repeat may (Acme may sell assets and may make capital expenditures), or say Acme may sell assets or make capital expenditures, or it may do both; with three or more, say may do any one or more of the following.
exceptions: When the first act logically leads to the second (Parent may dissolve Sub and liquidate its assets), "together" is likely intended (11.33).
severity_basis: can change meaning or invite dispute

section: Part Versus the Whole > And
statement: Objects-of-preposition ambiguity: nouns joined by and as objects of a preposition alongside a direct object (Delta shall issue a promissory note to Echo and Foxtrot) can mean one to each, or one to them jointly; may and shall not multiply the meanings.

trigger.signal: a direct object plus two or more objects of a preposition joined by and (issue a note to X and Y)

test: Ask whether each named recipient gets one, or one is shared.
fix: Say to each of Echo and Foxtrot, or to Echo and Foxtrot jointly.
exceptions: When the objects can't be considered collectively (construct a factory in California and Florida), the scope narrows (11.35).
severity_basis: can change meaning or invite dispute

section: Part Versus the Whole > And
statement: Adjectives-linked-by-and ambiguity: two adjectives joined by and before a plural noun (temporary and part-time employees) can mean those who are temporary and those who are part-time, or only those who are both; with may there are five meanings.

trigger.signal: two adjectives joined by and modifying one plural noun

test: Ask whether something must have both attributes or either.
fix: Repeat the noun with each adjective (temporary employees and part-time employees), or say who are both.
exceptions: Mutually exclusive attributes (full-time and part-time) reduce the ambiguity (11.38).
severity_basis: can change meaning or invite dispute

examples.before: Tango shall terminate the employment of Acme's temporary and part-time employees.
examples.after: Tango shall terminate the employment of Acme's temporary employees and part-time employees.

section: Part Versus the Whole > And
statement: Every-X-and-Y ambiguity: every or each before nouns linked by and (indemnify every director and officer) can mean every director and every officer, or every person who is both.

trigger.signal: every or each followed by two nouns joined by and

test: Ask whether one person must hold both roles.
fix: Say every director and every officer.
severity_basis: can change meaning or invite dispute

examples.before: Acme shall indemnify every director and officer of Widgetco.
examples.after: Acme shall indemnify every director and every officer of Widgetco.

section: Part Versus the Whole > And
statement: Optional-element ambiguity: and linking a required element to one meant to be optional (on the basis of dues deduction authorization and other evidence) invites a fight over whether both are required.

trigger.signal: and followed by other, additional, or further [noun] where that element is optional

test: Ask whether the provision fails if the second element is absent.
fix: Insert any after and (and any other evidence).
severity_basis: County of Du Page v. Illinois Labor Relations Board (Ill. 2008): the court held and meant or

section: Part Versus the Whole > And
statement: Two-trigger ambiguity: and joining two triggering events in a time or condition provision (during the six-month period following (x) Termination and (y) a Restrictive Covenant Breach) leaves unclear whether the right runs after each event or only after both. The listed and ambiguities aren't exhaustive.

trigger.signal: and joining two triggering events after following, after, upon, or on

test: Ask whether the provision is triggered by either event or only by both.
fix: State whether the right arises after either event or only after both of them.

section: Part Versus the Whole > Or
statement: Or presents alternatives and entails at least one. Its "not and" implicature (that not all alternatives are true) is implied, not part of its meaning, so or doesn't mean only one alternative is true; either strengthens the implicature but doesn't make it meaning. Under negation, an or-coordination usually equals an and-coordination of negative clauses, but wide-scope readings remain possible.
severity_basis: Cambridge Grammar of the English Language at 1293-98

section: Part Versus the Whole > Or
statement: Inclusive-versus-exclusive or: or between alternatives that aren't mutually exclusive (Acme shall dissolve Subsidiary A or Subsidiary B) can mean one but not both, or one or both, in every category of contract language except prohibition.

trigger.signal: or joining alternatives that could both occur or both be chosen

test: Ask whether both alternatives could happen or be chosen, and whether that should be allowed.
fix: Say ... or Subsidiary B, but not both; or ... or Subsidiary B, or both. Don't rely on the not-and implicature or on either for an exclusive meaning, or on context for an inclusive one.
exceptions: Some ors can only be exclusive (Parent shall incorporate Sub in Delaware or New York) (11.61).
severity_basis: Mintz v. Pazer (N.Y. Sup. Ct. 2014) (either may push a court to an exclusive reading); SouthTrust Bank v. Copeland One (Ala. 2003) (ambiguous or construed against the drafter)
notes: "Winning a fight is a distant second-best to avoiding the fight" (11.63).

section: Part Versus the Whole > Or
statement: Or-under-negation ambiguity: shall not X or Y (Acme shall not dissolve Subsidiary A or Subsidiary B) most likely prohibits each, but can be argued to prohibit only doing both, only doing one, or more; the same arises in negative statements of fact and conditional clauses.

trigger.signal: or inside a prohibition or negative statement

test: Ask whether a court could read the prohibition as applying to only one of the alternatives.
fix: Say Acme shall not dissolve Subsidiary A and shall not dissolve Subsidiary B, or Acme shall dissolve neither Subsidiary A nor Subsidiary B. Don't assume a court will apply De Morgan's laws.
severity_basis: Alloy Bellows & Precision Welding v. Cole (N.D. Ohio 2016): a prohibition equivalent to "You may not eat ice cream on Saturday or Sunday" was held to apply to only one day

section: Part Versus the Whole > Or
statement: Conditional-item-in-or-series ambiguity: when one item in an or-series is modified by a conditional clause (with Fred or, if she's in town, Nancy), it is unclear whether the conditional item is simply one more alternative or takes priority when the condition is met; setting the item apart with its own or makes the priority reading likelier.

trigger.signal: or, if [condition], [item] within a series

test: Ask whether the conditional item must be chosen whenever its condition is met.
fix: State the intended meaning in full: X or Y; if Y is unavailable, X (alternatives), or Y if [condition]; if not, X (priority).
severity_basis: Brooks Capital Services v. 5151 Trabue (Ohio Ct. App. 2012): a statute with this structure was held ambiguous

section: Part Versus the Whole > Or
statement: Or-with-plural-noun ambiguity: subjects or objects of a preposition linked by or with a plural noun (Able or Baker shall submit invoices to Charlie; Acme shall sell apples or oranges) leave unclear whether one party handles all, each item is handled by one, items may be handled jointly, or the alternatives may alternate or run concurrently.

trigger.signal: subjects or objects joined by or together with a plural noun

test: Ask who may handle which items, and whether alternatives may alternate or combine.
fix: State the intended allocation expressly, using wording that tracks the intended meaning (for example, whether the items may be split, shared, or must all go to one).
severity_basis: can change meaning or invite dispute

section: Part Versus the Whole > Or
statement: "Cumulation of attributes": an or-coordination of attributes that aren't mutually exclusive (one Acme temporary or part-time employee) raises whether it also covers something combining them (an employee who is both).

trigger.signal: two non-exclusive adjectives joined by or

test: Ask whether something with both attributes should be covered.
fix: To preclude cumulation, say ... temporary or part-time but not both (not doing so would be reckless); to make cumulation explicit, say temporary or part-time or both, weighing certainty against wordiness.
exceptions: It doesn't arise with mutually exclusive attributes (full-time or part-time employee) (11.85).
Economy of hypothesis suggests cumulation is covered, perhaps strongly enough that there is no real ambiguity (11.86).
severity_basis: vagueness, dispute risk, or legally significant usage

section: Part Versus the Whole > Or
statement: Adjectives-linked-by-or ambiguity with plural nouns: Tango shall terminate the employment of Acme's temporary or part-time employees can mean those who are temporary or those who are part-time, or all of both groups; may adds more meanings.

trigger.signal: two adjectives joined by or modifying one plural noun

test: Ask whether the provision reaches only one group, either group, or all members of both groups.
fix: Repeat the noun for each adjective (temporary employees or part-time employees).
severity_basis: can change meaning or invite dispute

examples.before: Tango shall terminate the employment of Acme's temporary or part-time employees.
examples.after: Tango shall terminate the employment of Acme's temporary employees or part-time employees.

section: Part Versus the Whole > And/Or and And ... Or
statement: Don't use and/or; say X or Y or both, one or both of X and Y, or one or both of the following: X; and Y. If and/or seems to offer significant economy, restructure.
severity_basis: a less clear usage invites a disgruntled party to use it as a stick (Redmond v. Sirius International, E.D. Wis. 2014); it is misused where only or is possible, states an obligation two ways, and is unclear with three or more items

examples.before: Acme shall purchase Widget A and/or Widget B.
examples.after: Acme shall purchase Widget A or Widget B and may purchase both.

section: Part Versus the Whole > And/Or and And ... Or
statement: And-or scope ambiguity: in a string of three elements with and between two and or between the others (Acme shall hire Able and Baker or Charlie; If A and B, or C, then D), the meaning depends on which conjunction has scope over the other.

trigger.signal: and and or in the same series of three or more elements

test: Group the elements both ways ((A and B) or C; A and (B or C)) and ask whether both groupings make sense.
fix: Enumerate (Acme shall hire (1) Able and Baker or (2) Charlie); use either to mark the or-coordination (Able and either Baker or Charlie); or use on the one hand ... on the other hand. For conditions: If A and B, or if C, then D; or If A and either B or C, then D.
severity_basis: Snukal v. Flightways Manufacturing (Cal. 2000) (Cal. Corp. Code § 313); BL Partners Group v. Interbroad (Pa. Super. Ct. 2017)

section: Part Versus the Whole > And/Or and And ... Or
statement: And-for-or mistake: and used where or makes sense (or the converse), as in a guarantee that terminates upon (1) ..., (2) ..., and (3) ..., where requiring all three events makes no sense.

trigger.signal: a list of alternative triggering events joined by and

test: Ask whether the provision should operate when only one listed event occurs.
fix: Use or when any one suffices; to prevent an argument that more than one occurring defeats the provision, put one or more of the following before the alternatives and and after the next-to-last.
severity_basis: 2014 Caesars Entertainment indenture dispute over whether the parent guarantee terminated on the first of three events

section: Part Versus the Whole > Every, Each, All, and Any
statement: Every/each/all-in-discretion ambiguity: in language of obligation these words are clear, but with may (Acme may purchase every vehicle included in the Lee Assets) they can mean no fewer than all, or one or more.

trigger.signal: may followed by every, each, or all; for a single item, also the whole or the entire

test: Ask whether the party may take only some.
fix: Say may purchase one or more of the vehicles, or may purchase the vehicles, but only all of them.
exceptions: For a single item, the ambiguity afflicts equivalents to all, including the whole and the entire (11.106, second printing).
severity_basis: can change meaning or invite dispute
notes: Second printing (spring 2024) revised the last sentence of 11.106: "(In the case of a single item, ambiguity afflicts equivalents to all, including the whole and the entire.)" The first printing (our PDF, p. 535) tied this to mass nouns. Source: https://www.adamsdrafting.com/changes-made-to-the-2d-printing-of-the-5th-edition-of-mscd/

section: Part Versus the Whole > Every, Each, All, and Any
statement: Any ambiguity: in language of obligation, any can mean all (shall purchase any vehicle, as in "take the name of any person who comes through the door") or one ("pick any card"), and may imply there may be none; in language of discretion, it can mean only one or one or more.

trigger.signal: any after shall, must, or may, or any in a condition

test: Ask whether any means each one, just one, or one or more.
fix: Say each, one, or one or more, as intended; refer to "a single term" or "one or more terms."
severity_basis: Endeavor Energy Resources v. Energen (Tex. 2020): "accumulate unused days in any 150-day term"

section: Part Versus the Whole > Every, Each, All, and Any
statement: Failure-or-inability ambiguity: every, each, all, and any in a sentence expressing failure or inability (inability to perform any duty; if all of the Conditions have not been discharged; prevents a Party from performing any of its obligations) can mean failure as to all, as to none, or as to one or more.

trigger.signal: every, each, all, or any combined with failure, inability, prevention, or not

test: Ask whether the provision is triggered by failure as to one item or only as to all.
fix: Say inability to perform one or more duties, or inability to perform all duties; if one or more of the Conditions has not been satisfied.
severity_basis: Dooba Developments v. McLagan Investments [2016] EWHC 2944 (Ch): "strict Boolean logic" read "if all of the Conditions have not been discharged" as requiring all four to be unsatisfied; courts can't be expected to sort this out unaided

examples.before: "Disability" means the Employee's inability to perform any duty under this agreement.
examples.after: "Disability" means the Employee's inability to perform one or more duties under this agreement.

section: Part Versus the Whole > Case Study and Practical Considerations
statement: Don't ignore part-versus-whole ambiguity; it confuses practitioners, clients, and judges.
severity_basis: Meyer v. CUNA Mutual Insurance Society (3d Cir. 2011) was decided incorrectly because the court found ambiguity where a reasonable reader would find none

section: Part Versus the Whole > Case Study and Practical Considerations
statement: Read "unable to perform any of the duties of his occupation or any occupation for which he is reasonably qualified" as a negated or-coordination: the natural meaning is unable to perform any duties of his own occupation and unable to perform any duties of any qualified occupation. The alternative reading (either inability suffices) makes half the provision redundant and so is unreasonable.
severity_basis: the ambiguity of or is a question of English usage, not a narrow legal question (11.130); overlap such as omitting other (any other occupation) is common and benign (11.137-.138)

section: Part Versus the Whole > Case Study and Practical Considerations
statement: Treat a provision as ambiguous only if each competing meaning is reasonable.
test: For each candidate meaning, ask whether a reasonable reader, using ordinary English usage, could adopt it.
severity_basis: can change meaning or invite dispute

section: Part Versus the Whole > Case Study and Practical Considerations
