statement: Weigh the reasonableness of alternative meanings independently; defects in one meaning don't bolster the reasonableness of the other.
severity_basis: can change meaning or invite dispute

section: Part Versus the Whole > Case Study and Practical Considerations
statement: Stay alert to part-versus-whole ambiguity, or you will likely miss alternative meanings until they cause a dispute; don't expect judges, increasingly reliant on dictionaries, to sort out a part-versus-whole mess sensibly.
severity_basis: can change meaning or invite dispute

section: Part Versus the Whole > Case Study and Practical Considerations
statement: Decide how far to go in eliminating alternative meanings: they are virtually inescapable with and and or; leave language as is if the alternative meaning isn't reasonable, but consider redrafting if an unreasonable meaning could cause mischief if a court adopted it.
exceptions: Revising "a medically determined sickness or accidental bodily injury" or "education, training or experience" to rule out combined readings would be outlandish (11.154).
severity_basis: vagueness, dispute risk, or legally significant usage

section: Part Versus the Whole > Case Study and Practical Considerations
statement: Balance expediency against risk: in The Seller has complied with all laws applicable to the Business and [or] the Acquired Assets, the natural meaning with and and with or is the same (each law applicable to either), and prose stylists would avoid extra verbiage; expediency might well prevail.

examples.before: The Seller has complied with all laws applicable to the Business and the Acquired Assets.
examples.after: The Seller has complied with all laws applicable to the Business and all laws applicable to the Acquired Assets.

section: Part Versus the Whole > Case Study and Practical Considerations
statement: Expect that eliminating part-versus-whole alternative meanings often becomes part of broader redrafting rather than a targeted adjustment.
severity_basis: vagueness, dispute risk, or legally significant usage

examples.before: unable to perform any of the duties of his occupation or any occupation for which he is reasonably qualified by education, training or experience
examples.after: (2) the member is able to perform none of the duties of the member's occupation and each other occupation for which the member is reasonably qualified by education, training, or experience

notes: The 11.159 revision is quoted in part; the full model language also restates the first-12-months standard as clause (1).

section: Syntactic Ambiguity > Modifiers
statement: Syntactic ambiguity arises from word order and the grammatical relations among words and phrases; it features in litigation more often than part-versus-whole ambiguity. A modifier is a word or phrase that changes the meaning of a word or phrase to which it is grammatically related.
severity_basis: can change meaning or invite dispute

section: Syntactic Ambiguity > Modifiers
statement: Preceding-modifier ambiguity: a modifier before two or more nouns (only children's apparel, accessories, and footwear) can modify only the first noun or all of them.

trigger.signal: an adjective or noun modifier before a series of two or more nouns

test: Ask whether the modifier should apply to every noun in the series.
fix: If only the first: enumerate (only (1) children's apparel, (2) accessories, and (3) footwear), use semicolons, or put that noun last. If all: repeat the modifier before each noun, or restate (only the following items for children: apparel, accessories, and footwear).
severity_basis: Regency Commercial Associates v. Lopax (Ill. App. Ct. 2007) ("fast food restaurant or restaurant facility"); In re Mobilactive Media (Del. Ch. 2013) ("interactive video programming and advertising content")

examples.before: Acme may sell in the Stores only children's apparel, accessories, and footwear.
examples.after: Acme may sell in the Stores only the following items for children: apparel, accessories, and footwear.

section: Syntactic Ambiguity > Modifiers
statement: Trailing-modifier ambiguity: a modifier after two or more nouns or clauses (incur any debt or make any capital expenditure in excess of $500,000) can modify only the last element or all of them.

trigger.signal: a modifier after the last of two or more nouns, verbs, or clauses

test: Ask whether the modifier should reach every element before it.
fix: If only the last: put that element first (make any capital expenditure in excess of $500,000 or incur any debt), or use semicolons. If all: repeat the modifier after each element. Enumeration alone can't fix it; tabulation works but is disfavored for short clauses.
severity_basis: Anderson v. Hess (8th Cir. 2011) ("drilling or reworking operations"); ECB USA v. Chubb (S.D. Fla. 2021); Batty v. UCAR International (Del. Ch. 2019) ("paid or payable")

examples.before: Acme shall not incur any debt or make any capital expenditure in excess of $500,000.
examples.after: Acme shall not incur any debt in excess of $500,000 or make any capital expenditure in excess of $500,000.

section: Syntactic Ambiguity > Modifiers
statement: Don't rely on the rule of the last antecedent, or on the "comma test" (a comma before a modifier following a series makes it apply to the whole series), to resolve a modifier's reach; eliminate the ambiguity.
severity_basis: the rule "has little weight or value" (Kimble, 16 Scribes J. Legal Writing 5 (2015)); the comma test conflicts with English usage, and relying on it would be "beyond reckless"

section: Syntactic Ambiguity > Modifiers
statement: Preceding-and-trailing-modifier ambiguity: with modifiers both before and after two noun phrases (Delaware corporations and LLCs qualified to do business in New York), four meanings are possible.

trigger.signal: a series with both a leading and a trailing modifier

test: List the four combinations of which noun each modifier reaches.
fix: Repeat a modifier to show it reaches both nouns (Delaware corporations qualified to do business in New York and Delaware LLCs qualified to do business in New York); switch the order of the noun phrases to show it doesn't.
severity_basis: United Rentals v. RAM Holdings (Del. Ch. 2007): "in no event shall the Company seek equitable relief or seek to recover any money damages in excess of such amount"; what matters is that the parties fought

section: Syntactic Ambiguity > Modifiers
statement: Medial-modifier ambiguity: a modifier after one noun in a string (the Lee Assets, excluding the Miller Assets, the Chang Assets, and the Meyer Assets) leaves unclear whether later nouns fall within it.

trigger.signal: excluding, including, other than, or except inside a series

test: Ask whether the later nouns are part of the exception or additional items.
fix: Use enumeration or parentheses: the Lee Assets (excluding the Miller Assets), the Chang Assets, and the Meyer Assets; or the Lee Assets (excluding the Miller Assets, the Chang Assets, and the Meyer Assets).
severity_basis: can change meaning or invite dispute

section: Syntactic Ambiguity > Modifiers
statement: Squinting-modifier ambiguity: a modifier placed between two elements could modify what comes before or after it (If Acme rejects any Asset within 10 days the Seller shall reimburse Acme).

trigger.signal: a time or condition phrase sitting between a conditional clause and the main clause with no comma, or with only a comma to show its attachment

test: Read the modifier with the preceding element, then with the following one; if both make sense, it squints.
fix: Move the modifier, and if needed use it twice: If no later than 10 days after the Closing Acme rejects any Asset, the Seller shall no later than 10 days after receiving the notice of rejection reimburse Acme. Don't rely only on a comma.
severity_basis: can change meaning or invite dispute

section: Syntactic Ambiguity > Modifiers
statement: Uncertain-length ambiguity: it can be unclear whether a modifier incorporates a following relative clause (any item of apparel not constituting a Product that Widgetco has ... sold).

trigger.signal: a negative or participial modifier followed by a relative clause

test: Ask whether the relative clause belongs to the modifier (not constituting a Product that Widgetco sold) or to the head noun (item of apparel that Widgetco sold).
fix: Place the modifier in a conditional clause: any item of apparel, on condition that it does not constitute a Product that Widgetco has ... sold (or ... that Widgetco has sold, on condition that the item does not constitute a Product).
severity_basis: can change meaning or invite dispute

section: Syntactic Ambiguity > Modifiers
statement: Misplaced-modifier ambiguity: a modifier separated from what it modifies (... to an account designated by Galactic no later than five Business Days after the closing ...; a motor vehicle included in the Assets that is in Acme's possession) can attach to the wrong element.

trigger.signal: a time phrase or relative clause placed after an intervening noun

test: Ask what the nearest preceding element is and whether the modifier is meant for it.
fix: Put the modifier next to what it modifies, or move it to the front of the sentence (No later than five Business Days after the closing of a sale, the Sellers shall deliver the Proceeds of that sale to Galactic).
severity_basis: can change meaning or invite dispute

examples.before: every certificate of title relating to a motor vehicle included in the Assets that is in Acme's possession
examples.after: every certificate of title that is in Acme's possession relating to a motor vehicle included in the Assets

section: Syntactic Ambiguity > Modifiers
statement: Opening-or-closing-modifier ambiguity: a phrase that opens or closes a sentence containing two or more clauses (Other than in the Ordinary Course of Business, Acme shall not incur debt and Acme shall not make any capital expenditures; ..., unless and until terminated by one year prior notice) can modify one clause or all.

trigger.signal: an opening or closing phrase in a sentence with two or more clauses

test: Ask whether the phrase should govern every clause.
fix: If it modifies both and the clauses share a subject, combine them and put the phrase in front (Other than in the Ordinary Course of Business, Acme shall not incur debt or make any capital expenditures). If only the first, put it after the first clause; if only the second, reverse the clauses and put it after the new first clause.
severity_basis: Rogers Communications v. Aliant (CRTC): "the comma that costs 1 million dollars" in a renewal clause that made a five-year term illusory

section: Syntactic Ambiguity > Modifiers
statement: Offsetting-comma ambiguity: meaning that turns on whether a closing modifier is set off by commas (100% of the Redemptive Value [,] as of the Cut-off Date [,] of the Asset; all Acme inventory, including ... fertilizer materials [,] that Widgetco sold to Acme).

trigger.signal: a phrase whose attachment depends on the presence or absence of one or two commas

test: Read the sentence with and without the commas; if the meaning changes, the commas carry too much.
fix: Restructure so the meaning doesn't depend on commas. Be wary of ostensibly offsetting commas where the part before the first comma can stand alone.
severity_basis: Shelby County State Bank v. Van Diest Supply (7th Cir. 2002): the court ignored the absence of a comma

section: Syntactic Ambiguity > Modifiers
statement: To eliminate offsetting-comma confusion where two clauses share a prepositional phrase, move the shared preposition before each comma so the reader knows something is yet to come (or use two sentences).
severity_basis: someone might argue the Vendor isn't liable at all, and the original causes a miscue until the second comma

examples.before: The Vendor will not be liable to Acme or any Buyer, and neither Acme nor any Buyer will be liable to the Vendor, for any damages that are not a reasonably foreseeable consequence of breach.
examples.after: The Vendor will not be liable to Acme or any Buyer for, and neither Acme nor any Buyer will be liable to the Vendor for, any damages that are not a reasonably foreseeable consequence of breach.

section: Syntactic Ambiguity > That and Which
statement: A restrictive clause gives essential, distinguishing information (The cakes that George baked were delicious); a nonrestrictive clause gives a supplemental aside (The cakes, which George baked, were delicious). Usage authorities recommend that for restrictive clauses and comma-which for nonrestrictive ones.
severity_basis: vagueness, dispute risk, or legally significant usage

section: Syntactic Ambiguity > That and Which
statement: Restrictive-versus-nonrestrictive ambiguity: when drafters blur that and which (which in restrictive clauses, comma-which used for that, dropped commas before which), a relative clause can be read as limiting the noun or as an aside (all Contracts other than Assumed Contracts which are subject to section 4.3).

trigger.signal: which introducing a relative clause, with or without a preceding comma

test: Ask whether the clause is meant to narrow the noun (restrictive) or merely add information (nonrestrictive), and whether a reader could take it the other way.
fix: Use that for restrictive clauses; don't use nonrestrictive clauses; if the noun the clause modifies is unclear, use parentheses around any intervening phrase.
severity_basis: AIU Insurance v. Robert Plan (N.Y. Sup. Ct. 2006) treated a comma-which clause as restrictive

examples.before: There is no fact known to any Credit Agreement Party or any of its Subsidiaries which has had, or could reasonably be expected to have, a Material Adverse Effect.
examples.after: There is no fact known to any Credit Agreement Party or any of its Subsidiaries that has had, or could reasonably be expected to have, a Material Adverse Effect.

section: Syntactic Ambiguity > That and Which
statement: Don't use nonrestrictive clauses in contracts; either tackle an issue head-on or omit it.
severity_basis: a nonrestrictive clause risks being construed as restrictive (AIU Insurance), and nonrestrictive asides don't belong in contracts

section: Syntactic Ambiguity > That and Which
statement: Use that, not which, in restrictive clauses.
severity_basis: with which in restrictive clauses, only a comma distinguishes restrictive from nonrestrictive, which is asking for trouble

section: Syntactic Ambiguity > That and Which
statement: Using that may not be enough when it is unclear which noun the clause modifies (any Employee Benefit Plan, other than a Multiemployer Plan, that is subject to Title IV); put parentheses around the intervening phrase.
fix: Put parentheses around other than a Multiemployer Plan.
severity_basis: can change meaning or invite dispute

examples.before: "Pension Plan" means any Employee Benefit Plan, other than a Multiemployer Plan, which is subject to the provisions of Title IV of ERISA ...

section: Syntactic Ambiguity > The Serial Comma
statement: Use the serial comma (a comma before the conjunction joining the last two elements of a series of three or more).
severity_basis: standard in American English outside journalism (Chicago Manual of Style 6.19); it avoids the ambiguities in 12.60-.73

section: Syntactic Ambiguity > The Serial Comma
statement: Combined-element ambiguity: without a serial comma, the last two elements of a series can read as one combined element (raspberry, chocolate chip and cherry).

trigger.signal: series of three or more with no comma before the final and/or

test: Ask whether the last two elements could be one item.
fix: Add the serial comma, and if an element is itself a combination, reorder or restructure so it can't be misread.
severity_basis: can change meaning or invite dispute

section: Syntactic Ambiguity > The Serial Comma
statement: Apposition ambiguity: omitting the serial comma can make the second element read as an appositive explaining the first (To my parents, Ayn Rand and God), and the serial comma itself can create apposition (To my mother, Ayn Rand, and God).

trigger.signal: a series in which the second element could be read as renaming the first

test: Ask whether the second element could be read as a description of the first.
fix: Add the serial comma where it prevents apposition; where it creates apposition, reorder the elements or restructure.
severity_basis: Telenor Mobile v. Storm (S.D.N.Y. 2008): a "control" definition listed two or three alternatives depending on punctuation; a serial comma before "or otherwise" would have helped
notes: MSCD disagrees with Garner's Modern English Usage that the serial comma never creates an ambiguity (12.64).

section: Syntactic Ambiguity > The Serial Comma
statement: Shared-preposition ambiguity: without a serial comma, a final item can read as a second object of a preposition in the preceding item (packing for shipment or distribution of), changing who or what is covered.

trigger.signal: a series whose last item contains a preposition followed by X or Y

test: Ask whether the last noun is a separate item in the series or a second object of the preposition.
fix: Use parentheses (packing (for shipment) or distribution), reorder, or use semicolons, enumeration, or tabulation; don't rely on the comma alone.

section: Syntactic Ambiguity > The Serial Comma
statement: Use the serial comma, but don't rely on a comma to establish meaning; instead of or in addition to it, use another technique (parentheses, reordering, semicolons, enumeration, or tabulation) to eliminate the ambiguity.
severity_basis: parties and judges can't be counted on to understand commas, and a disgruntled party may argue a comma out of existence (Medfusion; ECB USA v. Chubb; State v. Khalil; Glasser v. Hilton Grand Vacations; Princeton Excess v. Hub City)

section: Syntactic Ambiguity > Delimiting Commas, Multiple Ambiguities, Restructuring
statement: Delimiting-comma ambiguity: offsetting commas meant to make the part after the second comma modify both preceding parts (in redeeming, or protecting any Grantor's interest in, the Excluded Assets) work only if both outer parts are fragments; if the part before the first comma can stand alone, the hint is too subtle.

trigger.signal: X, or Y, Z, where Z is meant to complete both X and Y

test: Check whether the part before the first comma and the part after the second are fragments that can't be read in isolation; if either can stand alone, the structure is ambiguous.
fix: Repeat the shared element: in redeeming the Excluded Assets or protecting any Grantor's interest in the Excluded Assets ("three words well spent"). Use delimiting commas only if both parts are fragments and the economy is significant.
severity_basis: can change meaning or invite dispute

examples.before: in redeeming, or protecting any Grantor's interest in, the Excluded Assets
examples.after: in redeeming the Excluded Assets or protecting any Grantor's interest in the Excluded Assets

section: Syntactic Ambiguity > Delimiting Commas, Multiple Ambiguities, Restructuring
statement: Each additional instance of syntactic ambiguity in a sentence doubles the possible meanings (three instances in one Georgia statute line yield eight).
test: Count the ambiguous attachments in a sentence; with two or more, restructure rather than patch.
severity_basis: can change meaning or invite dispute

section: Syntactic Ambiguity > Delimiting Commas, Multiple Ambiguities, Restructuring
statement: Sometimes, instead of remedial work on an awkward structure, start afresh; for example, eliminate an abstract noun that creates the ambiguity.
severity_basis: can change meaning or invite dispute

examples.before: Upon occurrence of a Change in Law or a Force Majeure Event that adversely affects the Seller's performance under this agreement, the Buyer and the Seller shall negotiate in good faith ...
examples.after: If a Change in Law or a Force Majeure Event adversely affects the Seller's performance under this agreement, the Buyer and the Seller shall negotiate in good faith ...

section: Selected Usages > ABROGATE
statement: Don't use abrogate in contracts; it is archaic and obscure.
fix: Use plain wording, for example 'will not affect'.

examples.before: ... and does not diminish or abrogate any rights of Indemnitee thereunder.
examples.after: ... and will not affect any rights of Indemnitee thereunder.

notes: KB verdict label: Don't use.

section: Selected Usages > ACTION OR PROCEEDING
statement: Instead of action or proceeding, use just proceeding; proceeding encompasses action.
fix: Use 'proceeding' alone.
notes: KB verdict label: Don't use. Authorities: Black's; 1A C.J.S. Actions s. 22 (13.3).

section: Selected Usages > ACTIVELY
statement: Don't use actively (or proactively) with a verb structure that connotes activity; it is redundant.
fix: Delete actively.
exceptions: To distinguish levels of activity (for example, to exclude an employee on leave), state the distinction explicitly (13.5); see R-13.5-actively-levels.

examples.before: which are being actively contested in good faith
examples.after: which are being contested in good faith

notes: KB verdict label: Don't use.

section: Selected Usages > ACTIVELY
statement: If you use actively to distinguish levels of activity (as in while actively employed, to exclude an employee on leave), instead state the distinction explicitly.
fix: Say explicitly what status counts, for example whether an employee on leave qualifies.

section: Selected Usages > ACTUAL, ACTUALLY
statement: Use actual only to draw a contrast with some other attribute (any actual or alleged damage) or where a word arguably has a non-actual meaning; otherwise delete it as padding.
test: Does actual contrast with alleged, potential, estimated, or another attribute? If not, delete it.
fix: Delete actual where it is padding.
exceptions: Keep actual where it draws a contrast (actual or alleged; actual or potential) or where the word it modifies arguably has a non-actual meaning (13.6).

examples.before: permits in Seller's actual physical possession
examples.after: permits in Seller's physical possession

examples.before: a copy of the actual proposed Lease
examples.after: a copy of the proposed Lease

notes: KB verdict label: Use only in a stated context. In the page image, 'before the actual taxes and special assessments payable during such year are known' (13.6) is shown unstruck; the text does not say why.

section: Selected Usages > ACTUAL, ACTUALLY
statement: Delete actually; it is rhetorical emphasis and can be deleted without affecting meaning.
fix: Delete actually.

examples.before: cash dividends per share actually paid by the Company
examples.after: cash dividends per share paid by the Company

notes: The first 13.7 example ('all Expenses actually and reasonably incurred by Indemnitee') is shown unstruck in the page image; the text does not say why.

section: Selected Usages > AFFIRMATIVELY, AFFIRMATIVE
statement: Generally, delete affirmatively; it is rhetorical emphasis.
fix: Delete affirmatively.
exceptions: For votes, see R-13.9-affirmative-vote; for affirmative action, see R-13.10-affirmative-action; for the heading Affirmative Covenants, see R-13.11-affirmative-covenants.

examples.before: unless the Employee affirmatively elects otherwise
examples.after: unless the Employee elects otherwise

examples.before: The Recipient hereby affirmatively consents to
examples.after: The Recipient hereby consents to

notes: KB verdict label: Don't use.

section: Selected Usages > AFFIRMATIVELY, AFFIRMATIVE
statement: Instead of the affirmative vote of a majority of the outstanding shares, say what is meant: by vote of the shareholders in which a majority of the outstanding shares vote in favor of the action.
fix: by vote of the shareholders in which a majority of the outstanding shares vote in favor of the action

section: Selected Usages > AFFIRMATIVELY, AFFIRMATIVE
statement: In affirmative action, affirmative is redundant unless you are referring to employment or higher-education admissions policies; delete it otherwise.
fix: Delete affirmative (for example, 'take any action').

examples.before: will not be required to take any affirmative action to cause delivery
examples.after: will not be required to take any action to cause delivery

section: Selected Usages > AFFIRMATIVELY, AFFIRMATIVE
statement: Don't use Affirmative Covenants as a heading; Certain Obligations would be an improvement.
fix: Use the heading Certain Obligations.

section: Selected Usages > ALLONGE
statement: Don't use the term of art allonge. Use indorsement supplement, indorsement addendum, or indorsement certificate; where allonge means an amendment of a promissory note, use amendment.
fix: indorsement supplement, indorsement addendum, or indorsement certificate; amendment (for FIRST ALLONGE TO PROMISSORY NOTE)
severity_basis: obscure term of art whose meaning has drifted
notes: KB verdict label: Don't use.

section: Selected Usages > ALSO, IN ADDITION
statement: Be restrained in using also and in addition; contract provisions on discrete topics should be able to stand on their own.
fix: Delete where the provision stands on its own.
notes: KB verdict label: Use with care. The author does not ban these words; he says be restrained.

section: Selected Usages > AMONG OTHER THINGS
statement: Use among other things only when it refers to something treated fully elsewhere (in this or another contract). Where it is equivalent to includes or including, use that word; where only the items specified are relevant, delete it.
test: Are the other things treated fully elsewhere? If yes, keep. If the phrase introduces examples, use includes/including. If only the stated items matter, delete.
fix: includes / including, or delete
exceptions: Benign when it refers to something treated fully elsewhere (13.15).

examples.before: 'Reasonable Efforts' means, among other things, ...
examples.after: 'Reasonable Efforts' includes ...

examples.before: Each Letter of Credit must, among other things, (1) provide for
examples.after: Each Letter of Credit must (1) provide for

notes: KB verdict label: Use only in a stated context. On the risks of includes as a definitional verb, see 6.38.

section: Selected Usages > AMONG OTHER THINGS
statement: Don't use the Latin inter alia.
fix: Use the English treatment in R-13.15-among-other-things.

section: Selected Usages > AMONGST, WHILST
statement: Use among, not amongst, and while, not whilst; this applies to British drafters too.
fix: among; while
notes: KB verdict label: Don't use. Garner's Modern English Usage; Google Ngram (13.20).

section: Selected Usages > ANNIVERSARY
statement: Use anniversary only for a yearly recurrence; don't use it to mark a milestone in months or weeks. Instead of 12-month anniversary, say on the anniversary of or 12 months after.

trigger.signal: anniversary used with months or weeks

fix: one month after [event]; on the anniversary of [event]; 12 months after [event]

examples.before: monthly beginning on the one-month anniversary following the First Closing Date
examples.after: monthly beginning one month after the First Closing Date

notes: KB verdict label: Use only in a stated context.

section: Selected Usages > ANNIVERSARY MONTH
statement: Don't use anniversary month; spell out the month meant.
fix: the month in which the anniversary of [event] occurs; the month of that year corresponding to [month]

examples.before: annually during each anniversary month thereafter
examples.after: annually during the month in which the anniversary of the Effective Date occurs

notes: KB verdict label: Don't use. By default forward-looking, but used backward-looking and for a corresponding month of a later year (13.25-13.26).

section: Selected Usages > ANNUAL MEETING
statement: Be specific about what qualifies as the annual meeting for a given year; for example, say that a meeting qualifies if it is held anytime in that year.
fix: State which meeting counts as the annual meeting for each year.
notes: KB verdict label: Use with care. Airgas, Inc. v. Air Products & Chemicals, Inc., 8 A.3d 1182 (Del. 2010) (13.29).

section: Selected Usages > ANYONE
statement: If a provision encompasses anyone, consider using anyone (If anyone commences an involuntary case against the Company); it is more concise than any person or entity or any Person.
fix: anyone; or the passive without a by-agent (If an involuntary case is commenced against the Company)
exceptions: Don't use anyone in a sensitive context; there is little relevant caselaw (13.30). See R-13.30-anyone-sensitive.
notes: KB verdict label: Use with care.

section: Selected Usages > ANYONE
statement: Don't use anyone in a sensitive context, because there is little relevant caselaw; use a defined term such as Person instead.
fix: Use the defined term (for example, any Person).
severity_basis: untested usage in a sensitive provision

section: Selected Usages > APPLICABLE > Applicable Plus Noun
statement: You may use applicable before a noun to mean 'whichever is relevant' (the applicable benefit plan). Don't use it where it suggests the provision applies to a subset of a whole when it applies to the whole, as in applicable law or applicable taxes.
test: Does applicable select one of several relevant items? If it merely restates that the thing applies (applicable law), delete it.
fix: Delete applicable where redundant.

examples.before: Recipient shall pay all applicable taxes incurred
examples.after: Recipient shall pay all taxes incurred

examples.before: the bulk transfer laws of any applicable jurisdiction
examples.after: the bulk transfer laws of any jurisdiction

notes: KB verdict label: Use with care. The third 13.33 example ('do not violate any applicable law') shows no strike in the page image although the text calls applicable redundant there.

section: Selected Usages > APPLICABLE > Applicable Plus Noun
statement: Don't use applicable if greater precision is required; restate the provision so it is clear which item is meant.
fix: Restate explicitly (for example, 'with respect to a given anniversary').

examples.before: on condition that the Employee is employed by the Company on the applicable anniversary
examples.after: except that the Company will not be required to make a payment with respect to a given anniversary if the Employee is then no longer employed by the Company

section: Selected Usages > APPLICABLE > The Verb To Be Plus Applicable
statement: Generally, instead of be applicable, use the verb apply.
fix: apply / applies

examples.before: will be applicable solely to work that the Tenant performs
examples.after: will apply solely to work that the Tenant performs

section: Selected Usages > APPLICABLE > As Applicable
statement: You may use as applicable; it is unobjectionable and more concise than as the case may be.
fix: Keep; prefer it to as the case may be.

section: Selected Usages > APPURTENANT
statement: Use appurtenant only to express its primary real-estate meaning (easement appurtenant); start by replacing ancillary uses of appurtenant and appurtenance, in real-estate contracts or elsewhere.
fix: offered at; that are part of; associated with; located in; its
exceptions: Entrenched real-estate uses (easement appurtenant; a definition of Appurtenances in a real-estate contract) need not be replaced (13.39-13.40).

examples.before: similar areas and facilities appurtenant to the Project
examples.after: similar areas and facilities that are part of the Project

examples.before: the federal court appurtenant thereto
examples.after: the federal court located in King William County

notes: KB verdict label: Use only in a stated context.

section: Selected Usages > ARISING OUT OF OR RELATING TO
statement: Don't rely on arising out of or relating to to set the scope of dispute-resolution, liability-limitation, or release provisions; it combines two nonspecific standards. To bring in a broad but predictable set of claims, refer to the contract and to the activities the parties will engage in as part of the transaction, and drop or relating to.

words: arising out of or relating to
arising out of or related to
arise out of or relate to
arises out of or relates to

fix: any dispute arising out of this agreement or [named transaction activities]
notes: KB verdict label: Don't use. Moskin treatise states the conventional view (13.44). In re TFT-LCD (Flat Panel) Antitrust Litigation, 2011 WL 2650689 (N.D. Cal. 2011) (13.46). Appendix A fn 185 keeps arising out of alone.

section: Selected Usages > ARISING OUT OF OR RELATING TO > An Alternative Approach
statement: Say what the subject matter is rather than arising out of the subject matter of this agreement; that phrase trades one nonspecificity for another and has generated litigation.

words: any action or proceeding brought to enforce any provision of this agreement

fix: Name the activities (for example, ownership of any Interest, or management or operations of the Company).

examples.before: any action or proceeding brought to enforce any provision of this Agreement
examples.after: any dispute arising out of this agreement, ownership of any Interest, or management or operations of the Company

notes: Henderson v. Henderson Investment Properties, L.L.C., 227 P.3d 568 (Idaho 2010) (13.49).

section: Selected Usages > ARISING OUT OF OR RELATING TO > An Alternative Approach
statement: If you want to limit a dispute-resolution provision to claims under the contract, include a provision excluding extracontractual liability; don't assume arising out of alone does it.

trigger.signal: dispute-resolution provision meant to cover only contract claims

fix: Add an express exclusion of extracontractual (tort, statutory) claims.
severity_basis: scope of covered claims can be disputed
notes: Maynard v. BTI Group, Inc., 157 Cal. Rptr. 3d 148 (Ct. App. 2013) ('any dispute' included tort claims) (13.51). Relying on arising out of alone would be 'reckless' (13.52).

section: Selected Usages > ARISING OUT OF OR RELATING TO > The Risk of the Unknown
statement: Recognize that deciding which claims a provision covers can backfire; if you do many transactions, apply a flexible, reasoned (not copy-and-pasted) dispute-resolution strategy and focus, deal by deal, on eliminating sources of dispute and confusion.

trigger.signal: governing-law or forum provision that sweeps in all claims

fix: Choose coverage deliberately for each transaction type.
notes: Example: choosing California law for all claims because it favors you on one issue, then facing a dispute where it works against you (13.53).

section: Selected Usages > AS AMENDED
statement: Don't use as amended to modify references to statutes or other contracts. When referring to compliance, don't tack on as amended; compliance can be measured only against the text as then in effect.

words: as amended from time to time
as the same may be amended

fix: Delete as amended in compliance references.
exceptions: For a reference to an element of a statute or contract (such as a definition), see R-13.58-as-in-effect.

examples.before: Acme shall comply with the Securities Act, as amended
examples.after: Acme shall comply with the Securities Act

notes: KB verdict label: Don't use. Appendix A fn 65 drops as amended.

section: Selected Usages > AS AMENDED
statement: When referring to an element of a statute or another contract (for example, a definition), make clear whether you mean it as in effect on the date of this agreement (to freeze it) or as then in effect (to pick up later amendments); if that leaves room for confusion, be more specific (as in effect on exercise of the Option).

trigger.signal: cross-reference to a definition or provision of a statute or other contract

test: Can a reader tell which version of the referenced text applies at the relevant time?
fix: as in effect on the date of this agreement / as then in effect / as in effect on [event]
severity_basis: unclear point in time; as amended makes no sense if no amendment occurred

section: Selected Usages > AS BETWEEN THE PARTIES
statement: Don't use as between the parties; a contract is between the parties and no one else, so the phrase is in effect read into every provision.
fix: Delete it.
exceptions: If a nonparty might be implicated, address that explicitly (13.61); see R-13.61-as-between-nonparty.

examples.before: As between the parties, Acme will be solely responsible for the cost of Development
examples.after: Acme will be solely responsible for the cost of Development

notes: KB verdict label: Don't use.

section: Selected Usages > AS BETWEEN THE PARTIES
statement: If you are tempted to use as between the parties because a nonparty might somehow be implicated, address the nonparty issue explicitly instead.
fix: State the nonparty arrangement expressly.

section: Selected Usages > AS LIQUIDATED DAMAGES AND NOT AS A PENALTY
statement: When providing for liquidated damages, include a characterization of the payment, but don't rely on the formula as liquidated damages and not as a penalty. Use a fuller acknowledgment (damages difficult to estimate and prove; the parties intend compensation, not a penalty) and explain why actual damages are difficult to estimate.

words: as liquidated damages and not as a penalty

fix: Acme acknowledges that the actual damages likely to result from breach ... are difficult to estimate on the date of this agreement and would be difficult for Widgetco to prove. The parties intend that ... would compensate Widgetco ... They do not intend for it be a penalty ...
exceptions: Don't simply drop the characterization; some courts give it weight (13.64-13.65).
notes: KB verdict label: Use with care. 24 Williston s. 65:1 (13.62); Restatement (Second) of Contracts s. 356 cmt. c (13.63); Ludlow Valve Mfg. Co. v. City of Chicago, 181 Ill. App. 388 (1913) (13.64).

section: Selected Usages > AS THE CASE MAY BE
statement: As the case may be can make a choice made in one sentence flow through to later sentences, but generally express the meaning more concisely (the transferee instead of Baker or Charlie, as the case may be) or use as applicable.
fix: the transferee (or another concise reference); as applicable
notes: KB verdict label: Use with care.

section: Selected Usages > AS THE CASE MAY BE
statement: Don't use as the case may be after simple alternatives; that is a misuse.

trigger.signal: as the case may be after 'X or Y' in the same clause

fix: Delete it.
notes: Book's misuse example (13.70): 'Date of Termination' means the date on which a Covered Change in Control Termination or Covered Termination Prior to a Change in Control occurs, as the case may be.

section: Selected Usages > AT LEAST ONE OF X AND Y
statement: Use at least one of X and Y (with and), never at least one of X or Y; or say one or more of X and Y, which is simpler. Courts and drafters should ignore SuperGuide's suggestion that or changes the result.

trigger.signal: at least one of / one or more of followed by a list joined by or

test: Is the list after at least one of joined by or? If so, change or to and.
fix: at least one of X, Y, and Z; one or more of X, Y, and Z
severity_basis: misreading invited by SuperGuide; ungrammatical with or
notes: KB verdict label: Use. SuperGuide Corp. v. DirecTV Enterprises, Inc., 358 F.3d 870 (Fed. Cir. 2004) (13.72-13.75).

section: Selected Usages > AT LEAST ONE OF X AND Y > Recommendation
statement: If at least one of refers to categories, or to units within categories, say so explicitly, and say whether you mean units in all categories or in fewer than all; if it refers to units, nothing more is needed.

trigger.signal: at least one of before a list of categories that each contain units

test: Could one of mean one item within a category or one category? If so, the provision is ambiguous.
fix: at least one of the following categories: ...; at least one unit in each of the following categories: ...; at least one unit in [at least] one of the following categories: ...

section: Selected Usages > ATTORN
statement: Don't use the term of art attorn (or attornment). In a provision effecting an attornment, use consent; the same applies to the Canadian use of attorn for consent to court jurisdiction.
fix: consent (Tenant shall consent to any party's succeeding to the Landlord's interest ...)
exceptions: If you feel you must refer to attornment, use Attornment as a section heading (13.89); see R-13.89-attornment-heading.

examples.before: Tenant shall attorn to any party's succeeding to the Landlord's interest
examples.after: Tenant shall consent to any party's succeeding to the Landlord's interest

notes: KB verdict label: Don't use.

section: Selected Usages > ATTORN
statement: If you feel you must refer to attornment, use Attornment only as a section heading, with consent in the provision itself.
fix: Heading: Attornment; text: consent.

section: Selected Usages > AUTOMATICALLY
statement: Omit automatically where it is dispensable. Use it where, without it, a passive-voice provision could suggest that party action is required, as with automatic extension of a term.
test: Without automatically, could a reader think a party must act (a missing by-agent)? If not, delete it.
fix: Delete; keep for automatic extension of a term.

examples.before: restrictions on any such awards will automatically lapse at midnight
examples.after: restrictions on any such awards will lapse at midnight

notes: KB verdict label: Use only in a stated context.

section: Selected Usages > AUTOMATICALLY
statement: Don't use automatically where a legal fiction is being established; use deem.
fix: will be deemed to have been ...

examples.before: will be automatically modified to conform to the tax law requirements
examples.after: will be deemed to have been modified to conform to the tax law requirements

section: Selected Usages > BASIS (INCLUDING TIMELY)
statement: Replace adverbial basis phrases with the adverb: on a daily basis -> daily; on a weekly basis -> weekly; on a regular basis -> regularly; on a pro-rata basis -> pro rata; on a timely basis, in a timely manner, in a timely fashion -> timely. Some basis phrases need a bigger fix; for on an ongoing basis, say how often or at Acme's request.
fix: daily; weekly; regularly; pro rata; timely; periodically / monthly / at Acme's request

examples.before: Interest will accrue on a daily basis.
examples.after: Interest will accrue daily.

examples.before: ability to perform on a timely basis its obligations
examples.after: ability to timely perform its obligations

examples.before: unless that transaction is made on an arm's-length basis and has been approved
examples.after: other than an arm's-length transaction that has been approved

notes: KB verdict label: Don't use. Garner's Dictionary of Legal Usage at 895: adverbial timely is archaic in British English (13.98).

section: Selected Usages > BECAUSE
statement: Whenever you use because in a contract (typically in a conditional clause, If X because of Y, then Z), consider being specific about the type of causation required, such as sole cause or but-for cause.
test: Must Y be the sole cause or only one of several causes? If the provision doesn't say, it invites dispute.
fix: State the causation standard (solely because of; but for).
notes: KB verdict label: Use with care. Gross v. FBL Financial Services, Inc., 557 U.S. 167 (2009) (statutory 'because of' requires but-for causation) (13.102).

section: Selected Usages > BELIEF
statement: Don't state categorically the legal implications of facts as they exist on signing (This agreement complies with section 409A); have the party give its opinion (The parties believe this agreement complies). It would be clearer, though not necessarily convenient, to qualify by belief statements of fact that present legal opinions (formation, enforceability, no violation of law), backed by indemnification or another risk-allocation mechanism.

trigger.signal: statement of fact asserting a legal conclusion

fix: The parties believe that ...; supplement with indemnification, a termination fee, or another risk-allocation mechanism.
exceptions: Qualifying by belief often goes against long-established convention (13.106).
The parties intend that ... offers less comfort than believe (13.104); on intend that, see 3.491-.500.
severity_basis: statement purporting to preempt judicial determination
notes: KB verdict label: Use.

section: Selected Usages > BETWEEN OR AMONG
statement: Instead of between or among, use just between; there is no basis in English usage for reserving between for two and among for more than two. To avoid any confusion about contracts between the parties, say agreements between two or more of the parties.
fix: between; agreements between two or more of the parties
notes: KB verdict label: Don't use.

section: Selected Usages > BOOKS AND RECORDS
statement: Drop books from books and records; books are an example of records.
fix: records
exceptions: If an explicit link to a statute is required (for example, Delaware GCL s. 220), say in accordance with the statute rather than parroting it (13.113).
notes: KB verdict label: Don't use.

section: Selected Usages > BOOKS AND RECORDS
statement: To capture the narrower accounting meaning, use accounting records (the UK Companies Act 2006 term) or financial records; a narrower term may spare a party a surprise when the other side asks to audit many kinds of records.

trigger.signal: audit or inspection right over records

fix: accounting records / financial records

section: Selected Usages > BOTH X AND Y, EITHER X OR Y
statement: Generally, don't use both to emphasize the link between two things, or either to emphasize that an or is exclusive; contracts aren't the place for degrees of emphasis.
fix: Delete both / either.
exceptions: When the linked items are lengthy, both (or either) signals in advance the conjunction to come; restructuring may still be better (13.116-13.117). See R-13.116-both-lengthy.

examples.before: certified by a physician acceptable to both Acme and the Employee
examples.after: certified by a physician acceptable to Acme and the Employee

notes: KB verdict label: Don't use.

section: Selected Usages > BOTH X AND Y, EITHER X OR Y
statement: When the two linked items are lengthy, both (or either) can signal in advance that the link is and (or exclusive or); but restructuring the provision might be a better fix.

trigger.signal: both/either before two long coordinated items

fix: Keep both/either, or restructure (for example, enumerate).

section: Selected Usages > BUY, PURCHASE
statement: Use the verb purchase, not buy; buying and bought are more awkward than purchase and purchased, and related verb and noun forms help the reader.
fix: purchase / purchases / purchasing / purchased
severity_basis: consistency of verb and noun forms
notes: KB verdict label: Use. 13.119 shows the rejected change purchase -> buy. The defined term Buyer is not addressed in the detail notes.

section: Selected Usages > BYLAWS
statement: Spell it bylaws (no hyphen).
fix: bylaws
notes: KB verdict label: Use. British English uses byelaw for local-authority regulations (Garner's, 13.123).

section: Selected Usages > CERTAIN
statement: Don't use certain if its connotation of a subset of a whole doesn't apply or is unnecessary.
test: Does the provision refer to an unnamed subset? If the items are identified (listed in a schedule), certain is wrong.
fix: the, or delete

examples.before: certain assets listed in schedule B
examples.after: the assets listed in schedule B

examples.before: Executive may provide certain services to Acme
examples.after: Executive may provide services to Acme

notes: KB verdict label: Use only in a stated context.

section: Selected Usages > CERTIFY
statement: In contexts such as the Customer shall certify in writing to the Seller that the Customer has complied, don't use certify, which implies a formal certificate; say the Customer shall notify the Seller that ...
fix: notify (and drop 'in writing' if the notices provision already requires writing)
notes: KB verdict label: Don't use. The objection is to implied formality 'in such contexts' (13.126); a formal certificate requirement is a different matter.

section: Selected Usages > CHANGE IN CONTROL, CHANGE OF CONTROL
statement: Change in control and change of control are both acceptable; pick one and use it consistently.
test: Does the document or document set use both forms?
fix: Use one form throughout.
notes: KB verdict label: Use.

section: Selected Usages > CLOSING
statement: When closing means the moment a transaction is consummated, it is a gerundial noun; use it with the definite article (on or before the Closing).
test: Is closing used for the moment of consummation without the? Then add the.
fix: the Closing
notes: KB verdict label: Use. Omitting the wouldn't cause confusion, but get it right (13.139).

section: Selected Usages > COGNIZANT
statement: Usually dispense with cognizant, a formal word for knowledgeable; use aware of or omit.
fix: aware of
exceptions: Use cognizant agency only to invoke the statutory federal-contracting arrangement (13.141); see R-13.141-cognizant-agency.

examples.before: the Contributor is fully cognizant of and understands all of the risk factors
examples.after: the Contributor is aware of all of the risk factors

notes: KB verdict label: Use only in a stated context.

section: Selected Usages > COGNIZANT
statement: Use cognizant agency only to invoke the federal-contracting arrangement provided for by statute; where the meaning is simply relevant agency, say so.
fix: relevant agency (unless the statutory arrangement is meant)
severity_basis: term of art defined by statute

section: Selected Usages > COMPETITIVE
statement: Use competitive only to mean 'of, involving, or based on competition' or 'likely to succeed in competition'. Where the meaning is competing, use competing or the verb compete.
fix: competing; competes with

examples.before: 'Competitive Business' means any business that is similar to or competitive with the business of the Company
examples.after: 'Competing Business' means any business that is similar to or competes with the business of the Company

notes: KB verdict label: Use with care. Appendix A fns 124 and 136 replace competitive with that competes with.

section: Selected Usages > COMPLETE AND ACCURATE
statement: Generally, do without some or all of complete and accurate. First determine whether you can drop the phrase entirely; if you keep one element, consider keeping the whole phrase, to avoid a fight over whether the remainder is comprehensive enough.
fix: See the context rules R-13.148 to R-13.152.
notes: KB verdict label: Use with care.

section: Selected Usages > COMPLETE AND ACCURATE
statement: By context: for an obligation to compile data, drop complete, and if possible drop both (Acme shall maintain a database that lists for all customers the following information); to confirm data meet a contract requirement, refer to compliance with the requiring provision (Acme has complied with its obligations under section 5); for copies, drop both, or if nervous keep complete and drop accurate.
fix: Acme shall maintain a database that lists ...; Acme has complied with its obligations under section 5; a copy of ...

examples.before: Excelsior shall maintain complete and accurate books of account.
examples.after: Excelsior shall maintain accurate books of account.

section: Selected Usages > CONSEQUENTIAL DAMAGES
statement: Don't exclude consequential damages; the term is confusing. Courts equate it with Hadley's second branch (special circumstances), but Black's treats it as indirect damages, a causation concept, so it is lexically ambiguous. Address the parties' concerns more clearly using the alternatives in 13.166-13.174.
fix: Exclude damages not reasonably foreseeable (13.167); cap damages; describe included damages; address special circumstances explicitly; consider liquidated damages.
severity_basis: lexical ambiguity; courts acknowledge unclear meaning
notes: KB verdict label: Don't use. Hadley v. Baxendale (1854), 156 E.R. 145 (13.158); West & Duran, 63 Bus. Law. 777 (2008) (13.160-13.163); Applied Data Processing v. Burroughs, 394 F. Supp. 504 (D. Conn. 1975) (13.165). 13.162-13.163 refer to 'the example in 13.154', printed in 13.155.

section: Selected Usages > CONSEQUENTIAL DAMAGES > Consequential Damages Is Confusing
statement: Don't exclude both special damages and consequential damages; U.S. courts generally treat them as synonyms, and special damages means something else in tort, so the pairing adds confusion.
fix: Use the alternatives in R-13.167-foreseeable-damages and R-13.170-special-circumstances.

section: Selected Usages > CONSEQUENTIAL DAMAGES > Consequential Damages Is Confusing
statement: Don't exclude both direct and indirect damages; that could lead to a fight over whether all damages are excluded or the contract is void.
fix: State which damages are recoverable.
notes: Innovate Technology Solutions, L.P. v. Youngsoft, Inc., 418 S.W.3d 148 (Tex. App. 2013) (13.164).

section: Selected Usages > CONSEQUENTIAL DAMAGES > Alternatives to Confusion
statement: To exclude remote damages, exclude damages that aren't reasonably foreseeable: Neither party will be liable for breach-of-contract damages that the breaching party could not reasonably have foreseen at the time of breach.

trigger.signal: limitation-of-liability provision

fix: Neither party will be liable for breach-of-contract damages that the breaching party could not reasonably have foreseen at the time of breach.
notes: It states what a court would likely conclude anyway but might prevent a fight (13.167). West & Duran at 806 (13.167).

section: Selected Usages > CONSEQUENTIAL DAMAGES > Alternatives to Confusion
statement: If the seller wants to exclude otherwise recoverable damages, agree to an absolute cap; if it wants to limit types of damages, describe what damages are included rather than excluded (for a sale of goods, expectancy damages and cover minus contract price, without those terms of art, perhaps with a cap). A buyer might accept a limited range of damages in exchange for liquidated damages.

trigger.signal: limitation-of-liability provision

fix: cap; description of included damages; liquidated damages

section: Selected Usages > CONSEQUENTIAL DAMAGES > Alternatives to Confusion
statement: If you want to exclude damages, don't use consequential damages; use the Hadley second-branch meaning, expressed as special circumstances. For a sale, have the buyer state that, except as described, it has no knowledge of special circumstances that would render otherwise unforeseeable damages foreseeable, and describe any special circumstances the seller acknowledges.
fix: The Buyer states that [except as described in section x,] it has no knowledge of any special circumstances to which it is subject that would render reasonably foreseeable any damages ... that otherwise would not have been reasonably foreseeable.
exceptions: A buyer aware of special circumstances can keep the right to claim for them (the bracketed exception) or waive it (13.171).

section: Selected Usages > CONSEQUENTIAL DAMAGES > Alternatives to Confusion
statement: Exclude other kinds of damages only if doing so serves your interests, not from a copy-and-paste urge, and beware pitfalls such as excluding lost profits.
fix: Delete exclusions that don't serve the client.
notes: Book's example of an improvised list (13.155): punitive damages, lost profits, diminution of value, consequential damages, special damages, incidental damages, indirect damages, exemplary damages, or other similar unforeseen damages.

section: Selected Usages > CONTINUOUSLY, CONTINUOUS
statement: Generally, omit continuously (and continuous), adjusting the wording if needed; unless you specify otherwise, a provision applies continuously, and continuously could be read as nonstop, every-minute activity.
fix: Delete; adjust the verb (keeps substantially all of its assets invested).
exceptions: Where you must emphasize nonstop activity, use constant, nonstop, or 24 hours a day, seven days a week (13.178).
Keep the securities term of art continuous offering (13.180).

examples.before: shall diligently and continuously enforce the material obligations
examples.after: shall diligently enforce the material obligations

examples.before: money market mutual fund that has substantially all of its assets invested continuously
examples.after: money market mutual fund that keeps substantially all of its assets invested

notes: KB verdict label: Don't use. In the 13.179 image only the first continuously is struck; 'continuous services' is not struck.

section: Selected Usages > CONTINUOUSLY, CONTINUOUS
statement: Where you must emphasize nonstop activity, use constant, nonstop, or 24 hours a day, seven days a week instead of continuously.

trigger.signal: obligation that really requires uninterrupted activity

fix: constant; nonstop; 24 hours a day, seven days a week

section: Selected Usages > CONTINUOUSLY, CONTINUOUS
statement: Keep continuous in the securities term of art continuous offering (an offering made on a continuous basis).
fix: Leave it.

section: Selected Usages > CONTRACTUAL
statement: Don't use contractual; say contract terms and contract obligations instead of contractual terms and contractual obligations, and contracts instead of contractual instruments or contractual arrangements.
fix: contract terms; contract obligations; contracts
notes: KB verdict label: Don't use.

section: Selected Usages > COSTS AND EXPENSES
statement: Don't use the doublet costs and expenses; costs are a type of expense. Refer to court costs, other litigation costs, and any other expenses (or a variant), or use only expenses.
fix: expenses; court costs, other litigation costs, and any other expenses

examples.before: the Company shall pay all costs and expenses, including reasonable attorneys' fees and costs, incurred in connection with that action
examples.after: the Company shall pay all expenses ... incurred in connection with that action

notes: KB verdict label: Don't use.

section: Selected Usages > COTERMINOUS
statement: Don't use coterminous or conterminous; refer to the contract terminating when the other contract terminates.
fix: that terminates when [the other contract] terminates

examples.before: a license coterminous with the Lease Term
examples.after: a license that terminates when the Lease Term terminates

notes: KB verdict label: Don't use.

section: Selected Usages > COTERMINOUS
statement: When one contract is to terminate when another does, say explicitly whether early termination of one contract terminates the other or whether they operate independently.

trigger.signal: contract whose term is tied to another contract

fix: State whether early termination of either contract carries over to the other.

section: Selected Usages > COUPLED WITH AN INTEREST
statement: Before saying a power of attorney is coupled with an interest, ask whether the power should last beyond the principal's death or incompetence. If not, drop the phrase; saying the power is irrevocable serves your purpose. If so, ask whether the agent has an interest in the subject matter of the power; if not, the phrase likely won't help.
test: (1) Must the power survive death or incompetence? (2) Does the agent have an interest in the subject matter of the power (not just the proceeds)?
fix: irrevocable; or the explanatory provision in 13.200
severity_basis: legal effect depends on facts, not label
notes: KB verdict label: Use only in a stated context. 3 Am. Jur. 2d Agency ss. 49, 56, 58; Crowe v. Trickey, 204 U.S. 228 (1907) (13.193-13.197).

section: Selected Usages > COUPLED WITH AN INTEREST
statement: If the agent has an interest in the subject matter of the power and the power should survive death or incompetence, use an explanatory provision instead of the bare formula.
fix: [The principal] acknowledges that this power of attorney is coupled with an interest, because the agent has an interest in [the subject of the power]. As a result, in addition to any other consequences under law, this power is irrevocable and will survive [the principal's] death or incompetence.
notes: This conflicts with not saying the same thing twice (1.56), but the benefits outweigh that (13.201).

section: Selected Usages > CURING BREACH
statement: Provide for cure only where it seems appropriate, for example a missed payment; the concept is overused, and giving across-the-board permission to breach is indulgent. Provisions allowing cure can exclude breaches not amenable to cure by covering only breaches that are.
fix: Limit cure to appropriate breaches (for example, payment) and to breaches amenable to cure.
notes: KB verdict label: Use with care. Some breaches can't be cured ('you can't unbreak an egg') (13.204-13.205).

section: Selected Usages > CURING BREACH > Amenable to Cure
statement: Use amenable to cure, not capable of being cured.
fix: amenable to cure

section: Selected Usages > DEEM
statement: Use deem only to create a legal fiction: to treat a thing as what it is not or might not be, or as having qualities it does not or might not have. Don't use deem where no legal fiction is established.
test: Is the provision treating something as what it is not, or might not be? If not, delete deemed (to be).
fix: Delete deemed to be; state the consequence directly.

examples.before: Any violation ... will be deemed to be a breach by Acme of this section 4.2.
examples.after: Any violation ... will be a breach by Acme of this section 4.2.

examples.before: The date of exercise will be deemed to be the date on which the Company receives notice of exercise.
examples.after: The date of exercise will be the date on which the Company receives notice of exercise.

notes: KB verdict label: Use only in a stated context. Appendix A fns 126 and 192 remove unnecessary deem.

section: Selected Usages > DEEM
statement: Use deem with will, not shall (Any notice will be deemed to have been received on delivery), and in the passive, not the active voice (not The parties will deem).
test: Has-a-duty test: substitute 'has a duty to'; shall be deemed fails.
fix: will be deemed
notes: Benign overuse of shall can be let pass on the other side's draft (Introduction; 3.103).

section: Selected Usages > DEEM > Making a Release Automatic
statement: To make a release automatic, use deem instead of language of obligation: instead of If X, Acme shall release Widgetco, say If X, Acme will be deemed to have released Widgetco.
fix: Acme will be deemed to have released Widgetco
severity_basis: release depends on a party's act
notes: Management Strategies, Inc. v. Housing Authority of New Haven, 2009 WL 1958170 (Conn. Super. Ct. 2009) (13.213).

section: Selected Usages > DEFAULT > Default or Event of Default
statement: In the paired defined terms Default (a latent event of default) and Event of Default, use Potential Default and Default instead; the traditional pair look the same and don't signal their definitions. Don't use Incipient Event of Default.
fix: Potential Default; Default
severity_basis: defined terms that don't signal meaning
notes: KB verdict label: Use with care. Traditional definition (13.217): 'Default' means any event that with notice or passage of time, or both, would constitute an Event of Default.

section: Selected Usages > DEFAULT > Has Occurred and Is Continuing
statement: In conditions to performance, consider referring to cure instead of has occurred and is continuing; is continuing fits a status (pendency of a lawsuit) but not an event (filing a lawsuit), and an inaccurate statement of fact doesn't continue. Where possible, phrase events of default as statuses.
fix: no Potential Default or Default has occurred and, if it is amenable to cure, has not been cured as of the date that Loan is made
exceptions: Phrasing as a status won't always be possible (13.223); the cure formulation leaves open whether an event is amenable to cure (13.226).

section: Selected Usages > DEFAULT > Event of Default or Default Event
statement: If you won't shorten event of default to default, say default event, which is more concise.
fix: default event

section: Selected Usages > DELIVER BY HAND
statement: Treat deliver by hand as a relic: its meaning is unclear (who is 'yourself'; is UPS a courier?). Use a notices provision that reflects current delivery methods, such as the author's form.
fix: Use a notices provision that names current delivery methods.
notes: KB verdict label: Don't use. The text does not say 'don't use' in those words; the author calls the phrase a relic and points to his notices provision (13.229).

section: Selected Usages > DEROGATE
statement: Don't use derogate in contracts; there is always a simpler way to say it. An obscure word with two very different meanings (transitive 'disparage'; intransitive 'detract from') is unpromising.
fix: except that the Lessee may ...; does not affect
notes: KB verdict label: Don't use. Example (13.234): 'The aforesaid shall not derogate from the right of the Lessee to conduct a proceeding'; simpler: except that the Lessee may, combined with the preceding sentence (13.235).

section: Selected Usages > DEROGATE
statement: If you use derogate intransitively (to detract), say derogate from; without from it reads as the transitive 'disparage'.

trigger.signal: derogate followed directly by an object noun

fix: derogate from (better, a simpler wording)
severity_basis: wrong sense of an ambiguous word
notes: Example (13.236): 'Section 5.01(p) shall in no event derogate or diminish the obligations'; the drafter meant the intransitive sense.

section: Selected Usages > DIRECTLY
statement: Usually use a clearer alternative to directly, and omit it where a direct connection is implicit, which is the case unless the context suggests otherwise.
fix: through the Company; or its subsidiaries; delete

examples.before: owned by the Company, directly or through subsidiaries
examples.after: owned by the Company or its subsidiaries

examples.before: Ms. Lopez shall report directly to the board of directors
examples.after: Ms. Lopez shall report to the board of directors

notes: KB verdict label: Use with care. One 13.239 example ('directly to that broker or dealer') is not struck in the image. Appendix A fn 71 removes 'direct or indirect'.

section: Selected Usages > DIRECTLY
statement: To express urgency, use promptly, not directly.
fix: promptly

section: Selected Usages > DISCLAIM
statement: When a party disclaims something (usually warranties), generally use a simpler and clearer alternative, such as will not be liable or is not making any warranty; UCC s. 2-316 speaks of excluding or modifying warranties, not disclaiming them.
fix: will not be liable for; is not making any warranty

examples.before: The Agent Parties expressly disclaim liability for errors or omissions
examples.after: The Agent Parties will not be liable for errors or omissions

examples.before: The Seller disclaims any warranty of merchantability
examples.after: The Seller is not making any warranty of merchantability

notes: KB verdict label: Don't use. Conspicuousness requirements for warranty exclusions are addressed in 16.25.

section: Selected Usages > DISPARAGEMENT
statement: Instead of prohibiting disparaging remarks, consider prohibiting the person from saying to anyone, in writing or orally, anything critical; disparage is ambiguous (one definition requires falsity), and adding falsity makes breach much harder to show.
fix: shall not say to anyone, in writing or orally, anything critical of ...
exceptions: The approach may seem overbroad, but a criticized party that can't show damages can't sue, and such provisions are usually used when the person bound is being given something, presumably on separation (13.244).
notes: KB verdict label: Don't use.

section: Selected Usages > DUE OR TO BECOME DUE
statement: Replace due or to become due with clearer wording.

words: due or to become due and payable

fix: that are then due or that become due

examples.before: any payments due or to become due in respect of that Collateral
examples.after: any payments that are then due or that become due in respect of that Collateral

notes: KB verdict label: Don't use.

section: Selected Usages > DULY
statement: Outside terms of art with broader substantive implications, omit duly; the verb it modifies usually already includes 'in a proper manner'. Duly is often paired with the equally unnecessary validly.
fix: Delete duly (and validly).
exceptions: Keep duly in terms of art such as duly incorporated and duly organized (13.252-13.254); see R-13.252-duly-terms-of-art.

examples.before: have been duly and validly authorized
examples.after: have been authorized

examples.before: will be deemed to have been duly given when delivered
examples.after: will be deemed to have been given when delivered

notes: KB verdict label: Use only in a stated context. Garner's Dictionary of Legal Usage at 301 (13.249).

section: Selected Usages > DULY
statement: Leave duly alone in terms of art with broader substantive implications, such as duly incorporated and duly organized; there it is shorthand for a parcel of issues.
fix: Keep it.
notes: Glazer & FitzGibbon on Legal Opinions s. 6.2 (13.252).

section: Selected Usages > DURING ... EMPLOYMENT
statement: Instead of during X's employment, be more specific: it could mean the entire calendar period of employment, including nights and weekends, or only work hours.
fix: State the period (for example, at any time from the start date until employment ends, whether or not during working hours).
notes: KB verdict label: Don't use. Mattel, Inc. v. MGA Entertainment, Inc., 616 F.3d 904, 912 (9th Cir. 2010) (13.256).

section: Selected Usages > DURING THE TERM OF THIS AGREEMENT
statement: Usually omit during the term of this agreement when it modifies language of obligation, discretion, or prohibition; by default, provisions addressing party actions apply only during the term.

words: during the term of this agreement

fix: Delete it.
exceptions: Use it when deviating from the default to specify duration (13.259); see R-13.259-during-term-duration.

examples.before: During the term of this agreement, the Company shall pay Jones an automobile expense allowance
examples.after: The Company shall pay Jones an automobile expense allowance

notes: KB verdict label: Use only in a stated context. Appendix A fns 40 and 42 address this redundancy.

section: Selected Usages > DURING THE TERM OF THIS AGREEMENT
statement: Use during the term of this agreement when deviating from the default rule to specify duration, as in During the term of this agreement and for five years thereafter, the Recipient shall not disclose ...

words: during the term of this agreement and for

fix: Keep it.

section: Selected Usages > DURING THE TERM OF THIS AGREEMENT
statement: Don't use during continuance of this agreement, and don't use continuance to mean duration; in legal usage continuance usually means postponement of a proceeding.

words: during the continuance of this agreement

fix: during the term of this agreement (only when needed)

section: Selected Usages > EFFLUXION OF TIME
statement: Don't use effluxion (or efflux or affluxion) of time. You could use passage of time, but better refer specifically to the relevant period or date, or overhaul the provision so no substitute is needed.
fix: the specific period or date; passage of time
notes: KB verdict label: Don't use. Example (13.262): 'terminated (except by mere effluxion of time or in the case of Total Loss of a Borrower Ship)'.

section: Selected Usages > END, TERMINATE
statement: Use the verb terminate, not end; the noun forms of end are awkward (at the end of this agreement could mean the back of the document), and related verb and noun forms help the reader.
fix: terminate / termination
severity_basis: consistency of verb and noun forms
notes: KB verdict label: Use. 13.265 shows the rejected change terminate -> end.

section: Selected Usages > ESPECIALLY, PARTICULARLY, IN PARTICULAR
statement: It's best not to use especially, particularly, or in particular; they signal that something is particularly important, which suggests everything else is less important and could affect interpretation. Use disciplined including to bring something within a provision.
fix: including (used as in 13.377)
exceptions: Where especially means specifically, use specifically (13.270); see R-13.270-specifically.
severity_basis: can affect interpretation of the rest
notes: KB verdict label: Don't use. Example (13.267): 'If the scope of work of a Work Order changes, especially the estimated timelines, ...'.

section: Selected Usages > ESPECIALLY, PARTICULARLY, IN PARTICULAR
statement: Where especially means 'specifically' (a separate committee created especially for this purpose), use specifically.
fix: specifically

section: Selected Usages > ETC.
statement: Delete etc.; it is casual, and either redundant (after examples) or hazardous because the provision's reach is uncertain. Ideally, specify a class and nothing else or make the list exhaustive; if neither is possible, use including.
fix: Name the class; make the list exhaustive; or use including
notes: KB verdict label: Don't use. Example (13.273): 'levels of noise, dust, obstruction of access, etc. that are in excess of ...'.

section: Selected Usages > ET SEQ.
statement: When a contract refers to a statute, don't use et seq. after the first section; better still, don't state the section at all, since the statute's name is enough.
fix: the Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification Act (no codification)
notes: KB verdict label: Don't use.

section: Selected Usages > EXECUTE AND DELIVER > Executing a Contract
statement: Don't refer to executing a contract; execute is ambiguous between signing and performing and could lead to a dispute.
test: Does execute mean sign or perform? If sign, say sign; if entry into the agreement, say enter into.
fix: sign; enter into; perform
notes: KB verdict label: Don't use. Akorn, Inc. v. Fresenius Kabi AG, 2018 WL 4719347, at *29 (Del. Ch. 2018) (13.279). On execute and deliver in the concluding clause, see 5.8-.12.

section: Selected Usages > EXECUTE AND DELIVER > Execute and Deliver
statement: In contexts such as a statement of power and authority, refer to entry into the agreement (enter into this agreement) instead of execute and deliver.
fix: enter into this agreement

examples.before: The Company has all requisite corporate power and authority to execute and deliver this agreement.
examples.after: The Company has all requisite corporate power and authority to enter into this agreement.

notes: As printed, only 'execute and' is struck and 'deliver' is not; the evident intent is enter into. Appendix A fn 173 uses enters into.

section: Selected Usages > EXECUTE AND DELIVER > Execute and Deliver
statement: Where a party must enter into a contract or sign an ancillary document, or entry is a condition, refer to signature and delivery: have the party sign and deliver a signed copy, the surest way to verify performance or satisfaction of the condition.

trigger.signal: obligation or condition to enter into or sign a document

fix: shall sign and deliver to [party] a signed copy of ...
exceptions: Be prepared for someone to insist on execute rather than sign (13.284).

section: Selected Usages > FAILS TO
statement: Usually use does not or another alternative instead of fails to; fails to is often used where no failure is involved, and invoking failure is never necessary.
fix: does not; not to; unless ... timely delivers

examples.before: and CRISPR fails to bring any such action
examples.after: and CRISPR does not bring any such action

examples.before: if the Indemnified Party fails to timely deliver the Indemnity Notice
examples.after: unless the Indemnified Party timely delivers the Indemnity Notice

notes: KB verdict label: Don't use.

section: Selected Usages > FAITHFULLY
statement: Don't use faithfully and comparable adverbs (diligently, competently, industriously) to state an employee's standard of performance; be specific about the employee's duties.
fix: State the employee's duties and any measurable targets.
notes: KB verdict label: Don't use. Example (13.289): 'shall diligently, faithfully, and competently perform her duties'. A claim for unfaithful performance depends on agency law, not the word (13.290).

section: Selected Usages > FAX
statement: Use fax, not facsimile, telefacsimile, or telecopier, for both the machine and what it transmits. Don't use Telecopier generically (a brand name), and don't write fax in all capitals (not an acronym).
fix: fax
notes: KB verdict label: Use. Unless you work in an industry that still relies on fax, the advice should be irrelevant (13.293).

section: Selected Usages > FIXED FEE
statement: When specifying the amount of a fee, don't use flat fee or fixed fee; use those phrases only when referring generally to a kind of payment.
fix: Delete 'a fixed fee of' before the amount.

examples.before: The Bank shall pay AZ Financial a fixed fee of $37,500
examples.after: The Bank shall pay AZ Financial $37,500

notes: KB verdict label: Use only in a stated context.

section: Selected Usages > FOR ANY REASON OR NO REASON
statement: In referring to termination, for any reason on its own suffices; don't add or no reason. There is always a reason, and any reason doesn't imply a good reason.

words: for any reason or no reason

fix: for any reason
notes: KB verdict label: Don't use.

section: Selected Usages > FOR ANY REASON OR NO REASON
statement: If the aim is to avoid having to explain a termination, say the company won't have to provide an explanation.

words: for any reason or no reason
trigger.signal: termination right where the terminating party doesn't want to give reasons

fix: State that the company won't have to provide an explanation.
exceptions: A company might be required by law to give an explanation (13.299).

section: Selected Usages > FOR ANY REASON OR NO REASON
statement: Using for any reason or for no reason doesn't mean the employee has waived the implied duty of good faith; to address that duty, have the employee acknowledge factors the company need not consider. In other contracts, don't use the phrase (instead of at its sole discretion) as an attempt to circumvent the implied duty of good faith.
fix: Add an acknowledgment of the factors the company need not consider.

section: Selected Usages > FORCE AND EFFECT
statement: Omit force from force and effect (no force and effect, the same force and effect, full force and effect); it is redundant, and contract language doesn't aim to persuade, so emphasis has no place.
fix: effect (no effect; the same effect; in effect)
notes: KB verdict label: Don't use. Examples in 13.302 are not redlined in the book.

section: Selected Usages > FORMAL, FORMALLY
statement: Omit formal and formally where redundant; they suggest that unspecified procedures matter. If you have particular procedures in mind, make them explicit.
fix: Delete; or state the procedures.

examples.before: making formal demand for the Rents
examples.after: making demand for the Rents

examples.before: litigate or formally contest any proceedings
examples.after: litigate or contest any proceedings

notes: KB verdict label: Don't use.

section: Selected Usages > FORM AND SUBSTANCE
