statement: Don't use in form and substance (an opinion of counsel in form and substance satisfactory to the Buyer); say an opinion of counsel satisfactory to the Buyer.
fix: satisfactory to the Buyer
notes: KB verdict label: Don't use. Appendix A fn 167 drops in form and substance.

section: Selected Usages > FORM AND SUBSTANCE
statement: Best, attach the document as an exhibit and require it to be in that form or, for flexibility, in a form substantially similar to the exhibit; this avoids preclosing haggling.

trigger.signal: closing deliverable described only by a satisfaction standard

fix: in the form of exhibit X / in a form substantially similar to exhibit X
exceptions: If the document relates to a future transaction whose terms are unknown, an exhibit may not be feasible (13.311).

section: Selected Usages > FOR THE AVOIDANCE OF DOUBT
statement: Don't use for the avoidance of doubt; it is filler (sometimes doubly pointless), rhetorical emphasis, and a buried verb. What follows must stand on its own; strike language that states the blindingly obvious.
fix: Delete the phrase and let the text stand alone; strike the obvious.

examples.before: For the avoidance of doubt, this arbitration agreement does not apply to any dispute under the Indemnification Agreement.
examples.after: This arbitration agreement does not apply to any dispute under the Indemnification Agreement.

examples.before: For the avoidance of doubt, nothing in this agreement gives Acme any rights
examples.after: Nothing in this agreement gives Acme any rights

notes: KB verdict label: Don't use.

section: Selected Usages > FOR THE AVOIDANCE OF DOUBT
statement: Where for the avoidance of doubt adds a second sentence to a definition, restructure the definition as a single sentence.

trigger.signal: definition followed by a 'for the avoidance of doubt' sentence

fix: ... and excludes ...

examples.before: immediately before the Company's IPO. For the avoidance of doubt, Insider Shares will not include any IPO Shares
examples.after: immediately before the Company's IPO and excludes any IPO Shares

section: Selected Usages > FOR THE AVOIDANCE OF DOUBT
statement: Where for the avoidance of doubt introduces a fact, have the party acknowledge the fact instead.

trigger.signal: 'for the avoidance of doubt' before a statement of fact

fix: [Party] acknowledges that ...

examples.before: For the avoidance of doubt, Invest Bank has implemented reasonable policies
examples.after: The Seller acknowledges that Invest Bank has implemented reasonable policies

section: Selected Usages > FOR THE AVOIDANCE OF DOUBT
statement: The phrase for clarity raises the same issues as for the avoidance of doubt; don't use it.
fix: Delete it; make the text stand on its own.

section: Selected Usages > FRAUD AND INTENTIONAL MISREPRESENTATION
statement: In exceptions to indemnification limits, referring to both fraud and intentional misrepresentation is safer than fraud alone, because the elements differ and a court might treat fraud as a distinct claim. Clearer still, avoid the terms of art and describe the conduct.
fix: any claim that the Indemnifying Party intentionally supplied one or more Indemnified Parties with information that the Indemnifying Party knew [or should have known] was inaccurate or any claim that the Indemnifying Party intentionally withheld information from one or more Indemnified Parties
severity_basis: terms of art with varying meanings in a key carve-out
notes: KB verdict label: Use with care. 26 Williston s. 69:2 (13.321); Restatement (Second) of Torts s. 526 (13.322). The conduct-based wording uses more words and is novel, but it is clearer (13.327).

section: Selected Usages > FROM THE BEGINNING OF TIME
statement: Don't use from the beginning of time (or from the beginning of the world) in release language; it is quaint and redundant, because a release of all claims already covers all periods.

words: from the beginning of the world

fix: Delete it.
notes: KB verdict label: Don't use.

section: Selected Usages > FULL-TIME
statement: Be more specific than full-time when referring to work: state the minimum hours per day and days per week, how long that level must be maintained, and whether the person must be employed (and whether volunteer or independent-contractor work counts).
fix: State minimum hours and days, duration, and what kinds of work count.
notes: KB verdict label: Don't use. In re C.P.Y., 364 S.W.3d 411 (Tex. App. 2012) ('returns to work on a full time basis') (13.330).

section: Selected Usages > GUARANTEE, GUARANTY
statement: In all circumstances, use guarantee as both verb and noun; don't use guaranty. Insisting on a noun distinction invites confusion.
fix: guarantee
notes: KB verdict label: Use. Garner's Dictionary of Legal Usage 399 (13.333); New Fowler's 343 (13.334).

section: Selected Usages > GUARANTEE, GUARANTY
statement: Don't use guarantee as the counterpart of guarantor to mean the person to whom a guarantee is given; given the word's primary meaning, that invites confusion.

trigger.signal: guarantee used as a noun for the person benefiting

fix: Use a defined term for the beneficiary (for example, the Lender).

section: Selected Usages > GUARANTEE (THE VERB) AS TERM OF ART
statement: Recognize that the verb guarantee, followed by a noun, is an unnecessary term of art: hereby guarantees, read in isolation, means 'will be liable for', as does indemnifies. Whether replacing it is feasible is a matter of inertia and expediency, not semantics.
fix: will be liable for (optional)
notes: KB verdict label: Explanatory (no verdict). Example (13.340): 'The New Borrower hereby guarantees payment and performance when due ... of all Obligations.' No command is stated.

section: Selected Usages > GUARANTEES THAT
statement: Consider using guarantees that followed by a clause to create a guarantee (Acme guarantees that Widgetco will comply with its obligations); the verb form is clearer and more concise than guarantees plus an abstract noun (Acme guarantees Widgetco's compliance).
fix: Acme guarantees that Widgetco will comply with its obligations under this agreement.

examples.before: Acme guarantees Widgetco's compliance with its obligations under this agreement.
examples.after: Acme guarantees that Widgetco will comply with its obligations under this agreement.

notes: KB verdict label: Use with care.

section: Selected Usages > GUARANTEES THAT
statement: Don't use guarantees that as throat-clearing (for example, before an obligation or statement of fact that needs no guarantee label); that is a different, disfavored use.
fix: State the obligation or statement of fact directly.

section: Selected Usages > GUARANTEES—ABSOLUTE, CONTINUING, IRREVOCABLE, AND UNCONDITIONAL
statement: Omit absolutely, unconditionally, irrevocably, and the adjectives absolute, continuing, irrevocable, and unconditional from guarantees; be specific about the deal terms instead. They are unclear terms of art, add words, don't prevail over the law (a guarantor may revoke as to future advances), and don't prevail over the deal terms.
fix: Delete the adverbs and adjectives; state the deal terms specifically.
exceptions: A guarantee is irrevocable unless you say otherwise, subject to the law's limit on revocation as to future advances (13.348-13.349).
severity_basis: unclear terms of art; false certitude
notes: KB verdict label: Don't use. Restatement (Third) of Suretyship and Guaranty s. 8 (13.347); Darmstadter: 'Phrases like absolute and unconditional are the bane of legal drafting' (13.351).

section: Selected Usages > HABENDUM
statement: Don't use habendum or to have and to hold; they are hopelessly archaic. Address any substantive implications in standard English.
fix: State the interest granted and its conditions in standard English.
notes: KB verdict label: Don't use.

section: Selected Usages > HERE- AND THERE- WORDS
statement: Don't use here- words (herein, hereof, hereunder, hereto), except hereby in language of performance; for example, use in this agreement instead of herein. Use there- words only to avoid awkward or long-winded repetition. Here- words cause ambiguity, and both kinds sound archaic and legalistic.
fix: in this agreement; under this agreement; to it; of it
exceptions: hereby in language of performance (13.356; see 3.50).
there- words to avoid awkward or long-winded repetition (13.356).
notes: KB verdict label: Use only in a stated context. Where scope matters (herein meaning this section or the whole agreement), treat as an ambiguity issue (7.23-.25). Appendix A fns 35, 190, and 207 remove here- words.

section: Selected Usages > HERE- AND THERE- WORDS
statement: Keep hereby in language of performance (Acme hereby assigns ...).
fix: Keep hereby with language of performance; delete it elsewhere.

section: Selected Usages > HERE- AND THERE- WORDS
statement: A there- word is acceptable to avoid awkward or long-winded repetition (... and any amendments thereto); any amendments to it would also work, though most drafters would need to get used to it.
fix: Keep only if the alternative is awkward; otherwise to it / of it.

section: Selected Usages > IN ACCORDANCE WITH, ACCORDING TO
statement: Use in accordance with rather than according to to express 'in accordance with'; according to has other meanings ('depending on'; 'as reported by'). Use neither if under would do.
fix: under; in accordance with
notes: KB verdict label: Use with care. Example (13.357): 'Any dispute must be resolved by arbitration according to the procedures stated in this section 12.10.' Appendix A fn 55 replaces pursuant to with under / in accordance with.

section: Selected Usages > INCLUDING, INCLUDES
statement: Of the five uses of including, use only the one that introduces an item that, because the class is uncertain, might not otherwise be considered part of it (an enlarging item: fruit, including tomatoes). Introducing a list of obvious examples is standard but problematic; introducing an exhaustive list, an item outside the class, or an item affected by a class modifier should be avoided.
test: Is each item after including at the margins of the class (one a reader might doubt belongs)? If the items are obvious members, a court may read the class as limited to items like them.
fix: Use including only for enlarging items; otherwise see the related rules.
notes: KB verdict label: Use only in a stated context. Federal Land Bank of St. Paul v. Bismarck Lumber Co., 314 U.S. 95 (1941) (illustrative meaning) (13.362); restrictive readings: Frame v. Nehls, 550 N.W.2d 739 (Mich. 1996) (13.365); Dept. of Treasury of Indiana v. Muessel, 32 N.E.2d 596 (Ind. 1941) (13.366).

section: Selected Usages > INCLUDING, INCLUDES > An Unhelpful Fix
statement: Don't rely on without limitation or but not limited to (or but is not limited to, including without limiting the generality of the foregoing, including without implication of limitation); they are usually redundant and courts have held including restrictive despite them. Use including and includes in a targeted way instead.

words: includes but is not limited to
including without limiting the generality of the foregoing

fix: including (targeted use)
notes: Shelby County State Bank v. Van Diest Supply Co., 303 F.3d 832 (7th Cir. 2002); Horse Cave State Bank v. Nolin PCA, 672 S.W.2d 66 (Ky. Ct. App. 1984); Holy Angels Academy v. Hartford Ins. Group, 487 N.Y.S.2d 1005 (Sup. Ct. 1985) (13.371-13.373). The author rejects Garner's contrary view (13.385-13.391). Appendix A fn 156 replaces including but not limited to with including.

section: Selected Usages > INCLUDING, INCLUDES > Avoiding Uncertainty
statement: If you rely on the general word's everyday meaning, don't follow it with a list of obvious examples; fruit, including oranges, lemons, and grapefruit invites a court to limit fruit to citrus.

trigger.signal: general word followed by including and several obvious members of the class

fix: Delete the obvious examples, or use an enlarging item.

section: Selected Usages > INCLUDING, INCLUDES > Avoiding Uncertainty
statement: If you feel compelled to name an obvious member (fruit, including oranges, because oranges matter to the client), a court might have a hard time restricting the class when only one item is named; the more items you add, the greater the risk.

trigger.signal: including followed by a single obvious example

fix: Name only one item, or use the approach in 13.384.

section: Selected Usages > INCLUDING, INCLUDES > Avoiding Uncertainty
statement: If the general word has a specialized meaning (different from everyday use, or created by the contract, such as excluded liabilities), don't use including; provide an exhaustive list, perhaps as a definition with the noun as the defined term. In any event, select the general word with care; the more specific it is, the less mischief including can cause.

trigger.signal: including after a term the contract itself creates

fix: exhaustive definition ('Excluded Liabilities' means ...)

section: Selected Usages > INCLUDING, INCLUDES > Putting the General Word at the End
statement: Putting the general word last (oranges, lemons, grapefruit, and other fruit) likely increases the risk of a restrictive reading, because most courts apply ejusdem generis to a list followed by a catchall. Avoid a limited list of obvious members wherever placed; if the client's needs leave no choice, put the general word last and block the limiting implication by adjusting it (and other fruit, whether or not citrus).

trigger.signal: list of specific items followed by a catchall general word

fix: oranges, lemons, grapefruit, and other fruit, whether or not citrus

section: Selected Usages > INCLUDING, INCLUDES > Related Problematic Usages
statement: Don't use for example or e.g. before a list of items after a general word; it raises the same issues as including, and an enlarging item doesn't work after for example.
fix: including (enlarging item) or a precise class
exceptions: For example can introduce illustrative scenarios, such as how a formula might operate (13.392).

section: Selected Usages > INCLUDING, INCLUDES > Related Problematic Usages
statement: Don't use including with limitation (perhaps a misguided attempt at 'consisting of') or excluding without limitation (what is excluded is limited to what is designated).
fix: consisting of / comprising; excluding

section: Selected Usages > INCLUDING, INCLUDES > Don't Use Including to Introduce an Exhaustive List
statement: Don't use including to introduce an exhaustive list (Great Britain, including England, Wales, and Scotland); use comprising, or delete the class and list only the components.

trigger.signal: including before what is meant as a complete list

fix: comprising; or list the components only
severity_basis: readers may wonder what else is included

section: Selected Usages > INCLUDING, INCLUDES > Don't Use Including to Bring Within the Class What Otherwise Would Not Be Part of the Class
statement: Don't use including to bring in something categorically outside the class (fruit, including carrots; equipment, including software and software license fees); use and (fruit and carrots).

trigger.signal: including followed by an item that is not a member of the class

fix: X and Y
severity_basis: forces an unnatural meaning on the class

section: Selected Usages > INCLUDING, INCLUDES > Using Including to Introduce Items That Might or Might Not Be Part of the Class Due to a Modifier That Applies to the Class
statement: When a modifier applies to the class (red fruit, including apples; any American automobile, including any truck), a court would likely apply the modifier to the items after including, but with a vague modifier (disruptive activity, including playing music) one might argue it doesn't. Be explicit about which meaning you intend.

trigger.signal: modifier on the class noun before including

test: Does the class modifier apply to the items after including? If the reader can't tell, the provision is ambiguous.
fix: State whether the modifier applies (for example, add 'that constitute consequential damages', or use and instead of including).
notes: Massachusetts v. E.P.A., 549 U.S. 497, 557 (2007) (Scalia, J., dissenting) (13.400); Dow Chemical Canada ULC v. Nova Chemicals Corp., 2018 ABQB 482 (13.406-13.407).

section: Selected Usages > INCORPORATED BY REFERENCE
statement: Don't use incorporated by reference in a contract. Stating that schedules or exhibits are incorporated herein by reference accomplishes nothing (a reference in the body brings them in); saying one contract incorporates another because both are parts of one transaction is redundant and can have unexpected effects; and a contract can be subject to another contract's provision without incorporating it.

words: made a part of this agreement

fix: Delete; refer to the schedule in the body; state the interplay between the contracts.
notes: KB verdict label: Don't use. MRC Total Build Ltd. v F&M Installations Ltd., 2019 BCSC 765 (subcontract incorporating the prime contract imported its arbitration provision) (13.411).

section: Selected Usages > INCORPORATED BY REFERENCE
statement: Don't incorporate recitals by reference into the body of the contract.

words: recitals set forth above are incorporated

fix: Delete the incorporation sentence.

section: Selected Usages > INCORPORATED BY REFERENCE
statement: Incorporation by reference is the right concept for importing, without repeating them, provisions of a separate agreement; even then, describe what is happening rather than use the jargon.

trigger.signal: provisions of another agreement imported into this one

fix: Baker hereby makes to Charlie, as if they were in this agreement, all statements of fact made by Able to Baker in the Able-Baker Purchase Agreement.

section: Selected Usages > INDEFINITELY, PERPETUALLY
statement: Use perpetually, not indefinitely, to mean 'perpetually'; indefinitely also means 'without limit' (a limit could be set later).
fix: perpetually
exceptions: Indefinitely in the 'without limit' sense is unobjectionable (13.415): if Acme discontinues or indefinitely suspends development.

examples.before: During the term of this agreement and indefinitely thereafter
examples.after: During the term of this agreement and perpetually thereafter

notes: KB verdict label: Use with care.

section: Selected Usages > INDEFINITELY, PERPETUALLY
statement: Where the idea of 'perpetually' is followed by until, drop it; until already sets the end point.
fix: Delete indefinitely/perpetually.

examples.before: the Securities must be held indefinitely until they are registered
examples.after: the Securities must be held until they are registered

section: Selected Usages > INDEFINITELY, PERPETUALLY
statement: Don't perpetually (or forever) release someone; you release once. Avoid forever and until (or to) the end of time or of the world.

words: until the end of the world

fix: hereby releases; delete forever

section: Selected Usages > INDEMNIFY > Function
statement: Use indemnification deliberately. It can bring in deep pockets, cover disclosed liabilities, external events, and nonparty losses, and recover legal fees; it can give the indemnifying party a cap, time limits, and a basket. If you don't need deeper pockets, don't need to address disclosed liabilities, and nonparty claims are remote or modest, indemnification is probably more trouble than it's worth; address fee-shifting separately.
test: Do the likely claims justify full-blown indemnification provisions?
fix: Omit indemnification, or tailor it; see the related INDEMNIFY rules.
notes: KB verdict label: Use with care. Procedures add predictability only if indemnification is the exclusive remedy for such claims (13.431).

section: Selected Usages > INDEMNIFY > Function
statement: If you want indemnification to cover claims between the parties (not just nonparty claims), say so in the indemnification provisions, or risk a fight.

trigger.signal: indemnification provision silent on direct claims between the parties

test: Does the provision say whether it covers claims by one party against the other?
fix: State expressly that indemnification covers claims between the parties (or only nonparty claims).
notes: Mobil Oil Canada v. Beta Well Service (1974), 43 D.L.R. (3d) 745 (A.B.C.A.); Hot Rods, LLC v. Northrop Grumman, 242 Cal. App. 4th 1166 (2015); NevadaCare v. Dept. of Human Services, 783 N.W.2d 459 (Iowa 2010) (13.437).

section: Selected Usages > INDEMNIFY > Say Shall Indemnify, Not Hereby Indemnifies
statement: Use shall indemnify (language of obligation), not hereby indemnifies (language of performance); don't combine the two.
fix: shall indemnify
notes: Combination to avoid (13.439): 'Tenant hereby indemnifies and at all times shall indemnify and hold harmless the Landlord'.

section: Selected Usages > INDEMNIFY > Don't Use Indemnify and Hold Harmless
statement: Use just indemnify, not indemnify and hold harmless (or save harmless); never use hold harmless. Some courts and commentators give hold harmless a different meaning, so the redundancy is risky.
fix: indemnify
severity_basis: inherently confusing usage (flagged in the Introduction)
notes: Same meaning: Majkowski v. American Imaging Mgmt., 913 A.2d 572 (Del. Ch. 2006) and others (13.442); different meaning: Queen Villas HOA v. TCB Property Mgmt., 56 Cal. Rptr. 3d 528 (Ct. App. 2007); Stewart Title v. Zeppieri, [2009] O.J. No. 322 (13.444-13.445).

section: Selected Usages > INDEMNIFY > Don't Use Indemnify and Hold Harmless
statement: Address directly whether indemnification covers only losses paid or also liabilities incurred: have the indemnifying party indemnify against both losses and liabilities, or better, use a defined term (Indemnifiable Losses or a variant) that states exactly what is covered, for example including judgments so the indemnified party needn't pay a judgment first; address litigation expenses in the procedure provisions.

trigger.signal: indemnification provision that relies on hold harmless to cover incurred liabilities

fix: Define Indemnifiable Losses to state what is covered (including judgments).

section: Selected Usages > INDEMNIFY > Don't Use Shall Indemnify and Keep Indemnified
statement: Don't use shall indemnify and keep indemnified; it serves no discernible purpose.
fix: shall indemnify

section: Selected Usages > INDEMNIFY > Defend Is Inadequate
statement: Don't rely on adding defend; address explicitly, in the indemnification procedure provisions, how defense of nonparty claims is handled.
fix: Procedures stating who controls the defense, counsel, expenses, and settlement.
severity_basis: obligation to defend is not an obligation to advance costs
notes: Fillip v. Centerstone Linen Services, LLC, 2014 WL 793123, at *4 (Del. Ch. 2014) (13.452). The author points to his blog post 'My Indemnification Language' (13 Aug. 2013).

section: Selected Usages > INDEMNIFY > Prepositions
statement: Use a single preposition after indemnify (for, from, or against, depending on what follows); don't use the rhetorical triplet for, from, and against. Courts have relied on prepositions to hold that indemnification doesn't cover claims between the parties, but that happens only when the drafter doesn't express the key issues, so address them.
fix: indemnify ... against [Indemnifiable Losses]
notes: Jacobson v. Crown Zellerbach Corp., 539 P.2d 641 (Or. 1975); Cecil Lawter Real Estate School v. Town & Country Shopping Center, 694 P.2d 815 (Ariz. Ct. App. 1984) (13.454). 13.457 prints 'against, from, and against' (apparent typo).

section: Selected Usages > INDEMNIFY > Consider Not Using Indemnify
statement: Consider not using indemnify in the operative provisions: say what is covered, for example will be liable to those Acme Persons for, rather than shall indemnify those Acme Indemnitees against. An interim step is to use indemnification only as a heading. This wording also attracts less attention from counterparties skittish about indemnification obligations; but pick your battles.
fix: will be liable to [persons] for [losses]

section: Selected Usages > INDENTURE
statement: No command: indenture is a synonym of contract used for a limited group of contracts, with only tradition going for it; bond agreement or trust agreement would be unobjectionable.
fix: bond agreement; trust agreement (optional)
notes: KB verdict label: Explanatory (no verdict).

section: Selected Usages > IN OTHER WORDS
statement: Don't use in other words, or i.e., that is, namely, or to wit; state the concept clearly the first time.
fix: Restate the concept once, clearly.
notes: KB verdict label: Don't use.

section: Selected Usages > INURE
statement: Don't use inures to the benefit of (or enure); use benefits. Obscure wording often signals an expendable provision, such as the pointless successors-and-assigns provision.
fix: benefits

examples.before: the issuance of Letters of Credit for the account of Subsidiaries inures to the benefit of the Borrower
examples.after: the issuance of Letters of Credit for the account of Subsidiaries benefits the Borrower

notes: KB verdict label: Don't use. Appendix A fn 182 drops the successors-and-assigns sentence (13.473).

section: Selected Usages > INURE
statement: In trademark licenses, instead of saying goodwill inures solely to the benefit of the licensor, address the goodwill issue directly.

words: inure solely to the benefit of the licensor

fix: State directly who owns the goodwill arising from the licensee's use.
notes: Adams, Inures to the Benefit and Trademark Licensing, 105 Trademark Reporter 944 (2015) (13.474).

section: Selected Usages > IT BEING UNDERSTOOD THAT
statement: Don't use it being understood that; there's always a better alternative. Where it clarifies or supplements preceding language, delete it and make what follows a separate sentence; where the parenthetical is unnecessary, delete it entirely; where it inserts one provision into another, make it a separate sentence.
fix: separate sentence; delete; or acknowledges
notes: KB verdict label: Don't use. Example (13.477): '(it being understood that the Company may but shall not be obligated to do so)' deleted entirely.

section: Selected Usages > IT BEING UNDERSTOOD THAT
statement: Where it being understood that means a party accepts as accurate a fact asserted by another party, use acknowledges.

trigger.signal: it being understood before a statement of fact

fix: The Borrower acknowledges that ...

examples.before: it being understood and agreed, however, that failure to obtain a Collateral Access Agreement might
examples.after: The Borrower acknowledges that failure to obtain a Collateral Access Agreement might

section: Selected Usages > JOINDER
statement: Call the document by which someone becomes party to an existing contract an amendment, not a joinder, joinder agreement, or accession agreement; repurposing an unrelated legal term of art is unnecessarily legalistic.
fix: ... will become a Holder under this agreement by signing an amendment to this agreement to that effect.
notes: KB verdict label: Don't use.

section: Selected Usages > JOINT AND SEVERAL
statement: Don't use joint and several; express the concept directly: the claimant may recover the full amount of the collective liability from any one or more obligors and may bring one or more separate actions against any one or more of them.
fix: Acme may elect to recover from any one or more Widgetco Entities the full amount of any collective liability of the Widgetco Entities under this agreement, and Acme may bring one or more separate actions against any one or more Widgetco Entities regarding any such liability.
severity_basis: archaic term of art with procedural implications
notes: KB verdict label: Don't use. Williston s. 36:1; Restatement (Second) of Contracts ss. 288-289 (13.486-13.493). Joint is subsumed by several; several is archaic (13.494).

section: Selected Usages > JOINT AND SEVERAL
statement: Don't use several but not joint; where it is meant to apportion liability among owners pro rata, state the pro rata recovery and the right to bring separate actions.
fix: Acme may recover from each Shareholder a proportion of any collective liability of the Shareholders under this agreement equal to the proportion of all Shares then outstanding represented by the Shares then owned by that Shareholder. Acme may bring one or more separate actions ...
severity_basis: risk of confusion with the broader meaning of several

section: Selected Usages > JOINT AND SEVERAL > Relevance of Statutes
statement: Statutes in many jurisdictions make joint promises joint and several or presume joint and several duties; expressing the several concept explicitly won't hurt even if a statute would supply it, and it tells the parties what the law provides.

trigger.signal: two or more obligors under one obligation

fix: State the recovery rule explicitly.
notes: 13.498 says 'as proposed in 13.496'; the general several concept is in 13.495 (as printed).

section: Selected Usages > KNOWLEDGE > The Function of Knowledge Qualifications
statement: Consider a knowledge qualification in a statement of fact if the party can't determine whether the statement is accurate, usually because the matters might be hidden (contamination) or under others' control (threatened litigation). It means the party claims only that it isn't aware of anything suggesting inaccuracy; who bears unknown risk is a risk-allocation question.
fix: To the Seller's knowledge, ...
severity_basis: risk allocation in statements of fact
notes: KB verdict label: Use with care. Practice: threatened-litigation statements almost always carry a knowledge qualifier; capitalization statements never do (13.503).

section: Selected Usages > KNOWLEDGE > The Function of Knowledge Qualifications
statement: Don't refer to the best of someone's knowledge; best is a rhetorical flourish and could suggest a duty to investigate or heightened knowledge.

words: to the best of its knowledge

fix: to Acme's knowledge
severity_basis: could imply a duty to investigate

section: Selected Usages > KNOWLEDGE > The Function of Knowledge Qualifications
statement: Don't use knowledge and belief; it is redundant and invites a disgruntled party to invest it with meaning.
fix: knowledge

section: Selected Usages > KNOWLEDGE > Defining Knowledge
statement: Consider making Knowledge a defined term to address whose knowledge counts (narrow for the stating party, broad for the other) and the level of knowledge (actual knowledge, or knowledge after inquiry of specified employees or after reasonable investigation, using knows or should have known). In a sale of a business, consider whether to include its managers. Avoid reasonable knowledge as unclear.
fix: Autonomous definition of Knowledge naming the individuals and the level of investigation.
notes: The template definitions [1]-[3b] are in ocr-tables.md.

section: Selected Usages > KNOWLEDGE > Defining Knowledge
statement: Use a rule 405 (Securities Act) reference to define executive officers in a knowledge definition only if the party benefiting from the qualification is a U.S. public company.
fix: Name the individuals instead (unless a U.S. public company).

section: Selected Usages > KNOWLEDGE > Don't Use Is Unaware Of
statement: Use knowledge, not is unaware of; it would be reckless to assume a contract can create a meaningful distinction between absence of knowledge and knowledge of absence, and knowledge is more versatile.
fix: to the Company's knowledge, no facts exist that would form a reasonable basis for any such claim

examples.before: the Company is unaware of any facts that would form a reasonable basis for any such claim
examples.after: to the Company's knowledge, no facts exist that would form a reasonable basis for any such claim

section: Selected Usages > LATINISMS
statement: Omit Latinisms, including those the book lists from EDGAR contracts, and express the meaning in standard English.
fix: Standard English equivalent
exceptions: Ingrained Latinisms such as pro rata, status quo, and vice versa can be accepted as English (13.515).
notes: KB verdict label: Don't use. The 13.514 list cites 'mutatis mutandis (see 13.546)'; the entry is at 13.575 (book cross-reference error).

section: Selected Usages > LATINISMS
statement: Accept Latinisms so ingrained they are English, such as pro rata, status quo, and vice versa.
fix: Keep them.

section: Selected Usages > LEGAL FEES INSTEAD OF ATTORNEYS' FEES
statement: Use legal fees rather than attorneys' fees (or lawyers' fees); it needs no apostrophe, covers paralegal fees, and works outside the U.S.
fix: legal fees
exceptions: If you do use attorneys' fees, put the apostrophe after the s, to avoid fights over whether it means one attorney's fees (13.516).
notes: KB verdict label: Use.

section: Selected Usages > LEGAL FEES INSTEAD OF ATTORNEYS' FEES
statement: If you use attorneys' fees, put the apostrophe after the s; attorney's fees invites a fight over whether it means one attorney's fees.
fix: attorneys' fees (better, legal fees)

section: Selected Usages > LEGALLY
statement: No command; a caution. After Dark Horse Express, legally (legally must pay; unless legally prohibited) may be read to cover contractual obligations as well as obligations imposed by law; say which you mean.
test: Does legally mean imposed by law only, or also by contract or settlement?
fix: Say whether obligations under contracts and settlements count.
notes: KB verdict label: Explanatory (no verdict). Dark Horse Express, LLC v. Lancer Insurance Co., 733 F. App'x 826 (6th Cir. 2018) (13.518). The fix is a KB inference from the caution; the book gives no wording.

section: Selected Usages > LIKELY
statement: Be aware of the uncertain meaning of likely (more or less than 50%? synonymous with probable?); in some contexts you can't avoid it. You could state a percentage probability instead, though debating 49% versus 51% is often meaningless for contract provisions.
fix: has a probability of greater than 50% of [result]

examples.before: a physical or mental incapacity or disability that has rendered, or is likely to render, the Executive unable to perform
examples.after: a physical or mental incapacity or disability that has rendered, or has a probability of greater than 50% of rendering, the Executive unable to perform

notes: KB verdict label: Use with care. State v. Green, 480 N.E.2d 1128 (Ohio App. 1984); Anderson v. Bell, 303 S.W.2d 93 (Mo. 1957) (13.523).

section: Selected Usages > LIKELY
statement: Don't say reasonably likely; it adds vagueness to a degree of probability, and reasonableness has nothing to do with likelihood.
fix: likely

section: Selected Usages > LOOK TO
statement: Instead of A shall look only to B for X, consider C will not be liable for X; if C has more than one member, consider Only B will be liable for X. Look to is oddly colloquial and wrongly phrased as an obligation.
fix: Parent will not be liable for payment on this note; Only the Issuer will be liable for payment on this note
notes: KB verdict label: Don't use.

section: Selected Usages > LOST PROFITS
statement: No single command; a caution. Excluding lost profits can have unexpected results: whether lost profits are consequential depends on context; saying consequential damages include lost profits may still leave lost profits classed as general damages outside the exclusion; and excluding lost profits alone is arbitrary. Consider the alternatives to the traditional liability-limiting provision (13.166-13.173).
fix: Use the alternatives in R-13.167-foreseeable-damages and related rules; if all lost profits are to be excluded, say so with and, not including.
notes: KB verdict label: Explanatory (no verdict). Biotronik A.G. v. Conor Medsystems Ireland, Ltd., 11 N.E.3d 676 (N.Y. 2014); Luminara Worldwide v. Liown Electronics, 2017 WL 1064887 (D. Minn. 2017) (13.531).

section: Selected Usages > LUMP SUM
statement: Where lump-sum payment is a clumsy alternative to single payment and the contract specifies when payment is due, consider omitting it; its benefits are marginal.
fix: Delete in a lump sum where the payment date is specified.
exceptions: In construction and some other fields, lump sum has a specialized meaning (13.537).
Keep single-payment language if you want to bar installments on that one day (13.539).

examples.before: which amount the Company shall pay in one lump-sum payment on the 30th day after the Date of Termination
examples.after: which amount the Company shall pay on the 30th day after the Date of Termination

notes: KB verdict label: Use only in a stated context. Appendix A fn 121 treats lump-sum cash as redundant.

section: Selected Usages > LUMP SUM
statement: Keep lump sum where it has a specialized meaning, as in construction and some other fields (for example, a lump-sum contract price).
fix: Keep it.

section: Selected Usages > MERELY, MERE
statement: Don't use merely or mere; it has a dismissive quality unsuited to contract language. Depending on context, delete it or use just or only.
fix: delete; just; only

examples.before: the Plan constitutes a mere promise by the Company
examples.after: the Plan constitutes only a promise by the Company

examples.before: and not merely amounts contributed under Code Section 401(k)
examples.after: and not only to amounts contributed under Code Section 401(k)

notes: KB verdict label: Don't use.

section: Selected Usages > MONEY—STATING AMOUNTS OF > Use Only Digits
statement: State amounts of money in digits only, even though numbers up to ten are otherwise stated in words; don't use words and digits together (One Million Dollars ($1,000,000)).

trigger.signal: amount written in words followed by digits in parentheses

severity_basis: redundant convention that creates mismatch risk
notes: KB verdict label: Use only in a stated context. If the words and digits disagree, see R-14.7-words-digits-mismatch.

section: Selected Usages > MONEY—STATING AMOUNTS OF > Decimal Fractions
statement: Use zeros after a decimal point only when fractional amounts appear in the same context ($2, not $2.00, unless the provision also refers to, say, $3.94); don't add and 00/100 dollars; for less than a whole unit, use $0.32, not 32 cents written with the cent sign.
notes: Follows The Chicago Manual of Style 9.20 (13.546).

section: Selected Usages > MONEY—STATING AMOUNTS OF > Decimal Fractions
statement: Decimal and thousands separators vary by country; pick conventions and apply them consistently.

trigger.signal: amounts using both 1,000.00 and 1.000,00 styles

fix: Use one separator convention throughout.

section: Selected Usages > MONEY—STATING AMOUNTS OF > Large Amounts
statement: A mix of words and digits for large amounts ($4.4 billion; $3 million) is acceptable and can aid reading, but don't switch to it if other numbers in the same context use all digits, and don't go beyond two decimal places.
fix: $4.4 billion (max two decimals; consistent with nearby amounts)

section: Selected Usages > MONEY—STATING AMOUNTS OF > Large Amounts
statement: Billion means a thousand million in the U.S. but a million million in Germany and many non-English-speaking regions; if confusion might arise in an international transaction, use only digits for amounts of one thousand million units or more.
fix: Digits only (1,000,000,000)

section: Selected Usages > MONEY—STATING AMOUNTS OF > Currencies
statement: Specify the currency, by currency sign or ISO 4217 three-letter code (EUR; NOK), but not both. Where a sign is shared (the dollar sign for dollar and peso currencies), use a code or a modified sign (A$, Mex$) in contracts between parties from different countries. An autonomous definition ("Dollars" and "$" mean United States dollars) is another way, but don't use a definition as an excuse to use a bare $ for Australian dollars; use A$ every time.

trigger.signal: bare $ or dollars in a cross-border contract

test: Could the currency sign refer to more than one currency? Is both a sign and a code used for one amount?
fix: US$ / A$ / Mex$ or USD / AUD / MXN
notes: Define dollars only if you use words and digits, which the manual advises against (13.555).

section: Selected Usages > MONEY—STATING AMOUNTS OF > Currencies
statement: Spacing: always a space between a code and the number (EUR 2,400,000); a space after a letter sign (SFr. 334,583); no space after a symbol, even with prefixed letters (C$655,000). Placement of the sign before or after the amount varies; pick one and apply it consistently.

trigger.signal: currency code without a space, or symbol followed by a space

section: Selected Usages > MORAL TURPITUDE
statement: Don't use moral turpitude; it is insufficiently specific (Black's: conduct contrary to justice, honesty, or morality), yet it is a fixture of cause definitions and loan-agreement statements.
fix: Use plain criteria for a termination-for-crime provision (see R-13.571-termination-for-crime).
notes: KB verdict label: Don't use. Marmolejo-Campos v. Gonzales, 503 F.3d 922 (9th Cir. 2007) (13.559).

section: Selected Usages > MORAL TURPITUDE
statement: When drafting a termination-for-crime provision, decide: what crime (crime is preferable to criminal offense; felony and misdemeanor aren't recognized everywhere and vary by state); involving what offense (labels such as dishonesty or fraud, or a crime related to the employee's employment); other criteria (carve-outs such as noncustodial penalties or DWI); at what stage (commission, arrest, indictment, charge, or conviction or plea); which jurisdiction (name one if terminology varies); and whether to combine kinds of crime or stages.
fix: See R-13.571-termination-for-crime.

section: Selected Usages > MORAL TURPITUDE > Recommendation
statement: In a termination-for-crime provision, keep it simple unless you have a good reason to complicate it. A reasonable pro-employer formulation: the Employee is charged with a crime that (1) is punishable by a custodial penalty, instead of or in addition to a fine or other noncustodial penalty, or (2) is related to the Employee's employment. An employment agreement might add a broader right to terminate for conduct the employee knew, or a reasonable person would have known, would reasonably be expected to have a material adverse effect on the company's business or reputation.

trigger.signal: cause definition that refers to crimes

fix: the Employee is charged with a crime that (1) is punishable by a custodial penalty, instead of or in addition to a fine or other noncustodial penalty, or (2) is related to the Employee's employment
notes: The book cautions to see 11.85 on the wording of this provision.

section: Selected Usages > MUTATIS MUTANDIS
statement: Instead of mutatis mutandis, use a phrase such as together with any necessary conforming changes; make major adjustments explicit.
fix: together with any necessary conforming changes
notes: KB verdict label: Don't use. Example of explicit adjustments (13.575): each reference to 'Lease' will be deemed a reference to 'Sublease' ...

section: Selected Usages > MUTUAL, MUTUALLY
statement: Use mutual for 'pertaining to both parties' (for their mutual benefit) and mutually for reciprocity (mutually acceptable press releases); otherwise see the related rules.
fix: See related rules.
exceptions: Don't combine mutual with each of them (for the mutual benefit of each of them) (13.581).
notes: KB verdict label: Use only in a stated context.

section: Selected Usages > MUTUAL, MUTUALLY
statement: Don't use mutual with agreement, or mutually with agree or agreeable; reciprocity is inherent in agreement.
fix: agreement; agree; agreed; acceptable to both parties

section: Selected Usages > MUTUAL, MUTUALLY
statement: Instead of by mutual consent of the parties for amendments, state that an amendment must be in writing and signed by both parties.
fix: An amendment must be in writing and signed by both parties.

section: Selected Usages > MUTUAL, MUTUALLY
statement: Don't use mutually when you mean jointly.
fix: jointly

examples.before: a nationally recognized independent public accounting firm mutually selected by the Stockholders' Representatives and Acme
examples.after: a nationally recognized independent public accounting firm jointly selected by the Stockholders' Representatives and Acme

section: Selected Usages > NEGLIGENCE, GROSS NEGLIGENCE
statement: Using negligence doesn't involve undue uncertainty. But unless you can research the tort law of each relevant jurisdiction, don't use gross negligence, a vague tort term of art with no settled meaning; for misconduct beyond negligence, use reckless, recklessly, or recklessness, and don't try to distinguish reckless from wanton conduct.
fix: reckless / recklessly / recklessness
exceptions: In jurisdictions that don't recognize degrees of negligence (Pennsylvania, for example), a negligence standard might apply (13.597, 13.601).
Courts in many jurisdictions hold advance releases of liability for gross negligence unenforceable (13.588).
severity_basis: vague term of art; meaning varies by jurisdiction
notes: KB verdict label: Use only in a stated context. Sommer v. Federal Signal Corp., 79 N.Y.2d 540 (1992); City of Santa Barbara v. Superior Court, 161 P.3d 1095 (Cal. 2007) (13.591-13.592).

section: Selected Usages > NEGLIGENCE, GROSS NEGLIGENCE
statement: Use intentional or intentionally instead of willful or willfully, and make the labels relate to the consequences of the party's action, not the action itself; one can act intentionally without intending damage.
fix: intentionally causing those consequences
severity_basis: ambiguity of what the intent attaches to

section: Selected Usages > NEGLIGENCE, GROSS NEGLIGENCE
statement: Adjust tort-based standards to the governing law; if it doesn't recognize U.S. concepts, don't insist on them. Don't define recklessness or any form of it; a definition adds verbiage without certainty.

trigger.signal: definition of reckless or gross negligence; non-U.S. governing law

fix: Delete the definition; adapt to the governing law.

section: Selected Usages > NEGLIGENCE, GROSS NEGLIGENCE
statement: Consider not using tort-based standards for performance under the contract; the contract already gives a remedy for nonperformance. In particular, a recklessness or intentional-misconduct carve-out from an indemnification cap could undermine the cap if indemnification covers failure to comply with obligations; such a carve-out makes more sense for losses from relations with nonparties.

words: except in the case of gross negligence
except for gross negligence or willful misconduct

fix: Limit the carve-out to nonparty-related losses, or drop it.

section: Selected Usages > NEGLIGENCE, GROSS NEGLIGENCE > A Sample Provision
statement: Model provision replacing willful misconduct or gross negligence: liability only to the extent that, as a result of reckless disregard for the consequences of an act or failure to act, or of intentionally causing those consequences, the party causes damages.
fix: The Processor will not be liable to any party or nonparty for damages arising from an act or failure to act on its part in connection with its performance under this agreement, except to the extent that as a result of its reckless disregard for the consequences of that act or failure to act, or its intentionally causing those consequences, the Processor causes the party or nonparty to suffer damages.

examples.before: except to the extent such conduct constitutes its own willful misconduct or gross negligence
examples.after: except to the extent that as a result of its reckless disregard for the consequences of that act or failure to act, or its intentionally causing those consequences, the Processor causes the party or nonparty to suffer damages

section: Selected Usages > NO LATER [OR EARLIER, MORE, OR LESS] THAN
statement: Use no later than (not not later than), no earlier than, and no more than; they are less formal and more natural.
fix: no later than; no earlier than; no more than
notes: KB verdict label: Use. Appendix A fn 49 replaces within / not later than with no later than (10.70).

section: Selected Usages > NO LATER [OR EARLIER, MORE, OR LESS] THAN
statement: Use not less than, not no less than; no less connotes surprise, while not less is matter-of-fact.
fix: not less than

section: Selected Usages > NOT BE CONCERNED TO SEE TO
statement: Instead of shall not be concerned to see to (or to enquire into, inquire into, and variants), use will not be responsible for; the Commonwealth phrases are obscure.

words: shall not be concerned to see to the application

fix: will not be responsible for

examples.before: the Buyer will not be concerned to see to the application thereof
examples.after: the Buyer will not be responsible for the application thereof

notes: KB verdict label: Don't use.

section: Selected Usages > NOTICE > Notice and Prior Notice
statement: Consider using the verb notify instead of the noun notice. Notice can mean advance intimation or simply giving information, so Acme shall provide Karlsson with notice of any change of address is ambiguous about timing; notice is also a buried verb. Prior or advance adds nothing to ten days' notice.
test: Is it clear whether the notice must come before or after the event?
fix: Acme shall promptly notify Karlsson if it changes its address; Acme shall notify Karlsson at least ten days in advance if Acme changes its address.

examples.before: Acme shall provide Karlsson with prompt notice of any change of address
examples.after: Acme shall promptly notify Karlsson if it changes its address

examples.before: Acme shall provide Karlsson with at least ten days' prior notice of any change of address
examples.after: Acme shall notify Karlsson at least ten days in advance if Acme changes its address

notes: KB verdict label: Use with care.

section: Selected Usages > NOTICE > Termination with Prior Notice
statement: Don't say Acme may terminate this agreement upon (or by giving, or with) 60 days' prior notice; upon and by giving suggest termination when notice is given, and with is unclear. A date or event restriction (After X, Acme may terminate ...) leaves unclear whether it applies to terminating or to giving notice. State that if the party notifies the other that it is terminating, the agreement terminates a stated period after the other party receives that notice.
fix: If [after X] Acme notifies Widgetco that Acme is terminating this agreement in accordance with this section 4, this agreement will terminate 60 days after the day Widgetco receives that notice.
severity_basis: ambiguity about the effective date of termination

section: Selected Usages > NOTICE > Notice—Using an Apostrophe with Periods of Time
statement: When referring to prior notice, use an apostrophe with the period of time: one week's notice, five days' notice.
fix: five days' notice; one week's notice

section: Selected Usages > NOTIFY
statement: Use notify in the sense 'to inform someone' (Acme shall promptly notify Widgetco of any Security Incident), not the English sense 'to make known' (notify any Security Incident to Widgetco).

trigger.signal: notify + thing + to + person

fix: notify [person] of [thing]
notes: KB verdict label: Use.

section: Selected Usages > NOTWITHSTANDING, SUBJECT TO, EXCEPT AS PROVIDED IN > Notwithstanding
statement: There are good reasons not to use notwithstanding: it operates remotely, so readers may accept a provision unaware it is undercut elsewhere; an agreement-wide notwithstanding clause leaves the reader to work out which provisions are affected (possibly none); and competing notwithstanding clauses compound confusion. Prefer subject to.

words: notwithstanding anything in this agreement to the contrary

fix: Qualify the provision being undercut with subject to section X.
notes: KB verdict label: Use with care. Schepisi v. Roberts, 974 N.Y.S.2d 446 (App. Div. 2013) (competing notwithstanding clauses) (13.636). Notwithstanding may go at the front of the phrase (13.637). Appendix A fn 32 removes notwithstanding.

section: Selected Usages > NOTWITHSTANDING, SUBJECT TO, EXCEPT AS PROVIDED IN > Notwithstanding
statement: Notwithstanding the foregoing is ambiguous: the foregoing might refer to the previous sentence, all preceding text, or something in between.
test: Can the reader tell exactly which text the foregoing refers to?
fix: Name the provision (subject to section 3.2).

section: Selected Usages > NOTWITHSTANDING, SUBJECT TO, EXCEPT AS PROVIDED IN > Subject To
statement: Qualify the provision being undercut with subject to section X rather than prefacing the undercutting provision with notwithstanding; don't use both; and generally be specific about which provision does the undercutting.
test: Does subject to name the specific undercutting provision? Is notwithstanding also used for the same relationship?
fix: Subject to section 5, ...
notes: Example (13.638): qualify section 4 (payment of purchase price) with 'Subject to section 5' instead of prefacing section 5 with 'Notwithstanding section 4'.

section: Selected Usages > NOTWITHSTANDING, SUBJECT TO, EXCEPT AS PROVIDED IN > Subject To
statement: Notwithstanding has a use even for drafters who normally use subject to: when proposing a change to the other side's draft that undercuts other provisions, especially a last-minute change, it lets you make one change rather than add the provision plus cross-references.

trigger.signal: markup of the other side's draft

fix: Acceptable in a markup of the other side's draft.

section: Selected Usages > NOTWITHSTANDING, SUBJECT TO, EXCEPT AS PROVIDED IN > Subject To
statement: Subject to the terms of this agreement before key language of performance or obligation can be superfluous, since rights and obligations come from the contract as a whole; but when a key obligation (such as to cause a merger) is subject to conditions and termination rights, it is generally simpler to say Subject to the terms of this agreement than to list the sections.

words: subject to the terms of this agreement
subject to the terms and conditions of this agreement

fix: Keep for key obligations subject to conditions and termination rights; delete elsewhere.

section: Selected Usages > NOTWITHSTANDING, SUBJECT TO, EXCEPT AS PROVIDED IN > Except as Provided In
statement: Know the difference: except as provided in marks the other provision as an exception, so it is narrower than subject to, which could mean an exception or a supplement (such as a condition on a right). By extension, except as otherwise provided in this agreement is narrower than subject to the terms of this agreement.

words: except as otherwise provided in this agreement

test: Is the other provision an exception, or does it supplement (for example, impose a condition)? Choose except as provided in only for an exception.
fix: except as provided in section X (exception); subject to section X (other interplay)

section: Selected Usages > NOTWITHSTANDING, SUBJECT TO, EXCEPT AS PROVIDED IN > Confusing Interplay
statement: Besides expressing which provision prevails, express clearly the nature of the interplay between the provisions.

trigger.signal: two provisions that address the same subject differently

fix: Say what the overriding provision does to the other (excepts, conditions, limits).
notes: BDC Finance L.L.C. v. Barclays Bank PLC, 974 N.Y.S.2d 39 (App. Div. 2013) (13.643).

section: Selected Usages > NOTWITHSTANDING, SUBJECT TO, EXCEPT AS PROVIDED IN > Eliminating Nullified Provisions
statement: Don't leave in the contract language nullified by new text (signaled with subject to, notwithstanding, or provisos); a party can claim the ostensibly nullified language still has life. Delete it.

trigger.signal: provision overridden in full by a later provision but left in the text

fix: Delete the nullified language.
exceptions: Keeping the other side's language may help get the deal done (13.645), but the risk remains.
notes: United Rentals, Inc. v. RAM Holdings, Inc., 937 A.2d 810 (Del. Ch. 2007) (13.645).

section: Selected Usages > NOVATION
statement: Instead of saying an amendment does not effect a novation, say it will not result in any of the Obligations being replaced; novation is a term of art many readers won't know.
fix: will not result in any of the Obligations being replaced
exceptions: If you think it important to keep novation, combine the approaches: does not effect a novation of the Obligations, in that it will not result in any of the Obligations being replaced (13.648).
notes: KB verdict label: Don't use.

section: Selected Usages > NOVATION
statement: If keeping the word novation matters, combine it with the explanation: does not effect a novation of the Obligations, in that it will not result in any of the Obligations being replaced.
fix: does not effect a novation of the Obligations, in that it will not result in any of the Obligations being replaced

section: Selected Usages > ONLY
statement: Place only immediately before the words it is meant to limit, not by reflex before the verb; the farther it sits from its correct position, the greater the risk of ambiguity.
test: Which words does only limit? Move it immediately before them.
fix: The Tenant may move furniture ... only during nonbusiness hours

examples.before: The Tenant may only move furniture ... during nonbusiness hours
examples.after: The Tenant may move furniture, fixtures, and equipment into and out of the Premises only during nonbusiness hours unless Landlord gives approval otherwise

notes: KB verdict label: Use with care. Garner's Modern English Usage (13.649). 13.652 deletes a doubled only.

section: Selected Usages > ON THE ONE HAND ... ON THE OTHER HAND
statement: Use on the one hand ... on the other hand only to bifurcate a list of three or more items: to show which conjunction has scope over the other when one pair is joined by and and the other by or, or to divide into two categories a list that uses and as the only conjunction (the relationship between A, on the one hand, and B and C, on the other hand). Otherwise omit it.
fix: Omit unless bifurcating three or more items; enumeration also works.
notes: KB verdict label: Use only in a stated context.

section: Selected Usages > ON THE ONE HAND ... ON THE OTHER HAND > Used Unnecessarily
statement: Omit on the one hand ... on the other hand with a list of only two items, or with a list of three or more items that doesn't need bifurcating.

trigger.signal: the phrase used with two items or an undivided list

fix: The Corporate Taxpayer, the Partnerships, and the applicable Limited Partner acknowledge that ...

section: Selected Usages > ON THE ONE HAND ... ON THE OTHER HAND > Used Unnecessarily
statement: Where one of two items is plural and the phrase is used to show that its members act together, say so with (considered collectively), placing the plural item first to avoid syntactic ambiguity.

trigger.signal: plural party group paired with a single party

fix: The Sellers (considered collectively) and the Purchaser are each responsible for paying half the Transfer Taxes

section: Selected Usages > ON THE ONE HAND ... ON THE OTHER HAND > Used Unnecessarily
statement: Don't use on the one hand ... on the other hand in the introductory clause to group parties by role; recitals are for indicating roles.

trigger.signal: the phrase in the introductory clause

fix: Indicate roles in the recitals.

section: Selected Usages > PARENTHESES > Function
statement: Don't use parentheses for explanations or asides. Use them to eliminate syntactic ambiguity, with enumeration, to create a defined term after an integrated definition, for paired alternative arrangements that apply in different circumstances, and for two alternative scenarios of even modest complexity instead of delimiting commas.

trigger.signal: parenthetical aside or explanation in operative text

fix: Delete the aside or make it a sentence.
severity_basis: contract prose is not for asides
notes: KB verdict label: Use only in a stated context. Appropriate use (13.664): 'Acme shall give the Customer whatever advance notice is required by law (or, in the absence of such a requirement, reasonable advance notice) to allow the Customer to retrieve any Customer Data.'

section: Selected Usages > PARENTHESES > Parentheses Within Words
statement: Don't use parentheses within a word, such as (s) on a singular noun (say one or more), (sub)licensee, (sub)contractor, (self)insured, or (s)he.
fix: one or more registration statements; one or more certificates; gender-neutral drafting

examples.before: a registration statement(s)
examples.after: one or more registration statements on Form S-3

examples.before: the certificate(s)
examples.after: one or more certificates

section: Selected Usages > PARTY AS AN ADJECTIVE
statement: Use party as an adjective to be more concise: Acme is party to a confidentiality agreement with Widgetco; Acme and Widgetco are party to a confidentiality agreement.
fix: is party to; are party to
notes: KB verdict label: Use.

section: Selected Usages > PERCENTAGES
statement: Don't use 100% where it would be simpler to omit it or use all (all outstanding shares; fully covered). Use half rather than 50%, and drop of if you can (half the shares).
fix: all; the number of; fully; half
exceptions: Use 100% and 50% for a numerical value in a provision that includes other percentages (13.670).

examples.before: distribute to its shareholders 100% of the outstanding shares
examples.after: distribute to its shareholders all outstanding shares

examples.before: will be 100% covered
examples.after: will be fully covered

notes: KB verdict label: Use with care.

section: Selected Usages > PERCENTAGES
statement: Use 100% and 50% when the provision includes one or more other percentages (a target award-date value of 100% of the Base Salary and a maximum award value of 150% of the Base Salary).
fix: Keep the percentage.

section: Selected Usages > PERCENTAGES
statement: Don't use fractions other than half (one-quarter, one-fifth); use percentages. But use a fraction that would require a recurring decimal as a percentage, such as one-third or two-sevenths.
fix: 25%; 20%; 10% (keep one-third, two-sevenths)

section: Selected Usages > PERSONAL DELIVERY
statement: Don't use personal delivery or deliver ... personally; it is unclear whether personal relates to the person delivering (must the party deliver it itself?) or to the recipient (must it be handed to the recipient?). Deliver by hand raises similar issues.
fix: Use a notices provision that names current delivery methods (the author's form).
notes: KB verdict label: Don't use. Ener-G Holdings plc v. Hormell [2012] EWCA Civ 1059 (13.674).

section: Selected Usages > PERSONNEL
statement: Don't use personnel undefined: some read it as employees, others more broadly (even companies), which could lead to a dispute. If you mean employees, say employees; if you mean employees and other representatives, use the defined term Representative.
fix: employees; Representatives
exceptions: If the group includes more than employees and representatives, you could use a defined term Personnel, but consider whether you need such an unwieldy group (13.680).
notes: KB verdict label: Don't use.

section: Selected Usages > PLEASE
statement: Don't use please in contracts; contracts aren't the place for courtesy, and please can be read as precatory rather than mandatory.
fix: language of obligation (shall)
notes: KB verdict label: Don't use. Landmark American Insurance Co. v. Lonergan Law Firm, PLLC, 809 F. App'x 239 (5th Cir. 2020) (13.682).

section: Selected Usages > PREVAILING PARTY
statement: If you want to recover legal fees and other expenses, say so in the contract; in the U.S. they generally aren't recoverable otherwise. But prevailing party (or successful party) has spawned much litigation; specifying what determines prevailing (judgment or dismissal; substantially what was sought; net winner) each has tradeoffs, and the risks of setting rules in advance might outweigh the benefits.
fix: State fee recovery expressly; decide deliberately whether to define prevailing.
exceptions: In California, Cal. Civil Code s. 1717(b)(1) defines prevailing party for contract claims, and the definition can't be altered by contract (13.689).
notes: KB verdict label: Use with care. Rossi, 1 Attorneys' Fees s. 6:8 (13.684); Exxess Electronixx v. Heger Realty Corp., 75 Cal. Rptr. 2d 376 (Ct. App. 1998) (13.689).

section: Selected Usages > PREVAILING PARTY
statement: For contracts governed by California law, the Cal. Civil Code s. 1717(b)(1) definition of prevailing party for contract claims is mandatory; a contract definition can't alter or avoid it.

trigger.signal: California governing law

fix: Don't rely on a contract definition of prevailing party under California law.

section: Selected Usages > PRINCIPLE OF LEAST PRIVILEGE
statement: If you use principle of least privilege, consider telling the reader what it means; if you explain it, it might make sense to omit the phrase unless it helps as a defined term. Involve an information-security specialist, because the principle reaches beyond access to information.
fix: ... shall apply the 'principle of least privilege' in granting access ..., so a user or a process has access only to such information as is required to perform a legitimate business function.
notes: KB verdict label: Use with care.

section: Selected Usages > PRODUCT, UNITS OF THE PRODUCT
statement: Use the defined term Product for a product line and refer to units of the Product for individual samples; Product alone is ambiguous between the two.
fix: units of the Product
notes: KB verdict label: Use.

section: Selected Usages > PROPRIETARY
statement: Don't use proprietary in defining Confidential Information: proprietary information sweeps in nonconfidential information, and proprietary and confidential excludes confidential information that isn't proprietary (such as information a third person disclosed under a confidentiality agreement).
fix: confidential
notes: KB verdict label: Don't use. Proprietary is overused in contracts (13.695). Appendix A fn 132 replaces proprietary with confidential.

section: Selected Usages > PROVIDED THAT
statement: Don't use provided that (or ; provided, however, that, or provided further). The proviso is archaic and signals imprecisely whether what follows is an exception, limitation, condition, or addition; use the precise alternative: except that (exception), and in any event (limitation), on condition that (condition), and (addition).
test: Classify what follows: exception, limitation, condition, or addition.
fix: except that; and in any event; on condition that; and

examples.before: ; provided, however, that, the Warrant Shares may be subject to restrictions
examples.after: except that the Warrant Shares may be subject to restrictions on transfer

examples.before: ; provided, however, that the Closing must occur, no later than 1 December 2023
examples.after: and in any event no later than 1 December 2023

examples.before: ; provided, however, that the Consultant shall obtain,
examples.after: on condition that the Consultant obtain Acme's written consent

notes: KB verdict label: Don't use. Jacobsen v. Katzer, 535 F.3d 1373 (Fed. Cir. 2008): the wrong lesson is to use provided that for conditions (13.700). Appendix A fns 24, 31, 130 remove provisos.

section: Selected Usages > PROVISION
statement: Delete provision(s) where it is redundant (in accordance with the provisions of this section 4.1.1), delete terms and provisions, and don't use provisions in section and article headings.
fix: in accordance with this section 4.1.1; The Purchase Agreement ... will remain in effect; Interpretation; Definitions; Patents
exceptions: Unspecific uses (antidilution provisions in the Notes) are the word's function and aren't struck (13.702).

examples.before: in accordance with the provisions of this section 4.1.1
examples.after: in accordance with this section 4.1.1

examples.before: Other Interpretive Provisions
examples.after: Interpretation

examples.before: Patent Provisions
examples.after: Patents

notes: KB verdict label: Use with care.

section: Selected Usages > PUBLIC DOMAIN > Used in the Exception to the Definition of Confidential Information
statement: Don't use in the public domain to mean that information is public; it is wordy, primarily British, and confusing because the phrase has a more entrenched intellectual-property meaning.
fix: public; publicly available; available to the public; publicly known
notes: KB verdict label: Use only in a stated context.

section: Selected Usages > PUBLIC DOMAIN > Used Regarding Intellectual Property
statement: If you use in the public domain in its intellectual-property sense (works no longer subject to copyright), consider explaining it; simpler still, omit it and say what you mean.
fix: Except for portions in the public domain (that is, not subject to copyright protection), ...
severity_basis: term of art unknown outside IP circles

section: Selected Usages > REASONABLE, REASONABLY
statement: Where reasonable doesn't refer to the reasonableness of the thing modified, say what is meant: instead of to the reasonable satisfaction of Acme (or reasonably satisfactory to Acme), say to the satisfaction of Acme, determined from the perspective of a reasonable person in Acme's position.
fix: to the satisfaction of Acme, determined from the perspective of a reasonable person in Acme's position
notes: KB verdict label: Use with care. In a reasonable fee and in reasonable detail, reasonable refers to reasonableness of the thing and is fine (13.714). Courts would likely give satisfactory the objective meaning anyway (13.761).

section: Selected Usages > REASONABLE, REASONABLY
statement: Omit reasonably where it is redundant: with verbs that inherently involve reasonableness (cooperate reasonably), with promptly and other such adverbs (reasonably promptly), and in reasonably likely.
fix: cooperate; promptly; likely
exceptions: Whether reasonably is redundant with a verb depends on the verb (reasonably requests, reasonably determines mean 'in a reasonable manner') (13.715).

section: Selected Usages > REASONABLENESS AND GOOD FAITH > Whether to Use a Reasonableness Standard or a Good-Faith Standard
statement: Generally prefer a reasonableness standard (objective) for a counterparty's conduct, for example reasonable efforts rather than good-faith efforts; a good-faith standard is subjective.
fix: reasonable / reasonably / appropriate
exceptions: If your client is the one subject to the provision, you might prefer a good-faith standard (13.721).
notes: KB verdict label: Use with care.

section: Selected Usages > REASONABLENESS AND GOOD FAITH > Whether to Use a Reasonableness Standard or a Good-Faith Standard
statement: Use a good-faith standard when a party is taking a position (contesting taxes in good faith, claiming that something happened, filing a complaint), and use good faith to qualify an obligation to negotiate; you can't be forced to agree just because a reasonable person would have.
fix: contested in good faith; negotiate in good faith

section: Selected Usages > REASONABLENESS AND GOOD FAITH > Whether to Use a Reasonableness Standard or a Good-Faith Standard
statement: Don't use good faith with words that refer to a party's actual state of mind; good-faith belief makes no sense.
fix: believes
notes: With believes, satisfactory, and other state-of-mind words, a reasonableness standard refers to a reasonable person in the party's position (13.724, citing 13.761-.762).

section: Selected Usages > REASONABLENESS AND GOOD FAITH > Whether to Use a Reasonableness Standard or a Good-Faith Standard
statement: In jurisdictions recognizing the implied duty of good faith, stating a good-faith standard isn't necessary, though a reminder can help. The difference between the standards can be more apparent than real, since courts often judge good faith by how others behaved, which may help if the other side balks at reasonableness.

trigger.signal: express good-faith standard

fix: Optional reminder.

section: Selected Usages > REASONABLENESS AND GOOD FAITH > Using Both Standards Together
statement: Usually don't use both standards in one provision; reasonable good-faith efforts and reasonable good-faith judgment are redundant. You might want both where conduct must be reasonable and not a pretext (taxes contested in good faith by appropriate proceedings), but both can be overkill (a customer disputing charges reasonably and in good faith invites an argument of bad faith).
fix: reasonable efforts; in good faith by appropriate proceedings (pretext concern)

section: Selected Usages > REGARD SHALL BE HAD TO
statement: Don't use regard shall be had to (passive, with a shall that fails the has-a-duty test); one approach is the active voice with take into account, consider, or include.

words: regard is to be had to

fix: [the actor] shall take into account / consider / include
notes: KB verdict label: Don't use. Example (13.730): 'In computing the majority when a poll is demanded, regard shall be had to the number of votes to which each Member is entitled by the Articles.' Not amenable to a quick fix (13.731).

section: Selected Usages > REMEDIATE
statement: Using remediate for cleanup or treatment of environmental contamination is acceptable; remediation has a specialized environmental meaning, and remedy could mean money, penalties, or an injunction.
fix: Keep remediate for environmental cleanup; otherwise remedy.
notes: KB verdict label: Use only in a stated context.

section: Selected Usages > REMIT, REMITTANCE
statement: Use pay and payment instead of remit and remittance, which are old-fashioned; where possible, replace the abstract noun remittance with the verb pay.
fix: pay; payment (transfer or refund in some contexts)

examples.before: If legal restrictions prevent the prompt remittance of
examples.after: If by law Acme is prevented from paying promptly any royalties

notes: KB verdict label: Don't use.

section: Selected Usages > RESPECTIVE, RESPECTIVELY > Respective
statement: Use respective only where components of one group are considered separately in pairing them with components of another group (Acme, Widgetco, or any of their respective Affiliates). Delete an extraneous respective (or use in question), don't use it with a singular construction, use any where no pairing is involved, and consider making the groups singular.
test: Does respective pair each member of one group with its own counterpart in another group? If not, remove it.
fix: in question; any; singular construction (Each capitalized term ... has the meaning given to it)

examples.before: the first day of the respective Class Year
examples.after: the first day of the Class Year in question

examples.before: 'Release Date' means the respective dates
examples.after: 'Release Date' means any date on which

examples.before: All capitalized terms that are used but not defined in this SOW have the respective meanings given to them
examples.after: Each capitalized term used but not defined in this SOW has the meaning given to it

notes: KB verdict label: Use only in a stated context.

section: Selected Usages > RESPECTIVE, RESPECTIVELY > Respectively
statement: Use respectively only to pair each item in an earlier list with its counterpart in a following list with the same number of items, both joined by and, not or; it is redundant without a preceding list to echo.
test: Are there two lists of equal length joined by and? If not, delete respectively.
fix: employed by each of XYZ, the Company, and the Bank in a senior executive capacity

examples.before: The Executive is employed by XYZ, the Company, and the Bank in senior executive capacities, respectively
examples.after: The Executive is employed by each of XYZ, the Company, and the Bank in a senior executive capacity

section: Selected Usages > RIGHTFULLY, RIGHTFUL
statement: Consider replacing rightfully and rightful (and wrongfully, wrongful) with a clearer statement of the basis for entitlement; in the confidentiality exception (information the Licensee rightfully obtains), it is unclear whether the source owed no confidentiality duty, the recipient broke no law, or both.
fix: State the basis (for example, from a Person that was not under a duty to keep that information confidential).
notes: KB verdict label: Don't use.

section: Selected Usages > RIGHT, TITLE, AND INTEREST
statement: Consider using only interest instead of right, title, and interest, a bloated legalism; interest includes the others. If interest alone is inadequate, add only what is needed; if the concern is that the transferor might retain something, have it acknowledge that after the transfer it is left with nothing relating to the asset.
fix: interest
notes: KB verdict label: Don't use. The manual 'won't offer a blanket rule' given the many contexts (13.756). In re Baldwin's Estate, 134 P.2d 259 (Cal. 1943) (13.754).

section: Selected Usages > SAID USED AS A POINTING WORD
statement: Don't use said in place of the pointing words this, that, these, and those; it is annoyingly legalistic and less clear.

trigger.signal: said used as an adjective before a noun

fix: this; that; these; those

examples.before: shall immediately refer said dispute to arbitration
examples.after: shall immediately refer that dispute to arbitration

examples.before: members of said board on the first day of such period
examples.after: members of that board on the first day of that period

notes: KB verdict label: Don't use.

section: Selected Usages > SAME USED AS A PRONOUN
statement: Don't use same as a pronoun; use it, its, them, they, or their, or repeat the noun, perhaps with a pointing word; sometimes more revision is needed.

trigger.signal: the same used as a pronoun

fix: it; them; they

examples.before: before the same become delinquent
examples.after: before they become delinquent

examples.before: upon the depositing of the same in the U.S. mail
examples.after: when it is deposited in the U.S. mail

notes: KB verdict label: Don't use.

section: Selected Usages > SATISFACTORY
statement: Satisfactory to Acme is ambiguous between the objective meaning (a reasonable person in Acme's position would be satisfied) and the subjective meaning (Acme must actually be satisfied, subject to good faith). Courts prefer the objective meaning; to make it clear, say reasonably satisfactory to Acme.
fix: reasonably satisfactory to Acme (objective)
exceptions: For the subjective meaning, drafters say at its discretion, which strictly doesn't go to the meaning of satisfactory; the explicit formula is 'satisfactory to Acme, with Acme's satisfaction in this instance being a function of whether Acme is actually satisfied (subject to any implied duty of good faith), rather than whether a reasonable person in Acme's position would be satisfied' (13.762), which a counterparty is unlikely to accept.
notes: KB verdict label: Use with care. Corbin s. 5.32; Williston s. 38:22 (13.761). Compare 13.718, which says spelling out the reasonable-person perspective is clearer than reasonably satisfactory.

section: Selected Usages > SETOFF, OFFSET
statement: The nouns setoff and offset mean the same thing, as do the verbs set off and offset; pick one noun, use it consistently with the corresponding verb, and spell the noun setoff (not set-off or set off) and the verb set off (two words).
