test: Is more than one form used for the same concept? Is the noun hyphenated?
fix: setoff (noun) / set off (verb), or offset throughout
notes: KB verdict label: Use. Citizens Bank of Maryland v. Strumpf, 516 U.S. 16 (1995) (13.765).

section: Selected Usages > SHAREHOLDER OR STOCKHOLDER?
statement: You may use either stockholder or shareholder for a holder of shares of a Delaware corporation, for all purposes including contract drafting; they are synonyms.
test: Is only one form used throughout?
fix: Either; be consistent.
notes: KB verdict label: Use.

section: Selected Usages > SHAREHOLDERS AGREEMENT
statement: Call a contract between shareholders a shareholders agreement (plural attributive noun, no apostrophe); shareholders' agreement and shareholder agreement are defensible. The same applies with stockholder.
fix: shareholders agreement
notes: KB verdict label: Use.

section: Selected Usages > SIGNATORY
statement: Don't use signatory; it is ambiguous (a person that signs and becomes a party, or anyone who signs for a party). Use party for a person that signs and thereby becomes a party, say the individual signing this agreement for Acme for an individual signing for a party, and consider signer, including in signature blocks.
fix: party; the individual signing this agreement for Acme; signer
exceptions: Don't say on behalf of Acme; it could be read as referring to an agent rather than an Acme officer (13.776).
In a signature block, signatory clearly refers to the individual signing (13.777).
notes: KB verdict label: Don't use.

section: Selected Usages > SILENT ON
statement: Instead of This agreement is silent on ..., say This agreement does not address [the issue in question].
fix: This agreement does not address ...
notes: KB verdict label: Don't use.

section: Selected Usages > SOLE, EXCLUSIVE > Sole, Exclusive in Licensing
statement: In licensing, rather than rely on sole to mean that the licensor keeps the right to practice the licensed subject matter, state that in a separate sentence; sole versus exclusive license is jargon, less clear than it seems. Exclusive (except as to the Licensor) is another way; avoid coexclusive.
fix: State in a separate sentence that the licensor retains the right to practice the licensed subject matter.
notes: KB verdict label: Use with care. Drafting License Agreements s. 1.02; Milgrim on Licensing ss. 15.08, 15.33 (13.780-13.781).

section: Selected Usages > SOLE, EXCLUSIVE > Sole and Exclusive
statement: Don't use sole and exclusive: say sole remedy or only remedy instead of sole and exclusive remedy; exclusive jurisdiction in a forum-selection provision; and Acme owns all those interests instead of the sole and exclusive property of Acme. At its sole and exclusive option raises the same issues as at its sole discretion.
fix: sole remedy / only remedy; exclusive jurisdiction; Acme owns

section: Selected Usages > SOLICIT
statement: In no-solicit provisions, use solicit to be hired, not bare solicit (solicit them for what?) or solicit to employ (awkward); solicit employees to accept employment is clearest but wordy.
fix: solicit [employees] to be hired
notes: KB verdict label: Use with care.

section: Selected Usages > SPECIFIC
statement: If tempted to use specific, try omitting it; if that doesn't work, consider a different word (individual; specified). The entry excludes specific performance.
fix: delete; individual; specified
exceptions: specific performance is outside the entry (13.791).

examples.before: it is the specific intent of the parties that
examples.after: the parties intend that

examples.before: in specific cases
examples.after: in individual cases

examples.before: relate solely to a specific earlier date
examples.after: relate solely to a specified earlier date

notes: KB verdict label: Don't use. The last 13.791 example prints 'Nosuch employees' without a visible strike (possible production error).

section: Selected Usages > SPOUSE
statement: Use spouse instead of wife or husband; it works whatever the sex of the party and of the person the party is married to.
fix: spouse
notes: KB verdict label: Use.

section: Selected Usages > SUBROGATION
statement: In provisions that relate only to the parties, replace the terms of art subrogation and subrogate with simpler alternatives.
fix: Acme hereby waives any of the rights of the Administrative Agent ...

examples.before: Acme will not be entitled to be subrogated to any of the rights of the Administrative Agent
examples.after: Acme hereby waives any of the rights of the Administrative Agent

notes: KB verdict label: Use only in a stated context.

section: Selected Usages > SUBROGATION
statement: In insurance-requirement provisions, changing subrogation terminology means presenting insurers with novel wording; consult an insurance specialist or leave well enough alone.
fix: Leave as is, or consult an insurance specialist.
notes: 13.798 cites 13.949 as a combining technique; 13.200 fits better (possible cross-reference mismatch in the source).

section: Selected Usages > SUBSISTING > In Leases
statement: Don't use subsisting when referring to leases; references to the status of contracts use in full force and effect or valid and enforceable.
fix: valid and enforceable; in effect
notes: KB verdict label: Don't use. Example (13.799): 'held under valid, subsisting, and enforceable leases'.

section: Selected Usages > SUBSISTING > Relating to Intellectual Property
statement: Don't parrot the copyright statute's subsists (Copyright Act s. 102) in statements about IP; use the word that makes sense more broadly, such as exists.
fix: exists; valid and enforceable
exceptions: Subsisting patent is a term of art (issued and alive but not necessarily valid or enforceable); the author offers no alternative (13.804).

section: Selected Usages > SUBSISTING > Instead of Existing
statement: Subsisting is sporadically used instead of existing; where a state issues a certificate of subsistence rather than a certificate of good standing (Pennsylvania is one), it is easy to see why a drafter would use subsisting for an entity formed there.
fix: existing (unless tracking a certificate of subsistence)
notes: The entry states no other verdict here.

section: Selected Usages > SUCH AS
statement: Don't use such as; it may be unclear whether the such as phrase narrows the preceding noun (restrictive) or just gives examples (nonrestrictive), and it would be rash to rely on a comma to tell them apart. Describe the class precisely; if its boundaries might be uncertain, use including as recommended in 13.375-.380.
fix: a precise class; including (enlarging item)
notes: KB verdict label: Don't use. Lawler Manufacturing Co. v. Bradley Corp., 280 F. App'x 951 (Fed. Cir. 2008) (13.813-13.814).

section: Selected Usages > SUCH USED AS A POINTING WORD
statement: Use such with a noun echoing an antecedent only when it means 'of this kind', often after any or no (any such deposit; No such default exists). Otherwise use this, that, these, or those; if that would follow the that of a that-clause, use the.

trigger.signal: such + noun referring back to a specific antecedent

fix: this; that; these; those; the
severity_basis: one word for different meanings; legalism

examples.before: under common control with such Person
examples.after: under common control with that Person

examples.before: within such ten-day period
examples.after: within that ten-day period

examples.before: except to the extent that that loss
examples.after: except to the extent that the loss

notes: KB verdict label: Use only in a stated context. Appendix A fns 28 and 188 replace such with pointing words.

section: Selected Usages > SUFFER > Intransitive
statement: Don't use suffer to mean 'undergo, experience'; use incur, or, because suffer is used with abstract nouns, sometimes an adjective.
fix: incur; restate with an adjective or verb
exceptions: Suffer meaning 'to submit to or be forced to endure' is unobjectionable (13.820).

examples.before: the Company would suffer irreparable harm to its business and goodwill
examples.after: the Company's business and goodwill would be irreparably harmed

notes: KB verdict label: Don't use.

section: Selected Usages > SUFFER > Transitive
statement: Suffer meaning 'to allow, especially by reason of indifference' (suffer to exist) is pompous and archaic; usually use permit.
fix: permit

examples.before: create, incur, assume, or suffer to exist any Lien
examples.after: create, incur, assume, or permit to exist any Lien

section: Selected Usages > SURVIVAL
statement: In each of three contexts (claims, provisions, statements of fact), survival language is unnecessary or inferior to an alternative.
fix: See the context rules.
notes: KB verdict label: Don't use.

section: Selected Usages > SURVIVAL > Survival of Claims
statement: Don't state that claims arising before termination survive termination; terminating, even for breach, doesn't preclude a damages claim.
fix: Say nothing.
exceptions: Stating settled law can help because parties won't necessarily know the law (13.825).
notes: Farnsworth on Contracts s. 8.15 (13.824).

section: Selected Usages > SURVIVAL > Survival of Provisions
statement: To make an obligation continue after termination, build its duration into the obligation (during the term of this agreement and for five years thereafter) rather than stating that the provision survives; don't state that dispute-resolution and other boilerplate survive termination.
fix: During the term of this agreement and for five years thereafter, the Recipient shall not ...

section: Selected Usages > SURVIVAL > Survival of Statements of Fact
statement: Instead of stating how long statements of fact survive, address time limits on indemnification claims directly and more broadly in a section entitled Time Limits; survival periods address only one basis of claims and don't limit claims for breach of obligations.
fix: A Time Limits section stating when indemnification claims may be brought.
notes: GRT, Inc. v. Marathon GTF Technology, Ltd., 2011 WL 2682898, at *14 n.79 (Del. Ch. 2011) notes the manual's approach (13.831).

section: Selected Usages > TERMINATION, EXPIRATION > What to Use in Termination Provisions
statement: Use terminates, not expires, in termination provisions, and treat expiration as one form of termination; This agreement terminates on [date] is unambiguous. Using expires forces ponderous constructions (expires or is terminated) elsewhere, and failing to use them can cause disputes.
fix: terminates; termination
notes: KB verdict label: Use with care. Hamden v. Total Car Franchising Corp., 2012 WL 3255598 (W.D. Va. 2012); Holtzman Interests 23 v. FFC Sugarloaf, 2012 WL 468257 (Mich. Ct. App. 2012) (13.838).

section: Selected Usages > TERMINATION, EXPIRATION > What to Use in Termination Provisions
statement: Don't use terminate and expire together; it shows inconsistency or redundancy.
fix: terminate
notes: Example (13.839): 'This agreement will terminate and expire upon cessation of commercial operation of the Plant.'

section: Selected Usages > TERMINATION, EXPIRATION > Referring to Termination Provisions
statement: Be careful how you refer to termination. If the contract states its term with the noun term, refer explicitly to both the end of the term and party termination if you mean both (better, refer to the sections). If you mean only termination without party action, refer to those sections. If you mean only termination by a party, use the active voice (if either party terminates this agreement), not if this agreement is terminated.
test: Does the reference mean end of term, termination by a party, or both? Can a disgruntled party argue end of term is expiration?
fix: if either party terminates this agreement; on termination of this agreement under section 9.2 or 9.3

section: Selected Usages > TERMINATION FOR CAUSE
statement: Use termination for cause only in employment agreements; in other contracts, for cause is redundant, because grounds for termination vary widely and one label wouldn't work.
fix: Delete for cause outside employment agreements.

examples.before: Acme may terminate this agreement for cause effective when Acme notifies Widgetco
examples.after: Acme may terminate this agreement effective when Acme notifies Widgetco

notes: KB verdict label: Use only in a stated context.

section: Selected Usages > TERMINATION FOR CONVENIENCE
statement: Leave termination for convenience in government contracts, where it refers to the government's right to terminate without breach. Elsewhere, convenience is wishy-washy and a litigator might argue it requires some burden; say Acme may terminate this agreement for any reason by giving the Vendor at least 30 days' prior notice. You may drop at any time, but don't drop both phrases.
fix: may terminate this agreement for any reason by giving ... at least 30 days' prior notice
notes: KB verdict label: Use only in a stated context.

section: Selected Usages > TERMINATION FOR CONVENIENCE > What To Use Instead
statement: If the contract also provides for termination for cause, you could use termination without cause instead of for any reason, for symmetry. Eliminate or for no reason. For a heading, if Termination for Any Reason seems blunt, use Unrestricted Termination or group by who may terminate (Buyer Termination).

words: for any reason or for no reason

fix: without cause (symmetry); Unrestricted Termination (heading)

section: Selected Usages > TERMS AND CONDITIONS
statement: Say terms instead of terms and conditions (a condition is a kind of term); the same goes for terms, conditions, and exceptions and terms and provisions. It might be clearer to say any provision of this agreement, because term in the singular could be read as duration.
fix: terms; any provision of this agreement
notes: KB verdict label: Don't use. Appendix A fns 174 and 197 collapse these doublets.

section: Selected Usages > THAT CERTAIN
statement: Use a or an instead of that certain when referring to an agreement; it is an archaism.
fix: a / an

examples.before: party to that certain credit agreement
examples.after: party to a credit agreement dated 12 August 2022

notes: KB verdict label: Don't use.

section: Selected Usages > THE EARLIER [OR LATER, GREATER, OR LESSER] OF X AND Y
statement: Use and between the alternatives (the later of (1) ... and (2) ...); you are selecting one item from a group. With three or more items, use earliest, latest, greatest, or least.

trigger.signal: the earlier/later/greater/lesser of ... or ...

fix: the later of (1) ... and (2) ...
severity_basis: logic; courts have bungled both versions
notes: KB verdict label: Use. Dan's Hauling & Demo v. GMMM Hickling, 147 N.Y.S.3d 805 (App. Div. 2021); Andros v. Colliers Macaulay Nicolls, 2019 ONCA 679 (13.866-13.867). The author rejects Garner's preference for or (13.864).

section: Selected Usages > THE EARLIER [OR LATER, GREATER, OR LESSER] OF X AND Y
statement: If you use whichever is, use or ((1) ... or (2) ..., whichever is later), and reserve it for items described succinctly, because it puts the basis of selection at the end.
fix: X or Y, whichever is later (short items only)

section: Selected Usages > THERE CAN BE NO ASSURANCE THAT
statement: Don't use there can be no assurance that (from securities offerings); it creates a fake subject and verb and fits no category of contract language. Have whoever would benefit acknowledge that the thing might not happen.
fix: The Owner acknowledges that the Owner might not receive that notice in time ...
notes: KB verdict label: Don't use.

section: Selected Usages > THEREFOR
statement: Delete therefor if context makes clear what is referred to; otherwise be explicit. If you use it, expect people to try to change it to therefore.
fix: Delete, or name the thing.

examples.before: will be entitled to receive in exchange therefor the purchase price
examples.after: will be entitled to receive in exchange the purchase price

notes: KB verdict label: Don't use.

section: Selected Usages > THING
statement: Instead of any thing or all things, refer to the acts or pieces of property meant.
fix: Name the acts or property.
notes: KB verdict label: Don't use.

section: Selected Usages > THIRD PARTY
statement: Don't use third party; it derives from party of the first part and is anomalous (party means one who has entered into the contract). Use Person when the parties needn't be excluded, any Person other than a party or nonparty when they must be, and the defined term Nonparty instead of Third Party or Third-Party Claims.
fix: Person; any Person other than a party; nonparty; Nonparty

examples.before: similar right of a third party
examples.after: similar right of any Person

examples.before: disclosed to the receiving party by a third party
examples.after: disclosed to the receiving party by a Person other than a party, on condition that that Person was not under a duty to keep that information confidential

notes: KB verdict label: Don't use.

section: Selected Usages > THIRD PARTY
statement: You can't dispense entirely with third party: keep it in terms of art such as third-party beneficiary and where legislation uses it.
fix: Keep it.

section: Selected Usages > THROUGHOUT THE UNIVERSE
statement: Use worldwide instead of throughout the universe if the grantee has no prospect of using the rights in space, in satellites or otherwise.
fix: worldwide
notes: KB verdict label: Don't use.

section: Selected Usages > TIME IS OF THE ESSENCE
statement: Don't rely on time is of the essence (or of the essence); it is jargon, too general, silent on consequences, may have no legal effect, and courts have ignored it. Use a termination provision instead, supplemented if appropriate by an acknowledgment that breach of specified sections is material breach; for a drop-dead date, have the parties acknowledge that no time beyond that date will be required.

words: time shall be of the essence

fix: Termination provision; acknowledgment that breach of section x is material breach; drop-dead-date acknowledgment (13.895)
exceptions: Termination for any tardiness might make sense in some contexts (13.892).
notes: KB verdict label: Don't use. Corbin s. 37.3 (13.889, 13.891); Restatement (Second) of Contracts s. 242 cmt. d (13.894).

section: Selected Usages > TOGETHER WITH, AS WELL AS
statement: Outside its use in boosting defined terms (6.77), replace together with with and, with, or plus; apply the same fixes to as well as.
fix: and; with; plus
exceptions: Together with is acceptable when boosting defined terms (6.77).

examples.before: the Site together with the Buildings
examples.after: the Site and the Buildings

examples.before: together with an explanation
examples.after: with an explanation

examples.before: the advanced funds together with interest
examples.after: the advanced funds plus interest

notes: KB verdict label: Use with care.

section: Selected Usages > TO THE EXTENT PERMITTED BY LAW
statement: Use to the extent permitted by law if conduct contemplated in the contract might result in a party breaking the law (To the extent permitted by law, Acme may incinerate the Excess Materials); it makes it hard for Acme to argue that its unlawful conduct doesn't give the other side grounds to terminate or sue.

words: to the extent permitted by law
to the fullest extent permitted by law
to the maximum extent permitted by law
to the extent permitted by applicable law

fix: Keep only where contemplated conduct might be unlawful.
notes: KB verdict label: Use only in a stated context.

section: Selected Usages > TO THE EXTENT PERMITTED BY LAW
statement: In language of performance such as a jury-trial waiver, to the extent permitted by law does nothing except tell the parties the waiver might or might not be enforceable; if you want to signal willingness to have an unenforceable provision modified, use a severability provision instead.

words: to the extent permitted by law
to the fullest extent permitted by law
trigger.signal: the phrase in a waiver (jury trial, claims)

fix: Delete the phrase; rely on a severability provision.
notes: The author disagrees with Negotiating and Drafting Contract Boilerplate 155 (Stark ed. 2003) (13.901).

section: Selected Usages > TRADEMARKS—REFERENCES TO
statement: Drop the registration symbol in contracts. In trademark license agreements and other contracts about rights in a trademark, use all capitals for that trademark; where a trademark simply identifies goods or services, use initial capitals.

trigger.signal: trademark in all capitals or with a registration symbol

fix: Drop the symbol; all capitals only in trademark-rights contracts; initial capitals elsewhere
notes: KB verdict label: Use with care. Gilson on Trademarks s. 2.02; Kane on Trademark Law s. 5:2.1 (13.906).

section: Selected Usages > TRADEMARKS—REFERENCES TO > Registration Symbol or No Registration Symbol?
statement: Contracts can drop the registration symbol: they aren't disseminated publicly, and a party is unlikely to need notice in a contract for Lanham Act recovery (15 U.S.C. s. 1111). A concerned owner should address unauthorized use expressly.
fix: Drop the symbol; add an express provision on unauthorized use if needed.

section: Selected Usages > TRADEMARKS—REFERENCES TO > Relationship to Trademark Guidelines
statement: If your client has strict rules on referring to its trademarks (all capitals and the symbol every time), follow them even if they add clutter, but use judicious defined terms (the Licensed Mark; the Product) to limit references to the trademark.

trigger.signal: client trademark guidelines

fix: the Licensed Mark; the Product

section: Selected Usages > UNLESS AND UNTIL
statement: Use just unless; unless and until signals a hoped-for condition might not be met, a rhetorical nuance that suits speech or persuasive writing, not contracts.
fix: unless
notes: KB verdict label: Don't use.

section: Selected Usages > UNLESS THE CONTEXT OTHERWISE REQUIRES
statement: Eliminate unless the context otherwise requires (or requires otherwise); it adds uncertainty a litigator might exploit. If you want to deviate from an across-the-board convention, be specific.

words: unless the context clearly requires otherwise
except where the context otherwise requires

fix: Delete; state any specific deviation.
notes: KB verdict label: Don't use. Example (13.920): 'Unless the context otherwise requires, capitalized terms used in this agreement have the following meanings.'

section: Selected Usages > UNLESS THE PARTIES AGREE OTHERWISE
statement: Generally don't use unless the parties agree otherwise; the parties may waive, amend, or delete any provision whether or not the contract says so.

words: unless otherwise agreed by the parties

fix: Delete it.
exceptions: It is appropriate if reminding everyone that the parties might later agree on a different arrangement would ease negotiation of a provision (13.922).
notes: KB verdict label: Use only in a stated context.

section: Selected Usages > UTMOST
statement: Omit utmost, in this context and everywhere else; with the utmost dispatch is an idiosyncratic alternative to reasonable efforts, and in utmost good faith, utmost care, and utmost diligence it adds only rhetorical emphasis. If you have something specific in mind, express it clearly.
fix: Delete; state the specific standard.
notes: KB verdict label: Don't use.

section: Selected Usages > VERY
statement: Very (like extremely and highly) is not a meaningful indication of magnitude in contracts; the reader can't tell where it falls between nothing and everything.
fix: Delete, or state the magnitude.
notes: KB verdict label: Don't use. The entry states no explicit instruction; it notes very occurs infrequently in contracts.

section: Selected Usages > VEST
statement: Vesting in the sense of gaining rights to an asset over time (stock options; employer-matched contributions) is the term's ordinary use. When vest is used to express transfer of property, say instead that the thing becomes someone else's property.
fix: will become the property of the Surviving Corporation
notes: KB verdict label: Use only in a stated context. Example (13.925): 'all of the assets ... of Merger Sub and ABC shall vest in the Surviving Corporation'. The fix wording paraphrases 13.926.

section: Selected Usages > VIRGULE, ALSO KNOWN AS THE FORWARD SLASH
statement: Don't use the virgule (forward slash) in contracts other than to state a fraction; writers use it for per, or, and, or a vague disjunction, and there is almost always a better choice.

trigger.signal: slash between words

fix: or; and; per; one or more of
notes: KB verdict label: Use only in a stated context.

section: Selected Usages > VOLUNTARILY, INVOLUNTARILY
statement: Depending on context, voluntarily and involuntarily might not make sense; delete or replace them (voluntarily or involuntarily terminated -> ceases to be an employee for any reason). Freely is similarly usually redundant.
fix: ceases to be an employee for any reason; delete
exceptions: If involuntarily (in a prohibition on encumbering shares) addresses a legitimate issue, address it some other way (13.929).
notes: KB verdict label: Don't use. 13.930 example: 'The Landlord may freely lease' (freely struck).

section: Selected Usages > WAIVER OF PRESENTMENT
statement: No explicit instruction: The guarantor waives protest, presentment and notice of dishonor is a relic under post-1990 UCC article 3 (adopted by all states except New York and South Carolina); per Darmstadter, all suretyship defenses can be waived with I waive defenses based on suretyship or impairment of collateral.
fix: I waive defenses based on suretyship or impairment of collateral (states with post-1990 art. 3)
notes: KB verdict label: Explanatory (no verdict). Darmstadter, Hereof, Thereof, and Everywhereof 197 (2d ed. 2008) (13.931).

section: Selected Usages > WARRANT, WARRANT CERTIFICATE, WARRANT AGREEMENT
statement: Distinguish the warrant (the intangible right: exercise of the warrant) from the document evidencing it; call the document a warrant agreement if issuer and holder sign it and a warrant certificate if only the issuer signs.

trigger.signal: warrant used for both the right and the document

fix: warrant (right); warrant agreement / warrant certificate (document)
notes: KB verdict label: Use. 13.934 cites 13.938-.952 for the verb warrant; that entry runs 13.937-13.951.

section: Selected Usages > WARRANTY, THE VERB WARRANT > Using the Verb Warrant to Introduce a Statement of Fact
statement: Use states instead of warrants to introduce a statement of fact (consistent with states instead of represents); represents and warrants is pointless and confusing. A statement needn't be called a warranty to be one.
fix: states
notes: KB verdict label: Use with care. 13.939 prints 'section 2-303 of the Uniform Commercial Code' (confirmed in pdf/pages/p793.txt); the quoted express-warranty language appears to be UCC s. 2-313, so the section number is likely a misprint (unverified against the UCC text here).

section: Selected Usages > WARRANTY, THE VERB WARRANT > Using the Verb Warrant to Introduce a Statement of Fact
statement: In sale-of-goods contracts, you can instead combine the warranty and its remedy in one sentence: make the actual or future fact a conditional clause and the remedy the matrix clause.

trigger.signal: product warranty followed by a separate remedy provision

fix: If at any time during the six months after the date of this agreement the Equipment does not conform to the Specifications, the Vendor shall modify or replace the Equipment.
notes: Actual-fact version (13.946): 'If no later than 15 days after the date of this agreement the Buyer notifies the Vendor that the Equipment is not in good working order, the Vendor shall fix or replace the Equipment.'

section: Selected Usages > WARRANTY, THE VERB WARRANT > Don't Use the Verb Warrant to Introduce an Obligation
statement: Don't use warrants to introduce an obligation (Acme warrants that it shall perform routine maintenance); it is throat-clearing.
fix: Acme shall perform routine maintenance ...

section: Selected Usages > WARRANTY, THE VERB WARRANT > Using the Word Warranty
statement: The noun warranty may refer to provisions in a contract or absent from it (Acme makes no warranties, express or implied), and it is appropriate to head a section Warranty or Warranties if that is what it consists of. But whether a provision is a warranty depends on content, not label.
fix: Keep the noun and heading; don't rely on the label.

section: Selected Usages > WELL AND TRULY
statement: Don't use well and truly; it is an idiomatic coupling meaning completely, invariably redundant, with a rhetorical function from oaths that doesn't fit contracts.
fix: Delete it.
notes: KB verdict label: Don't use.

section: Selected Usages > WILLFUL, WILLFULLY
statement: Instead of willful or willfully (as in willful misconduct), use intentional or intentionally and specify that the party's intent pertains to the consequences of its action; willful is vague and ambiguous as to whether intent attaches to the act or its consequences.
fix: intentionally causing those consequences (see 13.607)
exceptions: Have the intent pertain to taking the action if, in context, that makes more sense (13.956).
notes: KB verdict label: Don't use. Johnson & Johnson v. Guidant Corp., 525 F. Supp. 2d 336 (S.D.N.Y. 2007) (13.955). Appendix A fn 94 replaces willful with intentional.

section: Selected Usages > WITHOUT LIMITING THE GENERALITY OF THE FOREGOING
statement: Don't use without limiting the generality of the foregoing; express the relationship more concisely: use including in one sentence; don't use both the phrase and including; put the examples first and make the general concept a catchall; or keep two sentences with includes; and if what follows isn't an example, delete the phrase. Do without in furtherance of the foregoing (and not in limitation thereof).

words: without limiting the generality of the foregoing

fix: including; examples first with a catchall; The General Partner's duties include the following:
exceptions: If the general concept and the examples are sufficiently unwieldy, the phrase might make sense, but that is unlikely (13.964).
notes: KB verdict label: Don't use.

section: Selected Usages > WITHOUT PREJUDICE
statement: Instead of without prejudice, a litigation term of art, use does not affect or will not affect; with prejudice (claims dismissed so as to bar future action) is unobjectionable.
fix: does not affect; will not affect

examples.before: That right of setoff is without prejudice and in addition to any other right
examples.after: That right of setoff does not affect any other right

examples.before: will be without prejudice to the contract rights
examples.after: will not affect the contract rights of the Trust

notes: KB verdict label: Don't use.

section: Selected Usages > WORKMANLIKE
statement: Unless you are referring to the implied warranty of workmanlike performance recognized in construction law, consider competent and competently instead of workmanlike, a dated, gender-specific term of art; better still, be specific about the work expected.
fix: competent / competently; specific requirements
exceptions: Keep it when referring to the implied warranty of workmanlike performance (13.969, 13.971).
notes: KB verdict label: Use only in a stated context. Example (13.969): 'All Tenant Improvements must be done in a first-class workmanlike manner.' J.W. Hancock Enterprises v. Registrar of Contractors, 617 P.2d 19 (Ariz. 1980); Melody Home Mfg. v. Barnes, 741 S.W.2d 349 (Tex. 1987) (13.970).

section: Numbers and Formulas > Words or Digits > Problems
statement: Don't state numbers in words followed by digits (six (6)); it is tedious, says the same thing twice (a source of inconsistency), interferes with phrasal-adjective hyphens (five (5)-year periods), and a digit in parentheses can look like an enumerated clause.

trigger.signal: number in words followed by the same number in digits in parentheses

fix: Use the words-or-digits convention in R-14.15-words-then-digits.
notes: Appendix A fn 122 uses 24 instead of twenty-four (24).

section: Numbers and Formulas > Words or Digits > Problems
statement: If a number stated in words and digits disagrees, flag it: under the judicial principle and statutes such as UCC s. 3-114 ('words prevail over numbers'), the words govern, which may yield a meaning contrary to intent because a mismatch more likely comes from changed digits. Big numbers are more prone to mismatch, since few read the words.

trigger.signal: words and digits for the same number that differ

test: Convert the words to a number and compare with the digits.
fix: Correct the mismatch; then state the number once (digits for amounts of money).
severity_basis: conflict resolved by law, possibly against intent
notes: Fetch Interactive Television v. Touchstream, 2019 WL 193921 (Del. Ch. 2019) ('fifteen (30) days') (14.3); Charles R. Tips Family Trust v. PB Commercial LLC, 459 S.W.3d 147 (Tex. App. 2015) ($1,007,000 in words vs. $1,700,000 in digits) (14.13-14.14).

section: Numbers and Formulas > Words or Digits > Using First Words, Then Digits
statement: Use words for whole numbers one through ten and digits for 11 and above, for ordinal (seventh, 22nd) as well as cardinal numbers. The fix for digit errors is proofreading.

trigger.signal: numbers above ten in words, or one through ten in digits in running text

fix: ten days; 30 days; seventh; 22nd
exceptions: Use digits for numbers below 11 in lists of numbers, where numbers occur frequently, in percentages, in amounts of money, and in times of day (14.16).
Use words for numbers 11 and over at the beginning of a sentence (14.16).
Which system you use matters less than being consistent (14.16).
notes: Garner's Modern English Usage at 762 recommends the same; Chicago Manual 9.2 uses words through 100 (14.15).

section: Numbers and Formulas > Words or Digits > Using First Words, Then Digits
statement: Use digits even for numbers below 11 in lists of numbers, where numbers occur frequently, in percentages, in amounts of money, and in times of day; use words for numbers 11 and over at the beginning of a sentence; above all, be consistent.

trigger.signal: percentages, money, times of day, or number lists

fix: 5%; $5; 9:00 a.m.; Twenty-five ... (sentence start)

section: Numbers and Formulas > Words or Digits > Using First Words, Then Digits
statement: Use just digits for the big number in a contract (for example, the loan amount in loan documentation); don't assume words and digits help. A mix of words and digits can be appropriate for very large amounts of money.

trigger.signal: principal amount stated in words and digits

section: Numbers and Formulas > Words or Digits > Using Only Digits for All Numbers
statement: The manual doesn't recommend using digits for all numbers (it can seem intrusive in prose), but you can elect to do so; it is a relatively harmless choice.

trigger.signal: digits used for one through ten

fix: Optional.
notes: Eagleson, Numbers: Figures or Words, 50 Clarity 32 (2003) argues for digits only (14.19).

section: Numbers and Formulas > Formulas > Using Prose > Simple Formulas
statement: For a single calculation, use an amount equal to X [plus] [minus] [multiplied by] [divided by] Y; don't put a comma before plus, minus, multiplied by, or divided by; when calculating money, insert an amount equal to; and with simple formulas, omit end-product phrases such as the sum of X plus Y or the excess of X over Y. A quantum can be a percentage (an amount equal to 5% of the Overdue Amount).
fix: an amount equal to X plus Y; an amount equal to X minus Y
exceptions: End-product phrases have uses in other contexts (14.29, 14.31, 14.37).

section: Numbers and Formulas > Formulas > Using Prose > Specifying the Order of Operations
statement: When a formula mixes operations, specify the order. In equations, use parentheses even where mathematical convention would make them unnecessary ((2 x 3) + 4; (10 - 4) + 2), because a lawyer may not know the convention and left-to-right can't be counted on.

trigger.signal: formula combining plus/minus with multiplied by/divided by

test: Could the operations be performed in a different order and give a different result?
fix: Use the result of, enumeration, or parentheses in an equation.

section: Numbers and Formulas > Formulas > Using Prose > Specifying the Order of Operations
statement: In prose, whenever priority is to be given to one or more operations, use the result of before the isolated operation, or enumeration (equivalent to parentheses around each enumerated clause). Express each operation as X [plus] [minus] [multiplied by] [divided by] Y; don't use and for addition.

trigger.signal: formula in prose with mixed operations

fix: ... multiplied by the result of the Parent Stock Value divided by the Parent Opening Stock Value; or (1) ... multiplied by (2) ...
exceptions: Because the result of is open-ended, it eliminates ambiguity only if its operation occurs at the end of the formula (14.30).

section: Numbers and Formulas > Formulas > Using Prose > Specifying the Order of Operations
statement: Prefer the result of over the [sum] [difference] [product] [quotient] of; readers may not know those terms (other than sum), and the quotient of X divided by Y is tautological.
fix: the result of
exceptions: Occasionally use these phrases to avoid repetition (14.31, 14.37-14.40).

section: Numbers and Formulas > Formulas > Using Prose > Specifying the Order of Operations
statement: Whatever the context, avoid the amount by which A exceeds B (wordy), the excess of A over B (A over B can express a fraction), and the difference between A and B (5 and 7 could give 2 or -2).
fix: A minus B

section: Numbers and Formulas > Formulas > Using Prose > Specifying the Order of Operations
statement: A variant way to fix order of operations: put the isolated operation first, refer afterward to its result, and use the present participle of the verb of calculation (by dividing X by Y and multiplying the result by Z).
fix: determined by dividing X by Y and multiplying the result by Z

section: Numbers and Formulas > Formulas > Using Prose > When a Formula Contains Three or More Sequential Operations
statement: For nested operations, use enumeration ((1) and (A) act as opening parentheses), and insert the result of or another filler phrase between adjacent enumerations; don't place enumerations next to each other without intervening text. Where the result of would appear three times, use alternatives (the product of, the sum of) despite the tautology.

trigger.signal: formula with three or more sequential operations

fix: (1) the result of (A) ... divided by (B) ... plus (2) ...

section: Numbers and Formulas > Formulas > Using Prose > An Instance of Formula Ambiguity
statement: Watch for a percentage or multiplier followed by a phrase that could apply before or after another operation (23.4% of the price in excess of X less the Costs and Incentives); use enumeration to state the intended meaning unambiguously. Likewise watch whether a minimum or maximum modifies the whole product or only one factor.
fix: Enumerate: (1) 23.4% of (A) ... minus (B) ...
notes: Chartbrook Ltd v. Persimmon Homes Ltd [2009] UKHL 38 (14.41-14.44); Tyll v. Stanley Black & Decker Life Ins. Program, 403 F. Supp. 3d 27 (D. Conn. 2019) (14.45).

section: Numbers and Formulas > Formulas > Using Prose > An Instance of Formula Mistake
statement: Check where the amount by which sits relative to a multiplier: the amount by which (a) 4.8 times EBITDA exceeds (b) $2,000,000 is not 4.8 times the amount by which (a) EBITDA exceeds (b) $2,000,000. Consider an equation to catch such errors.
test: Run sample numbers through the formula as written and as intended.
fix: Restate as an equation or with enumeration.
notes: Unnamed Quebec Superior Court opinion; the drafter's client faced a C$6,203,632 claim (14.46-14.48).

section: Numbers and Formulas > Formulas > Using Prose > Fractions
statement: Use a fraction (a fraction, the numerator of which ... and the denominator of which ...) only when a number is being prorated; otherwise state the calculation as one number divided by another.

words: a fraction, the numerator of which

fix: X divided by Y

section: Numbers and Formulas > Formulas > Using Prose > Expressing Results as a Percentage
statement: Express results as percentages where more comprehensible (22.45% rather than 0.2245), using a fraction, expressed as a percentage, the numerator of which ... or the result, expressed as a percentage, of X divided by Y; use division rather than the ratio, expressed as a percentage, of X to Y; and you needn't say multiplied by 100.
fix: the result, expressed as a percentage, of X divided by Y

section: Numbers and Formulas > Formulas > Using Prose > Rounding
statement: Generally provide for rounding of a formula's result: choose the increment by what is rounded (shares to the nearest whole share; interest rates often to 1/100th of 1%); say whether to round up, down, or to the nearest increment; say how to treat an amount exactly halfway; and address rounding inside the formula or, if there are several formulas, in an internal rule of interpretation.

trigger.signal: formula with no rounding rule

test: Does the formula say the increment, the direction, and the treatment of halves?
fix: All calculations in this agreement are to the nearest cent (with $.005 being rounded upward) and to the nearest one-tenth of a share (with .05 of a share being rounded upward).
notes: The decimal convention of nearest rounding and rounding a half up can't be counted on to be recognized (14.58-14.59).

section: Numbers and Formulas > Formulas > Using Prose > Rounding
statement: When a fixed quantity is allocated pro rata, round down; rounding up risks over-allocation, and purchasers would presumably accept an adjustment for leftovers.
fix: rounded down to the nearest whole share

section: Numbers and Formulas > Formulas > Using Prose > Tabulation
statement: You could tabulate a formula's enumerated clauses, but a formula complex enough to benefit from tabulation would likely benefit more from a mathematical equation.

trigger.signal: long formula in run-in text

fix: Tabulate, or use an equation.

section: Numbers and Formulas > Formulas > Using Mathematical Equations
statement: The more complex the formula, the more likely an equation is clearer; use a prose lead-in, the equation, and a legend (In this formula, the following applies:). For a particularly complicated equation, consider a schedule with a sample set of calculations.

trigger.signal: formula with several nested operations stated only in prose

fix: Lead-in + equation + legend; sample calculations in a schedule.

section: Numbers and Formulas > Formulas > Using Mathematical Equations
statement: Don't use the percent sign in equations (3 / 4% could mean 75% or 0.75%); if you want a percentage result, say so in the prose preamble.

trigger.signal: % inside an equation

fix: State the percentage result in the lead-in.

section: Numbers and Formulas > Consecutive Ranges of Numbers > Distinguishing between Stepped Rates and Shifting Flat Rates
statement: A tiered rate schedule is ambiguous unless it says whether the rate for the band in which the total falls applies to the whole amount (a shifting flat rate) or each rate applies only to the amount within its band (a stepped rate). For a stepped rate, state increments in prose (5% of the first million dollars ...), use an IRS-style table with a cumulative base, or state in the preamble that each percentage applies only within its range; for a shifting flat rate, say the percentage for the range in which the year's revenue falls applies to all of it, or add of total gross annual revenue after each percentage. Incremental rates is not clear enough.

trigger.signal: table or list of rates by revenue or volume band

test: At a total in a higher band, does the higher rate apply to all of it or only to the excess?
fix: ... of total gross annual revenue (flat); 5% of the first $1 million, 6% of the next $1 million ... (stepped)
notes: Tennessee Excavating Co. v. Morrison-Knudsen Co., 1992 WL 113426 (Tenn. Ct. App. 29 May 1992) (14.69). The author coins 'shifting flat rate' and 'stepped rate'.

section: Numbers and Formulas > Consecutive Ranges of Numbers > Gaps and Overlaps
statement: Avoid overlap between consecutive ranges (1-10 and 10-20 leave ten unclear; use 1-10 and 11-20). For ranges that can run to decimals (dollars), don't use from $1,000 to $2,000 and from $2,000 to $3,000; use over $1,000 but not over $2,000. Don't fix overlap by creating a gap (from $1,000 to $1,999 leaves $1,999.01-$1,999.99 unplaced).

trigger.signal: consecutive ranges sharing an endpoint, or leaving a gap

test: Does every possible value fall in exactly one range?
fix: over $1,000 but not over $2,000; over $2,000 but not over $3,000
exceptions: A gap is appropriate if the unit comes only in whole units (1-10 / 11-20 widgets) (14.77).
Overlap matters more under a shifting flat rate than a stepped rate (14.75).

section: Numbers and Formulas > Consecutive Ranges of Numbers > Gaps and Overlaps
statement: For consecutive date ranges, take care with ambiguous prepositions (from, to, until, through, between).

trigger.signal: consecutive date ranges

fix: Use the time-reference rules in chapter 10.

section: Internal Rules of Interpretation > Introduction
statement: Treat internal rules of interpretation skeptically. They come in three types: rules comparable to autonomous definitions (might be useful); rules that state the obvious or do what other means do better (you can do without them); and rules that overreach in trying to create order (don't rely on them). If readers can't understand basic usages without help, something is amiss.

trigger.signal: section headed Interpretation or Construction

fix: Keep only the useful rules; delete the rest.

section: Internal Rules of Interpretation > Introduction
statement: Put autonomous definitions in the definition section, if the contract has one, not among the internal rules of interpretation.

trigger.signal: 'X' means ... inside an Interpretation section

fix: Move the definition to the definition section.

section: Internal Rules of Interpretation > Introduction
statement: Don't open an internal rule of interpretation with Unless the context otherwise requires; it undercuts the certainty the provision is meant to offer.
fix: Delete the phrase.
notes: The text names 'Unless otherwise specified' as another opening without criticizing it.

section: Internal Rules of Interpretation > These Might Be Useful
statement: A rule such as All references to time are based on the time in [location] might be useful; it spares stating a time zone after each reference. It matters only for parties in different time zones or business conducted across zones.
fix: All references to time are based on the time in [location].

section: Internal Rules of Interpretation > These Might Be Useful
statement: A rule that an action due on a day that is not a Business Day may be taken on the next Business Day might be useful, but it is redundant in a contract that measures all periods in business days.
fix: If any date specified in this agreement as the only day, or the last day, for taking action falls on a day that is not a Business Day, then that action may be taken on the next Business Day.

section: Internal Rules of Interpretation > These Are Unnecessary, or Should Be
statement: Don't include a rule that references to articles, sections, exhibits, and schedules are to those of this agreement; it states the obvious.
fix: Delete it.

section: Internal Rules of Interpretation > These Are Unnecessary, or Should Be
statement: Don't include a rule that definitions apply to the singular and plural; that is true without the provision, and defining terms in both singular and plural just adds clutter.

words: equally applicable to both the singular and plural

fix: Delete it.

section: Internal Rules of Interpretation > These Are Unnecessary, or Should Be
statement: Don't include rules that a reference to an agreement means it as amended, or that a reference to a statute includes amendments and successor provisions; adding as amended is unnecessary, so these rules are too.

words: as amended from time to time
as the same may be amended

fix: Delete it; address timing where it matters (13.58).

section: Internal Rules of Interpretation > These Are Unnecessary, or Should Be
statement: A rule that party refers only to a named party (to keep a no-third-party-beneficiary provision from reaching others) is unnecessary; a more economical fix exists (2.112).
fix: Use the approach in 2.112.

section: Internal Rules of Interpretation > These Are Unnecessary, or Should Be
statement: A rule that a pronoun applies to any gender is unnecessary if you draft gender-neutrally, which is always a good idea.
fix: Draft gender-neutrally and delete the rule.

section: Internal Rules of Interpretation > These Are Unnecessary, or Should Be
statement: A rule that here- words refer to the whole agreement is inaccurate for hereby in language of performance; more to the point, don't use here- words at all, except hereby in language of performance.

words: the words hereof, herein and hereunder

fix: Delete the rule and the here- words.

section: Internal Rules of Interpretation > These Are Unnecessary, or Should Be
statement: A rule that from means from and including and to and until mean to but excluding is fine as far as it goes but covers only a small part of time-reference ambiguity; a complete rule would be unwieldy, so purge each time reference of ambiguity instead.
fix: Fix each time reference (chapter 10).

section: Internal Rules of Interpretation > These Are Unnecessary, or Should Be
statement: A contra proferentem waiver (Because each party was involved in drafting ...) reflects how courts act anyway; courts would likely ignore it if it doesn't reflect how the contract was drafted.

words: no presumption against the drafting party
participated jointly in the negotiation and drafting

fix: Optional; it adds little.
notes: Senior Housing Capital v. SHP Senior Housing Fund, 2013 WL 1955012 (Del. Ch. 2013) (enforceable); Zimmerman v. Crothall, 62 A.3d 676 (Del. Ch. 2013).

section: Internal Rules of Interpretation > These Overreach by Trying to Create Order
statement: Don't rely on a rule that headings are for convenience only: where a heading is carelessly mismatched, it does only what a court would do anyway; where a heading arguably reflects intended scope, a court might ignore the rule. It is of questionable use.
fix: Draft accurate headings; don't rely on the rule.
notes: Infrassure, Ltd. v. First Mutual Transportation Assurance Co., 2016 WL 6775921 (2d Cir. 2016).

section: Internal Rules of Interpretation > These Overreach by Trying to Create Order
statement: Don't rely on a rule that including is to be read as followed by without limitation; it is unhelpful.

words: including shall be deemed to be followed by without limitation
the words include, includes and including

fix: Use including in a targeted way (13.377).

section: Internal Rules of Interpretation > These Overreach by Trying to Create Order
statement: Don't rely on rules that or is disjunctive and and is conjunctive, or that or is not exclusive; they grossly oversimplify the ambiguity of and and or (chapter 11), and on or the two provisions take opposite approaches.
fix: Resolve each and/or ambiguity in context (chapter 11).

section: Internal Rules of Interpretation > These Overreach by Trying to Create Order
statement: Don't rely on a rule that will means shall; it is a hopeless attempt to resolve will/shall confusion.

words: the word will shall be construed to have the same meaning

fix: Use shall only to impose a duty on a party that is the subject (3.89).

section: Internal Rules of Interpretation > These Overreach by Trying to Create Order
statement: A rule that shall is mandatory and may is discretionary is unnecessary if you use shall only to impose a duty on the subject of the sentence; courts have long recognized shall for obligations. Drafters who overuse shall shouldn't use the rule, since it couldn't apply to their drafting.

words: shall is mandatory and may is permissive

fix: Delete it; use shall correctly.

section: Internal Rules of Interpretation > These Overreach by Trying to Create Order
statement: Don't rely on a rule that the singular includes the plural and vice versa to prevent a singular/plural fight; if you mean one or more widgets, say so.

words: words in the singular include the plural

fix: one or more [nouns]

section: Internal Rules of Interpretation > These Overreach by Trying to Create Order
statement: Instead of a rule that a reference to a Person includes its successors and assigns, state to what extent a party may transfer elements of its performance.
fix: An assignment provision stating what may be transferred.

section: Typography > Fonts > The Usual Suspects
statement: Unless you are subject to institutional requirements, be open to alternatives to the default fonts; Times New Roman (designed for narrow newspaper columns) and Arial are overexposed and criticized, and Calibri and Constantia were designed for screen reading.

trigger.signal: document font

fix: Choose a readable font (the author uses Calibri).
notes: Appendix A fn 1: there are better font choices than Times New Roman. Microsoft announced in 2021 that it plans to replace Calibri as default (16.8).

section: Typography > Fonts > Constraints on Choice
statement: Use system fonts rather than purchased professional fonts; an unrecognized font displays in a fallback font, which disrupts signature-page exchanges and negotiations. For law firms and law departments you can assume Microsoft Office fonts.

trigger.signal: nonstandard font in a document to be exchanged

fix: Use a font available in Microsoft Office.

section: Typography > Fonts > Serif and Sans Serif
statement: There is no requirement to use a serif font; studies cast doubt on the assumption that serif fonts are easier to read.

trigger.signal: serif vs. sans serif choice

fix: Either is acceptable.

section: Typography > Justification
statement: Don't justify the margins of word-processed contracts; use ragged-right (flush-left) text. Word processors lack the spacing and hyphenation algorithms to make justified text readable; the professional look is a phony professionalism.

trigger.signal: justified text alignment

fix: Align left.

section: Typography > Emphasis > Emphasizing Names and Article Headings
statement: Use all capitals for article headings and for party names in the introductory clause and signature blocks; don't use all capitals for continuous body text.

trigger.signal: all-capitals body text

fix: Sentence case for body text.

section: Typography > Emphasis > Emphasizing Section Headings and Defined Terms
statement: Bold all section headings and each defined term where it is defined; don't use underlining for emphasis (a typewriter convention that overlaps descenders).

trigger.signal: underlined headings or defined terms

fix: Bold, not underline.
notes: Appendix A fn 20: bold headings, not underlining.

section: Typography > Emphasis > What Not to Emphasize
statement: Don't emphasize cross-references or references to attachments; it doesn't help the reader, and Word's find-and-replace is quicker and more reliable for checking them.

trigger.signal: bold or underlined cross-references

fix: Plain text for cross-references.

section: Typography > Emphasis > Emphasizing Provisions > What to Emphasize
statement: Don't emphasize any part of the provisions unless a statute or caselaw requires it (for example, statutes requiring capitals or 'conspicuous' text, such as UCC s. 2-316(2) for disclaimers of the implied warranty of merchantability), or unless you're counterbalancing a substantial disparity of bargaining power or sophistication. A provision needn't be emphasized to be conspicuous.

trigger.signal: emphasized provisions in the body

fix: Emphasize only where law requires or bargaining power is unequal.
notes: Ariz. Rev. Stat. s. 12-1366(A)(1); Fla. Stat. s. 718.202(3); Or. Rev. Stat. s. 93.040 (16.24); UCC s. 1-201(10) (16.26); Dresser Industries v. Page Petroleum, 853 S.W.2d 505 (Tex. 1993) (16.25); In re Bassett, 285 F.3d 882 (9th Cir. 2002) (16.27).

section: Typography > Emphasis > Emphasizing Provisions > What to Emphasize
statement: Jury-trial-waiver caselaw on conspicuousness is inconsistent; unless you can research it, make jury-trial waivers conspicuous regardless of the governing law.

words: waives any right to a trial by jury

fix: Set the waiver off with bold italics and/or a border.

section: Typography > Emphasis > Emphasizing Provisions > How to Emphasize It
statement: Unless a statute requires it, don't use all capitals to emphasize a provision; readers skim capitals and they may not even be conspicuous. Use bold italics and/or a border instead (also for stock-certificate legends), and don't use italics for emphasis, except perhaps in amendments.

trigger.signal: provision in all capitals

fix: Bold italics; a border.
notes: In re Bassett, 285 F.3d at 886 ('Lawyers who think their caps lock keys are instant make-conspicuous buttons are deluded') (16.29); Broberg v. Guardian Life, 171 Cal. App. 4th 912 (2009) (16.29).

section: Typography > Emphasis > Emphasizing Provisions > Acknowledging That Text Is Conspicuous
statement: Don't rely on an acknowledgment that text is conspicuous; it sits inside the provision, so if the provision is inconspicuous, so is the acknowledgment.

words: acknowledge that this provision is conspicuous

fix: Make the provision conspicuous instead.

section: Typography > Emphasis > Rhetorical Emphasis Through Typography
statement: Don't emphasize selected words for rhetorical emphasis (The Licensor shall NOT indemnify ...).

trigger.signal: a single word in capitals, bold, or italics for emphasis

fix: Plain text.

section: Typography > Font Size
statement: Font size depends on the typeface: 12 point Times New Roman and 10 point Arial are standard; 11-point Calibri is a safe choice, but you can experiment. Different sizes apply with a two-column format.

trigger.signal: font size

fix: 11-point Calibri or equivalent

section: Typography > Characters per Line
statement: Keep line length within the recommended 45 to 90 characters; the simplest fix is 1.5- to 2-inch side margins, though keeping blocks of text short mitigates long lines.

trigger.signal: lines exceeding about 90 characters

fix: Wider side margins; shorter blocks of text.
notes: 11-point Calibri on letter paper with one-inch margins gives 85-95 characters (16.40). The author hasn't increased his own margins (16.41).

section: Typography > Line Spacing
statement: Single spacing has been standard; consider experimenting with extra space (Typography for Lawyers recommends Word's Multiple at 1.03 to 1.24).

trigger.signal: line spacing

fix: Multiple 1.03-1.24 (optional)

section: Typography > Space After Punctuation
statement: Use one space, not two, after periods, question marks, exclamation marks, and colons.

trigger.signal: two spaces after punctuation

fix: One space.

section: Typography > "Curly" and "Straight" Quotation Marks and Apostrophes
statement: Make all quotation marks and apostrophes curly; mixed marks are a hallmark of a sloppy copy-and-paste job. Turn on Word's AutoFormat As You Type replacement and convert straight marks with Find and Replace.

trigger.signal: straight quotation marks or apostrophes, or a mix of straight and curly

fix: Curly marks throughout.

section: Typography > First-Line Indents
statement: Don't use both first-line indents and space between paragraphs; the manual's samples use no first-line indents.

trigger.signal: paragraphs with both first-line indents and spacing

fix: Space between paragraphs, no first-line indent.

section: Drafting as Writing > Don't Make Sentences Too Long
statement: Whittle down unnecessarily long sentences (contract sentences will usually exceed 20-25 words): a sentence is too long if it strings together clauses that would read better separately or includes unwieldy exceptions, qualifications, or conditions. Break it into components, state how they relate, and tabulate long lists of enumerated clauses.

trigger.signal: sentence over about 60 words, or with several qualifications

fix: Split into sentences; tabulate enumerated clauses.

section: Drafting as Writing > Keep Subject, Verb, and Object Close Together
statement: Keep subject, verb, and object close together and, if possible, at the start of the sentence; move intervening words to the beginning or end, or into a separate sentence.

trigger.signal: long phrase between subject and verb or between verb and object

fix: Acme shall not transfer the Shares to any Person without the prior written consent of Excelsior, which Excelsior shall not unreasonably withhold.

examples.before: Acme shall not without the prior written consent of Excelsior, which Excelsior shall not unreasonably withhold, transfer the Shares to any Person.
examples.after: Acme shall not transfer the Shares to any Person without the prior written consent of Excelsior, which Excelsior shall not unreasonably withhold.

section: Drafting as Writing > Don't Bury Verbs
statement: Whenever possible, use strong verbs instead of abstract nouns (buried verbs, nominalizations) or adjectives; they make prose bureaucratic, add prepositions and weak verbs, and let the drafter drop the actor.

trigger.signal: abstract noun ending -tion/-ment/-ance with a weak verb

fix: Immediately after Acme issues the Notes; If Smith fails to timely pay the Purchase Price; If this section violates any law; is liable
exceptions: Buried verbs are useful when dropping the actor helps (Upon exercise of the Option) (17.10).

examples.before: Immediately following issuance of the Notes
examples.after: Immediately after Acme issues the Notes

examples.before: If this section is violative of any law
examples.after: If this section violates any law

examples.before: The Warrants are not redeemable by Acme.
examples.after: Acme shall not redeem the Warrants.

section: Drafting as Writing > Don't Bury Verbs
statement: Like the passive, a buried verb is useful when dropping the actor helps: Upon exercise of the Option rather than When one or more Optionholders exercise the Option.

trigger.signal: nominalization whose actor is irrelevant

fix: Keep it.

section: Drafting as Writing > Avoid Gender-Specific Language
statement: For a group that includes or might include women and men, don't use exclusively he, his, him. Use a plural pronoun with conforming changes, repeat the noun, or add a feminine or neuter pronoun or both; singular they is acceptable but each drafter decides. Don't use singular they for a member of a group made up only of entities (use it), and be accurate however you handle pronouns.
fix: The Stockholders must surrender their stock certificates; Each Stockholder must surrender that Stockholder's stock certificate; his, her, or its

examples.before: Each Stockholder must surrender his stock certificates
examples.after: The Stockholders must surrender their stock certificates

notes: Total Recall Technologies v. Luckey, 2016 WL 199796 (N.D. Cal. 2016) (its for an individual suggested an intended beneficiary) (17.18). Appendix A fn 44 uses the Employee's for his.

section: Drafting as Writing > Don't Use Wordy Phrases
statement: Replace wordy phrases with simpler ones: prior to -> before; subsequent to -> after; in lieu of -> instead of; in the event that / in the event of -> if; pursuant to -> under, in accordance with, authorized by; set forth in -> stated in, in; until such time as -> until; in order to -> to; for the purpose of [verb]ing -> to [verb]; by reason of -> because of; due to the fact that -> because; despite the fact that -> although; is unable to -> cannot; is binding upon -> binds; per annum -> a year; with the exception of -> except for; and the other entries in the 17.19 table.

words: by virtue of the fact that

fix: See the 17.19 table (ocr-tables.md).
notes: Appendix A fns 27, 52, 55, 119, 120, 139 apply this table.

section: Drafting as Writing > Don't Use Wordy Phrases > To the Extent That
statement: Use to the extent that only when the degree of application depends on a variable (except to the extent that the federal securities laws apply); use if when satisfying a condition applies the provision in full.
test: Does the provision apply partly, in proportion to a variable? If it applies fully once the condition is met, use if.
fix: If any document is required to be filed ..., the Seller shall prepare and sign that document.

examples.before: To the extent that any document is required to be filed
examples.after: If any document is required to be filed

section: Drafting as Writing > Don't Use Wordy Phrases > The Fact That
statement: The fact that can almost always be improved (by virtue of the fact that -> because; The fact that there may be no Loans outstanding -> Whether any Loans are outstanding); notwithstanding the fact that and regardless of the fact that can always be replaced by although, even though, or even if.

words: in view of the fact that

fix: because; whether; although; even though; even if

examples.before: notwithstanding the fact that those shares were not outstanding
examples.after: even though those shares were not outstanding

notes: Appendix A fn 133 uses even if for notwithstanding the fact that.

section: Drafting as Writing > Don't Use Wordy Phrases > There Is and There Are
statement: Don't start a clause with there or it plus a form of to be; find the real subject and verb.
fix: If this agreement conflicts with ..., the terms of this agreement will control; No Governmental Authority is currently auditing ...

section: Drafting as Writing > Don't Use Wordy Phrases > With Respect To
statement: Replace with respect to with regarding or a single preposition (in, for, on), a shorter phrase (as to), or a bigger fix (a Fund's Borrowing Instructions).
fix: regarding; in; for; on; as to

examples.before: Borrowing Instructions with respect to a Fund
examples.after: a Fund's Borrowing Instructions

section: Drafting as Writing > Use Possessives
statement: Use possessives to make prose less wooden: Acme's board of directors; Smith's shares; the Lender's obligation to make Loans under this agreement.
fix: Acme's board of directors
notes: Appendix A fn 100 uses RMA's board of directors.

section: Drafting as Writing > Don't Overuse Initial Capitals
statement: Be restrained with initial capitals (following The Chicago Manual of Style): use lowercase for a particular contract unless it is a defined term, board of directors, officer and other titles (the president of Acme), organizational documents (certificate of incorporation, bylaws), capital stock (common stock), and article and section cross-references and references to exhibits, schedules, and other attachments.
fix: board of directors; section 4.2; exhibit A; common stock; the president of Acme
exceptions: Titles followed by a name take initial capitals (President Leah Greenberg), but that never happens in contracts (17.31).

Capitalize political-division words that follow a name as part of it; when they precede the name, capitalize them for countries but lowercase below the national level (New York State; the state of New York) (17.33).
notes: Appendix A fns 34, 69, 107 apply this rule.

section: Drafting as Writing > The Extraneous The
statement: Drop the before abstract nouns where it is extraneous (upon satisfaction; for purposes of calculating; caused by willful misconduct).
fix: Delete the.

examples.before: for the purposes of calculating
examples.after: for purposes of calculating

examples.before: applied to the repayment of Indebtedness
examples.after: applied to repayment of Indebtedness

section: Drafting as Writing > Contractions
statement: Don't use contractions in business contracts; contract prose is devoid of tone and rhythm.
fix: do not; will not; cannot

section: Drafting as Writing > Punctuation
statement: Use punctuation consistent with standard English without relying on it unduly. If a contract says punctuation is for ease of reference only and does not affect interpretation, insist that the provision be deleted.

words: for the purpose of easy reference

fix: Delete the punctuation-disclaimer provision.

section: Amendments > Amending, or Amending and Restating
statement: Amend (a new contract containing only the changes) when making a few discrete changes; amend and restate (the original revised to include prior and new amendments) when the changes are extensive or follow other amendments, making them hard to track.
fix: Choose by the number and complexity of changes.

section: Amendments > Amendment or Variation
statement: Don't use variation or vary for amending a contract; use amendment and amend. Synonyms cause waste and mischief, and in standard English a variation is something new, not a modified original.
fix: amendment; amend
exceptions: Variation in construction contracts (including FIDIC forms) for changed instructions about the work is unobjectionable (18.7).

section: Amendments > Title
statement: State in the title that the contract amends, or amends and restates, and name the type of agreement (AMENDED AND RESTATED MERGER AGREEMENT); number each amendment, at least from the second onward (AMENDMENT NO. 4 TO CREDIT AGREEMENT); don't include party names.

trigger.signal: amendment title

fix: AMENDMENT NO. 2 TO [TYPE] AGREEMENT

section: Amendments > Introductory Clause and Recitals
statement: In an amendment, don't refer to the amended contract in the introductory clause; refer to it in the recitals and, if feasible, briefly state why the parties are amending. Don't create the defined term this Amendment.
fix: Refer to this amendment (lowercase, undefined); identify the amended contract in the recitals.

section: Amendments > The Lead-In
statement: Use the same lead-in as for any contract; for an amended and restated contract, say The parties therefore amend and restate the [contract] to read in its entirety as follows.

trigger.signal: lead-in of an amendment

fix: The parties therefore amend and restate the [contract being amended] to read in its entirety as follows:
exceptions: If only one simple change is made, it can be wrapped into the lead-in (The parties therefore amend the Employment Agreement by deleting section 13 in its entirety.), unless you add general provisions such as governing law (18.10).

section: Amendments > Language of Performance
statement: Amending language is language of performance: prefer is hereby amended over is amended or is amended as of the date hereof; the passive is appropriate because it is clear who is amending.

words: is amended as of the date hereof

fix: is hereby amended

section: Amendments > Distinguishing between Amending and Supplementing
statement: An amendment changes the original; a supplement adds to it. A second agreement amends only if it says its provisions are added to the original; if its provisions are freestanding, call it a supplement, not the fusty Latinism addendum.
fix: supplement (freestanding) or amendment (changes the original)

section: Amendments > Adding, Deleting, and Replacing Language > Change Affecting Part of a Provision
statement: For a change to less than a whole section or subsection, either state only the exact change (by replacing '28 February 2019' with '30 April 2019') or restate the entire provision (is hereby amended to read in its entirety as follows); stating the change is concise but lacks context, restating gives context but is longer.

words: to read in its entirety as follows

fix: The definition of 'Termination Date' is hereby amended to read in its entirety as follows: ...
notes: The book's source definition states 28 February 2022 but the replacement example uses 2019 dates (inconsistent as printed).

section: Amendments > Adding, Deleting, and Replacing Language > Change Affecting an Entire Provision
statement: Add a provision with The Agreement is hereby amended by adding after section 10 the following new section 11; if the insertion isn't at the end, follow at once with a renumbering amendment. It is best to insert at the end of the agreement, section, or series, to avoid breaking internal cross-references and references in other contracts.
fix: (1) by adding after section 10 the following new section 11 and (2) by renumbering sections 11 through 19 as sections 12 through 20
exceptions: Fine-tuning and/or and the final period when adding a last clause is strictly required, but omitting it couldn't harm a party (18.20).

section: Amendments > Adding, Deleting, and Replacing Language > Change Affecting an Entire Provision
statement: Delete a provision with The Agreement is hereby amended by deleting section 10 in its entirety; if it isn't at the end, renumber or, more simply, keep the number and replace the text with the bracketed place-filler Intentionally omitted, which leaves cross-references intact.
fix: [Intentionally omitted]

section: Amendments > Layout
statement: When adding an entire section, subsection, or tabulated enumerated clause, indent it, set it in italics, and format it as in the amended contract, to distinguish it from the amendment's own text.

trigger.signal: added section text in an amendment

fix: Indented italic text formatted as in the original.

section: Letter Agreements > Function
statement: Don't give a regular contract the title letter of intent; it sends mixed signals. Letters of intent are by convention letter agreements.
fix: Use a title that reflects a binding contract.

section: Letter Agreements > Components
statement: A letter agreement consists of the sender's address, date, recipient's address, salutation, introductory sentence, substantive terms, closing sentence, sender's signature, and recipient's signature; a subject line is allowed, but a title isn't.

trigger.signal: letter agreement with a title

fix: Use a subject line instead of a title.

section: Letter Agreements > Components
statement: The sender is the party itself (for an entity, not its representative); its address can be typed or in letterhead. Date the letter as for an introductory clause. The recipients are the persons, other than the sender, to be bound; for an entity, usually add an Attention line naming a representative.

trigger.signal: letter agreement sent by an individual for an entity

fix: Sender: the entity; recipient: the entity, Attention: [representative]

section: Letter Agreements > Components
statement: For an individual recipient, use Dear plus the name, reflecting the relationship; for an entity, dispense with a salutation. Don't use Dear Sirs (gender-specific, old-fashioned), Dear Sirs and Madams, Ladies and Gentlemen, or To whom it may concern.
fix: Dear Susan / Dear Ms. Robbins; no salutation for an entity

section: Letter Agreements > Components
statement: Open with an introductory sentence such as The purpose of this letter agreement is to state the terms of [the transaction].

trigger.signal: letter agreement opening

fix: The purpose of this letter agreement is to state the terms of [the transaction].

section: Letter Agreements > Components
statement: Phrase the substantive terms as in a regular contract; you can drop section numbers and headings, but generally keep them. Use the third person, not you and we or us.
fix: Acme shall ...; Widgetco may ...

section: Letter Agreements > Components
statement: Use a closing sentence as in sample 14 (it can also refer to return of a signed copy). Place the sender's signature where a sender usually signs a letter; Yours sincerely isn't necessary; use regular-contract signature-block format, with an entity's block in the entity's name.
fix: Signature block in the entity's name

section: Letter Agreements > Components
statement: Give each recipient its own signature block, usually under the sender's, flush left, preceded by Agreed to (and accepted adds nothing). Generally include a date, or a court might apply the letter's date; if a particular date matters, state it (Agreed to on the date of this letter agreement) rather than leaving it blank. Prefer not to use an as of date.
fix: Agreed to on the date of this letter agreement:

section: Blog: no-ampersands-in-contracts
statement: Don't use an ampersand except where it appears in the name of a business or law firm; write and. In a heading, use a semicolon (Amendment; Waiver) or make separate sections.

trigger.signal: an ampersand outside a business or firm name

test: Is the ampersand part of a business or law-firm name?
fix: Replace with and; in a heading, use a semicolon or separate sections.
exceptions: Keep an ampersand that is part of a business or law-firm name.
notes: Post date: (not shown). Verified against the post on 5 Nov 2026. Key quotation: "I suggest that the only ampersands you use in a contract are those that appear in business (and law firm) names." Source: https://www.adamsdrafting.com/no-ampersands-in-contracts/. Adams: "With this post, I aim to set that right for the sixth edition!" MSCD5 doesn't address ampersands.

section: Blog: replacing-once-in-contracts-a-example-of-sweating-the-small-stuff
statement: Don't use once (or when) to introduce a condition; use if. If deleting once leaves an adjective phrase, just delete once.

trigger.signal: once or when as the subordinator of a conditional clause

test: Does once or when introduce a condition (an uncertain future event)? Both suggest an expectation that the circumstance will come to pass.
fix: Replace with if; or delete once where an adjective phrase remains (A Member may not withdraw a Redemption Notice once submitted).
exceptions: When used for timing of an event certain to occur, judge in context; the post addresses conditions.

examples.before: Once Client has initiated a Digital Asset withdrawal, the associated Client Digital Assets will be in a pending state
examples.after: If Client has initiated a Digital Asset withdrawal, the associated Client Digital Assets will be in a pending state

notes: Post date: (not shown). Verified against the post on 5 Nov 2026. Key quotation: "One possible fix would be to use when as the subordinator instead of once, but when too suggests an expectation that the circumstance in question will come to pass." Source: https://www.adamsdrafting.com/replacing-once-in-contracts-a-example-of-sweating-the-small-stuff/. Adams: "In the sixth edition ... you can expect to find the gist of this post in chapter 3" (Expressing Conditions Using a Conditional Clause).

section: Blog: a-new-variant-of-ambiguity-of-the-part-versus-the-whole
statement: A new variant of part-versus-whole ambiguity: when a quantity is attributed to more than one item (or a modifier such as monthly could attach to the noun or the verb), it can be unclear whether the quantity applies to each item or to all of them in the aggregate. Say each or in the aggregate.

trigger.signal: an amount or quantity attributed to plural items or periodic payments without each or in the aggregate

test: Could the amount be per item or a total?
fix: Say each or in the aggregate, depending on the meaning you intend.
